items.title: [Bug] Large HiCache UCX startup timeout on downstream build; not reproduced on v0.5.20
items.author: ByronHsu
items.body_excerpt:
### Result

**Not reproduced on the latest upstream image (v0.5.20).** A large HiCache pool triggered a UCX startup timeout on our earlier downstream build, but both HiCache and no-HiCache starts passed with the unmodified upstream image.

| Build | HiCache per rank | UCX initialization, all 8 ranks | Server ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Downstream `869abc0605`, NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21.0 | 234 GB | Six ranks explicitly timed out at 60s; none completed | No |
| Same downstream build, no HiCache | 0 | 3–4s | Yes |
| **Upstream v0.5.20, NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22.0** | **234 GB** | **~2s** | **234s after launch** |
| Same upstream image, no HiCache | 0 | ~2s | 62s after launch |

Each HiCache/control pair ran on the same eight-H200 node with fresh processes. The upstream pair used a different physical node from the downstream pair, and multiple software components changed: this does **not** identify a fix or prove the cause. Only startup was tested, with no inference requests. Both upstream runs registered all eight KV buffers, passed passive `/ready` checks for 30 seconds, and exited cleanly.

### Reproduction settings

8 H200s, approximately 2014 GiB host RAM; public `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite` real weights, revision `604d5664dddd88a0433dbae533b7fe9472482de0`.

Upstream image: `lmsysorg/sglang:latest` resolved to **v0.5.20**, source `94602c9c2b7cbdb8efd5c52802dac6a1c180089e`. Tested amd64 image digest:

```text
lmsysorg/sglang@sha256:b27fce60bc5494c118c4910702812bcfa8cee67abcdd1ff8b0902f21647552f4
```

No source overlay, serving patches, or dependency replacements. Download the model revision above into `$MODEL_DIR`, then run:

```bash
export SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_ENGINE_INIT_TIMEOUT=60
export SGLANG_NCCL_ALL_GATHER_IN_OVERLAP_SCHEDULER_SYNC_BATCH=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_STREAM_INTERVAL=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_CPU_IMAGE_PREPROCESSING=0

python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path "$MODEL_DIR" --trust-remote-code \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000 \
  --tp-size 8 --dp-size 8 --ep-size 8 --enable-dp-attention \
  --disaggregation-mode prefill --disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.7 --dtype bfloat16 --kv-cache-dtype bf16 \
  --page-size 64 --tokenizer-worker-num 4 \
  --context-length 150000 --max-running-requests 1024 \
  --skip-server-warmup --log-level debug --decode-attention-backend fa3 \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 234 \
  --hicache-write-policy write_through \
  --hicache-mem-layout page_first --hicache-io-backend kernel
```

Remove the five HiCache options for the control. CUDA graphs stay enabled; NIXL is the PD transport, not L3 storage. Actual pool allocation: **234,001,612,800 bytes per rank**, about **1.872 TB total**. Size is per rank and requires sufficient host/cgroup headroom.

### Original failure

The downstream run failed **during UCX backend creation, before KV registration**:

```text
RuntimeError: NIXL create_backend('UCX', {'num_threads': '8'}) did not return within 60s
```

Five seconds before failure: **141.6 GiB host headroom**, **39.2–39.4 GiB free per GPU**, no host OOM-counter increase or CUDA OOM. Host memory pressure and compaction were high. No native stack inside UCX was captured. A later audit found rank 0 in a debugger tracing stop at 21:29:30 UTC, inside the 60-second UCX window, as well as earlier allocation-stage attachments. The retained samples do not establish total pause duration. Other ranks also timed out without a recorded tracing stop, but this run was not free of measurement interference. A telemetry gap further limits the evidence.

The upstream HiCache run kept at least **120 GiB host headroom**, logged no OOM, and completed UCX startup quickly. The underlying reason for the older failure remains unresolved.

<details>
<summary>Upstream runtime</summary>

Python 3.12.3; PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130; NIXL/nixl-cu13 1.4.1; bundled UCX 1.22.0; CUDA 13.0; driver 595.71.05; Linux 6.8.12; FlashInfer 0.6.18; Transformers 5.12.1. THP mode remains `madvise`. The 60-second UCX deadline and eight prefill backend threads were unchanged.

</details>

### Follow-up: the extra host memory is DC receive buffers

On one exclusive node, with the same upstream source/image and **232 GB/rank** HiCache, we compared fresh server processes:

| Native backend | DC interfaces | Receive-buffer chunks | Scheduler anonymous huge pages | UCX startup span |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22 | 0 | 288 | 12.498 GiB | 2s |
| NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21 | 288 | 576 | 23.188 GiB | 4s |
| Same 1.3.0 package, only `UCX_TLS=^dc_mlx5` added | 0 | 288 | 12.502 GiB | 3s |

All three initialized all eight ranks, registered KV buffers, and held passive readiness for 30 seconds. No compaction stalls, THP fallbacks, or OOM occurred. No inference or PD transfers were tested. The third case is a diagnostic intervention, **not a verified timeout fix**.

UCX debug logs and per-scheduler memory maps identify the difference: **8 ranks × 9 workers × 4 ports = 288 DC interfaces**, each eagerly allocating a **38 MiB** receive buffer through `rc_recv_desc`. Those extra buffers account for **10.6875 GiB** of huge pages. Excluding only DC on the old package removes them and matches the newer package. Actual loaded UCX versions were verified in server logs.

The old binary includes DC; the new wheel omits it. [NIXL PR 1708](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/nixl/pull/1708) disables DC in the manylinux build. The v1.3.0 source tag also contains that flag despite the tested wheel including DC, so we report observed binary features rather than infer build history from tags.

During the **original failing UCX initialization window**, kernel counters rose by **10,496 compaction attempts, 10,492 failures, 3,407 THP fallbacks, and 3,668 direct-reclaim stalls**. They were flat just before UCX started. The examined SGLang NIXL startup and host-pool files are byte-identical between the downstream and upstream revisions.

This supports a host-memory compact

items.title: [torch.compile] config hashing refactor follow-ups
items.author: deleted-user
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### MOTIVATION.

[PR #26468](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/26468) moved vLLM config hashing toward an opt-out model so new compilation-relevant config fields are less likely to be accidentally omitted from torch.compile cache keys. 

This issue tracks the follow-ups and to-dos.

## TODOs
1. Refactor all locations of `compute_hash` to `compile_factors`.  `compute_hash` isn’t the right name because real computation of the hash is actually done by `utils.hash_factors`.
2. before calling `normalize value` in `get_compile_factors`, it needs to check if .compile_factors exists on the subobject. This allows us to avoid handling `PassConfig` specially as in the case for compilation.py 
4. Uniform use of `normalize_value` & `hash_factors` across configs with a compute_hash function.

comments.body:
I can't reproduce this on stock v0.21.0, and after tracing the whole streaming path I don't think stock code can produce this exact signature. Writing up what I found.

**What the glyphs are**

`Ċ`, `åĹ¯`, `ï¼Į` are exactly what `tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens()` returns for those token ids (verified with a DeepSeek-R1 family tokenizer: 198 -> `Ċ`, 106287 -> `åĹ¯`, 3837 -> `ï¼Į`). So the reasoning stream is raw token strings that never went through the byte-level decode step.

**Why stock v0.21.0 shouldn't be able to emit that**

The streaming chain with `--reasoning-parser deepseek_r1` is:

1. The engine detokenizer produces `output.text` (already byte-decoded, incremental).
2. serving_chat sets `delta_text = output.text` and feeds it to the unified parser that `ParserManager.get_parser(reasoning_parser_name="deepseek_r1")` builds, which delegates to `DeepSeekR1ReasoningParser`.
3. That parser only slices `delta_text` around the `</think>` boundary. I audited every branch of `basic_parsers.py` and `deepseek_r1_reasoning_parser.py`: each return value is a substring of `delta_text`. There is no `convert_ids_to_tokens` anywhere in `vllm/entrypoints`, `vllm/parser`, or `vllm/reasoning` (the only hit is the unrelated `/tokenize` endpoint).

Your control experiments are the tell. Without the parser, the same `output.text` arrives as clean content, and non-streaming is clean too. So your detokenizer output is clean. The parser can only cut up what it receives; slicing clean text cannot turn one field back into raw token strings while the other stays clean. Something in your deployment is replacing the reasoning path with a token-string implementation between the detokenizer and the wire.

**Verification I ran**

In-process simulation of the exact serving chain (real tokenizer, CJK reasoning stream, token-at-a-time detokenization, then the same `_WrappedParser.parse_delta` the server uses):

- v0.21.0 tag + transformers 5.8.1 (your versions), fast detokenizer path: clean
- v0.21.0 tag + transformers 5.8.1, forced slow `detokenize_incrementally` path: clean
- current main + transformers 5.14.1, both paths: clean

One related landmine worth knowing about for this exact checkpoint: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B` declares `tokenizer_class: LlamaTokenizerFast` on the Hub while shipping a byte-level BPE `tokenizer.json`. Under transformers 5.x that loads a `LlamaTokenizer` shim which drops all CJK at encode time and decodes to raw glyphs, tracked in huggingface/transformers#49252.

Your control experiments rule this out as the cause here (with that shim your Chinese prompt would tokenize to nothing and content would be glyph-laden too), but if your local `/models/deepseek` copy carries the Hub tokenizer files verbatim, your deployment is exposed to that separate bug as well. Easy check: `AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("/models/deepseek").encode("你好")` should return `[108386]`, not `[]`.

items.title: [Bug] lmcache CLI crashes on every subcommand without openai: bench engine imports it at parser registration
items.author: aeon-x
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

After a plain `pip install lmcache`, **every** `lmcache` CLI subcommand crashes at startup, including `lmcache server` and `lmcache --help`:

```
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'openai'
```

Root cause:

1. `lmcache/cli/main.py` registers every subcommand's argparse parser at startup, regardless of which subcommand is run.
2. Registering `bench engine` calls `EngineBenchCommand.add_arguments()`, which imports `engine_bench/command.py` → `engine_bench/config.py`, and `config.py:14` does a top-level `from openai import OpenAI`.
3. `openai` is not a dependency of the `lmcache` wheel. It is only listed in `requirements/cli.txt`, which is consumed by the separate `lmcache-cli` distribution (`pyproject_cli.toml`). The main `pyproject.toml` still installs the same `lmcache = "lmcache.cli.main:main"` console script, without those dependencies, and no `lmcache[cli]` extra exists (the only extras are `kafka` and `nixl`).

So the `lmcache` wheel ships an entry point that cannot start. It is masked in the `vllm-openai` images and in any environment where vLLM is installed, because vLLM itself depends on `openai`.

**To Reproduce**

```bash
python -m venv v && . v/bin/activate
pip install lmcache torch   # no vllm, no lmcache-cli
lmcache --help              # ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'openai'
lmcache server --help       # same
```

Reproduced on current `dev` (found while testing #5400's wheels in a clean venv): `lmcache --help`, `lmcache server --help`, `lmcache describe --help` all fail identically.

**Expected behavior**

`lmcache server` (and every subcommand that does not need it) works without `openai`. Only `lmcache bench engine` should require it, with a clear message.

**Possible fixes** (any one)

- Lazy-import `openai` inside the engine-bench code path that uses it (e.g. move `from openai import OpenAI` into the function that builds the client), so registration doesn't import it. Smallest change; other optional CLI imports may need the same treatment.
- Add `requirements/cli.txt` as a `cli` extra of the main package, and have `bench engine` raise a clear "pip install lmcache[cli]" error.
- Drop the `lmcache` console script from the main package if the CLI is meant to ship only via `lmcache-cli`. Note `lmcache server` is the documented way to start the MP server, so this probably isn't desirable.

items.title: llama-quantize: GGML_ASSERT(size mismatch) when quantizing mmproj files containing 3D conv tensors (gemma4v audio conv1d)
items.author: mrBenBern
items.body_excerpt:
Quantizing the gemma-4-E2B combined mmproj (vision+audio, gemma4v/gemma4a projectors) from F16 to Q8_0 aborts with:

  llama-quant.cpp:1365: GGML_ASSERT(gguf_get_tensor_size(...) == new_size) failed

Repro:
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize mmproj-F16.gguf out.gguf Q8_0

Fails at tensor `a.conv1d.0.weight` — shape [3,3,1,128] (3D conv1d from the audio encoder). The f32→f16 conversion changes the tensor size, and the split-output writer asserts on the mismatch. Every subsequent 3D tensor fails the same way (a.conv1d.1.weight [3,3,128,32], ...).

Workaround (verified): keep 3D tensors in f32 via tensor-type overrides —
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.0.weight=f32" \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.1.weight=f32" \
    mmproj-F16.gguf mmproj-F16-q8_0.gguf Q8_0

This works and the resulting Q8_0 mmproj is functionally correct on-device (Android, llama.cpp 4ebdf2c): vision outputs verified same-in-quality as F16 (sign-text reading), encode on a Helio G99 CPU improved 6.4x vs BF16 (37s -> 5.8s for a 91-token image).

Expected behavior: either skip/conversion-preserving handling for N-D tensors whose element count doesn't allow requantization, or a clean error message listing the offending tensors instead of an assert.

items.title: [Bug]: Qwen3.5-35B-A3B merged SFT BF16 intermittently produces NaN logits and exclamation-only output on H20 (v0.19.1; HF control finite)
items.author: ChenYahui210
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

Privacy-reviewed, targeted environment collection (not a full collect_env.py dump):

```text
GPU used by the reproduction: 1 x NVIDIA H20-3e
GPU memory reported by nvidia-smi: 143771 MiB

cuDNN reported by torch: 91002
Triton: 3.6.0
Transformers: 5.7.0
flash-linear-attention: 0.4.0
causal-conv1d: 1.6.0
```

Model: a private, merged SFT checkpoint based on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, loaded as BF16 with quantization=None. This report does not claim reproduction on the public unmodified base checkpoint. Both backends loaded the same verified checkpoint files. No runtime LoRA, training, sleep/wake, or speculative decoding was involved.

The vLLM package was not upgraded for this comparison. A newer release / current main and candidate patches have not yet been tested on these exact frozen inputs.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Summary

On a standalone vLLM 0.19.1 server, a frozen 11,686-token input produced exactly 2,500 exclamation marks (token ID 0), while `vllm:corrupted_requests_total` increased from 0 to 1 with `VLLM_COMPUTE_NANS_IN_LOGITS=1`. This happened during a **serial** request. A later identical request in the same server completed without a NaN-counter increment.

Using **the same merged BF16 weights and exactly the same frozen input token array**, Transformers generated 122 tokens and terminated normally on both replays; the two output token arrays were identical and every observed raw-logits tensor was finite.

Expected: finite logits and non-corrupted generation. I am not expecting bitwise equality between different backends. This report provides evidence of an intermittent numerical failure in the current vLLM execution stack, not a confirmed attribution to a particular kernel or cache bug.

## Observed sequence and results

Two inputs were selected because they had failed previously. A normal input was used as a control. Original generation budgets were retained; the tests were not shortened to a few output tokens.

| Input | Input tokens | Output budget | Historical failure | Transformers replay | vLLM replay |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 752 | 3200 | 3198 consecutive copies of one token | 187 output tokens; finite logits | 163 / 174 / 161 / 169 tokens; no NaN increment |
| B | 11686 | 2500 | 2500 copies of token 0 | 122 / 122 tokens; identical output arrays; finite logits | First serial request: 2500 copies of token 0 and NaN-counter +1. Later requests: 437 / 442 / 717 tokens without NaN increments |
| C (normal control) | 332 | 2500 | Normal | 177 tokens; finite logits | 171 tokens; no NaN increment |

Transformers order: A, B, C, B, all serial. Total: **4 requests, 608 forward/raw-logits checks, 0 nonfinite results**.

vLLM order on one fresh server: A, B, A, B serial; then A, B, A, B concurrently (4 requests); then C serial. Total: **9 requests, 1 NaN-corrupted request**. The failure was the second serial request, before the concurrent phase. There was no restart between the failed B request and its successful retries. These selected cases are not a representative failure-rate estimate.

Sanitized measurements around the failed serial request:

```text
corrupted_requests_total before: 0
corrupted_requests_total after:  1
usage.prompt_tokens:             11686
usage.completion_tokens:         2500
finish_reason:                  length
unique output token IDs:        [0]
longest identical-token run:    2500
returned text:                  "!" repeated exactly 2500 times
```

In the installed `vllm/v1/metrics/stats.py`, corruption is marked when `VLLM_COMPUTE_NANS_IN_LOGITS` is enabled and `output.num_nans_in_logits > 0`. Therefore this is not just a guess based on repetitive text. The request returned successfully at the HTTP level; the server remained alive. No CUDA exception, OOM, or resource-guard violation occurred during this replay.

## vLLM configuration

Normalized launch command (private path, device index, served name, and port replaced with placeholders/local defaults):

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 \
OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 MKL_NUM_THREADS=8 \
VLLM_COMPUTE_NANS_IN_LOGITS=1 \
python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \
  --model "$MODEL" \
  --served-model-name qwen35-debug \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 \
  --dtype bfloat16 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 1 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.60 \
  --max-model-len 40960 \
  --max-num-seqs 8 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 40960 \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --gdn-prefill-backend triton \
  --language-model-only \
  --seed 20260912 \
  --generation-config auto \
  --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_capture_sizes":[1,2,4,8],"max_cudagraph_capture_size":8}'
```

The server log confirms `enable_chunked_prefill=True`, `kv_cache_dtype=auto`, `quantization=None`, `enforce_eager=False`, and `speculative_config=None`. No MTP, prefix caching, adapter hot-loading, weight synchronization, or sleep/wake occurred. The server used fresh task-local compilation caches.

Requests used `/v1/completions` with pre-tokenized integer arrays, not server-side chat templating:

```python
payload = {
    "model": "qwen35-debug",
    "prompt": frozen_input_ids,  # same array used by Transformers
    "temperature": 0,
    "max_tokens": original_budget,  # 3200 for A; 2500 for B/C
    "seed": 20260912,
    "stop_token_ids": [248046, 248044],
    "skip_special_tokens": False,
    "return_token_ids": True,
}
```

`/metrics` was sampled before/after each serial request and before/after the concurrent group. Complete native output-token arrays, input hashes, request order, and metrics were retained locally.

## Transformers control

Transformers used the checkpoint tokenizer with `enable_thinking=True` to rebuild the saved full conversation, including prior tool-result context. The original incident did not log input token arrays: reconstructed lengths

items.title: [RFC]: CPU backend support for the vLLM connector + Mooncake Store L2 for multi-instance CPU serving
items.author: amd-lalithnc
items.body_excerpt:
## 1. Summary

This RFC proposes upstreaming two related contributions that enable **LMCache on the vLLM CPU backend** and make **cross-instance KV reuse** work for CPU serving:

1. **A CPU GPU-connector** (`VLLMCPUConnector`): a pure-torch gather/scatter path between vLLM's paged CPU KV cache and an LMCache `MemoryObj`, handling vLLM's 4D fused K/V CPU layout. This is the missing piece that lets LMCache run at all on `device=cpu`.
2. **Fixes to the Mooncake Store L2 connector** so it works on the CPU backend and shares KV **across instances** (fork-safe per-process client init, a correct `exists()`/lookup path, and a config-key alias).

Together these let multiple vLLM CPU instances behind a load balancer share one KV cache (SHM on a single box, or Mooncake Store over TCP across a cluster), instead of each instance recomputing the same prefixes.

Note that the CPU connector (contribution 1) is **backend-agnostic**: it is the shared foundation that unlocks the *entire* LMCache backend ecosystem on CPU (local DRAM L1, the shared SHM server, pickle, and remote L2s). Contribution 2 is one representative distributed L2 (Mooncake). We enable and validate **both** the default (SHM) and Mooncake paths because they target different deployment scopes (see §3.4).

We propose **two stacked PRs** (CPU connector, then Mooncake-on-CPU) plus this RFC to tie them together.

## 2. Motivation

- **CPU inference is growing** (cost, availability, disaggregated/CPU-tier deployments), and vLLM has a maturing CPU backend.
- **Multi-instance CPU serving needs *shared* KV.** vLLM's Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) is **per-instance**: behind a load balancer, instance B cannot reuse instance A's prefix KV, so shared system prompts / few-shot / documents are recomputed on every instance.
- **LMCache already solves cross-instance reuse**, but had **no CPU connector**, so it could not run on vLLM CPU at all; and the **Mooncake Store L2** path did not work on CPU or across instances (fork-safety + lookup bugs).
- **Measured impact** (Section 5): on a single-socket AMD EPYC, an external shared KV cache gives **+27-31% aggregate throughput at 3 instances** and **-28%/-34% p95/p99 tail latency** vs APC.

## 3. Design

### 3.1 Topology

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    LB[NGINX load balancer] --> V1[vLLM CPU inst 1]
    LB --> V2[vLLM CPU inst 2]
    LB --> V3[vLLM CPU inst 3]
    V1 <-->|store / load KV| L[(LMCache)]
    V2 <-->|store / load KV| L
    V3 <-->|store / load KV| L
    L <-->|put / get| S{{Shared KV: SHM  or  Mooncake Store L2 / TCP}}
```

### 3.2 CPU connector (`VLLMCPUConnector`)

**Why a CPU connector is needed.** Every existing GPU connector relies on CUDA custom ops (`c_ops`) and CUDA streams and assumes the GPU KV memory layout. None of that exists on CPU, so LMCache previously could not run on vLLM's CPU backend at all. `VLLMCPUConnector` fills that gap.

**What it implements.** The same connector interface, using **plain PyTorch tensor operations** (indexing + copy) with no CUDA kernels or streams:

- `from_gpu(...)` (**STORE / gather**): copy the KV for tokens `[start, end)` out of vLLM's paged CPU buffer into a contiguous `MemoryObj`.
- `to_gpu(...)` (**LOAD / scatter**): copy KV from a `MemoryObj` back into vLLM's paged buffer, placing each token's K/V into the slot given by vLLM's slot mapping.
- `batched_from_gpu(...)` / `batched_to_gpu(...)`: batched variants that handle several token ranges in one call.

**Handling vLLM's CPU KV layout.** vLLM's CPU backend stores each layer's cache as a single **4D fused K/V tensor** (K and V packed together), which is laid out differently from the GPU cache. For each layer the connector derives logical views shaped `[num_blocks, block_size, num_heads, head_size]` for K and for V (`_kv_token_views`), then uses the request's block/slot offsets to move exactly the right rows. This keeps gather/scatter correct without copying the whole buffer.

**Selection.** The connector is picked automatically when the device is CPU (`torch_device_type == "cpu"` in `CreateGPUConnector`), so no user config change is required.

**Plugging in as a `GPUConnectorInterface`.** So the CPU connector can subclass `GPUConnectorInterface` without importing the CUDA-heavy `gpu_connectors`/`utils` modules (which import `c_ops`, absent in NO_GPU_EXT builds), the interface ABC is extracted into a small `c_ops`-free `interface.py` that `gpu_connectors.py` re-exports. Existing GPU connectors are unaffected.

### 3.3 Mooncake Store L2 on CPU

The Mooncake client (Go runtime + multithreaded C++) is **not fork-safe**, and vLLM forks its scheduler/worker processes. Fixes:

- **Fork-safe, lazy per-process init**: the store/lookup client is created inside each process on first use (`_ensure_store()`), never inherited across a fork.
- **Correct lookup path**: `exists()`/`exists_sync()` now call `_ensure_store()` first (the contains/lookup path can run before any put/get on an instance) and compare `is_exist() == 1` (it returns `1/0/-1`) so an error never reads as a cache hit. Without this, cross-instance lookups were swallowed as misses and the instance recomputed.
- **Config-key alias**: accept `master_server_address` as an alias for `master_server_addr` in dict-based setup.

**Cross-instance key consistency (usage requirement, not connector code):** for a prefix computed on instance A to be found by instance B, the KV keys must hash identically across processes. Python's default randomized hashing breaks this; deployments must use a stable algorithm (e.g. `LMCACHE_PRE_CACHING_HASH_ALGORITHM=sha256` with `PYTHONHASHSEED=0`). This will be documented.

### 3.4 Why enable both paths (default SHM and Mooncake L2)

The CPU connector is transport/backend-agnostic, so a natural question is *why validate two L2 paths instead of one*. Because they are **complementary, not competing**: the right choice is dictated by deployment topology, and we want CPU users to be able to pick either without changing the connecto

items.title: [MP][engine_driven] ~0.55s fixed cost per transfer object on retrieve swamps wire time on PCIe hosts (pickle transport)
items.author: kaka86mm
items.body_excerpt:
## Environment
- PR #4410 head `2a79594` (hybrid multi-group engine-driven), CPU-only MP server `--supported-transfer-mode engine_driven`, transport = pickle (`Using pickle non-GPU transfer strategy`)
- 4× CMP 170HX (sm80, GPUs on PCIe 2.0 x4 host links, no P2P), vLLM 0.13.0 fork, PP=4
- MiMo-V2.6-Flash: 1 full-attention group + 5 sliding-window groups

## Measurement
Retrieval of a 69,376-token prefix across a restart (server untouched, engine restarted) shows a per-transfer-object fixed cost of ~0.55 s that dominates the wire time (~1.6 s total):

| server `--chunk-size` | transfer objects | retrieve TTFT | wire time (server log) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 256 (default) | 68 | 37.8 s | 1.6 s |
| 4096 | 17 | 9.8 s | 1.17 s |
| 8192 | 9 | 8.8 s | 0.28 s |

Plain local recompute of the same prefix is 26-30 s, so large chunks make the connector a ~3× win — but ~0.55 s of *fixed* cost per object means small-object workloads (many short prefixes, or default chunking) still lose to recompute on slow interconnects.

## Profile (with caveats)
py-spy `record -d 25 -r 50` on one PP worker during the retrieval phase. Caveat: py-spy samples **active threads only**, so this is a CPU-time profile, not wall-clock attribution — it can show where CPU went, not what blocked the main thread.

- MainThread (execute loop): essentially **absent** from CPU samples — blocked the whole time (separate stack dumps show it in `recv` / `shm_broadcast.acquire_read`)
- `_report_usage_worker` telemetry thread: burns a full core throughout retrieval (co-observation; not claiming causality)
- pickle-side work (`prepare_retrieve_multigroup_pickle`, `_load_from_bytes`, `msgspec_decode`): ~6-10% of CPU samples

So the wall-clock gap is not CPU-bound work in the worker; we suspect per-object round-trip/pacing in the transport.

## Questions
1. The server exposes `--shm-name` / pool size (`ShmTransferStrategy` with pickle fallback). Is the per-object cost expected to disappear under SHM (no serialize/TCP/unpickle per object)? We plan to A/B it in the next maintenance window and will report back.
2. The C++ transfer op records phase timings (`phase_timing_enabled` ← `is_observability_enabled()`, `pop_completed_phase_timings`). On the CPU-only server the `/metrics` endpoint only exposes lookup/lifecycle series — what is the supported way to export **engine-side** transfer-phase timings so the 0.55 s can be decomposed exactly?

Happy to share the raw flame data or a repro script (ffmpeg-free synthetic prompts against any checkpoint) if useful.

items.title: [RFC][MP] Hidden-state caching
items.author: Vivo50E
items.body_excerpt:
Cache a model's per-token hidden states alongside the KV they were produced with, so a consumer that conditions a downstream stage on them can still be fed after a KV hit skips prefill.

## Background

A multi-stage model can condition a later stage on an earlier stage's hidden states. In vLLM-Omni the talker is conditioned on the thinker's hidden states; Qwen3-Omni additionally uses intermediate layers named by `talker_config.accept_hidden_layer`.

KV offload breaks that. When LMCache serves a prefix, the engine skips prefill for those tokens, so no hidden states are produced for them. The talker is handed a suffix and the audio degrades — with no error anywhere, because from the KV path's point of view everything succeeded.

The fix is to cache the hidden states under the same keys as the KV they ride with, and restore them on a hit. This is implemented in-process today (`HiddenStateStore`, `lmcache/v1/hidden_state_store.py`, consumed by vllm-project/vllm-omni#1330) and does not exist in MP mode at all.

That PR would be the first consumer of an MP implementation too. The design below is written against its requirements, and we would do the port — so a first version gets exercised end to end rather than only specified.

## What the in-process implementation got wrong

Three properties this design has to have, each learned by shipping a bug without it:

**Keys must be derived exactly as the KV keys are.** Hidden states are only useful when they land under the same chunk hash as the KV for the same tokens, multimodal spans included — `mm_hash_to_token_values` substitution and all (`docs/design/integration/vllm/multimodal_cache_keying.md`). Deriving them separately produces a store that never hits, or worse, hits under the wrong identity. MP gets this for free if hidden states go through the same key derivation rather than a parallel one.

**Coverage must reach the scheduler.** In-process, hidden states live in a second pool with its own capacity and its own LRU, so the two quantities drift: the shipped defaults size them at 2 GB against 5 GB of KV, and a KV hit routinely outruns what hidden states can supply. Nothing detects it until the worker, by which point the prefill has already been skipped. The scheduler needs to commit to `min(KV, HS)` at `get_num_new_matched_tokens`, not to KV alone. LMCache#4824 adds this to the in-process lookup; the MP equivalent is the substance of this RFC's second half.

**Absolute token positions must survive a non-aligned hit.** Storage is chunk-aligned but a hit is not: a full-prompt hit leaves the engine recomputing the last token, so the first rows a worker produces after a restore start mid-chunk. Filing them at the rounded-down boundary stores them under earlier positions than they hold.

## Design

Hidden states are transient per-token activations with no paged home, and MP puts a process boundary between where they are produced and where they would be stored. Two ways across; the cheap one is good enough to start, and the other is below as a later optimization.

### Transport: a handler pair that ships bytes

`EngineDrivenTransferModule.commit_store` is the shape to copy — worker sends CPU bytes, server writes them, `prepare_retrieve` mirrors it:

```python
def commit_store(self, key: IPCCacheServerKey, instance_id: int,
                 cpu_data: bytes) -> bool:
    """Commit serialized CPU chunks to storage.
       cpu_data: Pickled list of CPU tensors produced by the worker."""
```

Copy the shape, not the handlers. `commit_store` opens with `entry, strategy = self._resolve_for_transfer(instance_id)`, which finds the engine-driven context the worker registered — and a CUDA deployment whose KV runs lmcache-driven never registered one. Reusing them would make the hidden state path inherit the KV path's transport mode, or force a second registration.

It does not need to. The transfer strategy exists to gather and scatter paged KV across block lists. Hidden states are a contiguous run of rows per request: there is nothing to gather. So the proposal is **a handler pair of its own — `store_hidden_states` and `retrieve_hidden_states` — taking and returning CPU bytes, resolving keys, and writing through the storage manager, with no transfer strategy involved**. CUDA and non-CUDA deployments take the same path, and whichever mode KV uses is not this path's concern.

The reason a copy is affordable here is size. A token of KV is `2 * num_layers * num_kv_heads * head_size` elements; a token of hidden state is `hidden_size`. On the Qwen2.5-Omni thinker that is `2 * 36 * 2 * 128 = 18,432` against a hidden size in the low thousands — **roughly a tenth**, or a third of it with three layers captured. The KV already crosses this boundary in an engine-driven deployment; a tensor a tenth its size does not change the shape of the cost.

### Keys

MP addresses objects with `ObjectKey`, not the in-process `CacheEngineKey`:

```python
class ObjectKey:
    chunk_hash: bytes
    model_name: str
    kv_rank: int
    object_group_id: int = 0
    cache_salt: str = ""
```

The chunk hash comes from `TokenHasher.compute_chunk_hashes`, so hidden states calling it on the same token ids land under the same hash as the KV — which is also how the `mm_hash_to_token_values` substitution comes along for free rather than being reimplemented.

What is left is telling the two apart. `object_group_id` is taken: it indexes KV kernel groups and carries a layout descriptor per group, which hidden states do not have. That leaves `model_name`, which is what Q already uses (`<model>##query`). Hidden states take `<model>##hidden`.

**One object per chunk, not one per layer.** If the layer set is declared once at registration (open question 1), every hidden-state object for a model has the same shape, `[chunk_size, num_layers, hidden_size]`, and a chunk needs exactly one key. https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF

Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Q4_K_M (arch=qwen3moe, pure attention) — UNAFFECTED on both builds

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Newer qwen models 3.5+ hybrid models were outputing mostly gibberish and crashing.  I've tested most of these models previously and they were working. Honestly thought I did something at first but then realized it was just an update I'm guessing.

Two related symptoms affect all hybrid architecture models (identifiable by 
ssm_d_conv / ssm_d_state / ssm_dt_rank fields in print_info) on Intel Arc Pro B60 
using server-intel latest (built 2026-06-03). Both are fixed by pinning to b8477.

SYMPTOM 1 - CRASH (qwen3next arch, e.g. Qwen3-Coder-Next):
Model loads fully into VRAM then crashes during warmup mul_mat on SSM/GDN weights.
crash at ggml_sycl_op_mul_mat line:3093.

SYMPTOM 2 - EMPTY/GIBBERISH OUTPUT (qwen35 arch, e.g. Qwen3.6-27B/35B):
Model loads and generates tokens but "content" field in API response is empty or 
contains number spam (e.g. 03129816571033482510583...). All output goes to 
"reasoning_content" as corrupted tokens. On b8477 the same models produce clean 
coherent output in "content".

IMPORTANT CONTEXT - why this is hard to diagnose:
server-intel is a rolling latest tag. Not sure when build/image broke but when I tried most recent build or 2026-06-03 get the broken build. Same 
image tag, completely different behavior depending on pull date. At one point I randomly tested Coder-Next about a week ago and although slow it worked. Now I randomly couldn't get any model 3.5 or above to work without gibberish outputs .... Coder-Next had been working in earlier sessions, then 
silently broke when the image updated i'm guessing, I just can't pinpoint when, unless this is known already.

Pure attention MoE models (qwen3moe arch, no SSM layers) are completely unaffected 
on both builds and work correctly throughout.

Steps to reproduce (using Docker):

1. Pull latest server-intel:
   docker pull ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-intel

2. Run with dual Arc Pro B60:

   docker run --rm \
     --device /dev/dri:/dev/dri \
     --group-add 993 --group-add 44 \
     -e ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=level_zero:0;level_zero:1 \
     -e ZES_ENABLE_SYSMAN=1 \
     -e UR_L0_ENABLE_RELAXED_ALLOCATION_LIMITS=1 \
     -e GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_LEVEL_ZERO=1 \
     -e GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_VMM=1 \
     -e GGML_SYCL_DISABLE_GRAPH=1 \
     -p 8010:8010 \
     ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-intel \
     --model /models/Qwen3-Coder-Next-UD-Q3_K_XL.gguf \
     --ctx-size 8192 \
     --host 0.0.0.0 \
     --port 8010 \
     -ngl 999 \
     --split-mode layer \
     --tensor-split 1,1 \
     --flash-attn off \
     --threads 1

3. For qwen3next: crash during warmup at ggml_sycl_op_mul_mat line:3093
   For qwen35: server starts, responds, but content field is empty or number spam

4. Replace image with server-intel-b8477 — identical command — both symptoms fixed

---

Side note for Ollama SYCL users:

This same regression affects users of https://github.com/eleiton/ollama-intel-arc
— an excellent community-maintained project providing native SYCL Ollama builds 
for Intel Arc GPUs. It is not a bug in that project. Ollama 0.30.2 pins 
LLAMA_CPP_VERSION=b9479 (confirmed via 
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ollama/ollama/v0.30.2/LLAMA_CPP_VERSION) which 
pulls the broken llama.cpp commit via FetchContent at build time.

Workaround: add this to ollama-sycl/Dockerfile after WORKDIR /ollama, then rebuild:

    RUN echo "ec2b787eb" > LLAMA_CPP_VERSION

Once this regression is fixed in llama.cpp master, Ollama SYCL builds will 
automatically pick up the fix.

### First Bad Commit

Working: server-intel-b8477 (ec2b787eb), image built 2026-03-23
Broken:  server-intel latest (~b9479), image built 2026-06-03

Regression window: somewhere between 2026-03-23 and 2026-06-03.
llama.cpp ships multiple builds per day so this window contains 
hundreds of commits. Have not bisected further.

A git bisect focusing on changes to ggml/src/ggml-sycl/ggml-sycl.cpp 
around the ggml_sycl_op_mul_mat function (line ~3093 in broken build) 
would likely narrow it down quickly.

Related: #21474 (same crash class on iGPU/Meteor Lake — that reporter 
also identified b8477 as working)  I just used this image to see if it would work, and it did!

Quick update. and sorry for the info dump.  I was able to narrow this down a lot more by testing the different images.

I tested the same stack, same hardware, same runtime flags, and the same model across each build to see where it worked and where it started producing bad output. The only thing I changed between tests was the image tag and container name.

The model used for every test was:

```text
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf
```

The model reports as:

```text
general.architecture = qwen35moe
general.name = Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
```

This does not look like the container itself is crashing. The container starts, the SYCL backend loads, the model loads, warmup finishes, and the server accepts requests. The actual issue is that it starts generating corrupted / gibberish tokens. Sometimes that then causes the server to return a 500 because the bad generated text breaks parsing around `<think>`.

This was the compose stack used for every build, with only the `image` tag and `container_name` changed for each build:

comments.author: CameronWeller
comments.body:
Still reproduces on current master (`67a17c17c`, 2026-09-02), single **Intel Arc Pro B60** (BMG G21), oneAPI DPC++ 2026.1, Level Zero 1.28.6, Mesa 26.0.8, kernel 7.0.0 (Ubuntu).

Models (both public GGUFs):
- `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF:Q4_K_M` — `arch=qwen35`
- `ornith-ai/Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B-GGUF` — `arch=qwen35moe`

**Extra data point that may help localise it:** on this box the failure is *not* the caught `ggml_sycl_op_mul_mat` exception during warmup — it's a hard **general-protection fault in libc during model load**, right after `llama threadpool init, n_threads = N` and *before* the warmup graph runs. Same faulting address every run (`libc.so.6 + 0x19a12b`). Kernel log:

```
traps: llama-server[…] general protection fault ip:…12b … in libc.so.6[19a12b,…+198000]
```

It behaves like a race / uninitialised read in the parallel tensor-upload path — it loads and runs **fine** under anything that perturbs timing:

- `gdb` (even with `MALLOC_CHECK_=3` / `MALLOC_PERTURB_`)
- `GGML_SYCL_DEBUG=1`

With `GGML_SYCL_DEBUG=1` the full graph executes on the GPU with no error. `--flash-attn off` lowers the crash rate but does not eliminate it. The CPU backend loads the same GGUFs in ~5 s and generates coherent output.

Minimal repro:

```
llama-server -hf unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF:Q4_K_M --no-mmproj -ngl 999 -c 4096 --port 8000
```

**Workaround:** the Vulkan backend (`-DGGML_VULKAN=ON`, Mesa ANV) loads and runs both `qwen35` and `qwen35moe` on the B60 with flash attention on and no crash — Qwen3.8-27B ~10 tok/s fully offloaded, Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B ~24 tok/s with `--n-cpu-moe`. `--spec-type draft-mtp` (the GGUF's own NextN head) also works on Vulkan and roughly doubles both.

items.title: [RFC]: Hot Standby Mode for Master Service Metadata High Availability
items.author: Libotry
items.body_excerpt: ## Introduction To address the issue where all metadata is lost after a master service failure and recovery, this solution proposes a **hot-standby synchronization mechanism** and a **hybrid approach** combining hot standby with snapshots, ensuring rapid data recovery following a master service failure. ## Motivation The current HA (High Availability) mode only supports rapid restart of the master service after a failure but cannot guarantee fast data recovery. The pain points of the current HA mode are as follows: | Issue | Impact | Severity | | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------- | | **Complete loss of metadata after Leader failure** | All KV cache location information is lost and must be rebuilt | 🔴 Critical | | **Follower lacks data pre-warming** | After successful election, the new Leader must start serving from scratch | 🟠 Medium | | **Long recovery time** | Relies on clients to re-register; may take several minutes to tens of minutes | 🟠 Medium | | **Service unavailability window** | Requests cannot be processed during Leader failover | 🟡 Low | ## Goals: 1. **Near-zero RPO**: Minimize the data loss window 2. **Fast failover**: Achieve second-level RTO (Recovery Time Objective) 3. **Data consistency guarantee**: Ensure correct synchronization between primary and standby 4. **Verifiability**: Include mechanisms to validate data integrity 5. **Low performance overhead**: Avoid impacting normal business operations ## Proposal ### 1. Core Design Approach **Use etcd as an intermediate reliability component to implement OpLog primary-standby synchronization**: - **OpLog Mechanism**: Primary Master records all state change operations to OpLog - **etcd Storage**: OpLog is written to etcd, leveraging etcd's strong consistency and persistence capabilities - **Watch Mechanism**: Standby Master receives OpLog in real-time through etcd Watch mechanism - **Ordering Guarantee**: Guarantee operation order through global sequence_id and key-level key_sequence_id ### 2. Architecture Design #### (1) Overall Architecture The overall architecture diagram shows the interaction relationships between Primary Master, etcd Cluster, and Standby Master: **Architecture Description**: - **Primary Master**: Handles client requests, records OpLog and writes to etcd - **etcd Cluster**: Acts as intermediate storage, providing strong consistency and Watch mechanism - **Standby Master**: Receives OpLog in real-time by watching etcd and applies to local metadata store #### (2) Data Flow Diagram The data flow diagram shows the complete flow from Client request to Standby synchronization: **Flow Description**: a. Client sends `PutEnd` request to Primary Master b. Primary Master records operation through `OpLogManager`, generating sequence_id c. `EtcdOpLogStore` writes OpLog to etcd d. etcd notifies Standby Master through Watch mechanism e. `OpLogWatcher` receives events and passes to `OpLogApplier` f. `OpLogApplier` checks order and applies to Standby's metadata store #### (3) Failover Sequence The failover sequence diagram shows the complete process from Primary failure to Standby promotion to Primary: **Flow Description**: a. **Normal Operation**: Primary maintains Lease, Standby continuously synchronizes OpLog through Watch b. **Primary Failure**: Primary's Lease expires, etcd notifies Standby c. **Standby Promotion**: Stop Standby service, initialize Lease, clean expired metadata, start leader election ### 3. Problem & Assumptions #### 1.1 Problem After a `Delete` (or eviction) on the primary master: - The primary frees a replica’s memory (returns buffer to allocator’s free list). - The `Delete` event is **not** replicated to the standby master. - The primary then crashes; the standby is promoted to new master. - The new master still believes that this replica exists, and returns its address to clients. - That buffer may already have been **reused by another object**, or may still contain **logically deleted data**. We must **never** return data that belongs to some other key/object/tenant due to buffer reuse, even if we allow some metadata loss. #### 1.2 Accepted Semantic Constraints We explicitly accept the following semantics: - **Metadata / delete operations may be lost across failover**: - A delete acknowledged by the old master may be “rolled back” after failover. - That is acceptable because the KV cache can be recomputed. - **Hard safety requirement**: - It is strictly forbidden to read data that **belongs to another key/object/tenant** as if it were the requested key. - In other words: buffer reuse must not cause **cross-key contamination**. Under these constraints, it is acceptable that: - A key that was “deleted” on the old master may reappear after failover (logical delete rolled back). - But it is **not** acceptable to read someone else’s data due to buffer reuse. --- ### 2. Idea We upgrade each replica from a “raw pointer” into a **versioned capability**: - In-memory layout of a replica buffer becomes: - The master generates a **64-bit version** for each successful `Put` of a key. - This `version` is stored: - In `ObjectMetadata` on the master. - In the `ReplicaDescriptor` returned to clients. - In the first 8 bytes of the actual buffer in the KV store. - On **Get**, the client always verifies: - Read the first 8 bytes of the buffer. - Compare with the expected version from `ReplicaDescriptor`. - If versions match → buffer still belongs to this key/epoch → safe to read payload. - If versions differ → buffer was reused by someone else → mark this replica invalid, do not use it. Thus, even if the physical address is reused for a different object, the client will detect it and reject the replica. --- ### 3. Data Model Changes #### 3.1 Version Type ```cpp using Version = uint64_t; ``` Version can be constructed as: - High bits: timestamp (e.g., microseconds since epoch). - Low bits: per-node monotonic sequence ID. Requirements: - For a single master process, each successful `Put` for a given key gets a **unique, monotonically increasing** version. - Version collisions are practically impossible within a process lifetime. #### 3.2 Replica Descriptor Extension Extend `Replica::Descriptor` (or equivalent) to carry version information: On `PutStart`, the master generates `version`, stores it in metadata, and includes it in each replica descriptor. --- ### 4. Write Path (Put) Design #### 4.1 Master: PutStart 1. Client invokes `Put(key, slices, config)`. 2. `MasterService::PutStart(key, slice_lengths, config)`: - Validates input. - Allocates replicas as it does today (segments, buffers, etc.). - Generates a new `Version version = MakeVersion()` for this key. - Stores `version` in `ObjectMetadata` for this key. - Fills `ReplicaDescriptor.version = version` for each allocated replica. - Returns the list of descriptors to the client. comments.author: ykwd
comments.body:
Thanks for sharing the proposal. Unfortunately, this approach is not safe and does not actually guarantee the hard safety requirement you described, for two reasons:

First, RDMA reads and writes do not provide ordering and atomicity guarantees, which breaks the version-only validation scheme. In your design, correctness relies on the assumption that the first 8 bytes (the version) and the payload are written and observed atomically and in order. That assumption does not hold.

Second, the allocator does not guarantee alignment between successive allocations, which makes the embedded-version assumption invalid. Your scheme assumes that when a buffer is freed and later reused, the next allocation will reuse the same start address and layout, so that the version stored in the first 8 bytes corresponds exactly to the logical object boundary.

items.title: [RFC]: Explicit Context Caching — Guaranteed KV Cache Eviction Protection
items.author: Colors-111
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

#  Explicit Context Caching — Guaranteed KV Cache Eviction Protection

## Summary

Introduce a `guaranteed_until` timestamp mechanism in Mooncake Store to implement Explicit Context Caching:

1. **Eviction protection**: Users mark `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` in `messages`, and the corresponding prefix KV Cache is marked as guaranteed (non-evictable within TTL) in the Store. After expiration, objects automatically degrade to regular objects
2. **Passive expiration**: Uses an absolute `guaranteed_until_` timestamp — BatchEvict naturally skips unexpired objects; expired objects automatically become eviction candidates. Zero new RPCs, crash-safe by design
3. **Zero state on inference engine side**: All guaranteed lifecycle management resides on the Master side. Inference engines (SGLang, vLLM, etc.) do not track or manage guaranteed cache; radix tree nodes require no new fields

## 1. Background and Motivation

### Problem 1: High-Value Prefixes Lack Eviction Protection

Mainstream inference engines (SGLang, vLLM, etc.) reuse KV Cache through prefix matching (RadixAttention / Automatic Prefix Caching). Shared prefixes (system prompts, RAG documents, few-shot examples) are frequently hit. The current eviction strategy in Mooncake Store sorts purely by lease timeout — least recently accessed objects are evicted first. This means:

- Under memory pressure, high-value long prefixes (e.g., a 4K-token system prompt) may be evicted first (because they may not have recent writes)
- After eviction, the next request requires full recomputation, causing P99 latency spikes and GPU compute waste

### Problem 2: OpenAI-Compatible cache_control Semantics Have No Backend Support

The OpenAI API introduced `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` markers, allowing users to declare "this prefix is important, don't evict it" in message content blocks. Frontend frameworks (e.g., LangChain, VLLM) widely support this semantic, but Mooncake Store has no corresponding eviction protection mechanism, rendering the marker effectively inert.

### Problem 3: Design Gap Between Explicit and Implicit Caching

Alibaba Bailian adopts a standalone CacheIndex + 20-block lookback window approach (multi-tenant cloud service), but this introduces a complex indexing system and inference-engine-side lifecycle management. For single-cluster self-deployment scenarios, we need a lighter approach.

**Goals**: Provide deterministic eviction protection (hard guarantee) for prefixes marked with `cache_control`. After TTL expiry, objects automatically degrade to regular objects. Zero new state on inference engine side. Zero regression risk.

## 2. Core Design

### Tiered Architecture

| Tier | Location | Role in Explicit Caching | Guarantee Level |
|------|----------|-------------------------|-----------------|
| L1 (GPU) | Inference engine Worker (local) | Temporarily held during inference, normal eviction | No guarantee |
| L2 (CPU) | Inference engine Worker (local) | Speedup on same-engine hit (bonus) | No guarantee |
| L3 (Mooncake Store) | Distributed storage | **Deterministic guarantee tier** | Hard guarantee |

L1/L2 do not participate in guarantees: requests may be routed to any engine instance, and L2 is only available on the local instance. Binding guarantees to L2 would require forced routing to a specific instance, breaking load balancing. L3 is shared across all engines, naturally supporting cross-engine reuse.

### Architecture Diagram

```
  Client (messages with cache_control markers)
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Inference Engine API Server          │
  │  - Parse cache_control → token offsets│
  └──────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                 │
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Inference Engine Worker Instance     │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ HiCache Controller (no change)│   │
  │  │ - radix tree normal prefix   │    │
  │  │   matching                   │    │
  │  │ - On write: check cache_     │    │
  │  │   control → write_through    │    │
  │  │   with guaranteed param      │    │
  │  │ - On read: check cache_      │    │
  │  │   control → GetReplicaList   │    │
  │  │   with guaranteed param      │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────┬───────────────────────────┘
             │
  ┌──────────▼───────────────────────────┐
  │  Mooncake Store (L3)                │
  │  - guaranteed_until_ timestamp guard │
  │  - BatchEvict skips unexpired objs  │
  │  - GrantLease auto-renewal          │
  │  - Guaranteed capacity limit+fallback│
  │  - SSD Offload priority protection  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Design 1: guaranteed_until_ Timestamp Scheme

Add `guaranteed_until_` (`SteadyClock::time_point`) to `ObjectMetadata`, defaulting to epoch (no guarantee). At PutStart, if `ReplicateConfig.guaranteed_until_ms > 0`, the Master converts it to an absolute timestamp.

**Core semantic**: `guaranteed_until_` unexpired → object is non-evictable (equivalent to hard pinned); expired → automatically degrades to a regular object.

**Why timestamps over reference counting / lease renewal**:

| Approach | New RPCs | Crash recovery | Complexity |
|----------|----------|----------------|------------|
| Reference counting | Requires ReleaseGuaranteed | Must clean residual counts | High |
| Lease renewal | Requires RenewGuaranteed | Depends on TTL patches | Medium |
| **guaranteed_until timestamp** | **Zero** | **Natural expiration, no orphans** | **Low** |

### Design 2: Zero State on Inference Engine Side

Inference engines (SGLang, vLLM, etc.) hold no guaranteed state. All lifecycle management is on the Master side:

- **Write path**: HiCache checks whether the current block falls within `cache_control`-marked token range → if yes, write_through to L3 with `guaranteed_until_ms`
- **Read path**: When a request carries `cache_control`, pass `guaranteed_ttl

[by Codex]

### Environment

- 2 x NVIDIA B300 in one NVLink domain
- `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.18-cu130`
- SGLang v0.5.18, FlashInfer 0.6.17

### Reproduction

1. Download only the public model configuration/tokenizer files and make a 24-layer dummy-weight configuration:

```bash
hf download nvidia/GLM-5.2-NVFP4 \
  --exclude '*.safetensors' \
  --local-dir /tmp/GLM-5.2-NVFP4-dummy

python3 -c 'import json; p="/tmp/GLM-5.2-NVFP4-dummy/config.json"; d=json.load(open(p)); d["num_hidden_layers"]=24; [d.__setitem__(k,d[k][:24]) for k in ("layer_types","mlp_layer_types","indexer_types") if k in d]; json.dump(d,open(p,"w"),indent=2)'
```

2. In the SGLang container, start the server:

```bash
export MC_FORCE_MNNVL=1
export NCCL_MNNVL_ENABLE=1
export NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=1

python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /tmp/GLM-5.2-NVFP4-dummy --load-format dummy \
  --tp-size 2 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
  --max-total-tokens 250000 --context-length 1048576 \
  --quantization modelopt_fp4 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
  --attention-backend nsa --nsa-prefill-backend trtllm --nsa-decode-backend trtllm \
  --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_trtllm \
  --flashinfer-allreduce-fusion-backend mnnvl \
  --chunked-prefill-size 32768 --max-running-requests 32 \
  --cuda-graph-config '{"prefill":{"backend":"breakable","max_bs":32768,"bs":[4,8,16,32,64,128,256,512,1024,2048,4096,8192,16384,26752,32768]}}' \
  --speculative-algorithm EAGLE --speculative-num-steps 5 \
  --speculative-eagle-topk 1 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 6 \
  --page-size 64 --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 160 \
  --enable-cache-report --enable-metrics
```

3. Save the example below as `hicache_hang_load.py` on the same host. It performs the cache-fill phase, verifies that eviction has started, keeps exactly 96 draw requests in flight, runs the CUDA-context churn workers on GPUs 0 and 1, and reports a reproduction after 120 seconds without a completion.

4. Run it while the server is healthy:

```bash
python3 hicache_hang_load.py --url http://127.0.0.1:30000
```

### Observed outcome

Within approximately 1-6 minutes, request progress permanently stops while both scheduler processes remain alive. One GPU becomes idle and the other stays at 100% utilization in a collective kernel. The busy GPU is typically stuck in FlashInfer's MNNVL `twoshotAllreduceKernel`; either TP rank can be the busy rank.

### Expected outcome

All requests complete without a permanent TP-rank hang.

items.title: fix(mlx): repeated chat returns unrelated text after native generation
items.author: coygeek
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On SGLang 0.5.20 with the native MLX backend, a successful chat request followed by native `/generate` changes the result of an identical deterministic chat request. The first chat answers Paris and finishes with `stop`; the second returns unrelated text and reaches the token limit. Disabling radix caching makes the mixed sequence pass. This report concerns observed sequential response correctness; the internal cause has not been established.

## Steps to reproduce

Use SGLang tag `v0.5.20`, commit `94602c9c2b7cbdb8efd5c52802dac6a1c180089e`, in an isolated Apple Silicon environment. The test used the public model `mlx-community/Qwen3-0.6B-4bit` at revision `73e3e38d981303bc594367cd910ea6eb48349da8`, copied into `./model`. The installation used the source Apple `all_mps` dependencies from `python/pyproject_other.toml`. See the [Apple Silicon installation guide](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.20/docs/docs/hardware-platforms/apple_metal.mdx) for backend setup.

Start a fresh server with the default radix cache enabled:

```sh
export SGLANG_USE_MLX=1
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=2
export MKL_NUM_THREADS=2
sglang serve --model-path ./model --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000 --context-length 2048 --mem-fraction-static 0.1
```

After `/health` returns HTTP 200, run this script. It discovers the served model name so the request body uses the same identifier as the server. Run only these three generation requests on the fresh server, in this order:

```python
import json
import urllib.request

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:30000"

def post(path, body):
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        BASE + path,
        data=json.dumps(body).encode(),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=120) as response:
        assert response.status == 200
        return json.load(response)

with urllib.request.urlopen(BASE + "/v1/models") as response:
    model = json.load(response)["data"][0]["id"]

chat = {
    "model": model,
    "messages": [{
        "role": "user",
        "content": "What is the capital of France? Answer in one sentence.",
    }],
    "max_tokens": 64,
    "temperature": 0,
    "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False},
}
native = {
    "text": "The capital of France is",
    "sampling_params": {"temperature": 0, "max_new_tokens": 24},
}

first = post("/v1/chat/completions", chat)
middle = post("/generate", native)
second = post("/v1/chat/completions", chat)

for label, result in [("first", first), ("second", second)]:
    choice = result["choices"][0]
    print(label, choice["finish_reason"], repr(choice["message"]["content"]))
print("native", middle["meta_info"]["finish_reason"], repr(middle["text"]))

for result in [first, second]:
    choice = result["choices"][0]
    assert choice["finish_reason"] == "stop", choice
    assert "Paris" in choice["message"]["content"], choice
```

For a control, restart the server and repeat with `--disable-radix-cache`. A consecutive chat/chat control before any native generation also passed in the retained run.

## Expected behavior

An unrelated, completed native request should not change the answer to the identical deterministic chat request. Both chat responses should answer Paris and finish with `stop`. The bounded native request may finish by length at its explicitly requested 24-token budget.

## Actual behavior

The first chat returned `The capital of France is Paris.`, with `finish_reason: stop` and 8 completion tokens. The native request returned 24 tokens with a length finish reason and reported 2 cached tokens. The second chat returned HTTP 200, `finish_reason: length`, and 64 completion tokens, beginning with the text below rather than answering the question:

```text
of the country that has the most number of people in the world. What is the name of the country?

A. China

B. Russia

C. India

D. United States

Answer: __________
Answer:
A
```

This is the beginning of the retained response; its final truncated question is omitted here. A later SDK request using the same chat arguments also returned unrelated text with a length finish reason. The immediate direct-HTTP chat after native generation already demonstrates the failure, without the SDK or subsequent completion/message requests.

## Affected area

Native MLX serving with default radix caching, sequential `/v1/chat/completions` and `/generate` requests. The failure is observable at the HTTP response boundary. No concurrency, cancellation, custom request IDs, or retraction was part of the minimized sequence.

## Runtime or environment

| Component | Observed value |
| --- | --- |
| SGLang | 0.5.20, source tag `v0.5.20`, commit `94602c9c2b7cbdb8efd5c52802dac6a1c180089e` |
| OS and hardware | macOS 27.0, ARM64, Apple M5 Pro, 64 GiB memory |
| Python | 3.12.13 |
| PyTorch | 2.13.0 |
| MLX | 0.32.3 |
| mlx-lm | 0.32.0 |
| Transformers | 5.12.1 |
| OpenAI SDK | 2.6.1, used only in additional checks |
| Native kernel | sglang-kernel 0.4.7, built with `setup_metal.py` |
| Model | `mlx-community/Qwen3-0.6B-4bit`, revision `73e3e38d981303bc594367cd910ea6eb48349da8` |
| Backend | `SGLANG_USE_MLX=1`, Metal available |

These values describe the retained 0.5.20 failure. A new isolated 0.5.21 runtime used source tag `v0.5.21`, commit `e00930c5489053f26d86b179cee0d087f846acbb`, the same public model snapshot, and the source `srt_mps` extra. MLX and mlx-lm were held at the same measured versions as the earlier run. Its dependency check passed for 150 packages. Optional native Metal kernels were not installed for the new check.

The following is the actual sanitized output of `SGLANG_USE_MLX=1 python3 -m sglang.check_env` from that 0.5.21 runtime:

```text
Python: 3.12.13 (main, Apr 14 2026, 14:33:40) [Clang 22.1.3 ]
MPS available: True
macOS Version: 27.0
macOS Build: 26A428
Apple Silicon: Apple M5 Pro
Unified Memory: 64.0 GB
CPU Cores (Total): 18
CPU Cores (Performance): 6
CPU Cores (Efficiency): 12
Me

items.title: [Feature] Upgrade Nsight Compute bundled by the CUDA devel base image
items.author: YouNeedCryDear
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

The runtime image ships Nsight Compute because the CUDA devel base installs it. SGLang does not apt-install this package.

`docker/Dockerfile` on `main` and at tag `v0.5.20` sets `ARG CUDA_VERSION=13.0.3`. The runtime stage is:

```dockerfile
# Note: Uses devel base for complete NVCC toolchain required by DeepGEMM JIT
FROM nvidia/cuda:${CUDA_VERSION}-cudnn-devel-ubuntu24.04 AS runtime
```

The comment above that stage says the runtime image is smaller than the framework stage and does not include dev tools such as nsight. That comment covers packages the framework stage installs (`nsight-systems-cli`). It does not cover the base image. `nvidia/cuda:13.0.3-cudnn-devel-ubuntu24.04` installs `cuda-nsight-compute-13-0` 13.0.3-1, which depends on `nsight-compute-2025.3.1` 2025.3.1.4-1.

The same two packages are installed in `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.18-runtime` and `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.20-runtime`. The deb unpacks a tree of about 1.3 GB at `/opt/nvidia/nsight-compute/2025.3.1` and vendors its own libraries. Versions read from that tree:

| Library | File | Version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenSSL | `host/linux-desktop-glibc_2_11_3-x64/libcrypto.so.3` | 3.0.16 (11 Feb 2025) |
| SQLite | `host/linux-desktop-glibc_2_11_3-x64/libsqlite3.so.0` | 3.46.0 |
| Qt | `host/linux-desktop-glibc_2_11_3-x64/libQt6Core.so.6` | 6.6.3 |

Those copies are behind published fixes:

- SQLite 3.46.0 is older than 3.50.2, so it is affected by [CVE-2025-6965](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-6965) (memory corruption when the number of aggregate terms exceeds the number of columns). Fixed in SQLite 3.50.2.
- OpenSSL 3.0.16 is affected by [CVE-2025-9230](https://openssl-library.org/news/secadv/20250930.txt) (Moderate: out-of-bounds read and write in RFC 3211 KEK unwrap; can crash or corrupt memory). The advisory says OpenSSL 3.0 users should upgrade to 3.0.18.
- The same 3.0.16 build is affected by [CVE-2025-9232](https://openssl-library.org/news/secadv/20250930.txt) (Low: out-of-bounds read in HTTP client `no_proxy` handling). The advisory says this vulnerable code was introduced in 3.0.16 and fixed in 3.0.18.
- OpenSSL 3.0.19 (27 Jan 2026) is a later security release on the 3.0 branch. Its [release notes](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/openssl-3.0.19/NEWS.md) fix further 3.0 issues, including CVE-2025-15467 (High: stack buffer overflow in CMS `AuthEnvelopedData` parsing), plus CVE-2025-68160, CVE-2025-69418, CVE-2025-69419, CVE-2025-69420, CVE-2025-69421, CVE-2026-22795, and CVE-2026-22796. The vendored copy is 3.0.16, so it has neither the 3.0.18 nor the 3.0.19 fixes.
- Qt 6.6.3 in this tree is the unpatched upstream build. Downstream security updates of that same version address [CVE-2025-5455](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-5455) and CVE-2025-30348.

Please upgrade this Nsight Compute pin. The current Nsight Compute release is 2025.4.1 (12 Jan 2026), which tracks CUDA Toolkit 13.1. Moving `CUDA_VERSION` to a 13.1 `cudnn-devel` tag, or otherwise replacing `cuda-nsight-compute-13-0` 13.0.3-1, is what drops `nsight-compute-2025.3.1` 2025.3.1.4-1. After the upgrade, please confirm the vendored OpenSSL is at least 3.0.19 and the vendored SQLite is at least 3.50.2.

Keep the devel base. DeepGEMM, Triton, and FlashInfer JIT still need `nvcc`, and upgrading Nsight Compute does not require removing `cuda-nvcc`.

I searched open and closed issues for this package and did not find an existing report. #33283 is about Nsight Systems process-tree profiling and does not cover this.

### Related resources

- Runtime stage: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.20/docker/Dockerfile
- Nsight Compute 2025.4.1 release: https://developer.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/get-started
- CVE-2025-6965: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-6965 and https://www.sqlite.org/cves.html
- OpenSSL advisory for CVE-2025-9230 and CVE-2025-9232: https://openssl-library.org/news/secadv/20250930.txt
- OpenSSL 3.0.19 release notes: https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/openssl-3.0.19/NEWS.md

Reproduction on the published runtime image:

```bash
docker run --rm --entrypoint bash lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.20-runtime -lc '
  dpkg-query -W cuda-nsight-compute-13-0 nsight-compute-2025.3.1
  H=/opt/nvidia/nsight-compute/2025.3.1/host/linux-desktop-glibc_2_11_3-x64
  strings "$H/libcrypto.so.3" | grep "^OpenSSL "
  strings "$H/libQt6Core.so.6" | grep "^Qt 6\."
  strings "$H/libsqlite3.so.0" | grep "^3\."
'
```

- **Usability**: Simple launch commands for a single engine and large-scale deployments, easy to use cookbook and docker images for common models.

items.title: [Bug] EAGLE/MTP same-checkpoint draft keeps redundant embed_tokens/lm_head copies resident during KV pool sizing → under-sized pool, startup OOM
items.author: paulalesius
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

With EAGLE/MTP speculative decoding and the draft taken from the **same checkpoint** as the target (the standard MTP setup, e.g. `nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4`), the draft worker loads full BF16 copies of `embed_tokens` and `lm_head`. Those copies are redundant: the MTP draft is supposed to share the target's embed/head, and the sharing code frees them (`EagleWorkerV2.init_lm_head()` → `set_embed_and_head()`/`set_lm_head_from_target()`, `python/sglang/srt/speculative/eagle_worker_v2.py:310-353`, `python/sglang/srt/models/qwen3_5_mtp.py:170-187`).

But the free only happens in `draft.alloc_memory_pool()`, which the scheduler (`python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py`, `init_memory_pools`) runs **after** the target pool is sized and **after** the draft pool is allocated:

```
init_target_memory_pool()      # target KV pool sized + allocated
draft_worker.alloc_memory_pool()
    -> TpModelWorker.alloc_memory_pool   # draft KV pool allocated  <-- OOM here
    -> init_token_map() / init_lm_head() # redundant copies freed    <-- too late
```

So both pools are sized while ~2.4 GiB/rank of about-to-be-freed weight traffic is still resident. The copies exist because for serialized NVFP4 ModelOpt checkpoints the draft is built unquantized (`_mtp_quant_config`, qwen3_5_mtp.py:65-69), and `load_weights` loads the checkpoint embedding into the draft's own tensor (qwen3_5_mtp.py:344-356): 2 x (248320/2 x 5120 x 2 B) = ~2.37 GiB per rank on this model. The draft worker also does not re-profile: `configure()` reuses the target's `memory_pool_config` (`kv_cache_configurator.py:366-370`), so the draft pool is built at the same token count into an already-exhausted GPU.

Measured impact, same machine and flags with vs. without a patch that runs the release before sizing:

| | without patch | with patch |
|---|---|---|
| free mem after draft load | 2.30 GB | 2.30 GB |
| target KV pool sized to | **106501** tokens | **139000** tokens (the requested `--max-total-tokens`) |
| free mem after pool alloc | 0.07 GB | 1.93 GB |
| outcome | `torch.OutOfMemoryError` at startup | healthy |

Pre-patch crash:

```
File ".../sglang/srt/speculative/eagle_worker_v2.py", line 226, in alloc_memory_pool
    self.draft_worker.alloc_memory_pool(...)
File ".../sglang/srt/mem_cache/kv_cache_configurator.py", line 376, in configure
    pools = self._init_pools(...)
File ".../sglang/srt/mem_cache/memory_pool.py", line 2453, in _create_buffers_normal
    torch.zeros(v_shape, dtype=self.store_dtype, device=self.device)
torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 54.00 MiB.
GPU 1 has a total capacity of 15.56 GiB of which 14.38 MiB is free.
```

### Proposed fix

Release the redundant copies **before** any pool is profiled. The sharing logic already exists and is idempotent; it just needs to run earlier. One-hunk patch to `python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py`:

```diff
@@ class Scheduler
      def init_target_memory_pool(self):
          ...
          self._release_draft_redundant_weights()   # NEW: before sizing
          self.tp_worker.model_runner.account_preloaded_weights(...)
          self.tp_worker.alloc_memory_pool()

+    def _release_draft_redundant_weights(self):
+        """Share the draft's embed/lm_head with the target before pool sizing."""
+        draft_worker = self.draft_worker
+        if draft_worker is None:
+            return
+        # The methods live on the inner worker (EAGLEWorkerV2 wraps it);
+        # resolve via the base-class property (None on non-last PP ranks).
+        inner = getattr(draft_worker, "draft_worker", None)
+        if inner is None or not hasattr(inner, "init_lm_head"):
+            return
+        try:
+            inner.init_token_map()
+            inner.init_lm_head()
+        except Exception:
+            logger.exception(
+                "Scheduler: early draft embed/lm_head release failed; the "
+                "release path in draft.alloc_memory_pool still runs"
+            )
+            return
+        logger.info("Scheduler: released draft embed/lm_head copies before pool profiling")
```

Why it is safe:

- **Idempotent.** The later `init_lm_head()` inside `draft.alloc_memory_pool` re-binds the same target tensors and repeats a harmless `empty_cache()`; the early call is a no-op for it.
- **Guards the inner worker.** The scheduler's `self.draft_worker` is the outer `EAGLEWorkerV2`; the methods live on the inner worker behind the `draft_worker` property (`base_spec_worker.py:191`). The `hasattr` check skips any draft without a share path (standalone EAGLE / different-checkpoint drafts, PP ranks that host no draft).
- **Fallback.** The try/except keeps the original late-release path alive if the early one fails.

Alternative: skip materializing the copies at load time (draft loader binds the target's embed tensor directly and skips allocating the draft `lm_head`, qwen3_5_mtp.py:344-356). That removes the waste at the source but is invasive (loader paths, PP stages, tie-words), whereas the scheduler-side fix is one guarded call site that works for every model family implementing `set_embed_and_head` (qwen2/3/3.5/3.8, glm, deepseek-v2/v4, gemma4, hunyuan, ...).


### Reproduction

```bash
          /home/noname/venv-sglang/bin/sglang serve \
              --trust-remote-code \
              --model-path /home/noname/.cache/huggingface/hub/models--nvidia--Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4/snapshots/482ca0f3832238542f8f5295dde86b5f22711d80 \
              --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
              --at

items.title: [Bug] big prefill blocks other requests on 2xRTX3090  for qwen3.8 27b
items.author: vargrant
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Here is situation when I tried to use sgalng for 2 concurrent queries when both requests not in cache. First big request coming with long time of prefill (it's can be minutes),  but second short request blocked due a time when first preill finished - this situation blocks inference for potential light query which arrival later but can be prefilled   and decoded faster then first hard request.

items.title: [Bug] /update_weights_from_disk: is_async / keep_pause / token_step have no effect, num_paused_requests is always 0
items.author: apex-mochen
items.body_excerpt:
On current main (`1818db4e54`), four parameters of `/update_weights_from_disk` are part of the API and documented in `docs/docs/advanced_features/sglang_for_rl.mdx`, but nothing in the tree reads them:

| name | kind | declared | documented as | who reads it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `is_async` | request | `io_struct.py:1879` | "Perform weight load asynchronously." (`sglang_for_rl.mdx:172`) | — |
| `keep_pause` | request | `io_struct.py:1883` | "Keep scheduler paused after update." (`:184`) | — |
| `token_step` | request | `io_struct.py:1887` | "Trainer step id for rollout bookkeeping." (`:196`) | — |
| `num_paused_requests` | response | `io_struct.py:1898` | "Number of paused requests during update." (`:241`) | only the producer, which hardcodes `0` (`scheduler_components/weight_updater.py:152`) |

For the three request fields the only occurrences in the whole tree are the declarations themselves and the docs rows (checked with `git grep`; unrelated hits: `is_async` in the flash-attn copy utils / marlin templates / tracing, and the `token_steps` sampling field). `num_paused_requests` is plumbed all the way into the HTTP/gRPC response (`http_server.py:1252,1258`, `grpc_bridge.py:571`, `tokenizer_manager.py:2210,2274,2283`), so callers do receive the field — it just can never be non-zero. (In DP>1 it comes back as a per-rank list of zeros while the documented type is `int` — `tokenizer_manager.py:2283`.)

I could not find a version where these were consumed either: the same greps on `v0.5.12.post1` and `v0.4.9` show no readers in the scheduler/tokenizer files that would have to read them, and no in-tree code sends them. So this looks like long-standing documentation/API drift rather than a fresh break.

### Impact

RL clients that follow the guide will pass `keep_pause` / `is_async` / `token_step` and silently get behavior other than what is documented, and `num_paused_requests` cannot be used to tell "nothing was paused" from "the counter is not wired".

### Proposed fix — happy to send a PR for whichever direction you prefer

- **A. Remove** the three request fields and their docs rows, and drop `num_paused_requests` from the response/docs. The pause lifecycle is caller-driven now (`/pause_generation` + `/continue_generation`, plus the begin/end weight-update session), so the async/keep-pause semantics have no home; removal converts a silent no-op into a loud error for out-of-tree callers.
- **B. Keep them for wire compatibility** but document them as deprecated no-ops.
- **C. Re-wire them**, if there is a live plan — e.g. `token_step` next to `weight_version`, and `num_paused_requests` sourced from the existing scheduler counter (the `sglang:num_paused_reqs` gauge, `observability/metrics_collector.py:493`).
