items.title: [Windows/Zen2 CPU-only] MinGW build decode 5.4× slower than MSVC on qwen4exp (b11160), plus CPU tuning findings, negative results and questions
items.author: geer1895
items.body_excerpt:
Hello llama.cpp maintainers,

First of all, thank you for this wonderful project — it has become the backbone of our local inference setup.

We recently spent several weeks tuning CPU-only inference on a workstation, and collected a set of findings we'd like to share back. The first item looks like a genuine build-related bug and is the main reason for opening this issue; the rest are smaller findings, negative results (documented so others don't repeat them), and a few questions. Everything below is **measured on real hardware**, with raw JSON/logs available on request. If you prefer, we're happy to split this into separate issues — just let us know.

## Environment

- **CPU**: AMD Threadripper PRO 3975WX, 32C/64T, Zen 2, AVX2 only (no AVX-512)
- **RAM**: 128 GB DDR4-2667, 4 channels populated (measured ~46.6 GB/s)
- **GPU**: Quadro P2000, 5 GB, sm_61 — effectively unusable for this model; **all measurements below are pure CPU** (`-ngl 0 -dev none`)
- **OS**: Windows (Server-class)
- **Model**: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, architecture `qwen4exp`, UD-Q3_K_XL quant (83.79 GiB), 176.9B total / ~10B active params, 48 layers, 512 routed experts (10 active per token) + 640 shared, hybrid SSM (36 linear-attention layers + 12 full-attention layers), 256K context
- **Reference build**: `unslothai/llama.cpp` `b11160-mix-a6922cc`, `windows-x64-cuda12-legacy` variant (MSVC 19.44) — the only release build we found that still covers sm_61
- **Self-built**: official `ggml-org/llama.cpp` tag `b11160`, MinGW-w64 gcc 16.2.0 (w64devkit v2.10.0), CMake 4.4.3

Benchmark method: `llama-bench -p 512 -n 128 -r 3`, fixed `-lm none -lzm off -ngl 0 -dev none`. Key conclusions were repeated 2–3 times and sample values are reported.

---

## Finding 1 (main): MinGW-w64 build decode is 5.4× slower than MSVC

Same source tag, same model, same machine, same parameters:

| Build | Compiler | ISA | pp512 (tok/s) | tg128 (tok/s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| unsloth release | MSVC 19.44 | haswell | **55.86** | **6.83** |
| self-built A | MinGW gcc 16.2.0 | `-march=native` (znver2) | 52.60 | **1.27** |
| self-built B | MinGW gcc 16.2.0 | haswell (multi-variant build) | 51.08 | **1.28** |

What we ruled out:

- **Not ISA-related**: two builds with completely different ISA targets (znver2 vs haswell) both land at 1.27–1.28.
- **Not multithreading sync**: with the gcc build, single-thread decode is 1.56 and 20 threads is 1.27 — *slower* than single thread. So the per-thread kernel quality itself is bad, not the barriers.
- **Prefill is barely affected** (−5.8%), so the problem is specific to the decode path. Decode is single-token matvec traversing the MoE expert-gather path; prefill is large-batch matmul. Our guess is code-quality issues in the MoE gather / lazy-table access path under gcc (vectorization failure, aliasing assumptions, or the lazy gather table handling), but we could not pin it down to a specific code path.

Reproduction:

```bash
wget https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/archive/refs/tags/b11160.tar.gz
tar xzf b11160.tar.gz && cd llama.cpp-b11160

cmake -B build -G "MinGW Makefiles" \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DGGML_CUDA=OFF -DGGML_NATIVE=ON -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF -DLLAMA_BUILD_TESTS=OFF
cmake --build build --target llama-bench -j 32

./build/bin/llama-bench.exe -m <qwen3.8.gguf> -p 512 -n 128 -t 20 -r 3 \
  -lm none -lzm off -ngl 0 -dev none
# expected: pp512 ≈ 52 (normal), tg128 ≈ 1.3 (should be ~6.8)
```

Also reproduces with the multi-variant shared-library build (`GGML_CPU_ALL_VARIANTS=ON -DGGML_BACKEND_DL=ON -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON`); the log confirms the `ggml-cpu-haswell.dll` backend was actually loaded. Results were identical (tg128 ≈ 1.28).

Controls we did **not** get to, which might help localize the cause: `-DGGML_OPENMP=OFF` (rule out libgomp vs MSVC OpenMP), `-O2` vs `-O3`, clang/MinGW combinations, and — most valuable — testing a **non-MoE model** to see whether only the MoE/decode path is affected (we had no other model available locally).

Since MinGW/MSYS2 is a fairly common way to build llama.cpp on Windows, we think this is worth investigating. Any hints from someone experienced with MinGW builds would be appreciated — we're happy to run further experiments on this machine.

---

## Finding 2: `llama-bench` does not support `-tb` (`--threads-batch`) — and it hides the biggest prefill lever

`llama-bench` rejects `-tb` with `error: invalid parameter`, while `llama-server` accepts `--threads-batch`. On our machine this parameter is the single largest prefill win we found, measured on llama-server (short prompt 68 tok / long prompt 1012 tok):

| Config | prefill (short) | prefill (long) |
|---|---|---|
| `-t 16` | 28.79 | 41.50 |
| `-t 20` | 32.74 | 48.80 |
| `-t 20 -tb 24` | **35.46** | **54.46** |

(+23–31% vs the t16 baseline; +8–12% vs t20 alone.) The reason it matters: prefill is compute-bound and decode is bandwidth-bound, so their optimal thread counts differ (24 vs 20 here; both regress at 32 due to SMT contention on Zen 2). Since llama-bench is the recommended tool for exactly this kind of scan — and can test many configs within one model load — not being able to sweep `-tb` there means most users will never discover this parameter. Any chance it could be added, to align with llama-server/llama-cli?

---

## Finding 3: default `--spec-draft-p-min 0` is not optimal; 0.30 is +10% here

With MTP speculative decoding on the same server and prompts (`-t 20 -tb 24`):

| Config | decode (tok/s) | acceptance |
|---|---|---|
| `p-min 0` (default) | 8.12 | 46.9% |
| **`p-min 0.30`** | **8.94** | 54.9% |
| `p-min 0.50` | 8.69 | **62.1%** |
| `n-max 5` | 7.10 | 33.8% |
| ngram-mod only (no MTP) | 6.86 | 0% |

Interesting details: `p-min 0.50` gives the highest acceptance but is *slower* than 0.30 (it filters out drafts that would have been accepted); `n-max 5` collapses acceptance to 33.8%, which confirms the document

items.title: [Kernel] Optimize triton decoding kernels for long context
items.author: merrymercy
items.body_excerpt:
We noticed the current triton decoding kernel is very slow on long context. This is due to a missing flash decoding like optimization.

## Reproduce
We test the decoding speed with a context length of 200 and 2,000.

triton backend: The decoding speed drops from 147.64 token/s to 126.41 token/s
```
$ python3 -m sglang.bench_offline_throughput --model meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --dataset-name random --num-prompt 1 --random-input 128 --random-output 2048 --random-range 1 --attention-backend triton

[2024-11-30 05:10:04 TP0] Decode batch. #running-req: 1, #token: 234, token usage: 0.00, gen throughput (token/s): 147.64, #queue-req: 0
... 
[2024-11-30 05:10:18 TP0] Decode batch. #running-req: 1, #token: 2154, token usage: 0.00, gen throughput (token/s): 126.41, #queue-req: 0
```

flashinfer backend: The decoding speed only drops from 144.17 token/s to 143.35 token/s
```
$ python3 -m sglang.bench_offline_throughput --model meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --dataset-name random --num-prompt 1 --random-input 128 --random-output 2048 --random-range 1

[2024-11-30 05:11:40 TP0] Decode batch. #running-req: 1, #token: 234, token usage: 0.00, gen throughput (token/s): 144.17, #queue-req: 0
...
[2024-11-30 05:11:54 TP0] Decode batch. #running-req: 1, #token: 2154, token usage: 0.00, gen throughput (token/s): 143.35, #queue-req: 0
```

## Possible solutions
We can learn from the flash decoding triton kernel from lightllm and improve the [current triton decoding kernel](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/triton_ops/decode_attention.py). Related links:
- https://github.com/ModelTC/lightllm/blob/main/lightllm/models/llama/triton_kernel/gqa_flash_decoding.py
- https://pytorch.org/blog/flash-decoding/
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.01282

items.title: Refactor: TRTLLMHAAttnBackend should not inherit from FlashInferAttnBackend when reuse is small
items.author: merrymercy
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`TRTLLMHAAttnBackend(FlashInferAttnBackend)` (in `python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/trtllm_mha_backend.py`) inherits from `FlashInferAttnBackend`, but it reuses very little from the parent. Almost all attention-specific behavior is overridden, and some inherited setup is allocated-but-never-used. We should reconsider this inheritance: **if the reuse is small, we should not inherit from `FlashInferAttnBackend`** — inheriting directly from the base `AttentionBackend` (and pulling in only the small bits of plumbing that are actually shared) would be cleaner.

### What is actually reused

The only real reuse comes from `super().__init__(...)`:
- `req_to_token_pool`, `token_to_kv_pool`
- `max_context_len`, `skip_prefill`, `use_sliding_window_kv_pool`
- the `kv_indptr` / `kv_last_page_len` buffers (used by the companion `TRTLLMHAAttnMultiStepDraftBackend` draft steps)
- `forward()` dispatch — which actually comes from the base `AttentionBackend`, not from FlashInfer.

### What is overridden (not reused)

Essentially all the attention logic:
- `init_forward_metadata`, `init_cuda_graph_state`, `init_forward_metadata_out_graph`
- `forward_decode`, `forward_extend` (call `flashinfer.decode.trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache` / `flashinfer.prefill.trtllm_batch_context_with_kv_cache` directly)
- `get_cuda_graph_seq_len_fill_value`, `_resolve_swa_kv_pool`
- it uses its own `TRTLLMMHAMetadata` and its own page-table builder.

### Inherited-but-unused / redundant work

Because the TRTLLM kernels use a completely different API, part of the parent `__init__` is wasted:
- Parent builds `prefill_wrapper_ragged`, `prefill_wrappers_paged`, `decode_wrappers`, and the `FlashInferIndicesUpdater*` objects — TRTLLM-MHA never uses them.
- Parent sets `self.workspace_buffer` to the shared `global_workspace_buffer`, but the child **replaces** it with its own zero-init `global_zero_init_workspace_buffer`.
- `max_context_len` and `_swa_kv_pool` are set by the parent and then re-set by the child.

### Proposal

- Evaluate inheriting `TRTLLMHAAttnBackend` directly from `AttentionBackend` instead of `FlashInferAttnBackend`.
- Move the small amount of genuinely shared init plumbing into a thin shared helper/mixin (e.g. pool/buffer setup) rather than dragging in the full FlashInfer wrapper/indices-updater allocation.
- Avoid allocating FlashInfer wrappers and updaters that the TRTLLM path never uses.
- Apply the same review to `TRTLLMHAAttnMultiStepDraftBackend(FlashInferMultiStepDraftBackend)`.

As a general guideline: **do not inherit from `FlashInferAttnBackend` when the reuse is little** — prefer inheriting from the base `AttentionBackend` and sharing only what is actually common.

### Good first issue

This is a good first issue: it is well-scoped, localized to `trtllm_mha_backend.py` (plus the base classes), and mostly a refactor with clear before/after behavior to validate against existing tests.

items.title: [Bug] Interrupted Mooncake trace download is reused as a complete cache
items.author: unravel1020
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

When SGLang downloads a Mooncake JSONL trace and the streamed HTTP response raises an exception after one or more chunks have been written, the partially written destination file is left in place. On the next `MooncakeDataset.load()`, the file-existence check treats that path as an available dataset and skips the download. The benchmark then reads only the records present in the partial file (or fails while parsing a truncated final line) instead of retrying the download.

This report concerns a path written by a failed download. It does not ask SGLang to remove arbitrary pre-existing user-provided dataset files.

### Reproduction

The following CPU-only reproduction uses a temporary destination that does not exist before the first load. The mocked response yields one complete JSONL record and then raises a connection error while the body is being streamed:

```python
import os
import tempfile
from unittest.mock import patch

import requests
from sglang.benchmark.datasets.mooncake import MooncakeDataset


class InterruptedResponse:
    headers = {"content-length": "200"}

    def raise_for_status(self):
        pass

    def iter_content(self, chunk_size):
        yield b'{"timestamp": 1, "hash_ids": []}\n'
        raise requests.exceptions.ConnectionError("simulated interrupted transfer")


with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as temp_dir:
    path = os.path.join(temp_dir, "trace.jsonl")
    dataset = MooncakeDataset(path, "conversation", 10)

    with patch(
        "sglang.benchmark.utils.requests.get",
        return_value=InterruptedResponse(),
    ):
        try:
            dataset.load()
        except requests.exceptions.ConnectionError:
            pass
        else:
            raise AssertionError("the first load should raise ConnectionError")

    print("final path exists:", os.path.exists(path))
    print("rows returned by the next load:", len(dataset.load()))
```

Observed on the commit below:

```text
first load: raises ConnectionError
final path exists: True
rows returned by the next load: 1
```

The second load does not issue another HTTP request because the destination path exists.

### Expected behavior

After a streamed download fails, SGLang should not leave a final path that a later load treats as a complete downloaded dataset. A subsequent load should retry the failed download or report that the downloaded dataset is unavailable; it should not silently benchmark from the partial trace.

### Environment

- SGLang source: `main` at `41812afe432a54308be1c361a4d587952356f958`
- OS: Ubuntu on WSL2, Linux 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2 x86_64
- Python: 3.12.14
- PyTorch: 2.13.0+cpu; `torch.cuda.is_available() == False`
- No model, server, or GPU is needed for this reproduction.
- `PYTHONPATH=python python -m sglang.check_env` currently fails on this CPU-only environment with `NameError: name 'env' is not defined`; this is unrelated to the reproduction above.

items.title: [Bug]: Fast Start WeightCacheKey hashes only safetensors headers, so an ipc_cache engine can silently map another checkpoint's weights
items.author: nien-hui
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text vLLM Version : 0.30.1rc1.dev426+g863475eb9 (git sha: 863475eb9) PyTorch : 2.13.0+cu130 Python : 3.12.14 OS : Ubuntu 22.04.3 LTS (x86_64) GPU : NVIDIA RTX A6000 (driver 580.178.04) ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug #### Summary `hash_checkpoint()` builds the `checkpoint` field of `WeightCacheKey` from each shard's file name and safetensors header only ([`protocol.py#L239-L272`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/863475eb9cd78ae6a4a22f1b90df7fe85e0af438/vllm/model_executor/model_loader/weight_cache/protocol.py#L239-L272)). The header holds tensor names, dtypes, shapes and offsets, but no weight values. Two local checkpoints with the same architecture and file layout (a base model and its fine-tune, `step_0` and `step_100`) therefore get the same key. If a daemon preloaded from checkpoint A is still running and an engine starts on checkpoint B with `--load-format ipc_cache`, the daemon's check ([`daemon.py#L399-L403`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/863475eb9cd78ae6a4a22f1b90df7fe85e0af438/vllm/model_executor/model_loader/weight_cache/daemon.py#L399-L403)) finds no mismatched field and serves A's tensors. The engine never reads B from disk and logs no warning, while the CLI and the API `model` field both say B. The [docs](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/863475eb9cd78ae6a4a22f1b90df7fe85e0af438/docs/features/preload.md?plain=1#L21-L23) promise a "Safe fallback" when the daemon's cached weights don't match the engine, and say the fingerprint covers "checkpoint content". A user would therefore expect a daemon that still holds a different checkpoint to be rejected. #### Reproduction with `vllm preload` Make two checkpoints that differ only in weight values. `q` is `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`; `q_mod` is a copy with `model.norm.weight` zeroed and the safetensors header untouched. ```bash hf download Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --local-dir q cp -r q q_mod ``` ```python import json import struct with open("q_mod/model.safetensors", "r+b") as f: (n,) = struct.unpack("

items.title: MP mode: remaining unbounded request-state retention in vLLM client and sidecar prefetch bookkeeping
items.author: wuwanxu
items.body_excerpt:
## Deployment

We run a production **3P1D** deployment with vLLM and `LMCacheMPConnector`. Each serving node has a per-node LMCache sidecar; LMCache uses `fs_native` as the L2 adapter backed by local SSD. P2P, CacheBlend, and engine-driven transfer are not enabled.

The previous client-side MQ no-response leak is tracked separately in #5270. During a follow-up audit of upstream `dev` (checked at `05fc77a`, 2026-09-24), we found the two request-state retention paths below. This issue only reports the observed behavior and asks maintainers to determine the intended lifecycle and remediation.

## 1. vLLM client: `_returned_finished` grows for the worker lifetime

`LMCacheMPWorkerAdapter` creates:

```python
self._returned_finished: set[str] = set()
```

`_process_finished_stores()` uses this set to prevent a request ID from being reported repeatedly through `finished_sending`, then records returned IDs with:

```python
self._returned_finished.update(ret_stores)
```

We could not find a `discard`, `clear`, TTL, or capacity-based removal path. Therefore every request ID once returned as `finished_sending` remains resident until the vLLM worker exits. This path is exercised by normal successful requests as well as failure paths.

The set appears to be needed for async-scheduling deduplication after neighboring tracking sets are drained, but it also produces monotonic process-lifetime growth. With UUID-like Python request IDs, the retained footprint is roughly 150-200 bytes per request before allocator overhead; at sustained high QPS this can become material in a long-lived worker.

Relevant code:
- `lmcache/integration/vllm/vllm_multi_process_adapter.py` (`_returned_finished`, `_process_finished_stores`)

### Questions for maintainers

1. Is process-lifetime retention of every completed `finished_sending` request ID required by the vLLM connector contract?
2. What lifecycle or retention semantics should this deduplication state have in a long-running worker?

## 2. sidecar: abandoned prefetch jobs and completion Bitmaps are never reclaimed

`LookupModule` registers every lookup in:

```python
self._prefetch_jobs: dict[str, _PrefetchJob] = {}
```

The job is removed when `QUERY_PREFETCH_STATUS` or `WAIT_PREFETCH_STATUS` obtains a non-`None` completion result. If a client aborts or disconnects after LOOKUP, or stops polling after an RPC timeout/unhealthy transition, the job is not consumed by that path.

The corresponding `PrefetchController` completion state has the same consumer-driven ownership:

```python
self._completed_lookups: dict[PrefetchRequestId, int] = {}
self._completed_results: dict[PrefetchRequestId, Bitmap] = {}
```

`query_prefetch_result()` pops both the Bitmap and the lookup result. The source comment notes that failing to consume the prefetch result leaks memory. `Bitmap` is native/C++ memory, so its growth may not be visible in Python GC or tracemalloc. `END_SESSION` removes the session and touches L1 keys but does not remove the prefetch job or controller completion state.

In production we also see frequent `Session ... not found, skipping touch` warnings (roughly 378-953 over two hours), consistent with request-lifecycle skew and making normal client polling an unreliable sole ownership mechanism.

Relevant code:
- `lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/lookup.py` (`_prefetch_jobs`, `query_prefetch_status`, `end_session`)
- `lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py` (`_completed_lookups`, `_completed_results`, `query_prefetch_result`)

### Questions for maintainers

1. What is the intended owner of a prefetch job and its completion result after the original client has abandoned the request?
2. Is there an existing cancellation or reclamation lifecycle that this MP path should use?
3. What cleanup ordering is required for an in-flight prefetch so that late completion cannot expose invalid L1 data or retain completion state?

## Expected behavior

For healthy-sidecar and abort/error paths alike, client and server request bookkeeping should have a defined bounded lifecycle. Abandoned request state should be reclaimable without requiring a vLLM worker or sidecar restart, while preserving correctness for normal in-flight requests.

## Reproduction direction

1. Run vLLM + `LMCacheMPConnector` + sidecar with an SSD-backed `fs_native` L2.
2. Send sustained requests and observe the vLLM worker: `_returned_finished` grows monotonically.
3. Submit LOOKUPs, then abort/disconnect before prefetch polling completes, or induce a prefetch-status timeout.
4. Observe `lmcache_mp.active_prefetch_jobs` and `PrefetchController.report_status()["completed_results_count"]`; entries can remain after the client has abandoned the request.

comments.author: neevmodh
comments.body:
Read through both paths in `upstream/dev` to check the analysis — can confirm both observations.

**Part 1 (`_returned_finished`):** Confirmed there's no eviction path on this set anywhere in `vllm_multi_process_adapter.py`. Looking at `_process_finished_stores`, the set's only real job is to stop the same `req_id` from being re-added to `ret_stores` if `finished_req_ids_from_engine` reports it again in a later call — but once vLLM's own engine stops mentioning a `req_id` (i.e. it's fully retired from the engine's tracking), `_returned_finished`'s entry for it can never be hit again by the loop that checks it, so it's dead weight from that point on. A conservative fix that doesn't touch the dedup semantics: at the end of `_process_finished_stores`, intersect `_returned_finished` with the union of `self.finished_stores` / `self.store_futures` / `finished_req_ids_from_engine`, so an ID is only retained while it's still reachable through one of the sets that could re-report it. Happy to send that as a small PR if a maintainer confirms there's no other call site relying on longer retention.

**Part 2 (prefetch jobs):** Confirmed `end_session` (`lookup.py:514`) is already the natural per-request teardown hook — it's called on `MP_REQUEST_END` and already knows the `request_id`. Adding `self._prefetch_jobs.pop(request_id, None)` there looks safe on the `LookupModule` side. The harder part is `PrefetchController`'s `_completed_lookups`/`_completed_results` (a *different* class, presumably reachable through session/controller wiring I didn't fully trace) — and your question #3 is the real blocker here: popping a `Bitmap` out from under a prefetch that completes *after* the client has already been torn down risks exactly the late-completion/invalid-L1-data race you flagged, since it's native memory. I don't think this half should be fixed without a maintainer confirming the intended ownership handoff at session end — happy to implement once that's settled, but I'd rather not guess at a fix that touches native memory lifecycle across processes.

comments.author: neevmodh
comments.body: Following up on my earlier analysis: opened #5363 for part 1 (the `_returned_finished` set). Rather than guess at exact removal timing (which depends on the vLLM engine-contract question I couldn't answer myself), it bounds the set with a small LRU cap instead — converts unbounded growth into bounded memory without needing that question resolved first. Part 2 (sidecar prefetch/completion state) is intentionally left alone, per my earlier comment on the native-memory ordering risk.

items.title: OTel tracing overhead cliffs at c=50 on TP=2 deployments — level/flush tuning has no effect
items.author: wangxf1987
items.body_excerpt:
## Title

OTel trace overhead benchmark on a production-style K8s deployment (TP=2, 2 replicas): throughput loss of 20-33% at c>=50, trace level and flush threshold have negligible effect

## Summary

We benchmarked `--enable-trace` overhead on a production-shaped K8s deployment (RBG + LeaderWorkerSet, not docker-compose), Qwen3.6-27B-CHO on sglang v0.5.18, TP=2 per replica x 2 replicas (4 GPUs total, not an exclusive full node). This complements the larger-scale results already discussed elsewhere for TP=8 exclusive-node setups, and shows the overhead shape is very different at smaller TP.

Full report (charts + tables): attached PDF (`report-en.pdf`). Raw data (`result.csv`, GPU/CPU logs) available on request.

## Environment

- sglang `v0.5.18` (community image), `SGLANG_TRACE_ASYNC=1`
- Deployment: K8s RBG + LeaderWorkerSet, TP=2 per replica, 2 replicas, 4x H20 GPUs
- Trace path: sglang engine -> local OTel Agent (DaemonSet, node-local endpoint) -> Gateway -> backend, i.e. a two-hop agent-gw architecture, not a direct hardcoded Gateway connection
- 4 configs compared:
  | Group | trace level | async | flush threshold |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | G1 baseline | disabled | - | - |
  | G2 | 2 | 1 | default |
  | G3 | 3 | 1 | default |
  | G4 | 2 | 1 | 50 |
- Load generator: fixed-prompt benchmark client, concurrency swept across 1/10/50/100/200, 3 repeats per level (median)

## Findings

1. **Overhead is mild at low concurrency (c<=10)**: ttft_p99 +6~71%, throughput loss only 3~4%.
2. **c=50 is a clear inflection point**: ttft_p99 jumps 4.6x (172ms -> 965ms) going from G1 to G2 — roughly equivalent to the G1 baseline's own c=100 latency level being pulled forward to c=50. In other words, enabling trace shifts the whole latency-saturation curve left by one concurrency tier.
3. **From c>=50 onward, throughput loss is stable at 20~33%**, and grows with concurrency (-20.3% at c=50, up to -33.1% at c=200).
4. **Trace level 2 -> 3 produced no measurable incremental overhead** at c>=10 (all deltas within noise, ±2%).
5. **`SGLANG_TRACE_ASYNC_FLUSH_THRESHOLD=50` vs. default also produced no measurable benefit** at c>=50 (within ±16%, mostly ±2%; one anomalous +132.9% ttft_p99 spike at c=10 looked like a transient one-off, not reproduced at other levels).
6. **Root cause for (4) and (5): CPU was never the bottleneck in this setup.** Host CPU utilization on the GPU node stayed at 2~3% across all 4 groups (vs. GPU sm% rising from 14.8% baseline to 16~19% with trace enabled). Both trace-level and flush-threshold tuning target CPU-side span processing cost — with only 2 TP ranks, span volume is low enough that CPU headroom is never exhausted, so those knobs have nothing to bite on at this scale.
7. This is a **much smaller overhead** than what we see at TP=8 on an exclusive full node (throughput loss there was 75~79%, itl_p99 spiking ~28x, with CPU pegged at 99% — happy to share that data too if useful). The magnitude gap tracks roughly linearly with TP rank count, since span generation scales with the number of ranks, and the TP=8 test used synchronous export while this one used async by default.

## Why we're filing this

- The community advice we've seen elsewhere ("lower `SGLANG_TRACE_LEVEL` to reduce overhead", "tune the async flush threshold") holds at high TP / high CPU pressure, but **doesn't transfer to smaller TP configs** — those knobs are simply inert until CPU saturates. Worth calling out in docs/guidance so users at TP<=2-4 don't spend time tuning a lever with no effect.
- The **c=50 inflection point** (throughput loss going from ~4% to ~20% within one concurrency step) suggests there may be a queueing/lock-contention effect on the trace export path that kicks in once concurrent in-flight spans cross some threshold, rather than a smooth linear cost per request. Might be worth profiling `trace_async.py`'s buffer/flush path under concurrent load to see if there's a lock or queue that serializes once request volume rises (in our TP=8 investigation, we found `trace_req_finish()`/`abort()` and `__getstate__` all trigger unconditional flushes regardless of the configured threshold, and `trace_req_start()`'s `tracer.start_span()` + `propagate.inject()` calls are synchronous OTel API calls on the request path — happy to dig further if maintainers think that's a productive direction).
- Production guidance: for small/mid TP deployments (TP<=2-4), default trace config (level=2, async on) is fine as-is. For TP=8-class deployments, overhead is materially higher and level-tuning is the effective lever — but this should probably be stated explicitly since it's not obvious from the trace docs which regime a given deployment falls into.

## Attachments

- `report-en.pdf` — full benchmark report with charts (ttft_p99 / itl_p99 / e2e_p50 / throughput vs. concurrency, delta% overview, GPU/CPU resource usage)
[Uploading report-en.pdf…]()

items.title: [Bug] Potential hybrid GDN Radix-cache selected-logprob drift on repeated branch scoring
items.author: furedericca-lab
items.body_excerpt:
## Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues and did not find an existing report that fully covers this request shape.
- [ ] I have not re-run this on today's latest main; the reproduction was observed on pinned main commit `2f5c9ac43d76eef11e8561c89c55a79db7db715a` (2026-09-25).
- [x] Environment details and a standalone `/generate` reproducer are included below.
- [x] This is a possible correctness issue rather than a general usage question.
- [x] Report is in English.

## Describe the bug

With a hybrid GDN Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 checkpoint, repeated selected-token logprob scoring is stable when Radix Cache is disabled, but the first Radix-enabled branch scoring pass differs substantially from subsequent identical passes.

The observation is:

| Cache configuration | Max repeated selected-logprob delta | Pattern |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Unified Radix Cache enabled | `2.551527976989746` | run 1 differs; runs 2 and 3 match exactly |
| Radix Cache disabled | `0.0` | runs 1, 2 and 3 match exactly |

The prefix is explicitly warmed before the repeated branch batches. With Radix enabled, the server log reports `#cached-token: 0` for the first branch batch and `#cached-token: 128` for later identical branch batches. With Radix disabled, the three repeated branch batches are bit-stable.

This strongly correlates the drift with the cache-hit execution path, but I do **not** want to over-attribute the root cause: the current evidence does not prove that a specific GDN recurrent-state checkpoint, restore, split, or other hybrid-cache internal operation is responsible.

This was found while gating a decision workload that consumes candidate-token logprobs directly, so cache-hit equivalence matters even when the top-1 decision itself does not change.

Related work:

- #22935 — Mamba Radix cache prefix/split behavior
- #34899 — bit-exact correctness coverage for Unified Radix Cache
- #38625 — interior/no-buffer checkpoint work

I am not assuming that #22935 or #38625 has the same root cause or fully covers this request shape. In particular, I would like to know whether a shared prefix followed by divergent option branches is expected to preserve selected-token logprobs under deterministic inference when the later identical branch requests hit the hybrid cache.

## Environment

Tested environment:

- SGLang source: `2f5c9ac43d76eef11e8561c89c55a79db7db715a`
- SGLang package: `0.5.21.dev612+g2f5c9ac43`
- Model: `ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27b-NVFP4`
- Model revision: `332d277a083ca395aa2f822842b82f5f2f3913a2`
- Architecture: `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`, hybrid GDN / full attention
- Quantization: ModelOpt mixed FP8/NVFP4
- GPUs: 2 × NVIDIA RTX 5090 (SM120), TP=2
- NVIDIA driver: `610.57.04`
- Kernel: `7.0.0-34-generic`
- Python: `3.13.11`
- PyTorch: `2.14.0a0.post20260925` (CUDA 13.4)
- Triton: `3.7.0`
- `sglang-kernel==0.4.7`
- `flash-attn-4==4.0.0b19`
- Attention backend: Triton
- Deterministic inference: enabled
- Prefill CUDA Graph: disabled
- Decode CUDA Graph: retained
- Unified Radix Cache: enabled for the failing case
- Observed Mamba strategy: `extra_buffer`
- Comparison case: identical server settings plus only `--disable-radix-cache`

A literal `python3 -m sglang.check_env` dump was not retained for this run; the exact pinned runtime versions above are from the same project environment used for the reproduction.

## Reproduction

Launch the candidate server with Radix Cache enabled:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /path/to/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27b-NVFP4 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30001 \
  --trust-remote-code --tp-size 2 \
  --attention-backend triton \
  --enable-deterministic-inference \
  --disable-prefill-cuda-graph
```

Then run this standalone script. It does **not** import Reflex. It warms the exact shared prefix using native `/generate`, then submits the same two divergent branch items three times and compares the selected A/B/C token logprobs.

<details>
<summary>Standalone /generate reproducer</summary>

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
import json
import math
import urllib.request
from uuid import uuid4

SYSTEM_PROMPT = (
    "You are a System One decision model. You read the State and answer each Question "
    "by choosing exactly one of the listed options. You never explain. You answer with "
    "the single option label only."

items.title: [Bug] Hybrid-SWA + radix cache: admission livelock when the SWA prefix lock pins a finished request's untrimmed last chunk
items.author: bill-h-lin
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

With a hybrid-SWA model, the radix cache on and a tight SWA pool, the scheduler can stop admitting a request forever: 1 waiting, 0 running, GPU idle, no log line. We hit it on MiMo-V2.6-Flash (sliding window 128, page size 1) and traced it to `SWAComponent.acquire_component_lock` pinning a whole tree node that holds a finished request's untrimmed last chunk of SWA, instead of one window.

**Sequence** (`--chunked-prefill-size 8192`, `--swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.06448` → SWA pool 8,451, `--context-length 131072`, `--max-running-requests 1`, overlap scheduler on):

1. A 32,768-token request with `max_new_tokens=1` (it finishes at its first token).
2. A request with the same 32,768 tokens, a different next token, then 4,999 more (37,768 in all).

Request 2 matches 32,768 cached tokens, needs 5,001 SWA slots and never runs. `/v1/loads` stayed at 1 waiting, 0 running for 43 minutes. The same sequence runs fine with `--chunked-prefill-size 4096` or with a 16,643-token SWA pool.

### Root cause (line numbers on `main` @ 6624999385)

1. Under the overlap scheduler, a request that finishes at its first token still gets one decode step prepared before its prefill result is processed: `alloc_for_decode` (`allocation.py:587`) commits one more token, and `release_kv_cache` → `insert_req(req, up_to=req.owned_kv_len())` keys `(origin_input_ids + output_ids)[:kv_committed_len]`. So it is cached with 32,769 tokens, its output token included.
2. `cleanup_after_caching_req` (`swa.py:1011`, the `not is_finished` guard at `:1023`) frees out-of-window SWA only for unfinished requests. So the request's final 8,192-token chunk keeps its SWA live. In the tree that is a node `[24,576, 32,641)` holding 8,065 live SWA slots, then the 128-token window leaf that `_maybe_split_leaf_for_swa_lock` (`swa.py:555`) capped "so locking it pins only one window".
3. Request 2 diverges at position 32,768, so its match splits the window leaf into 127 + 1. `acquire_component_lock` (`swa.py:811`) pins whole nodes until it has covered 128 tokens: the 127-token node, then the whole 8,065-token parent. **8,192 slots pinned** for a 128-token window.
4. `SWAPrefillBudget.check_prefill` (`prefill_budget.py:213`) sees 5,001 needed and 259 available. Since 5,001 fits an empty pool, it is not a permanent shortfall ("Transient pressure waits"), so the request waits for running requests to free slots. None exist.

The bound: only an untrimmed final chunk holds more than about one window of live SWA, so the lock over-pins by at most one chunk, while a request needs at most one chunk + 1. A pool of 2 × chunk + window + slack therefore always leaves enough (by 258 slots here), and one of chunk + window + slack, as above, can deadlock whenever a request reuses the path of one that finished at its first token (`max_tokens=1`, an immediate EOS or stop) and diverges inside its last window.

### Reproduction

- End to end: on a GPU (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell) with SGLang at 542a043, reproduced with the sequence above. That build carries local changes (an MoE expert-offload tier, and #41263's chunked-prefill SWA free order); none of them changes the radix tree, the SWA lock or `check_prefill` (#41263 only moves when a chunked request's out-of-window SWA is freed).
- On CPU, on the same build: the same four steps, with the scheduler's own `UnifiedRadixCache`, SWA allocator and `PrefillAdder` plus the orphan decode step, give 259 / 5,001 available / needed (not admitted) at chunk 8,192 / pool 8,451, and admit at chunk 4,096 (4,355 / 4,097) and at pool 16,643 (8,451 / 5,001).
- On `main`: the unit test in the linked PR builds a live parent + capped window leaf, matches a key that diverges on the last page and locks it; the lock pins the whole parent. Links 1, 2 and 4 are unchanged in the code on `main`; we have not run the end-to-end sequence on `main`.

### Proposed fix

In the lock walk, split a live, unlocked device-SWA node that is longer than what the window still needs, so only the in-window tail is pinned (the same idea as the leaf cap, applied to whatever node the walk reaches). PR: #41580.

Related: #27210 caps compute locks by splitting the lock's endpoint node. It does not cover this case: at page size 1 the match ends inside the capped leaf, the endpoint is shorter than a window, and the over-pin comes from its parent. #32379 fixed a different SWA admission livelock (decode headroom double-counted for cached resumes).

### Environment

SGLang 542a043 (end to end) and `main` 6624999385 (unit test), CUDA 13.0, torch cu130, one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm120), `--tp-size 1`, radix cache on, overlap scheduler on.

items.title: [Bug] DeepSeek V4 Pro loading on Lustre takes 95 minutes despite prefetch; limiting tensor-copy workers reduces it to 3.3 minutes
items.author: janbernloehr
items.body_excerpt:
## Describe the bug

Loading a DeepSeek V4 Pro FP8/NVFP4 checkpoint from Lustre on one 8-GPU B300
node takes approximately 95 minutes inside SGLang's model-loading phase,
even with `--weight-loader-prefetch-checkpoints` enabled. Prefetch finishes
in approximately 62–73 seconds, while the longest wait for outstanding
per-tensor loader futures is approximately 94 minutes.

In one sequential A/B experiment on the same node and container image,
changing only the tensor-copy executor in
`DeepseekV4ForCausalLM.load_weights` from the Python default of 32 workers
per rank to two workers per rank reduced the reported model-loading time
from **5717.04 s to 199.72 s**. Startup through HTTP readiness fell from
**6115.90 s to 325.52 s**. Both arms completed and served benchmark requests.

This concerns the executor used for per-tensor weight-loader calls, which
is separate from the checkpoint-prefetch and shard-reader thread counts.
The two arms retained mmap, four prefetch threads per rank, the serial
shard iterator, TP=8, and the same server arguments. DP-attention was disabled.

## Related upstream reports

- [Issue #20842](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/20842) proposed
  coordinated checkpoint prefetch for network storage. This report covers
  a remaining slowdown with that prefetch path already enabled.
- [Issue #29268](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/29268) reports
  DeepSeek loading hangs on network storage with async mmap-to-CUDA copies.
  It was closed after a suggestion to enable prefetch; the issue has no
  linked closing PR. Our case adds evidence with prefetch already enabled
  and without DP-attention. Our baseline eventually completed, so we are
  reporting an extreme slowdown rather than proving a deadlock.
- [PR #37806](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37806), currently
  open, proposes automatically enabling prefetch on NFS/Lustre. Its stated
  scope leaves `should_async_load()` and executor width unchanged. Since
  prefetch was explicitly enabled in both of our arms, auto-enabling that
  flag alone would not change our configuration.
- [PR #29821](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/29821) explored
  synchronous DeepSeek V4 tensor loading for an AMD/HIP slow-tail case.
  It closed without merging. That is related evidence about copy
  concurrency, but a different backend and experiment.

At inspected upstream commit
[`e8fab85a02c23e01260fb1adb030b00886f5999d`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/e8fab85a02c23e01260fb1adb030b00886f5999d/python/sglang/srt/models/deepseek_v4.py#L5556),
the DeepSeek V4 loader still constructs `ThreadPoolExecutor()` without an
explicit worker limit. Its
[`should_async_load()` helper](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/e8fab85a02c23e01260fb1adb030b00886f5999d/python/sglang/srt/model_loader/utils.py#L295)
still selects ordinary CPU tensors for async loading. This is a source
inspection; the measurements below use the pinned version listed under
Tested revision, not a GPU reproduction on latest main.

## Measurements

One allocation, one node, default arm first and two-worker arm second:

| Measurement | Default: 32 copy workers/rank | 2 copy workers/rank |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Startup through HTTP readiness | 6115.90 s | 325.52 s |
| Native model-loading duration, maximum of 8 ranks | 5717.04 s | 199.72 s |
| Outstanding copy-futures wait, maximum of 8 ranks | 5632.56 s | 131.71 s |
| Prefetch completion duration, range across ranks | 62.04–73.11 s | 66.59–75.82 s |
| Major page faults during copy-futures wait, sum across 8 rank processes | 143,578,881 | 318 |
| MHC JIT compile duration, maximum of 8 ranks | 289.0 s | 2.1 s |
| MHC rank synchronization, maximum of 8 ranks | 3880.9 s | 41.6 s |

The model-loading timer includes nested phases; these rows must not be
added together. The futures-wait measurement starts after iterator
consumption, so it does not cover all work performed by the executor.
Per-rank phase durations and fault deltas came from begin/end instrumentation
and process resource counters, present in both arms.

During the slow arm, sampled thread wait channels included
`cl_sync_io_wait` and `folio_wait_bit_common`. Earlier-finishing ranks then
spent a long time in MHC rank synchronization. This points to the loading
and page-fault path as a useful target, rather than treating the barrier
wait alone as the cause. We did **not** capture native CUDA stacks proving
the driver-lock mechanism described in #29268.

For a limited serving smoke test, aggregate output throughput with 1000-token
input/output requests was:

| Concurrency | Default (output tokens/s) | 2 workers (output tokens/s) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 110.30 | 109.32 |
| 16 | 1244.75 | 1294.89 |
| 64 | 2976.88 | 3051.67 |
| 128 | 4847.49 | 4847.73 |

These are single observations, not statistical performance or accuracy results.

## Reproduction

Use a single node with eight B300 GPUs and the checkpoint on a Lustre mount.
The measured checkpoint was `nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813-NVFP4`, revision
prefix `a6ed51e`, with **66 safetensors shards totaling 941,115,855,096 bytes
(876.48 GiB)**. The checkpoint contains mixed FP8/NVFP4 weights and E8M0
scales. It was already downloaded before either arm.

Run the pinned SGLang revision below. The command below uses generic paths and ports and omits the site's
NUMA binding. Both measured arms used identical NUMA placement:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /path/on/lustre/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813-NVFP4 \
  --served-model-name deepseek-v4-pro-861b \
  --tp 8 --nnodes 1 --node-rank 0 \
  --dist-init-addr 127.0.0.1:29500 \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.79 \
  --context-length 2048 \
  --cuda-graph-max-bs-prefill 2048 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
  --enable-metrics \
  --weight-loader-prefetch-checkpoints \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000
```

For the second arm, stop all server processes and apply this one-line change
inside `DeepseekV4Fo

items.title: [Bug][KV Cache] nvfp4 KV silently reuses the checkpoint's fp8-calibrated k/v_scale as NVFP4 global scale → deterministic long-context corruption (single-variable proof, sm_120)
items.author: chengye75-star
items.body_excerpt:
## TL;DR

Serving an NVFP4 KV cache (`--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4`) on a checkpoint whose `quantization_config.kv_cache_scheme` says `num_bits: 8` (e.g. unsloth's NVFP4 quants, which ship fp8-calibrated `k_scale`/`v_scale`) silently corrupts the KV cache: 32 tiny `[1]` bf16 scalars are loaded verbatim and consumed as the NVFP4 **global scale**. Removing exactly those 64 **bytes** flips long-context needle from 1/4 to 4/4 on an otherwise bit-identical 22.5 GB checkpoint. No log line ever mentions scales. Related but distinct: [#36121](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/36121) (fp4 scales not traveling through HiCache host transfers; footnote has our hybrid-path measurement), [#39942](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/39942) (fp8 KV scales silently *dropped* — opposite failure, same blind spot: nothing validates KV scale provenance).

## Setup

SGLang 0.5.21 (official PyPI wheel), torch 2.13.0+cu130, 2× RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB (sm_120, TP2), driver 595.91.07. Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` (hybrid 16 full-attention + 48 GDN layers, head_dim 256, compressed-tensors). Flags: `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4 --prefill-attention-backend flashinfer --decode-attention-backend trtllm_mha --disable-prefill-cuda-graph --context-length 195000 --page-size 64`, greedy, chat format. (Same rig as my [#36010 evidence post](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/36010#issuecomment-5788493111); this bug is **independent of spec decode** — it hits the plain no-spec nvfp4 path.)

## Symptom

With scales as shipped, long-context retrieval collapses: needle **1/4 (d50) / 0/4 (d500)**; answers degenerate into question-echoing after a short thinking block. Everything else looks healthy — boot logs clean, short prompts / tool calls / vision normal. Deterministic: completion tokens reproduce byte-for-byte across boots and repeats.

## Root cause (source walk; mechanism marked as inference)

1. The checkpoint carries 32 per-layer `*.self_attn.{k,v}_scale` tensors — `[1]` bf16 scalars calibrated for **fp8** KV (`config.json → kv_cache_scheme: {num_bits: 8, static_minmax, symmetric}`).
2. *(inference, from source)* At load, `weight_utils.maybe_remap_kv_scale_name()` attaches them to the attention modules unconditionally; the fp4 path (`layers/attention/kvfp4_tensor.py`, comment: *"The KV cache path passes preloaded per-layer scales already on device"*) consumes them as the NVFP4 `global_scale` in `x_fp4 * block_scale * global_scale`.
3. *(inference)* Nothing validates the checkpoint's KV scheme against the runtime `--kv-cache-dtype`. An fp8-geometry scalar (amax/448 family) applied under NVFP4 geometry (amax/6 family) is off by ~75× → every stored K/V is systematically mis-scaled.

## Single-variable proof (same box, same day, same prompts)

| config (one variable per row) | needle d50 | needle d500 |
|---|---|---|
| unsloth + nvfp4, scales as shipped | 1/4 | 0/4 |
| **unsloth + nvfp4, 32 scale tensors stripped (64 bytes total), `kv_cache_scheme=null`** | **4/4** | **4/4** |
| unsloth + fp8_e4m3 (scale geometry matches dtype) | 4/4 | 2/4 |
| `sakamakismile/Qwen3.8-27B-MTP-NVFP4` + nvfp4 (checkpoint ships no scales) | 4/4 | 1/4 |

The stripped copy is a hardlink farm with only `model.safetensors` rewritten (header offsets recomputed; post-check: 0 leftover scale tensors) — the rest of the ~22.5 GB is byte-identical. Same-checkpoint before/after is the control: 64 bytes of metadata move the score by three needle questions.

## Why this is not an edge case

The filename pairing (`…-NVFP4` weights + `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4`) is the natural reading, and unsloth's NVFP4 releases ship fp8-calibrated KV scales as a matter of their recipe. Everyone doing that pairing gets silently wrong KV with zero log evidence; needle-style evals are the only thing that notices, and most people don't run those. Checkpoints without shipped scales (dynamic path, row 4) are unaffected — which is presumably why this hasn't surfaced loudly.

## Asks

1. **Validate at load**: if the checkpoint carries `k_scale`/`v_scale` and `kv_cache_scheme.num_bits` disagrees with `server_args.kv_cache_dtype`, warn loudly and skip them (fall back to dynamic scales) instead of reinterpreting an fp8 scalar as an fp4 global scale.
2. Checkpoints whose scheme says `num_bits: 4` (e.g. NVIDIA/ModelOpt NVFP4-KV exports) *should* consume their scales — the bug is specifically the mismatched pair, not scale loading per se.
3. Optional `--load-kv-scales {auto,never}` for quick A/B without safetensors surgery (our workaround rewrites a 22 GB file's header — works in 3 minutes, but terrifying to recommend).

## Verified workaround & production numbers

Drop the 32 `*.self_attn.[kv]_scale` tensors from `model.safetensors`, rewrite header offsets, set `quantization_config.kv_cache_scheme = null`. The healthy config now serves our production: 185K-token cold prefill ~176 s, decode ~25 tok/s; with HiCache L2 (20 GB host, `write_through`, `page_first`, slru) a post-eviction 185K re-ask lands in **2.4–5.5 s** (vs 178 s cold) with the secret code word intact across the L2 round-trip (2/2 rounds, backup counters confirm real transfers); needle 4/4+4/4; tool-calls live. sm_120 hybrid-attention reference points are thin here — happy to post logs/transcripts.

Footnote re #36121: its fail-fast covers paths our hybrid assembly doesn't traverse (UnifiedRadixCache picks host pools in `hybrid_pool_assembler`), and in our exact combo (nvfp4 + HiCache + page_first + write_through) the fp4 block scales evidently *do* survive L2 as measured above — so the guard as drafted wouldn't cover this configuration either way. Full hybrid-path measurements posted as a review note on that PR.

items.title: [Bug] Scheduler aborts with `double free or corruption` inside the idle-loop invariant check (`session_held_tokens` walk); server hangs permanently afterwards
items.author: LUOSENGWA
items.body_excerpt:
# [Bug] Scheduler aborts with `double free or corruption` inside the idle-loop invariant check (`session_held_tokens` walk); server hangs permanently afterwards

### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version. (occurred on `nightly-dev-20261003-65f75914`)
- [x] I included environment info and logs. (full crash dump + `server_args` below; a py-spy capture will be added if it recurs)
- [x] This is a bug report.

### Describe the bug

On a single-GPU production deployment (Qwen3.5-27B-FP8, hybrid Mamba/GDN, MTP/EAGLE, context 262144, fp8 KV), after ~22h of normal serving the **scheduler process aborted with a heap-corruption fatal** while running the idle-loop invariant check:

```
[2026-10-04 10:32:27] Decode batch, #running-req: 1, #full token: 102547, ... #queue-req: 0   <- last normal line
double free or corruption (out)
Fatal Python error: Aborted

Current thread (most recent call first):
  File ".../sglang/srt/session/streaming_session.py", line 424 in session_held_tokens
  File ".../sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py", line 3543 in session_held_tokens
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler_components/pool_stats_observer.py", line 184 in session_held_tokens
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler_components/invariant_checker.py", line 113 in _check_full_pool
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler_components/invariant_checker.py", line 507 in _check_all_pools
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 4969 in on_idle
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 2003 in event_loop_overlap
  ... run_scheduler_process ...
Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault
```

The abort happened between two normal decode batches, with no preceding error/warning (no OOM, no CUDA error, no assertion). Immediately afterwards the whole pipeline goes permanently silent:

- `/health` reports: `Health check failed. Server couldn't get a response from detokenizer for last 20 seconds. ... last_heartbeat time: 10:32:27` — i.e. the tokenizer manager never receives another downstream message from the exact crash moment on.
- `/v1/models` and `/metrics` keep answering 200 — with **frozen counters** (`num_running_reqs` 0, `num_requests_total` no longer increments).
- Every generation request (`/generate`, `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions`) accepts the connection, receives the request body, and then **never returns a single byte**.
- ~2 hours later the container still lists `sglang::scheduler` / `sglang::detokenizer` processes (the scheduler's cumulative CPU time stops growing, i.e. it is wedged in/after the abort path; nothing detects the dead engine and restarts it).
- Manual `docker restart` recovers in 1-2 min; normal serving resumes.

The crash stack is inside the idle housekeeping walk: `on_idle()` → `invariant_checker._check_all_pools()` → `_check_full_pool()` → `pool_stats_observer.session_held_tokens()` → `unified_radix_cache.session_held_tokens()` → `streaming_session.session_held_tokens()` (`session/streaming_session.py:424`, iterating session slots). `double free or corruption (out)` = glibc detected heap corruption, most plausibly from a free/ownership bug in the session/mamba/KV release paths that the idle walk happens to detect (the walk itself performs only reads plus allocations).

### Environment

- Image: `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-20261003-65f75914` (digest `sha256:035f29e91cfdf3b7d031c28be43ef7bddc93bb1f025e35c02c62ac732b8ba59b`)
- 1× RTX PRO 5000 72GB (SM120), driver/CUDA per image; model: Qwen3.5-27B FP8 (`config model_type=qwen3_5`), hybrid GDN-Mamba + builtin MTP draft (EAGLE).
- Key `server_args`: `context_length=262144`, `kv_cache_dtype=fp8_e4m3`, `mem_fraction_static=0.9`, `chunked_prefill_size=2048`, `max_running_requests=32` (capped to 10 by `max_mamba_cache_size=32`), `speculative_algorithm=EAGLE` (steps=3, topk=1, draft=4), `max_mamba_cache_size=32`, `mamba_ssm_dtype=bfloat16`, `mamba_radix_cache_strategy=extra_buffer_lazy`, `radix_eviction_policy=lru`, `enable_streaming_session=False`, `disable_overlap_schedule=False`, `attention_backend=flashinfer`, `mamba_backend=flashinfer`, `cuda_graph_config`: decode full ≤bs256 + prefill breakable, `page_size=1`, `tp=dp=ep=1`.
- Env vars: `SGLANG_OPT_MAMBA_SKIP_DECODE_LOCK=1`, `SGLANG_IMAGE_MAX_PIXELS=2007040`.
- Serving profile: 24 small agents, mixed short chats + longer (~100-140K token) sessions, sparse multimodal; uptime before crash ~22h24m.
- `SGLANG_ENABLE_STRICT_MEM_CHECK_DURING_IDLE` left at its default (True) — we WANT the idle checks; the problem is what they caught.

### Related issues (checked, not duplicates)

- #26482 / #22511 / #10856 / #11925 — the *post-crash symptom* (`couldn't get a response from detokenizer` + all requests hang). #26482 was auto-closed (stale) without a crash dump; #22511 is the open tracking thread (still reported reproducible under load as of 2026-09). **None of them contain the actual crash stack, which is what this report adds.**
- #36205 — gated the *tree-cache* sanity check (perf/livelock); our crash is in the *pool* check path (`_check_all_pools`), which still runs.
- #40250 / #40252 (merged ~2026-09-25) — session/mamba free-path fixes ("mamba -1 sentinel free", session reap); our build is AFTER them, so if this is the same family the fix looks incomplete.
- #41617 (open) — radix-cache free/ownership bug (`release_kv_cache` frees slots the radix still owns) — same "free ownership" family, different trigger (`--strip-thinking-cache`, which we do not use).
- #34676 (open) — hybrid-Mamba prefill allocation failure that *kills* the scheduler; ours is a *heap-corruption abort during idle check*, not an allocation failure, so it looks distinct.

### Questions

1. Does the crash stack (idle `_check_full_pool` → `session_held_tokens` walk hitting `double free`) suggest a known free/ownership bug in the session slot / unified radix cache paths?
2. Should a scheduler abort be detected and the engine

items.title: [Bug] Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: CUBLAS_STATUS_INTERNAL_ERROR / illegal memory access in GDN path with prefix caching on GB10 (sm_121); --no-async-scheduling does not help
items.author: brainatworkharris
items.body_excerpt:
## Your current environment

- **GPU:** NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark), compute capability **12.1 (sm_121)**, 119.63 GiB unified memory
- **Driver:** 580.173.02 · **Arch:** aarch64 · **OS:** Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
- **vLLM:** `0.1.dev20073+g8e685d198` (the `release/qwen38next` recipe branch, PR #53896)
- **Image:** `vllm/vllm-openai:qwen38-flash-next@sha256:fc120ece0a388cc0aa1caad4a9f1cd92113484ab7ec2fd0efadd62585be05bf8`
- **Model:** `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`, revision `7b719225242aacd3dbd3f9407468c2ee9a9d2594` (ModelOpt NVFP4, experts-only)
- **Quant/kernels as selected at boot:** `quantization=modelopt_fp4`; NVFP4 MoE backend `FLASHINFER_CUTLASS`; GDN prefill `Triton/FLA`, GDN decode kernel `cuda`; attention backend `QWEN38_FLASH_NEXT_EXP_QSA_STATE`; `cudagraph_mode=PIECEWISE`

## Describe the bug

With `--enable-prefix-caching`, the engine dies with `CUBLAS_STATUS_INTERNAL_ERROR` followed by an
illegal memory access, in the model's own `forward`. It is reproducible and it is **not** triggered
by repeating a prompt — it is triggered by **prompts of differing lengths that share a prefix**,
i.e. a growing multi-turn conversation.

```
RuntimeError: CUDA error: CUBLAS_STATUS_INTERNAL_ERROR when calling `cublasGemmEx( handle, opa,
  opb, m, n, k, &falpha, a, CUDA_R_16BF, lda, b, CUDA_R_16BF, ldb, &fbeta, c,
  std::is_same_v<C_Dtype, float> ? CUDA_R_32F : CUDA_R_16BF, ldc, compute_type,
  CUBLAS_GEMM_DEFAULT_TENSOR_OP)`
torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered
vllm.v1.engine.exceptions.EngineDeadError

  File ".../vllm/models/qwen3_8_flash_next/nvidia/model.py", line 464, in forward
  File ".../vllm/models/qwen3_8_flash_next/nvidia/model.py", line 980, in forward
  File ".../vllm/compilation/piecewise_backend.py", line 380, in __call__
  File ".../vllm/compilation/cuda_graph.py", line 254, in __call__
```

### Three configurations tested — all fail identically

| `--mamba-cache-mode` | async scheduling | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `align` | default (on) | crash, `model.py:464` |
| `all` | default (on) | crash, `model.py:464` |
| `all` | **`--no-async-scheduling`** | **crash, `model.py:464`** |

`--no-enable-prefix-caching` never faults. That is the only working configuration we have found,
and it costs a full re-prefill of the entire history on every turn (23.5 s at 55K tokens).

### The trigger is NOT a repeated identical prompt

This matters because it is easy to miss. Under `--mamba-cache-mode all`:

- **Nine consecutive byte-identical ~50K-token prompts run clean**, with the cache hitting and
  TTFT collapsing from **24.38 s → 1.40 s (17.3×)**. No error.
- A sequence of prompts at **differing** lengths over the same prefix dies within a handful of
  requests — reproducibly, in every configuration above.

A benchmark that replays one fixed prompt will therefore report a large prefix-caching win and
never surface this. The failing access pattern is specifically "cache-hit resume where the new
request extends a cached prefix".

### Quality is unaffected right up to the crash

Deep-context accuracy with caching ON matches the caching-OFF baseline exactly — **12/12 synthesis
and 6/6 retrieval at ~64.7K prompt tokens, 0 errors** — on the same seed and items. So the cached
*values* are being computed and reused correctly. The fault appears to be in **state handling
across differing prefix lengths**, not in numerical corruption of the cache.

## Relationship to #50021

PR #50021 ("Bound accepted-token state lookups in GDN/KDA spec decode", open) describes a related
GDN + spec-decode + prefix-caching fault, and notes that
`gpu_model_runner` skips `num_accepted_tokens_event.synchronize()` when
`use_async_scheduling and mamba_cache_mode != "align"` — confirmed present in this build at
`v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py:2229`.

A third-party A/B in that thread (2× RTX 3090, sm_86) reports `--no-async-scheduling` resolving the
crash. **On GB10 / sm_121 it does not.** We verified the flag was actually in effect on the crashing
process (`docker inspect` shows `--no-async-scheduling` on the argv) rather than assuming it, and
the crash is unchanged in error, frame, and trigger.

We also confirmed async scheduling *was* implicitly on in our earlier runs — it is never logged, so
we traced `config/vllm.py` and found our lane falls through every auto-disable clause
(`UniProcExecutor.supports_async_scheduling() → True`; `mtp ∈ EagleModelTypes`) to
`async_scheduling = True`. So the sync-skip mechanism was genuinely active in the failing runs, and
closing it was not sufficient.

## Steps to reproduce

```bash
vllm serve RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 \
  --max-model-len 262144 --max-num-seqs 8 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.80 \
  --enable-prefix-caching --mamba-cache-mode all \
  --enable-chunked-prefill --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --kv-cache-dtype auto --no-enable-flashinfer-autotune \
  -cc.cudagraph_mode=PIECEWISE \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":2}'
```

Then issue chat completions whose message history shares a prefix but **grows** — e.g. a fixed
~40K-token conversation, then the same conversation plus one turn, then plus another. The engine
dies within roughly 5-10 such requests. Repeating a single fixed prompt will *not* reproduce it.

## Caveat: non-stock image (single-Spark PLE offload patch)

**Our image is not stock.** It carries a third-party patch
([blazux/qwen3.8-Flash-DGX](https://github.com/blazux/qwen3.8-Flash-DGX)) that serves the 47.7 GiB
n-gram (PLE) table from NVMe via `mmap` instead of keeping it resident — without it the 126 GiB
checkpoint does not fit a single 119.63 GiB Spark. The patch replaces
`Qwen3_8FlashNextNGramEmbedding` with an mmap-backed placeholder and registers a custom op
`vllm::ple_mmap_lookup` as a splitting op.

The crash is in the GDN attention path, not the PLE path, and the patch is a no-op when
`VLLM_PLE_MMAP` is unset — but **we have not reproduced this on an unpatched image**, and we cannot
on

items.title: [RFC]: Bound frontend drain latency for bulk aborts and long non-streaming completions
items.author: aoshen02
items.body_excerpt:
# Motivation.

Bulk abort is expected to be the fast path for pausing online RL generation,
but its latency can scale with all output retained by the frontend. In a
DP8/EP8/TP1 deployment with eight API server processes, aborting 2,000
non-streaming completion requests at a reported approximately 3,500 generated
tokens per request produced 96-177 seconds of frontend tail latency. Actual
returned means were 4,850-5,445 tokens because generation continued while the
frontend lagged. The engines had already accepted the abort; API processes
were still draining queued outputs,
detokenizing sampled logprobs, constructing response models, materializing
Python dictionaries, and encoding JSON.

The largest amplifier was API-process load imbalance. The parent enabled
`SO_REUSEPORT`, but all workers inherited copies of one socket and therefore
shared one accept queue. In one run, the busiest API process owned 1,492 of
2,000 requests. Balanced DP-engine load did not imply balanced frontend load.

This matters beyond RL pause. The same work appears when long non-streaming
completion requests finish or are aborted together, especially when sampled
logprobs or token IDs are returned. A fast model can produce outputs faster
than one Python frontend process can consume and serialize them.

This RFC follows the completed pause/resume API RFC #32103, whose follow-up
list explicitly called out better abort handling. It does not change pause
mode semantics or DPEP coordination. At RFC creation, searches of issues and open PRs using
pause/abort, frontend serialization, logprobs, API server, and reuseport terms
found no overlapping proposal or implementation. Related work is
complementary:

- #56754 drains in-process requests before sleep.
- #52875 reduces per-frame cost for simple streaming completions.
- #47933 preserves `finish_reason="abort"` for scale-out token streams.

## Reproduction and evidence

The primary setup used two GB200 nodes, DP8/EP8/TP1, eight API servers, 2,000
requests, and sampled `logprobs=0`. A four-layer checkpoint made the frontend
bottleneck easy to reproduce; the final candidate was also validated with the
full 78-layer MXFP8 checkpoint.

On the reduced model, the unmodified frontend took 96.18 and 177.12 seconds
from pause to its last response serialization in two runs. The measured
seven-file candidate took 3.38 seconds at 7.28 million returned tokens, and
5.18 seconds at 10.08 million returned tokens versus 96.18 seconds at 10.89
million unmodified. The six-file patch proposed here differs only by removal
of a null-result lazy-context change and was itself measured as the valid
2.924-second `no_lazy_context` leave-one-out arm.

On the full model, one unmodified baseline was 6.97 seconds frontend and 7.44
seconds through all client results, with a balanced 187-270 requests per
frontend. Four additional unmodified runs using a two-process client that
concentrated connections on fewer workers reached 8.92-21.10-second frontend
tails, with 462-907 requests on the busiest process. Two used the 3,500-token
trigger and two used 3,800. They have no patched counterpart and are baseline
evidence, not an A/B comparison.

Two seven-file-candidate repeats completed frontend serialization in 3.63 and
3.90 seconds and all client parsing in 3.81 and 4.19 seconds; waiting for both
the pause HTTP response and all client results took 3.81 and 7.67 seconds. This
validates parity and absence of regression at full scale. It does not reproduce
the reduced model's 100+ second tail in a matched A/B or isolate the listener
change. GPU response parity was also captured on this measured seven-file
candidate; equivalence to the shipped six-file state rests on hash identity
with the measured `no_lazy_context` arm rather than a separate post-trim GPU
capture.

We then ran an eight-arm, same-allocation leave-one-out experiment. Every arm
aborted and rendered exactly 2,000 responses. The complete candidate was
bracketed at 2.953 and 3.054 seconds, giving a 0.102-second drift bound.

| Removed optimization | Frontend-tail regression |
| --- | ---: |
| Independent `SO_REUSEPORT` listener per API worker | +6.199 s |
| Bounded single-token decode cache | +1.075 s |
| Flat sampled-logprob storage | +1.039 s |
| Direct Pydantic JSON serialization | +1.176 s |
| Explicit event-loop yields | +0.125 s |
| Lazy byte-fallback context lookup | -0.080 s |

The first four effects are 10-61 times the measured run drift. The lazy
context change was removed. Event-loop yields are retained for a deterministic
fairness invariant: without them, a ready output queue can consume 100 batches
before a waiting control task runs. Leave-one-out effects interact and must
not be summed to reconstruct the original 100+ second result.

The listener result is one stochastic draw for a client opening approximately
2,000 connections. Its +6.199-second effect is not a general point estimate;
keep-alive-heavy clients can see a different distribution or no benefit.

## Implementation update — 2026-09-23

Phase 1 is proposed in **#58278: [Frontend] Give API workers independent reuseport listeners** (draft, not merged). The narrowed implementation changes only listener selection and per-worker socket ownership. General CLI startup/shutdown behavior stays identical to the base; lifecycle refactoring is deferred. The following GPU measurements belong to historical head `377818881b`, not the current revision.

A prior **listener-only** GPU/HTTP ABBA experiment completed on node18 using one node with four GB200s, four-layer HY4-preview BF16, DP4/EP4/TP1, four default API processes, 250 requests per replica (1,000 total), non-streaming completions and sampled `logprobs=0`.

| Metric | Shared listener (A, two runs) | Independent listeners (B, two runs) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Last frontend serialization | 8.298 / 10.698 s | 4.551 / 4.746 s |
| Median frontend serialization tail | 9.498 s | 4.649 s (51.1% lower) |
| Last client response body received | 9

items.title: [Bug]: Illegal memory access (Xid 13) with SimpleCPUOffloadConnector on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next while an async CPU→GPU prefix load is in flight / sm120
items.author: maaaax
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

docker

### 🐛 Describe the bug

[vllm_tb.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32956928/vllm_tb.txt)

SimpleCPUOffloadConnector on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next while an async CPU→GPU prefix load is in flight

**Environment**
- Image `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly-e9757321527ca1ecd514c07c1418dd2c53da3d19` (`0.29.1rc1.dev573+ge97573215`, includes #56810), Model Runner V2
- 1× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120, 96 GB), PCIe Gen3, driver 615.71.09
- Model: `Inferact/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`, TP1

**Config**
```
env:
  VLLM_PLE_CPU_OFFLOAD=1
  TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.0f
  PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True

vllm serve Inferact/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4
  --max-model-len 262144 --tensor-parallel-size 1 --distributed-executor-backend mp
  --max-num-seqs 12 --max-num-batched-tokens 4096
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --kv-cache-memory=15679970304
  --enable-prefix-caching --no-enable-flashinfer-autotune
  --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}'
  --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml --reasoning-parser qwen3
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"SimpleCPUOffloadConnector","kv_role":"kv_both",
    "kv_connector_extra_config":{"cpu_bytes_to_use":68719476736,"lazy_offload":true}}'
```

Workload: agentic, 4–8 concurrent long-context requests (80k–185k tokens each), GPU KV pool 880,600 tokens, CPU tier 64 GiB (1518 blocks of 3200 tokens).

**Symptom**
The engine dies with:
```
torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered
  at vllm/v1/worker/gpu/async_utils.py:170 get_output -> self.copy_event.synchronize()
```
Kernel log at the same time:
```
NVRM: Xid 13, Graphics SM Warp Exception on (GPC 2, TPC 0, SM 0): Out Of Range Address
NVRM: Xid 13, Graphics SM Global Exception on (GPC 2, TPC 0, SM 0): Multiple Warp Errors
NVRM: Xid 43, pid=..., name=VLLM::Worker, channel 0x00000004
```

All crashes show the identical fault signature in dmesg: always GPC 2, TPC 0, SM 0, and byte-identical ESR values (`0x525730=0x101000e 0x525734=0x24 0x525728=0x1c81fb60 0x52572c=0x1174`) — i.e. the same instruction faulting deterministically. Always SM 0 suggests a single-CTA kernel (e.g. metadata/block-table preparation) rather than a large attention/MoE kernel.

Apart from that, offload works well: external prefix cache hit rate 80–90%, no output corruption observed, throughput roughly doubled compared to running without offload.

**Common signature across all 5 dumps** (from `dump_input.py`):

| UTC | kv_cache_usage | running / waiting / skipped_waiting | req with num_output_tokens=1 | connector_prefix_cache_stats hits / queries (GPU prefix hits = 0) | store in step |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 09-27 18:34 | 0.979 | 5 / 1 / 1 | yes | 96000 / 107026 | yes |
| 09-27 19:21 | 0.918 | 5 / 0 / 1 | yes | 73600 / 81165 | no |
| 09-30 11:50 | 0.944 | 4 / 0 / 1 | yes | 124800 / 132176 | no |
| 10-02 09:08 | 0.973 | 5 / 2 / 1 | yes | 118400 / 124640 | no |
| 10-02 10:25 | 0.962 | 6 / 1 / 1 | yes | 140800 / 148333 | no |

The server was idle between these sessions; under sustained load (4–8 concurrent long-context requests) the crash recurs roughly every 45–80 minutes (e.g. 18:34 → 19:21 and 09:08 → 10:25 UTC), so it reproduces quickly.

In every case:
- exactly one waiting request is skipped (`num_skipped_waiting_reqs=1`, shown as `Deferred: 1 reqs` in the stats log), i.e. an async CPU→GPU load of a 74k–141k-token prefix is in flight;
- the batch contains a request in its first decode step after prefill (`num_output_tokens=1`), with MTP (4 tokens scheduled per request);
- the KV pool is at 92–98%;
- the step's own `kv_connector_metadata` has `load_event=-1` (the load was issued in an earlier step);
- a concurrent GPU→CPU store is present in only 1 of 5 cases, so the store path seems uninvolved.

Example scheduler output (10-02 10:25):
```
num_computed_tokens=[131090, 140280, 125803, 1553, 836, 119148]
num_output_tokens=[1974, 1099, 628, 16, 11, 1]
total_num_scheduled_tokens=24
kv_connector_metadata=SimpleCPUOffloadMetadata(load_event=-1, load_gpu_blocks=[], load_cpu_blocks=[], load_event_to_reqs={}, store_event=-1, store_gpu_blocks=[], store_cpu_blocks=[], need_flush=false)
SchedulerStats(num_running_reqs=6, num_waiting_reqs=1, num_skipped_waiting_reqs=1, kv_cache_usage=0.9623, prefix_cache_stats=PrefixCacheStats(queries=148333, hits=0), connector_prefix_cache_stats=PrefixCacheStats(queries=148333, hits=140800))
```

**Hypothesis**
A race between the in-flight async load (possibly involving the non-prefix-cacheable QSA ring group, block size 8, or the GDN state of the loading request) and block reallocation for the running batch under high KV pressure. kv cache group sizes in this setup: `[3200, 3200, 3200, 3200, 8, 3200]`.

For reference: #56810 / #55033 were validated end-to-end only up to 24k tokens (GLM-5.3-Flash), with scheduler-level tests for the QSA ring; this setup is single-GPU SM120 with fp8 KV, MTP3 and 74k–185k-token restores.

**Possibly related**
- #53863 / #53860 — out-of-bounds `attrIdxs` in `cuMemcpyBatchAsync` (also in `vllm/v1/simple_kv_offload/cuda_mem_ops.py`); our restores are 74k–141k tokens, i.e. thousands of descriptors per load. Note though that the fault here is an SM exception (Xid 13), not a copy-engine MMU fault.
- #53505 — hybrid Mamba (align) + spec decode + KV connector corruption (closed); same combination of features as here.
- #51771 — MTP block drop + prefix caching untested for hybrid models with ≥3 attention groups (this model has 6 KV cache groups).

Full logs with all 5 dumps attached.
(docker-compose logs |grep -v GET |grep -v POST |grep -B50 -A500 Traceback)

---
*This report was prepared with AI assistance (Claude): the dumps were collected from my production instance, and the analysis and write-up were done together with Claude. I reviewed the content before submitting.*

items.title: [Bug]: FlashInfer with LHBNC on A100 asserts at startup
items.author: hyunnnchoi
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

vLLM 0.30.0 (ced6857), torch 2.13.0+cu129, flashinfer-python 0.6.18.post1, NVIDIA A100 80GB PCIe, driver 575.51.03. The code below is unchanged on main (1388100).

### 🐛 Describe the bug

On GPUs other than SM100, `FlashInferBackend.supported_kv_cache_layouts()` returns `None` ("any layout"), so layout resolution accepts LHBNC:

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/138810056093301f4881050fcf2b1786939da387/vllm/v1/attention/backends/flashinfer.py#L547-L553

FlashInfer only addresses NHD/HND pages, and `get_flashinfer_layout_string` has no LHBNC entry. Its assert message assumes the backend already rejected LHBNC:

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/138810056093301f4881050fcf2b1786939da387/vllm/v1/attention/backends/utils.py#L175-L190

Repro on A100:

```bash
VLLM_KV_CACHE_LAYOUT=LHBNC vllm serve meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct \
  --attention-backend FLASHINFER --enforce-eager
```

```text
INFO [utils.py:320] Using LHBNC KV cache layout.
ERROR [core.py:1366] AssertionError: KV cache layout LHBNC has no FlashInfer equivalent; FlashInfer rejects it in supported_kv_cache_layouts
```

Expected: resolution rejects LHBNC up front with the list of valid layouts, as it does for backends that declare their set. The other five layouts run fine with FlashInfer on A100. I have a small fix (declare those five on non-SM100) and will open a PR.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.
