items.title: Loop-carry detection skips `prev = cur` when both start as the same value, silently keeping the pre-loop value instead of carrying it
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


**TL;DR.** `CodeGenerator._find_carries` decides which variables of a `for` or `while` loop become `iter_args` by comparing IR values after one dry run of the body, instead of asking whether a value can differ between iterations. If `prev` and `cur` are the same IR value before the loop and the loop runs `prev = cur`, `prev` looks unchanged and is not carried, so it keeps its pre-loop value in every iteration and after the loop. Regression from #7200, first in 3.5.0 (3.4.0 is right). Possible fix: also carry every name that is assigned in the loop (as 3.4.0 did), or only those that share their initial IR value with another name.

**Why one dry run misses it.** `_find_carries` ([L485-L524](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L485-L524), the comparison is [L513](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L513)) runs the body once with every name bound to its pre-loop value. When `prev = cur` runs there, `cur` is still at its pre-loop value, so `prev` is bound to the value it already had. In the real body `cur` is a block argument, so `prev = cur` is a different value in every iteration. Seeing that takes a second pass that already knows `cur` is carried.

The smallest example. `prev` is `cur`'s value at the start of each iteration; `SAME=False` is the control, where `prev` is equal to `cur` but a different IR value:

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(out_ptr, n, SAME: tl.constexpr):
    cur = 0
    if SAME:
        prev = cur          # prev and cur are the same IR value
    else:
        prev = cur + 0      # control: equal to cur, but a different IR value
    for i in range(n):
        prev = cur          # prev is cur's value at the start of the iteration
        cur = cur + 1
    tl.store(out_ptr, prev)      # expected n - 1
    tl.store(out_ptr + 1, cur)   # expected n


n = 5
for same in (True, False):
    out = torch.zeros(2, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
    k = kernel[(1, )](out, n, same)
    print(f"SAME={same!s:5} prev, cur = {out.tolist()}, expected {[n - 1, n]}")
    print("   ", [l.strip() for l in k.asm["ttir"].splitlines() if "scf.for" in l][0].split(" : ")[0])
```
```
SAME=True  prev, cur = [0, 5], expected [4, 5]
    %cur = scf.for %i = %c0_i32 to %n step %c1_i32 iter_args(%cur_0 = %c0_i32) -> (i32)
SAME=False prev, cur = [4, 5], expected [4, 5]
    %prev:2 = scf.for %i = %c0_i32 to %n step %c1_i32 iter_args(%cur = %c0_i32, %prev_0 = %c0_i32) -> (i32, i32)
```
With `SAME=True` only `cur` is an `iter_arg`. 3.4.0 has two `iter_args` in both cases and returns `[4, 5]`. Without an `iter_arg`, `prev` is still bound to its pre-loop value when the body starts, and `enter_sub_region` restores that binding when the loop ends ([L146](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L146)).

**Why since 3.5.0.** Up to 3.4.0 every name that is assigned in the loop and live before it was carried ([visit_For](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/d4432f6b89ef554007a53ef90f2499d90792d7e7/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L1114-L1115), [visit_While](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/d4432f6b89ef554007a53ef90f2499d90792d7e7/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L1153-L1154)). #7200 (2025-06-23, "Improve detection of loop carries", for builtins that modify their arguments) replaced that with the comparison of IR values; v3.5.0 is the first tag that contains it. The existing tests for shared initial values (`test_loop_carry_shared_initial_value` and its while and tuple variants in test_frontend.py, #11369) update the aliased variables independently (`a = a + 1`, `b = b + 2`), so none has a copy between them.

**Possible fix.** Two variants, both tested as source patches on main @6fe3348e6.

Carry every name that is assigned in the loop, as 3.4.0 did, and keep the comparison:
```diff
--- a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py
+++ b/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py
@@ -493,6 +493,9 @@ class CodeGenerator(ast.NodeVisitor):
         self.scf_stack.pop()
         block.erase()
 
+        # A name that is assigned in the loop may have copied another one, which an unchanged handle doesn't show.
+        assigned = {n.id for n in ast.walk(node) if isinstance(n, ast.Name) and isinstance(n.ctx, ast.Store)}
+
         # If a variable (name) has changed value within the loop, then it's
         # a loop-carried variable. (The new and old value must be of the
         # same type)
@@ -510,7 +513,7 @@ class CodeGenerator(ast.NodeVisitor):
 
                 live_handles = flatten_values_to_ir([live_val])
                 loop_handles = flatten_values_to_ir([loop_val])
-                if live_handles != loop_handles:
+                if name in assigned or live_handles != loop_handles:
                     names.append(name)
                     init_tys.append(live_val.type)
                     init_handles.extend(live_handles)
```
The comparison was added by #7200 for builtins that modify their arguments in place. #8832 (2025-11-25) removed that case ("now that we ban mutations") together with its tests, attribute and item assignment raise, and aggregates cannot be assigned to after construction, so a name whose IR value changes is a name that is assigned. In test_frontend.py and the Gluon frontend tests, 57 of the 181 (name, loop) pairs that `_find_carries` looked at had a changed IR value, and all 57 are assigned in the loop. The set of assigned names comes from the AST, so it does not depend on what the dry run did; that also covers a branch that only the lowering takes (see below). items.title: Upgrade to Transformers v5
items.author: hmellor
items.body_excerpt:
## What is this issue?

This issue serves as a living tracker for the current issues preventing us from upgrading vLLM to Transformers v5.

We will use sub-issues to track individual failures and PRs should be made against these sub-issues.

The solutions to these issues may need to be applied to either:

- Transformers in the form of:
  - Adding missing backward compatibility (usually for custom code models)
  - General bug fixes/improvements to new features of v5
- vLLM in the form of:
  - Forward compatibility with how something is now done in v5
  - Edge case handling for issues that v4 ignored (such as config validation)

Sometimes, the issue is simply with the model checkpoint itself, for example if it:

- Contains a malformed `config.json` that cannot be used to instantiate the newly input validated `PreTrainedConfig` class
- Custom code* uses deprecated/removed APIs

In these situations, the best solution will likely be to skip these tests in vLLM and open a PR to Transformers to contribute this model. This will be faster and more sustainable than waiting for the model vendor to fix their custom model code, sometimes they nevert do.

Contributing the new model should be done using the new [Modular Transformers](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/modular_transformers) so that the implementation is easy to maintain and will remain maintained by the Transformers team.

_*particularly in the parts of the model implementation that vLLM tries to directly reuse, such as config/tokenizer/multimodal processor_

## Triage: this is an intermittent GPU hang, not a slow test

@yyihuang: the hang is in the Cake small-M head-dim-256 decode kernel added by #5369, `kernel_cake_fmha_decode_native_bf16_hd256_smallm_n64_p64`. It needs a kernel fix on main.

**Evidence (B200, CI images cu130/cu129, v0.7.1rc2 and main 7db28d561):**
- **Hanging params:** almost always `test_cake_decode_bf16_hd256_smallm_matches_flashinfer_reference[1-7-1-8-64-60000]`; the first hang was on `[1-8-1-8-64-60000]`.
- **Hang rates:**
  - whole file with a 240 s kill: rc2 2/25, main 1/25;
  - fresh process per single test: rc2 3/80;
  - the same shape through `_test_trtllm_batch_decode(backend="cake")`: main 1/40, and 3/27 with `CUDA_MODULE_LOADING=EAGER`.
- **No hang seen:** 300 back-to-back launches in one process (0/300), and the n64_p16 case (0/30). It mostly triggers on the first launch in a process.
- **Not compile time:** a cold run of the file is 179 s on rc2 (105 tests) and about 300 s on main (151 tests). One stuck kernel uses up the 2 h unit timeout, and the runner then marks every test "not executed". The first CI failure (2026-09-22) is the day #5369 landed.
- **cuda-gdb on the hung process:**
  - Only block 124 of 148 is still resident.
  - Every warp is parked in `mbarrier.try_wait`: softmax on `p_empty`, correction on `corr_scale`, warp 12 on `p_full`, warp 13 on `kv_empty[0]`.
  - There are no pending arrivals and no TMA bytes in flight, so this is a deadlock inside one CTA.
  - The other 147 CTAs left the cross-CTA merge spin after its 2^30-poll bound.
  - Suspected cause (not proven): an mbarrier phase race exposed by warp skew on a cold start.
- **Exposure:** new in 0.7.1 (rc1/rc2), and opt-in only (`backend="cake"`, BF16 head-dim-256 MTP/NEXTN decode on SM100/103). `backend="auto"` uses trtllm-gen.

**Release branch:** #5978 reverts #5369 on `release-v0.7.1` only. With it: 0/65 whole-file runs and 0/160 shape runs hung, and accuracy is unchanged on the compat route. The revert conflicts on main.

**Main:** until the kernel is fixed, consider skipping the 6 small-M GPU tests (the 5 reference cases plus `test_cake_decode_bf16_hd256_smallm_route_is_selected`) or gating the route off, so B200 CI stops hitting the 2 h timeout.

Not yet covered: SM103/B300 (it has its own sm_103a copy of the kernel), and the other small-M variants on their own.

items.title: llama : integer type consistency in `llama.h`
items.author: MarcusDunn
items.body_excerpt:
# Feature Description

llama.h should prefer to use `sized` (always) + `signed` (mostly) integers.

# Motivation

The integer types in `llama.h` right now are.

| Count | Type            |
|---------|------------------|
| 33      | `int`              |
| 10      | `int32_t`       |
| 24      | `uint32_t`     |
| 2        | `int64_t`       |
| 2        | `uint64_t`    | 

In #4540 there was a discussion around preferences for integer types on new methods. 

Avoiding `int` makes cross platform code simpler at essentially no cost.
Signed makes arithmetic simpler at the cost of some bits if you need something large.

# Possible Implementation

1. Change all `int`'s to `int32_t`
2. As code changes try to prefer signed integers.

We could also do some higher-impact things, but I'd take the lower-impact slower changes over a large find-and-replace.

items.title: [RFC]: [Store] Completing the cross-client move/migration control plane (DrainJob HA recovery, task lifecycle APIs, surface parity)
items.author: stmatengss
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

Mooncake Store already has a solid data plane for cross-client replica movement:

- the synchronous lease RPCs `CopyStart/CopyEnd/CopyRevoke` and `MoveStart/MoveEnd/MoveRevoke` (plus the `DynamicReplicaCopy*` variants),
- the asynchronous `REPLICA_COPY` / `REPLICA_MOVE` task queue (`CreateCopyTask` / `CreateMoveTask` / `QueryTask` / `FetchTasks` / `MarkTaskToComplete`), and
- the segment-level `DrainJob` that fans out into per-key move tasks.

The **control plane** around that data plane is incomplete, however. This RFC inventories the existing interfaces, lists the gaps, and proposes a phased completion plan:

1. **DrainJob HA persistence and resume** (correctness)
2. **Task/job lifecycle APIs**: register drain RPCs, add enumeration and per-task cancel (operability)
3. **Batching and granularity**: batch task creation, drain-by-client (ergonomics)
4. **Surface parity and documentation**: C API / Python / Admin HTTP / docs (adoption)

## Current state (inventory)

### Synchronous lease RPCs (executor client ↔ master)

| RPC | Shape | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CopyStart` / `CopyEnd` / `CopyRevoke` | 1 source → N targets | plus `DynamicReplicaCopyStart/End/Revoke` for dynamic replication |
| `MoveStart` / `MoveEnd` / `MoveRevoke` | 1 source → 1 target | `MoveStartResponse.target` is `optional` (degenerates to source-only removal when the target replica already exists); target allocation is memory-segment only |

All registered in `RegisterRpcService` ([rpc_service.cpp](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/main/mooncake-store/src/rpc_service.cpp)).

### Asynchronous task queue

- `CreateCopyTask(key, targets)` / `CreateMoveTask(key, source, target)` / `QueryTask` / `FetchTasks` / `MarkTaskToComplete`, all registered RPCs.
- A task is assigned to the client owning the source segment and executed by its background loop (`Client::PollAndDispatchTasks` → `ExecuteTask` → `Client::Copy` / `Client::Move`).
- Task state survives master failover: `task_manager` is one of the three snapshot payloads (`MasterSnapshotPayloads{metadata, segments, task_manager}`, see [master_snapshot_codec.h](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/main/mooncake-store/include/ha/snapshot/master_snapshot_codec.h)).

### Segment-level migration (DrainJob)

- `CreateDrainJob` / `QueryDrainJob` / `CancelDrainJob` are declared on `WrappedMasterService` but are **not registered as coro_rpc handlers**; they are exposed only through the admin HTTP server (`POST /api/v1/drain_jobs`, `GET /api/v1/drain_jobs/query`, `POST /api/v1/drain_jobs/cancel`, `GET /api/v1/segments/status`, see [master_admin_service.cpp](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/main/mooncake-store/src/master_admin_service.cpp)).
- The scheduler (`ScheduleDrainJobTasks` in [master_service.cpp](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/main/mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp)) expands a job into per-(tenant, key, segment) units, each executed as a `REPLICA_MOVE` task, bounded by `max_concurrency` (default 4) and retried up to `kMaxDrainUnitRetries`.
- Segment lifecycle `OK → DRAINING → DRAINED` (or back to `OK` on cancel/failure) **is** persisted: `MountedSegment.status` is covered by the segment snapshot payload.

### Cross-media migration (separate mechanism)

memory→SSD offload and SSD→memory promotion are heartbeat-driven (`OffloadObjectHeartbeat` / `NotifyOffloadSuccess`, `PromotionObjectHeartbeat` / `PromotionAllocStart` / `NotifyPromotionSuccess/Failure`), with `EvictDiskReplica` / `BatchEvictDiskReplica` for disk-replica cleanup. They are not task-based "moves" and are only listed here for completeness.

### Client surfaces

| Surface | move/copy/task | drain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MasterClient` (C++) | full | none |
| `RealClient` public API | `create_copy_task`, `create_move_task`, `query_task` | none |
| Python `MooncakeDistributedStore` | same three | none |
| C API ([store_c.h](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/main/mooncake-store/include/store_c.h)) | none | none |
| Admin HTTP | none | drain jobs + segment status |

## Gaps

### G1. DrainJob state is lost on master failover (correctness)

`drain_jobs_` is an in-memory map; the snapshot payloads are only `{metadata, segments, task_manager}`. After a failover:

- The job itself, its per-unit progress (`completed_unit_keys`, `terminal_failed_unit_keys`, `retry_counts`) and `migrated_bytes` are gone.
- The per-key move tasks it spawned **do** survive (they live in the task-manager payload) and will run to completion, but no job remains to consume their results.
- Segments the job marked `DRAINING` keep that persisted status, yet no job exists to drive them to `DRAINED` or back to `OK`. They stay non-allocatable indefinitely — and there is currently no admin endpoint to force a segment status change either.
- `CancelDrainJob` / `QueryDrainJob` on the new leader return `JOB_NOT_FOUND`; operators cannot even tell that a drain was in progress.

### G2. DrainJob has no RPC surface

The three drain methods exist on `WrappedMasterService` but are absent from `RegisterRpcService`, and `MasterClient` has no corresponding methods. Anything drain-related requires raw HTTP access to the admin server, bypassing the RPC path that gives clients service discovery, leader redirection, and retries.

### G3. No enumeration or per-task lifecycle

- No `ListDrainJobs`: a lost `job_id` makes the job invisible.
- No `ListTasks` / query-by-key: `QueryTask` is by UUID only.
- No `CancelTask`: an individual copy/move task cannot be canceled. Only a whole drain job can be, and only while it has no active tasks. A wrongly targeted `CreateMoveTask` can only be waited out.

### G4. No batch move primitive

`CreateCopyTask` / `CreateMoveTask` take a single key; `MoveStart` takes a single target. Migrating a key set (tenant compaction, rebalancer output) costs one RPC per key with no grouping handle. DrainJob covers the segment-level case only.

### G5. Drain gra

items.title: [docs] Slurm: fix multi-node example, add single-node and offline batch examples
items.author: holtwood
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

Contributes to #3244.

The existing multi-node example expands `$SLURM_NODEID` in the batch shell, before `srun` creates its per-task environments. Both launches can therefore receive the same node rank. The existing readiness loop also checks only whether a TCP port is open.

This PR covers basic multi-node serving, single-node serving, and offline batch inference. #29991 has a separate scope around PD disaggregation and Apptainer.

## Changes

- Evaluate `$SLURM_PROCID` inside each `srun` task and use Slurm `%n` patterns for per-node logs.
- Use configurable HTTP and distributed-init ports, a bounded `/health` check, and early process-exit detection.
- Add a single-node serving job with cleanup and an SSH forwarding hint.
- Add an offline job that writes a real Python file with a `__main__` guard, as required by the Engine multiprocessing setup.
- Document the log-directory prerequisite and cluster-specific scheduler, network, port, and model-cache settings.

## Validation

- `bash -n` on all three batch scripts.
- `mint validate`.
- `mint broken-links`.
- Parsed and mock-executed the offline Python example, including Engine context cleanup.

items.title: [Bug] `tree_speculative_sampling_target_only` rejects the only token with target mass when the coin equals the largest float32 below 1 and emits token id `vocab_size - 1`
items.author: clayboby
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

With top-k + top-p sampling, many decode steps end with a single-token nucleus. After `top_k_renorm_probs` → `top_p_renorm_probs` the surviving probability is often `0.99999994` (`1 - 2^-24`) instead of exactly `1.0`.

The acceptance test in the JIT verify kernel (`python/sglang/kernels/jit/include/sgl_kernel/speculative/sampling.cuh`) is strict:

```cpp
const bool has_target_mass = target_prob_single > DType(0);
if (has_target_mass && (coin < prob_acc / threshold_acc || target_prob_single >= threshold_single)) {
```

`torch.rand` (float32) returns multiples of `2^-24` in `[0, 1 - 2^-24]`, so `coin == 0.99999994` happens with probability `2^-24` per draw. Then `coin < 0.99999994` is false and `0.99999994 >= threshold_single` (default `1.0`) is false, so the only token with target mass is rejected. The kernel copies its probability into `draft_probs`, the residual `relu(target - draft)` is identically zero, `DeviceSamplingFromProb` finds no valid index, and the fallback `sampled_id = d - 1` emits the last vocabulary id.

**Expected:** a draft token that carries all of the target mass is always accepted (or, if rejected, is the token that gets re-sampled).

**Rate in real serving:** about `2^-24 ≈ 6e-8` per decode step that has a one-token nucleus with renormalized probability `1 - 2^-24`, i.e. roughly one unrelated token per ~10^7 generated tokens. Rare, but the emitted token has nothing to do with the distribution.

**Related:** #35771 / #35798 fixed the opposite edge (a draft token with zero target probability was accepted when `coin == 0.0`) by adding `has_target_mass` and switching `<=` to `<`. That strict comparison is what makes `coin == 1 - 2^-24` reject a token whose renormalized probability is also `1 - 2^-24`. The check is present on `main` and on tag `v0.5.21`.

**Suggested fix (any of):** keep the `has_target_mass` guard but compare with `<=` on the `prob_acc` branch; accept when the residual mass after the draft is zero; or treat `target_prob_single >= 1 - eps` as certain.

### Reproduction

No model needed; one GPU. The script below builds a one-token nucleus, uses it as the draft token, and fixes the coin at `0.99999994`.

<details>
<summary>repro.py (38 lines)</summary>

```python
"""Minimal repro: tree_speculative_sampling_target_only rejects the only token with
target mass when the coin is the largest float32 below 1, then emits vocab_size - 1.

Needs a CUDA GPU; no model weights. Run inside an environment with sglang v0.5.21."""
import torch
from flashinfer.sampling import top_k_renorm_probs, top_p_renorm_probs
from sglang.kernels.ops.speculative.sampling import tree_speculative_sampling_target_only

V, N, B, TOK = 248320, 4, 8, 1174  # vocab size, draft tokens per request, batch, the nucleus token
dev = "cuda"
p = torch.full((1, V), (1 - 0.9982) / (V - 1), device=dev)
p[0, TOK] = 0.9982
q = top_p_renorm_probs(top_k_renorm_probs(p, 20), 0.95)  # single-token nucleus
print("nucleus size:", int((q > 0).sum()), " renormalized prob:", repr(q[0, TOK].item()))

target = q.view(1, 1, V).repeat(B, N, 1).contiguous()
draft = torch.zeros_like(target)
cand = torch.full((B, N), TOK, dtype=torch.int64, device=dev)  # draft token == the nucleus token
ridx = (torch.arange(B, device=dev).view(-1, 1) * N + torch.arange(N, device=dev)).contiguous()
rnext = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3, -1], device=dev).repeat(B, 1).contiguous()  # chain
rsib = torch.full((B, N), -1, dtype=torch.int64, device=dev)

for coin in (0.5, 0.99999994):  # torch.rand(float32) returns 0.99999994 with probability 2^-24
    coins = torch.full((B, N), coin, dtype=torch.float32, device=dev)
    final = torch.rand((B,), dtype=torch.float32, device=dev)
    predicts = torch.zeros(B * N, dtype=torch.int32, device=dev)
    accept_index = torch.full((B, N), -1, dtype=torch.int32, device=dev)
    accept_num = torch.zeros((B,), dtype=torch.int32, device=dev)
    tree_speculative_sampling_target_only(
        predicts=predicts, accept_index=accept_index, accept_token_num=accept_num,
        candidates=cand, retrive_index=ridx, retrive_next_token=rnext, retrive_next_sibling=rsib,
        uniform_samples=coins, uniform_samples_for_final_sampling=final,
        target_probs=target, draft_probs=draft,
        threshold_single=1.0, threshold_acc=1.0, deterministic=True,
    )
    draft.zero_()
    print(f"coin={coin!r}: accepted drafts per row {accept_num.tolist()}, first emitted token per row {predicts.view(B, N)[:, 0].tolist()}")
# Expected: token 1174 in both cases. Observed with coin=0.99999994: 0 accepted, token 248319 (= V - 1).
```

</details>

Output inside the official `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.21` image:

```
nucleus size: 1  renormalized prob: 0.9999999403953552
coin=0.5: accepted drafts per row [3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3], first emitted token per row [1174, 1174, 1174, 1174, 1174, 1174, 1174, 1174]
coin=0.99999994: accepted drafts per row [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], first emitted token per row [248319, 248319, 248319, 248319, 248319, 248319, 248319, 248319]
```

In a 1,000,448-row run of the same setup: with `torch.rand` coins every row accepts and emits the nucleus token; with the coin fixed at `0.99999994` every row is rejected and emits `248319` (= `vocab_size - 1`).

### Environment

- sglang v0.5.21 (official `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.21` image; the same code is on `main`), flashinfer 0.6.18, PyTorch with CUDA 13
- GPU architecture: SM121
- Speculative decoding settings matching the repro: `speculative_num_draft_tokens=4`, `speculative_eagle_topk=1`, default ac

items.title: [Robustness]: Observations on missing defensive bounds checks in TritonGPU layout conversions
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
# [Robustness]: Observations on missing defensive bounds checks in TritonGPU layout conversions

**Target**: `lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/IR/LinearLayoutConversions.cpp`, verifiers, and layout lowering passes  
**Target Commit**: `42c5e89c3` / `main`  

---

### Summary

We identified several places in the `TritonGPU` dialect and its unified layout conversions (`toLinearLayout`) where invalid, edge-case, or malformed IR parameters are not caught by attribute/op verifiers. Instead of returning a diagnostic error (`emitError`), they crash `triton-opt` with unhandled process aborts (`SIGABRT`), segmentation faults (`SIGSEGV`), or hardware floating-point exceptions (`SIGFPE`).

These cases are not reachable from the standard high-level Python frontend under normal usage. However, for intermediate compiler passes, custom pass pipelines, or external IR emitters, adding defensive validation to the corresponding verifiers would improve the overall robustness and diagnosability of the compiler.

We disclose the main defect clusters below along with self-contained, minimal MLIR reproducers.

---

### 1. Integer Division by Zero (`SIGFPE`) on Swizzle Parameters

In `#ttg.swizzled_shared<{vec, perPhase, maxPhase, order}>`, the attribute verifier permits `perPhase = 0` and `maxPhase = 0`. During `swizzledSharedToLinearLayout`:

- Location: `lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/IR/LinearLayoutConversions.cpp:83`:
  ```cpp
  bases2D.push_back({row, (vec * ((row / perPhase) % maxPhase)) % numCols});
  ```
The compiler crashes with an unhandled hardware floating-point exception (`SIGFPE`, Signal 8) when `perPhase == 0` or `maxPhase == 0`.

#### Minimal Repro (`perPhase = 0`):
```mlir
// triton-opt repro.mlir --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx942 -o /dev/null
#s = #ttg.swizzled_shared<{vec = 1, perPhase = 0, maxPhase = 1, order = [1, 0]}>
#w1 = #ttg.amd_wmma<{version = 1, rank = 2, ctaLayout = {warp = [[0, 1], [1, 0]]}}>
#smem = #ttg.shared_memory
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas" = 1 : i32, "ttg.num-warps" = 4 : i32, "ttg.threads-per-warp" = 32 : i32} {
  tt.func @f(%a: !ttg.memdesc<64x32xf16, #s, #smem>) {
    %0 = ttg.local_load %a : !ttg.memdesc<64x32xf16, #s, #smem> -> tensor<64x32xf16, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 0, parent = #w1, kWidth = 8}>>
    tt.return
  }
}
```
*Note*: `maxPhase = 0` triggers the same SIGFPE on the modulo operation.

---

### 2. Unchecked Rank Assumptions & Array Bounds (`ArrayRef` OOB)

Several lowering routines assume specific tensor rank constraints without prior defensive checks:

- **Rank-4 local load (`rank4_local_load_oob`)**: In `NvidiaMmaEncodingAttr::dotOperandToLinearLayout` (`LinearLayoutConversions.cpp:1006`), `mma.getInstrShape()[rank - 2]` assumes `instrShape` has enough dimensions matching the tensor rank. For a rank-4 operand with a 2-element `instrShape = [16, 8]`, indexing at `[rank - 2]` (index 2) triggers an out-of-bounds assertion (`ArrayRef.h:247: Assertion 'Index < Length && "Invalid index!"'`).
- **Missing `warpsPerCTA` (`nv_missing_wpc_oob`)**: Omitting `warpsPerCTA` in `#ttg.nvidia_mma` causes an unchecked out-of-bounds read in `inferDotOperandCGALayout` (`Dialect.cpp:387`).
- **Extra `instrShape` dimensions (`nv_mmatile_m8`, `nv_mmatile_nkwidth`, `nv_mmatile_tilerank`)**: Having more `instrShape` dimensions than the tensor rank triggers hard assert failures inside `nvidiaMmaTile` (`LinearLayoutConversions.cpp:941/951/952`).

#### Minimal Repro (Rank-4 operand OOB):
```mlir
// triton-opt repro.mlir -o /dev/null
#shared = #ttg.swizzled_shared<{vec = 1, perPhase = 1, maxPhase = 1, order = [3, 2, 1, 0]}>
#mma1 = #ttg.nvidia_mma<{versionMajor = 2, warpsPerCTA = [1, 4, 1, 1], instrShape = [16, 8]}>
#smem = #ttg.shared_memory
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas" = 1 : i32, "ttg.num-warps" = 4 : i32, "ttg.threads-per-warp" = 32 : i32} {
  tt.func @f(%arg0: !ttg.memdesc<1x2x64x32xf16, #shared, #smem>) {
    %0 = ttg.local_load %arg0 : !ttg.memdesc<1x2x64x32xf16, #shared, #smem> -> tensor<1x2x64x32xf16, #ttg.dot_op<{opIdx = 0, parent = #mma1, kWidth = 8}>>
    tt.return
  }
}
```

---

### 3. Null-Pointer Dereference on Un-encoded Tensors (`SIGSEGV`)

When a `RankedTensorType` with no distributed layout encoding (where `getEncoding() == nullptr`) reaches function signature conversion in lowering:

- Location: `Dialect.cpp:132` via `convertTritonTensorType`.
- Behavior: `getUniqueElemsPerThread` unconditionally accesses members through `tensorType.getEncoding()`, leading to an immediate null-pointer segmentation fault (`SIGSEGV`).

#### Minimal Repro:
```mlir
// triton-opt repro.mlir --allocate-shared-memory-nv --triton-tensor-memory-allocation \
//   --triton-nvidia-gpu-tmem-barrier-insertion --convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm=compute-capability=100 -o /dev/null
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas" = 1 : i32, "ttg.num-warps" = 4 : i32, "ttg.threads-per-warp" = 32 : i32} {
  tt.func @p(%arg0: tensor<16x16xf8E4M3FNUZ>, %arg1: !tt.ptr<f8E4M3FNUZ>) {
    tt.return
  }
}
```

---

### 4. Process Abort via `report_fatal_error`

In `#ttg.linear`, when the base vectors do not form a surjective mapping:
- Location: `lib/Tools/LinearLayout.cpp:142` (`checkInvariants`).
- Behavior: Calls `llvm::report_fatal_error`, which unconditionally aborts the entire compiler process during MLIR parsing rather than returning a structured MLIR diagnostic error.

#### Minimal Repro:
```mlir
// triton-opt repro.mlir -o /dev/null
#l = #ttg.linear<{register = [[1, 0]], lane = [[4, 0], [8, 0]], warp = [], block = []}>
```

---

### Environment & Verification

All testcases above were verified on Triton commit `42c5e89c3` (with assertions enabled) using `triton-opt`.

items.title: TRITON_CODEGEN_BACKENDS cannot exclude nvidia/amd: core headers and libtriton include the backend trees
items.author: benkelaya
items.body_excerpt:
## Context

We build Triton from source on macOS arm64 to host an out-of-tree Apple GPU backend (the MLIR backend proposed in triton-lang/triton-ext#126). The machine has no NVIDIA and no AMD device and never will, yet every build compiles both backends and downloads the NVIDIA toolchain.

`CMakeLists.txt:27` declares `TRITON_CODEGEN_BACKENDS` as a cache variable, and `setup.py:297` already derives `-DTRITON_CODEGEN_BACKENDS` from the backend list, but `setup.py:399` fixes that list in code:

```python
backends = [*BackendInstaller.copy(["nvidia", "amd"]), *BackendInstaller.copy_externals()]
```

`TRITON_PLUGIN_DIRS` only adds externals, and no selector appears in the cmake passthrough list, so there is no supported way to ask for fewer in-tree backends from the Python build.

## What we tried, and what happened

We patched that one line to read `TRITON_CODEGEN_BACKENDS` from the environment, defaulting to `nvidia;amd` so nothing changes for anyone who sets nothing. The clean build with neither backend then fails after 107 seconds of compiling, because core code includes backend trees:

- `include/triton/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/Passes.h:5` includes `nvidia/include/Dialect/NVWS/IR/Dialect.h`, whose own line 31 needs the TableGen-generated `Dialect.h.inc` that exists only when the nvidia subtree builds. This is a public core header, so everything including it inherits the dependency.
- `lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/WarpSpecialization/PartitionLoops.cpp:10-11` includes the same NVWS dialect and its passes.
- `python/src/gluon_ir.cc:18-20`, inside libtriton itself, includes `third_party/amd/include/Dialect/TritonAMDGPU/IR/Dialect.h` and two AMD lib headers, whose dialect header needs AMD's generated `.h.inc`.

Seven core files in total, on commit `4a15f415`. So the selector the cmake side advertises cannot currently be honoured, and the hardcoded list at line 399 is arguably the accurate description of the tree rather than the bug.

## What it would be worth, measured

From a full build here, so these are measurements rather than estimates:

- the two backend subtrees are 625 MB of a 4405 MB build tree (nvidia 300 MB, amd 325 MB)
- the NVIDIA toolchain download is a further 662 MB, a pure skip on a machine that cannot use it
- roughly 290 MB of wheel payload

That is about 1.5 GB of an 8 GB footprint. In fairness, the single largest item is not the backends: `bin`, `test` and `unittest` come to 2887 MB and are already switchable today with `-DTRITON_BUILD_UT=OFF` and no patch at all. We mention it so the trade is judged honestly.

## The question

Is `TRITON_CODEGEN_BACKENDS` intended to be usable from the Python build, or are nvidia and amd considered mandatory in-tree components with the cmake variable serving another purpose? If the former, the minimum fix is either gating those seven includes behind the selector, which is the layering change, or always running the backends' TableGen while not building their libraries, which is smaller and uglier but honest.

We are happy to do the work and to test it on macOS arm64 on every pin move, but the direction is yours to set rather than ours to guess. We found no prior art for the split; #11485 looks adjacent in spirit, and #2048 is the old version of the same complaint from the other side. The one-line diff we tested is available if it is useful.

comments.author: woct0rdho
comments.body:
I'm also considering https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/issues/10329

(BTW there is Nvidia GPU on macOS arm64 with a custom driver but that's another story)

comments.author: benkelaya
comments.body:
Thank you, #10329 is the right home for this and I had missed it. Our report is effectively a macOS arm64 data point for it.

One thing worth noting for whoever picks it up: the sites we hit independently on macOS are the ones your guard set in triton-windows `155967dd` already touches. Our clean build with neither in-tree backend failed on `include/triton/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/Passes.h` pulling the NVWS dialect (your change guards the `.td` that generates it), on `lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/WarpSpecialization/PartitionLoops.cpp`, and on `python/src/gluon_ir.cc` including the AMD dialect inside libtriton, plus `setup.py`'s hardcoded backend list. Two platforms arriving at the same list of files is a reasonable sign that the list is complete, or close to it.

If it helps, we can build that guard set on macOS arm64 at the current Triton pin and report whether libtriton builds without either backend and whether the out-of-tree Apple backend from triton-lang/triton-ext#126 still loads and runs against it. I am happy to close this issue in favour of #10329 so the discussion stays in one place; say the word.

items.title: [Feature]: Share non-streaming chat message assembly between `OpenAIServingChat` and batch derender
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Tracking issue for the "Unify (not mirror) the assembly path" item in #42729, raised by @sagearc in the #48617 review (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48617#pullrequestreview-4695988048).

#### Why

Batch chat derender (`OnlineDerenderer._derender_chat`) builds the assistant message itself instead of  sharing the code in `OpenAIServingChat.chat_completion_full_generator`. Both run the same `Parser.parse()` over the same tokens. They differ in what happens after:

- which `tool_choice` branch applies
- `content or ""` for named / required tool choice
- tool call IDs
- the `finish_reason` rewrite to `tool_calls`

The two have already drifted three times:

- `null` vs `""` content, fixed in #48617
- `finish_reason`: batch derender passes through the generate side's `stop` for tool calls (fix in open PR #47931)
- tool call IDs: batch derender builds `ToolCall(id=random_uuid())` and drops the parser's ID, while coupled chat uses `tc.id or make_tool_call_id()`. Batch IDs lose the `chatcmpl-tool-` prefix, and Kimi K2 `functions.<name>:<idx>` IDs are lost. A fix will follow once #47931 merges, since both change the same block of `_derender_chat`.

The round trip parity test (`test_derender_parity.py`) missed the last two. It compares only tool names and arguments, and it feeds the coupled response's `finish_reason` into derender instead of the engine's.

#### Proposal

Pull the post parse message assembly out of `chat_completion_full_generator` into a helper that both paths call. It takes the parser output (`reasoning`, `content`, `tool_calls`), the request and the tool config and returns the `ChatMessage` fields and the final `finish_reason`. It owns:

- the `tool_choice` branches (none / named / required / auto)
- tool call IDs (`tc.id or make_tool_call_id()`)
- `content or ""` for named / required
- `auto_tools_called` and the `finish_reason` rewrite

Constraints:

- **Subclass hooks stay.** `_create_chat_message` and `_finalize_response_message` are overridden by the Cohere v2 handler (`cohere/serving.py`). The helper returns fields and serving still builds the message through the hooks. Derender doesn't subclass `OpenAIServingChat`.
- **No behavior change for `/v1/chat/completions`.** This is the hot non-streaming path.
- **Batch only.** Streaming is #57572.

#56851 `derender` level reuses `OnlineDerenderer.derender_chat`, so it picks this up without adding a third copy.

#### Done when

- [ ] Helper extracted from `chat_completion_full_generator`. Existing chat completion and tool / reasoning parser tests pass unchanged.
- [ ] `_derender_chat` uses it.
- [ ] #47931 and the tool call ID fix have landed first, so the refactor changes no behavior on either path. The tool call ID fix also makes `test_derender_parity.py` feed the engine's `finish_reason` and check tool call ID format.

### Alternatives

- **Rely on the parity test.** Cheaper  and it should be tightened anyway. But it runs one model with one parser configuration and it has already missed two of three drifts.
- **Fold this into #57572.** Both touch `OpenAIServingChat` but the streaming step works on deltas and this one builds a whole message. Keeping them apart keeps each serving change reviewable on its own. If the helpers end up sharing code (the `finish_reason` rewrite, tool call IDs), that can happen in whichever lands second.

### Additional context

- RFC #42729, "Unify (not mirror) the parse/assembly path"
- #48617 (parity test), #47931 (`finish_reason` fix, open). The tool call ID fix follows after #47931.
- #57572: streaming counterpart
- #56851: reuses `derender_chat` for its `derender` level

cc @sagearc @chaunceyjiang

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug] trtllm_mha for both prefill and decode on H200 (SM90) is accepted in v0.5.20 and returns wrong completions (gpt-oss-120b); v0.5.17 refused it; either half alone is correct
items.author: Ethan-ES
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

On **H200 (SM90)** with the `lmsysorg/sglang` **v0.5.20** image, launching gpt-oss-120b with `--attention-backend trtllm_mha` (i.e. trtllm_mha for **both** prefill and decode) **starts normally, reports `attention_backend='trtllm_mha'` in `/server_info`, serves at normal speed — and returns wrong completions**. The same command on the **v0.5.17** image refuses to start with `ValueError: TRTLLM MHA backend for prefill is only supported on Blackwell GPUs (SM100). Please use a different prefill backend.` So a configuration that used to be rejected became silently incorrect.

Each half alone is correct on v0.5.20: `--prefill-attention-backend trtllm_mha --decode-attention-backend fa3` and `--prefill-attention-backend fa3 --decode-attention-backend trtllm_mha` both pass our correctness probes; only the **both-trtllm_mha** combination fails (whether spelled as the single flag or explicitly).

### Environment

- Image `lmsysorg/sglang@sha256:06e4f2ed21afde4ff513cda65070124e727ba23ccaeff7712b8c40e1097d611f` (= tag `v0.5.20` / `latest` on 2026-09-23); inside: sglang 0.5.20, flashinfer 0.6.18 (python/cubin/jit-cache), torch 2.13.0+cu130, flash-attn-4 4.0.0b19
- Contrast image `lmsysorg/sglang@sha256:16aba8925507e631e1dc1e23d95d026533602591775f6a8db68b74ee99746155` (= tag `v0.5.17`): flashinfer 0.6.15.post1, torch 2.11.0+cu130
- 1 × NVIDIA H200 (143771 MiB), Kubernetes pod, cold caches (`HF_HOME` / `DG_CACHE_DIR` on emptyDir)
- Model: `openai/gpt-oss-120b`, snapshot `b5c939de8f754692c1647ca79fbf85e8c1e70f8a`; no speculative decoding, default KV dtype and memory settings

### Reproduction

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path /models/hub/models--openai--gpt-oss-120b/snapshots/b5c939de8f754692c1647ca79fbf85e8c1e70f8a \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 --attention-backend trtllm_mha
```
Then, with any OpenAI-compatible client at temperature 0 (`/v1/completions`):

| prompt (paraphrased) | v0.5.20, `--attention-backend trtllm_mha` | default (fa3) |
|---|---|---|
| "What is the capital of France?" | completion stops after **4 tokens, no "Paris"** | correct |
| "List the first five prime numbers." | runs to the 768-token budget, **never produces `2, 3, 5, 7, 11` in order** | correct |
| a short multiplication | correct | correct |

Observed on **5 of 6 fresh boots** of the failing configuration (identical failing prompts each time; on one boot a second pass recovered one of the two). The default server passed all three prompts on **4/4 boots, 8/8 passes**.

### Which half

| flags (v0.5.20) | `/server_info` prefill / decode | our 3-prompt probe |
|---|---|---|
| `--attention-backend trtllm_mha` | trtllm_mha / trtllm_mha | **fails** (4/4 boots) |
| `--prefill-attention-backend trtllm_mha --decode-attention-backend trtllm_mha` | trtllm_mha / trtllm_mha | **fails** |
| `--prefill-attention-backend trtllm_mha --decode-attention-backend fa3` | trtllm_mha / fa3 | passes (2/2) |
| `--prefill-attention-backend fa3 --decode-attention-backend trtllm_mha` | fa3 / trtllm_mha | passes (2/2) |
| default | fa3 / fa3 | passes (8/8) |

### What the server says at startup

Nothing: no warning, no fallback line, no SM90/SM100 message in the boot log of the failing configuration; `server_args` echoes `attention_backend='trtllm_mha'`; CUDA-graph capture logs the same `backend=breakable` (prefill) / `backend=full` (decode) strings as the fa3 server.

### Why report it

A configuration that fails loudly is safe; this one is accepted, fast (a 30-s probe on one boot gave ~+6 % tok/s over fa3 at concurrency 16) and wrong. Any selection process that checks "boots + serves + throughput" will grade it healthy. Either the SM90 guard for the trtllm_mha prefill+decode combination that v0.5.17 had should come back, or the combination needs a fix — and a correctness check for (prefill, decode) backend pairs newly accepted on a GPU generation would catch this class.

### Limitations of this report

One model (gpt-oss-120b: mxfp4 experts, GQA 64/8, head_dim 64, hybrid SWA), one GPU type, one image step in which three components moved together (sglang 0.5.17→0.5.20, flashinfer 0.6.15.post1→0.6.18, torch 2.11→2.13) — we cannot say which change opened the path or broke the numerics. We have not read the v0.5.20 source for the guard; the tables above are observations. n = 6 boots for the failing spelling, 1 boot each for the explicit half-splits.

items.title: [Feature]: Integrate Cake kernels via FlashInfer: model-by-model tracker
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**End-to-end validation and issue reporting:** Our shape coverage and correctness have not yet been validated end to end in model serving. If you encounter (1) end-to-end accuracy degradation, (2) unsuitable API requirements, such as unnecessarily requiring contiguous inputs, or (3) faster kernel benchmarks but worse end-to-end performance because the shapes optimized by the kernel do not cover the actual model-serving workload, please open an issue and tag @yyihuang with the affected kernel, the missing or problematic shape(s), and relevant model/serving details or a reproducer. We will resolve reported issues within **6 hours**.

## Motivation

Track integration of Cake kernels already delivered through FlashInfer into vLLM, grouped by the models that requested them. The upstream inventory is [flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#4254](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4254); model requirements below come from its subissues and the linked implementation PRs.

The proposed integration is through FlashInfer's public/prepared APIs. Each task should connect the relevant model operator, weight/cache layout, and execution mode to an eligible kernel, then measure the complete serving path. Upstream kernel benchmarks are useful starting points, not claims of vLLM end-to-end speedup.

**Snapshot: 2026-10-03 (UTC; October 2 in US Pacific); FlashInfer main [46340689a5ab](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/commit/46340689a5ab5665ab39f6281dac4d021d7ae94b).** “Merged” below means available in upstream FlashInfer, not necessarily in a released wheel or integrated here. Open follow-ups are explicitly marked and are not included in the merged coverage. Most listed kernels target SM100/SM103; exact architecture, SM-count, dtype, layout, and shape admission remain API-specific. Let the serving adapter retain its existing backend for configurations outside those contracts.

Notation: `T/M` = token rows, `B` = requests, `Q` = query tokens per request, `S` = KV length. MoE tuples are **(hidden size, expert intermediate size, number of experts, top-k)**; an intermediate size marked “local” is after TP sharding. Enumerated benchmark shapes are evidence points, not an assertion that every combination is supported.

## Integration and acceptance

- [ ] Pin a FlashInfer revision/release containing the required merged APIs and register backend selection at the existing operator boundary.
- [ ] Check the selected release branch separately: [#5978](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5978) is merged into `release-v0.7.1` only and reverts the BF16 head-dim-256 small-M speculative-decode route because of an intermittent B200 hang. This is a separate route from the E4M3/page-64 DCP entries below; a merge on the release branch does not establish a fix on main.
- [ ] Prepare weights, plans, output buffers, and workspaces before graph capture; account for changing request lengths, routing, state indices, and graph buckets.
- [ ] Validate each listed model/checkpoint, quantization recipe, TP/EP/CP configuration, and state/cache layout. Cover prefill, decode, speculative verification, ragged batches, and prefix-cache reuse where relevant.
- [ ] Compare against the current engine backend on model quality, TTFT, TPOT, throughput, and memory. Record the actual selected route and unsupported configurations before changing defaults.

vLLM already has FlashInfer hooks for several of these models. This tracker proposes selecting and qualifying the Cake implementations through those hooks and adding prepared adapters where needed.

## 1. Kimi-K3 / Kimi-K3-NVFP4 / Kimi-K3 vision

Requirements: [NVFP4 end-to-end #4568](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4568), [TP12 #4542](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4542), [ragged MLA/DCP #4658](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4658), [NVFP4 MLA #4644](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4644), [W4A8 SiTU #5156](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/5156).

Start from [`vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/tree/main/vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia): `kda.py`, `mla.py`, `latent_moe_runner.py`, `low_latency_gemm.py`, and `ops/attn_res.py`. The KDA module already calls FlashInfer recurrent/fused/packed APIs; connect explicit eligible Cake selection and its workspace/state contract through the existing wrappers rather than adding a parallel KDA implementation. Qualify ModelOpt weight preparation and the vision encoder separately.

| Integration task | Covered shape / contract | FlashInfer delivery / upstream status |
|---|---|---|
| KDA prefill and fused decode | D=128. Fused one-token decode includes H=8 for TP12, plus H=12/24/32/48/96; BF16/FP32 indexed recurrent states and width-4 convolution. Prefill consumes strided q/k/v views of packed `[T,3*H*128]` projection output without densification. Prefill checkpoint outputs are BF16; FP32 checkpoints and `checkpoint_state_indices` are not admitted by the Cake prefill route. Recurrent T=1 decode with explicit `cu_seqlens` is outside the explicit Cake contract; `auto` now respects that guard. | **Merged:** `recurrent_kda(..., backend="cake")` and `fused_kda_decode(..., backend="cake")`; [#5551](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5551), [#5846](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5846); selector/binding updates [#5901](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5901) and [#5919](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5919) preserve the public API and served shape contracts; explicit-`cu_seqlens` auto-dispatch fix [#5760](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5760); [API](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/flashinfer/kda.py). |
| Dense FP8 MLA and ragged/DCP MLA | Kimi latent=512, RoPE=64, E4M3 query/cache, page=64; registered H=12/96 decode and Q<=8 MTP paths. The separate var-Q DCP API accepts BF16 or FP8 query/cache, H<=128, registered pages 32/64/1

comments.body:
**Документация: Работа с `llama.cpp` b6286 (август 2025)**

**1. Изменения в архитектуре и API**

*   **Изменение публичного API:** Прямой доступ к внутренним библиотекам `ggml` и `gguf` через их заголовочные файлы (`ggml/ggml.h`, `ggml/gguf.h`) **больше не является публичным или рекомендуемым**. Функции вроде `gguf_init_from_file`, `gguf_get_n_tensors` и т.д. скрыты.
*   **Унификация API:** Всё взаимодействие с моделью, её метаданными и тензорами теперь должно происходить **только** через унифицированный API, предоставляемый в **`include/llama.h`** (и `include/llama-cpp.h` для C++).
*   **Изменение структуры `include`:** Публичные заголовки теперь находятся непосредственно в `include/`. Внутренние заголовки `ggml` перемещены в `ggml/include/`.

**2. Создание собственного примера/приложения (например, `qedit`)**

*   **Расположение:** Поместите исходный код примера (например, `qedit.cpp`) и его `CMakeLists.txt` в подкаталог `examples/<имя_примера>/` внутри корня проекта `llama.cpp`. Например: `llama.cpp/examples/qedit/`.
*   **`CMakeLists.txt` примера:**
    ```cmake
    cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
    project(<имя_примера> CXX) # Замените <имя_примера> на имя вашего проекта

    set(TARGET <имя_примера>)
    add_executable(${TARGET} <имя_файла>.cpp) # Замените <имя_файла>.cpp на имя вашего .cpp файла

    target_compile_features(${TARGET} PRIVATE cxx_std_17)

    # Указываем include-путь к llama.h
    target_include_directories(${TARGET} PRIVATE
        ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/include    # папка с llama.h
        # ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/common   # Если используете заголовки из common
        # ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/ggml/include # Только если требуется прямой доступ к внутренним ggml (не рекомендуется)
    )

    # Линкуем необходимые библиотеки
    target_link_libraries(${TARGET} PRIVATE
        # common     # Если используете утилиты из common
        llama        # ОСНОВНАЯ библиотека, предоставляющая API из llama.h
        # ggml       # Обычно не нужно явно указывать, так как llama зависит от ggml.
                     # Но можно оставить для ясности.
        # ggml-cuda  # НЕ НУЖНО. Отдельная цель ggml-cuda НЕ СОЗДАЕТСЯ.
                     # Функциональность CUDA интегрирована в основную библиотеку ggml.
        ${CMAKE_THREAD_LIBS_INIT} # Если требуется
    )
    ```
*   **Использование API:** В коде вашего примера используйте только функции, объявленные в `include/llama.h`. Примеры функций:
    *   `llama_backend_init()`, `llama_backend_free()`: Инициализация/деинициализация бэкенда.
    *   `llama_model_default_params()`: Получение параметров модели по умолчанию.
    *   `llama_load_model_from_file()`: Загрузка модели.
    *   `llama_model_meta_count()`, `llama_model_meta_key_by_index()`, `llama_model_meta_val_str_by_index()`: Доступ к метаданным модели.
    *   `llama_model_n_embd()`, `llama_model_n_ctx_train()`, `llama_model_n_params()`: Получение информации о модели (некоторые могут требовать активного контекста).
    *   `llama_free_model()`: Освобождение модели.

**3. Сборка проекта `llama.cpp`**

*   **Конфигурация CMake:**
    *   Используйте CMake для генерации проекта сборки.
    *   Для включения поддержки CUDA используйте опцию `-DGGML_CUDA=ON` (устаревшая `LLAMA_CUBLAS=ON` больше не поддерживается).
    *   Пример команды для Visual Studio 2022:
        ```bash
        cmake .. -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64 -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF -DLLAMA_BUILD_COMMON=ON -DLLAMA_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON
        ```
*   **Сборка библиотек:**
    *   При включении `GGML_CUDA=ON` и `BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON` (по умолчанию для MSVC):
        *   Исходники CUDA (`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/*`) добавляются в сборку основной библиотеки `ggml`.

items.title: ggml-hip: Q1_0 dp4a vec_dot + hipBLASLt prefill for ternary quants on RDNA4 (Q2_0 portion superseded by #26753)
items.author: The-Monk
items.body_excerpt:
### Update 2026-09-04: rescoped

The original version of this issue led with a Q2_0 `vec_dot` change for gfx1201. **That work has since landed independently in #26753** (native permute instructions replacing the `__byte_perm` lowering, +35% tg128 on a 9070 XT, merged 2026-08-30). That PR is a better-scoped version of what I described, and I have no interest in relitigating it -- it also establishes the precedent I was asking about, namely that arch-guarded ternary paths are acceptable here.

What follows is what remains unclaimed, plus a measurement finding that I think matters more than any single kernel.

---

### 1. A measurement correction that affects how these formats get evaluated

The common way to judge a quant kernel -- weight bytes divided by decode time, expressed as a percentage of memory-bandwidth roofline -- **systematically understates low-bpw formats**, and I think it has misdirected optimization work (certainly mine).

Holding the model fixed and varying only the weight encoding, decode time is linear in weight bytes with a large constant term:

| model | fit | R^2 |
|---|---|---|
| Bonsai-8B | `ms = 1.5556*GB + 2.275` | 0.99883 |
| Bonsai-27B | `ms = 1.6486*GB + 7.982` | 0.99924 |
| Qwen3.6-27B | `ms = 1.2841*GB + 15.089` | 0.99265 |

Three models, 4-6 points each, spanning up to 7.5x in weight bytes.

Subtract the constant and every format streams weights at the same rate:

```
Bonsai-27B Q2_0 : 7.154 GB / (19.753 - 7.735) ms = 600.1 GB/s
Bonsai-27B Q1_0 : 3.792 GB / (14.196 - 7.735) ms = 610.3 GB/s
Qwen3.6-27B     : 755.9 / 771.5 / 776.4 / 778.8 / 783.4 / 783.5 GB/s across
                  Q4_K_M, Q5_K_XL, MXFP6, Q6_K_XL, F8E4M3, Q8_0
```

The naive metric on that same Qwen data reads 460 -> 557 GB/s and looks like a 20% efficiency gradient across formats. There is no gradient. It is one constant divided by a shrinking numerator, so it *must* fall monotonically as bpw falls.

Concretely: Q2_0 measured "63% of roofline" and I spent a long time hunting the missing 37%. Corrected, it is at 100%. Five separate hypotheses (block layout, byte-granular loads, activation traffic, unpack ALU, visit width) all came back negative because there was nothing to find.

I would suggest that any future low-bpw kernel comparison subtract the per-token constant first, or compare kernel time directly rather than end-to-end decode.

### 2. Q1_0 vec_dot -- still unclaimed, and the win is much larger than I first reported

**Correction to the original version of this issue: I claimed +16%. Measured against clean upstream master it is +110%.** The original figure was taken on my own fork, where other changes had already recovered most of the loss, so the marginal gain there was small. Against master nothing masks it.

Measured on 1x Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201), interleaved runs, `-p 0 -n 64 -r 5`, Bonsai-27B Q1_0 (3.53 GiB):

```
master           29.69 / 29.11 t/s
master + patch   61.97 / 61.34 t/s
mean  29.402 -> 61.657 t/s   (+109.7%)
```

Mechanism: the current path issues **20 software `__byte_perm` calls per 32-element chunk** (2 for the nibble indices, 4 for the byte values, 4 to unshuffle -- twice per block). HIP has no hardware `__byte_perm`, so it lowers to a software routine and Q1_0 becomes VALU-bound rather than bandwidth-bound. Replacing it with 8 hardware `v_perm_b32` plus arithmetic removes the bottleneck.

The patch is one helper plus an `#if defined(GGML_USE_HIP)` / `#else`, matching the shape of the Q2_0 path merged in #26753. The `#else` branch is untouched.

Correctness:
- exhaustive equivalence over all 65536 possible `q` values, both paths compiled for gfx1201: **bit-identical**
- `test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT`: all 11 `q1_0` cases OK (n=1..9, k=256 and 4096)

Caveats stated plainly: single model, single card, and I have no NVIDIA hardware, so the CUDA path is unverified by measurement -- it is unchanged code inside the `#else`, but I have not run it.

Worth noting alongside this: Q1_0 will not beat Q2_0 on this class of hardware even with the fix, and that appears to be a property of sub-2-bpw formats rather than of any implementation. Independent confirmations:

- ikawrakow, ik_llama.cpp#45 on an RTX-4080: ternary at 305 t/s vs `IQ2_TN` at 320, attributed to "the bit twiddling we need to unpack the ternary bits"
- #19743, RTX 4090 Vulkan: TQ1_0 608 t/s vs TQ2_0 624 t/s

So the fix is worth having, but nobody should expect 1-bit to be the fast path.

### 3. hipBLASLt prefill routes -- unclaimed, and nothing comparable exists

pp1024 +37.5% Q2_0 / +17.8% Q1_0 (warm, self-tuning per-shape algo cache). As far as I can find, there is no ternary or sub-4-bit path through hipBLASLt or Tensile anywhere -- Tensile has no such datatype at all.

### 4. fp8 (E4M3/E5M2) tensor types -- unclaimed

ggml stops at MXFP4/NVFP4. I have working WMMA fp8 kernels on gfx1201, bit-exact verified. Flagging for interest only; happy to take this to a separate discussion if there is appetite.

### Closed negatives, recorded so nobody repeats them

- **Struct-of-arrays weight layout.** `block_q2_0` is 18 bytes with `qs` at offset 2, so its addresses are never 4-byte aligned, which is why the HIP path does 8 scalar byte loads and assembles `qs0`/`qs1` by hand. Splitting scales into a separate array makes the code stream contiguous and allows aligned dword loads. Tested with production arithmetic held fixed and the layout as the only variable, bit-exact: **2.39x at 4096x4096, but 0.99x once the working set exceeds Infinity Cache**. The unaligned loads are fully hidden behind DRAM latency. No win.
- **Activation-quant dedup across sibling matmuls** does not apply to a standard decode graph. ggml already quantizes once per distinct activation (measured 4.08 quantizes vs 6.87 matmuls per layer on a 64-layer model), so there is no sibling redundancy left to remove.

### Where the remaining time actually goes

For completeness, the per-token budget on Bonsai-27B Q2_0 (19.753 ms):

```
weight streamin

items.title: Misc. bug: llama-server (HIP/ROCm build) spins 2 threads at 100% CPU when idle in router mode (WSL2)
items.author: vecStardo
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

llama.cpp commit `030ebb558a5820b444a8f836ed5cdd46c9b4bd7a` (2026-08-11), built with GNU 11.4.0 for Linux x86_64, `GGML_HIP=ON` (ROCm), no CUDA.

### Operating systems

- [x] Windows (WSL2: Windows 11 10.0.26200, WSL 2.7.11.0, kernel 6.18.33.2, Ubuntu-22.04)

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

- [x] llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server --models-preset <models.ini> --host 0.0.0.0 --port 12347 -ngl 99 --models-max 2 --sleep-idle-seconds 300
```

Environment: `HSA_ENABLE_DXG_DETECTION=1`, `HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION=11.0.0`, `HSA_ENABLE_SDMA=0`.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`llama-server` built with the HIP/ROCm backend spins **2 threads at ~100% CPU each, continuously, while completely idle** in router mode on WSL2 with an AMD GPU (Radeon RX 7900 XTX, paravirtualized via dxg).

Reproduction:

1. Start llama-server in router mode: `--models-preset <ini> --host 0.0.0.0 --port 12347 -ngl 99 --models-max 2 --sleep-idle-seconds 300`.
2. Do not load any model (all models unloaded, no child processes).
3. Observe: two threads of the process are each pinned at ~100% CPU from process start, continuously, with zero HTTP traffic.

Evidence:

- `top -H`: TID 1905 `R` 99.9%, TID 1906 `R` 99.9%, `TIME+` identical and growing; main thread blocked in `futex_do_wait`.
- `/proc/<tid>/wchan` of the two spinning threads = 0 (pure user-space busy loop, no kernel blocking).
- No iowait (`wa=0`), no memory pressure (17 GB free, no swap).
- Not traffic-related: persists with zero requests for minutes.
- Not model-state-related: occurs with all models unloaded AND after a model enters sleeping state.
- `GPU_MAX_HW_QUEUES=1` (fix for idle GPU load, PR #24237) has no effect on this CPU spin.

Impact:

- 2 of 8 cores busy-waiting constantly while idle (~25% total CPU wasted).
- The CUDA equivalent busy-wait is addressed by `GGML_CUDA_BLOCKING_SYNC` (PR #26487); no HIP/ROCm equivalent found.
- Related discussion: #22238 (100% CPU single core usage while everything is fully offloaded to the GPU) and PR #27293 (`--poll` busy-spin / `--poll 0` recipe) — the default `--poll 50` polling loop accounts for ~1 core, but we observe **2 threads spinning even with no model loaded and no requests**, so this appears to be additional to the poll loop.

Expected:

- An idle llama-server with no models loaded / no requests in flight should block (epoll/futex) and use ~0% CPU.

Happy to run strace/gdb or provide more details.

### Relevant log output

No log output available (issue reproduces with zero requests). Evidence above is from `top -H` and `/proc/<tid>/wchan`.

---

AI usage disclosure: this report was drafted with AI assistance; every claim was verified by direct measurement (`top -H`, `/proc/<tid>/wchan`, resource counters) on the affected deployment before submission.

items.title: Misc. bug: a restored slot state prevents the prompt cache lookup, so a longer cached state is never found
items.author: loonylabs
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

version: 0.3.0-dev (build 378, commit 62850522e)
built with GNU 16.1.1 for Linux x86_64

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server -m model.gguf -c 204800 -np 1 \
  --slot-save-path /path/to/states --cache-ram 14336
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

* symptom: after POST /slots/{id}?action=restore the next turn prefills completely, even that the ram cache holds an even longer state of the conversation. this causes massive time to prefill 
* gate 1: server-context.cpp:1559: update_cache this is for two things: saving the outgoing state and finding a better state in cache. it is only set if f_keep < 0.5 ; the comment besides is only refering to the saving half. after a full restore f_keep is 1.0 and the search is never reached
* gate 2: server-task.cpp:1819 : if the slot is a complete prefix f_keep is 1.0 out of the box  and everything that is going beyond is naturally below that because exactly that is decreasing this value. such a slot is unbeatable, no matter how much further the cache is going beyond that
* why that is hitting me / what is my motivation: I am saving/persisting sessions because deep conversations (~11.5GB for 180k) are hitting my cache and getting them lost (your code says "making room for prompt cache entry, removing oldest entry" and I am refering to that) so that they are needed to getting prefilled which is super slow and causing long runs for about half an hour. slot persistence and ram cache using is exactly what breaks here

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. `git log -S` is unusable here: both lines live in files that were
split out of server.cpp, so the search points at the commit that created the
files rather than the one that introduced the condition. Not believed to be a
regression — it looks like the behaviour has been there since the RAM prompt
cache was added.

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>

```console
# Setup: state A (20000 tokens) saved to disk, the same conversation then grown
# to B (40000 tokens) and left in the RAM prompt cache by an LRU takeover.

# Arm 1 — continuation of B, no restore. The cache answers:
slot get_availabl: id  0 | task -1 | selected slot by LRU
prompt eval time =     320 ms /     4 tokens
cache_n = 40000                                      wall 0.32 s

# Arm 2 — identical request, with A restored first:
slot get_availabl: id  0 | task -1 | selected slot by LCP similarity, f_keep = 1.000
prompt eval time =  111510 ms / 20008 tokens
cache_n = 20000                                      wall 111.51 s
```
</details>

Three builds through one reproducer, differing only by the commits under test:

| build | arm 1 (no restore) | arm 2 (restore first) |
|---|---|---|
| 62850522e, unpatched | cache_n 40000 / 0.32 s | cache_n 20000 / 111.51 s |
| + gate 1 opened only | cache_n 40000 / 0.32 s | cache_n 20000 / 111.83 s |
| + both gates | cache_n 40000 / 0.35 s | cache_n 40000 / 0.53 s |

Arm 1 is the control and is stable across all three builds. The middle row
matters: opening only the first gate changes nothing, which is why this is
two separate conditions and not one.

The numbers behind the second gate, for this run:

| | f_keep | f_sim |
|---|---|---|
| slot (restored, 20000 tokens) | 1.00000 | 0.49990 |
| cache entry (40001 tokens) | 0.99998 | 0.99980 |

`f_keep_best < f_keep_cur && f_sim_best < f_sim_cur` is false: the entry covers
twice as much of the prompt and loses on f_keep by 0.00002.

items.title: Stall during long-prompt first prefill with DFlash2 spec decode (~120s for 75K tokens)
items.author: Songokou1983
items.body_excerpt:
**llama.cpp version tested**: ed262173 (also reproduced on master 9a4843cf)

**Hardware**:
- RTX 2000 Ada (PCH Gen 1 x4, 16 GB)
- RTX 3080 (Slot 2, CPU Gen 3 x16, 20 GB)
- RTX 3080 (Slot 1, OCuLink Gen 3 x4, 20 GB)
- 128 GB RAM, CUDA 13.2, driver 595
- Ubuntu 24.04

**Model**:
- Main: unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF UD-Q4_K_M (16.5 GB)
- Drafter: incoai/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2-Q4_K_M
- spec-type: draft-dflash, spec-draft-n-max 7
- -ts 27,36,36, -c 262144, ctk/ctv q8_0

**Symptom**:
Long prompt first request (cache miss) stalls in prefill for ~120 seconds before decode starts. Subsequent same-prompt requests (cache hit) take 4-25s normally.

**Repro**:
1. Launch llama-server with above config
2. Run 50-round benchmark with short prompt (5K tokens each) → no stall, mean 13.56s
3. Run 20-round benchmark with long prompt (50K-75K tokens each, cache cleared between rounds):
   - Run 1: prompt_n=75010, elapsed=**124.5s** = 27.3 t/s → STALL
   - Run 2-20: cache hit, all normal 4-25s

**Expected**: First prefill of 75K tokens @ ~800 t/s should take ~95 seconds (acceptable). NOT acceptable: 124s where normal prefill for this prompt size would be ~25-40 seconds.

**Diagnosis**:
- Stall rate: ~5% on long-prompt cache-miss requests
- Short prompts (< 5K) never stall across 50 rounds
- Looks like DFlash2 spec decode may stall on first cache-miss with long prompt

**Workaround**:
Disabling spec decode (vanilla decode) avoids the stall but cuts speed from ~44 t/s to ~22 t/s.

Tested with 3 different builds (ed262173, master 9a4843cf, DFlash drafter from incoai/z-lab) — all show same stall pattern.

Happy to provide more logs / reproduce on demand.

items.title: R9700 and other AMD Crashes - Gotchas and Possible Fixes
items.author: CircuitGuy
items.body_excerpt:
**TL;DR kernel settings** (may want to change):

    amdgpu.runpm=0             # headless card: never runtime-suspend (and evict VRAM to Host RAM)
    ttm.pages_limit=1572864    # cap GPU-pinned host RAM (6 GiB in 4 KiB pages); default is HALF your RAM

Plus a udev rule forcing `power/control=on` for the card. Then size `pages_limit` to your real GTT use plus ~2 GB of headroom.

This is mostly a problem caused by a 32 GB card with odd defaults. It gets much worse on a Proxmox **RAM-starved host** (aren't we all now adays - I'm not made of money) where **VMs with PCI passthrough lock their RAM** so it can never be swapped or reclaimed.

**Setup:** 
* Radeon AI PRO R9700 (32 GB, RDNA4), llama.cpp Vulkan/RADV, Proxmox host with 32 GB RAM.
* Two models on one card: currently a Qwen 27B for agents, a 4B vision model for camera analysis and light agent work. 
* A VM with an iGPU passed through locks 12 GB of RAM. The VM runs some self-hosted services and Frigate (which uses the iGPU for 'basic' person detection, video decoding, etc. and can lean on the vision LLM for threat analysis or detailed descriptions of a scene).
* The LLMs are running in nested LXC->Docker, independent of the Frigate VM.
* It's Proxmox running a home lab, so there's a few other things, not relevant, they're "boring" VMs or containers and can get evicted per below.

## The gotchas

1. **No monitor + runtime power management = host freeze.** With no display attached, amdgpu runtime-suspends the card after ~15 s idle and evicts ~30 GB of VRAM into system RAM. Telltale: `PSP is resuming` in dmesg. Fix: `amdgpu.runpm=0` plus the udev rule. The eviction into system RAM locked the kernel so hard that the keyboard caps lock light wouldn't work. *Interestingly it would respond to pings but couldn't log in physically or via ssh.*

2. **VRAM overcommit silently spills into system RAM.** When a load doesn't fit (two big models briefly overlapping, a restart racing a dying process, or just a tight fit), the driver quietly puts buffers in GTT (system RAM) instead of failing. By default it may pin up to **half of host RAM**. Two overlapping 27B loads did that, and I left it with a Codex babysitter and found it **locked for 6.5 hours with no OOM kill**. According to Claude's analysis of the logs, pinned GPU memory and passthrough RAM can't be reclaimed, so the kernel kept dropping and re-reading page cache (the mmap'd model files) and never decided it was out of memory. Swap didn't help. Fix: `ttm.pages_limit=`, which makes an overflow fail the allocation instead. (It only works on the kernel command line; changing it at runtime only triggers swap-out attempts.)

3. **Even "normal" loads can spill.** llama.cpp logged `failed to fit params to free device memory: n_gpu_layers already set by user to 99, abort` and loaded anyway; 1 GiB of its buffers ended up in system RAM. Check with `/proc/<pid>/fdinfo/<drm fd>`: `drm-total-vram` minus `drm-resident-vram` is your spill.

4. **Silent CPU fallback.** In an unprivileged container, a host rebuild changed the render group's GID, the render node became unopenable, and llama.cpp logged `no usable GPU found`, ignored `-ngl 99`, and loaded a 16 GB model into host RAM. The host froze again. Fix: map the GID explicitly (don't `chmod 666 /dev/dri`), and gate startup on `llama-server --list-devices` showing a `Vulkan0` device.

## Ideas for llama.cpp

I'm hoping this spurs a discussion, but these are the quick ones I came up with. Mostly, I'm hopeful the above helps someone with Radeon cards and hard crashes (the internet is FILLED with reports of this with no good resolutions). I think I'm out of the woods.

Anyway, here's the things that maybe would be in scope for llama.cpp

- **Fail instead of falling back:** when `-ngl` is set explicitly and no GPU is usable, exit non-zero (or add a `--require-gpu` flag).
- **A strict fit mode:** when the fit check fails, refuse to load rather than overcommit (for example `--fit strict`).
- **Report spill:** after load, say how many MiB of device buffers ended up in host memory. Vulkan can see this through `VK_EXT_memory_budget` / memory-type checks. Optionally fail above a threshold, and expose the number in `/metrics` or `/props`.
- **Document `--list-devices` as a preflight check** for container deployments.

items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

Commit: `7fe450e19305b828c199d602c23a8337aaa1f03b`.

```console
version: 0.5.0-dev (build 11146, commit 7fe450e19)
built with AppleClang 21.0.0.21000101 for Darwin arm64
```

CPU build:

```sh
cmake -B build -DGGML_METAL=OFF -DGGML_BLAS=OFF -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF -DLLAMA_OPENSSL=OFF -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --target llama-speculative llama-server
```

### Operating systems

Mac, Linux

macOS 27.0; the existing Linux reproduction used Ubuntu 24.04 and gcc 13.3.

### GGML backends

CPU

### Hardware

Apple M1 Pro. The existing Linux results used Intel Xeon CPUs at 2.10 GHz and 2.80 GHz.

### Models

Tiny random Llama target and a noised copy as draft: F32, 2 layers, vocabulary size 8. Each GGUF is 24,064 bytes. The vocabulary is `a` through `h`, with EOS at `h` (id 7). The prompt `bcdbc` is ids `1,2,3,1,2`.

The self-contained archive below has both models and `repro_l3.py`.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`llama-speculative` changes the output distribution at temperature greater than zero, even with `-np 1`.

On this fixture, after a first generated token of `f`, the next token is always `e`. The target's non-speculative distribution at that prefix gives `e` only about 0.345 probability, with the remaining mass on `g` and `h`.

Decode the archive below in the llama.cpp checkout, then run:

```sh
python3 repro_l3.py build/bin/llama-speculative target.gguf draft.gguf 1000
```

The script uses seeds 1 through 1000 and counts the token after a first generated `f`. It uses this command for each seed:

```sh
build/bin/llama-speculative -m target.gguf -md draft.gguf -p bcdbc -n 4 --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  -c 64 -t 1 --cache-type-k f32 --cache-type-v f32 -fa off \
  --samplers 'penalties;top_k;top_p;min_p;temperature' -np 1 \
  --temp 1.0 --top-k 3 --top-p 1.0 --min-p 0.0 --repeat-penalty 1.0 --repeat-last-n 64 -s 11
```

The reference probabilities come from non-speculative `llama-server` with prompt `bcdbcf`, the same sampler settings, `n_probs=8`, and `post_sampling_probs=true`: `e=0.3454894722`, `g=0.4516915679`, `h=0.2028189600`.

Two parts of the example seem to explain the result:

- It samples the draft, sorts its candidates, then takes `cur_p->data[is].id`. With `-np 1`, that is the top candidate, rather than the sampled candidate stored in `selected`. Verification still uses the ratio test with the draft probability.
- On rejection, it sorts the target and draft candidates by token id and subtracts probabilities by array position. With top-k/top-p/min-p truncation, the two arrays can contain different token ids at the same position.

Both lines remain in source at `a3a1c4747fdc0dcad40b3946108b89375d9a7d0e`: [draft selection](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/a3a1c4747fdc0dcad40b3946108b89375d9a7d0e/examples/speculative/speculative.cpp#L570) and [residual subtraction](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/a3a1c4747fdc0dcad40b3946108b89375d9a7d0e/examples/speculative/speculative.cpp#L346). That is a source check; the runtime reproduction above is on the pinned build.

This report concerns `examples/speculative`, rather than the server paths changed by #27694.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected.

### Relevant log output

Fresh Mac run:

```console
seeds 1..1000; runs with first token 'f' (5): 819
  next token 4 ('e'): 1.000   target: 0.345
  next token 6 ('g'): 0.000   target: 0.452
  next token 7 ('h'): 0.000   target: 0.203
```

The saved earlier run had 820 qualifying seeds, with the same next-token frequencies. The script retries the same seed when the example's stdout is incomplete.

Save the base64 block as `repro.zip.b64`, then decode and extract it:

```sh
python3 -c "import base64,pathlib; pathlib.Path('repro.zip').write_bytes(base64.b64decode(pathlib.Path('repro.zip.b64').read_text()))"
python3 -m zipfile -e repro.zip .
