### System Info

CPU only (parser logic, no GPU needed); TensorRT-LLM main @ 534e1f8a.

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

OpenAI function names may contain hyphens (`^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$`). With `--tool_parser kimi_k2`, a model output calling `functions.get-weather:0` (a tool named `get-weather`) is passed to `KimiK2ToolParser.detect_and_parse` / `parse_streaming_increment`.

### Expected behavior

One tool call named `get-weather` with its arguments.

### actual behavior

`detect_and_parse` returns no tool calls and the streaming path never emits one, so the call is silently dropped. The tool-call id and name patterns use `[\w\.]+`, which does not match `-`.

vLLM's Kimi K2 parser accepts such names. I have a fix with a regression test and will open a PR.

items.title: [Bug] Mooncake master startup failure leaves a partially published address behind
items.author: adenzhou1350
items.body_excerpt:
### Problem

On current main `80f1809362f1a1e5d5eafc5ac0e744b98e13f271`, `_published_address` writes every address file before entering its `try/finally`. If publishing the second path fails, the master is stopped by `running_master`/`provision_pool`, but the first address remains and points at the stopped master. A failed `os.replace` also leaves the staging file behind.

### Reproduction

Use a persistent `run_dir` and set `address_file` (or `PoolSpec.master_address_file`) to an existing directory. The first `run_dir/master.addr` is published; replacing the second target raises `OSError`. After context entry fails, the launched master is stopped, but `run_dir/master.addr` and `<address_file>.partial` still exist. This uses actual filesystem operations, not a mocked `os.replace`.

The relevant paths are [publication](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/80f1809362f1a1e5d5eafc5ac0e744b98e13f271/tensorrt_llm/_torch/pyexecutor/connectors/mooncake_store/master.py#L438-L463), [standalone master](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/80f1809362f1a1e5d5eafc5ac0e744b98e13f271/tensorrt_llm/_torch/pyexecutor/connectors/mooncake_store/master.py#L491-L498), and [pool provisioning](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/80f1809362f1a1e5d5eafc5ac0e744b98e13f271/tensorrt_llm/_torch/pyexecutor/connectors/mooncake_store/master.py#L537-L582).

### Proposed fix and checks

I prepared a [small fix with regression tests](https://github.com/adenzhou1350/TensorRT-LLM/commit/2e9863022): cover publication with `try/finally`, retract only successfully published paths, and clean the attempted staging file. The third regression ensures an unvisited path belonging to another master is preserved.

Windows and Linux CPU checks reproduce the three new failures on baseline; the patched master test file passes all 43 cases. These are **isolated leaf-module checks**: complete `config.py`/`master.py` and upstream tests are loaded, with package initializers bypassed and logging substituted; the suite's existing fake master process is used. This is not a claim that the full TensorRT-LLM package, Mooncake binary or GPU tests ran. Ruff lint/format and diff checks pass; the complete pre-commit hook suite was not run.

The same publication-before-finally structure is present in `_published_manifest` on #19171 at `997375ea351df93bf0b269fe8edf13871438bb89`; that renamed path was inspected statically, not executed. I can send the main-branch fix or help adapt it there, depending on the preferred review scope. Following CONTRIBUTING.md, I am requesting issue approval before opening a PR.

items.title: [Bug]: Nemotron dynamic-resolution tiler can return a zero-sized grid or divide by zero for panoramic images
items.author: adenzhou1350
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

Source: main at `f388b7c6a540364f356f200214497cdc34ce642e`.
CPU component reproduction with Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130 and Pillow on Linux. CUDA was hidden and never initialized. No model weights, TensorRT native extensions or server were used.

### Information / Tasks

A small custom CPU reproduction of the unchanged dynamic-resolution preprocessing component. This is not a full-model reproduction.

### Reproduction

From a checkout at the commit above, this runs the complete unchanged tiler class and its two helpers, without importing unrelated model/native dependencies:

```python
import ast
import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple, Union

import torch
from PIL import Image

path = Path("tensorrt_llm/_torch/models/modeling_nemotron_h_multimodal.py")
names = {"_get_media_dimensions", "DynamicResolutionParams", "DynamicResolutionImageTiler"}
tree = ast.parse(path.read_bytes())
nodes = [n for n in tree.body if getattr(n, "name", None) in names]
assert {n.name for n in nodes} == names
ns = dict(globals())
exec(compile(ast.Module(body=nodes, type_ignores=[]), str(path), "exec"), ns)
tiler = ns["DynamicResolutionImageTiler"](
    max_model_len=4096, patch_size=16,
    min_num_patches=256, max_num_patches=4096,
    downsample_ratio=0.5,
    norm_mean=[0.5] * 3, norm_std=[0.5] * 3,
)
for size in [(256, 256), (768, 256), (65536, 16), (16, 65536)]:
    for tokens in [64, 256]:
        try:
            params = tiler.compute_params([Image.new("RGB", size)], tokens)
            print(size, tokens, params[0].patch_size, params[0].num_embeddings)
        except ZeroDivisionError as error:
            print(size, tokens, type(error).__name__, str(error))
assert not torch.cuda.is_initialized()
```

### Expected behavior

Either return a positive patch grid satisfying the pixel-shuffle/token-budget constraints, or reject an unsupported image shape with an explicit validation error. A positive-size image should not result in zero height/width or an unhandled arithmetic exception.

### Actual behavior

Both ordinary-image controls return positive grids. The panoramic cases return:

```text
(65536, 16) 64  (724, 0) 0
(65536, 16) 256 ZeroDivisionError division by zero
(16, 65536) 64  (0, 724) 0
(16, 65536) 256 ZeroDivisionError division by zero
```

### Additional notes

[`process_media`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/f388b7c6a540364f356f200214497cdc34ce642e/tensorrt_llm/_torch/models/modeling_nemotron_h_multimodal.py#L365-L403) floors the scaled patch dimensions before enforcing the minimum patch count. A dimension can become zero. Above the minimum budget, the upscaling division then divides by zero; at the minimum budget, that branch is skipped and zero survives the subsequent divisibility checks.

The normal input-processing path calls this tiler through `_process_images_dynamic` / `compute_params`, but I have not run a real model/server or established a quality-preserving fix. Is there an intended aspect-ratio limit, or should this path handle/validate collapsed patch dimensions? I can contribute a focused regression and fix once the intended behavior is confirmed.

- [x] Searched existing issues/PRs and checked the current implementation. The existing dynamic-resolution feature PRs do not appear to address this boundary.

items.title: How to make Tensor static and only call kernel by pointer?
items.author: peterbjorgensen
items.body_excerpt:
I am trying to turn Python cute dsl kernels into TensorRT QDP Plugins. It restricts the kind of parameters the PTX can have to (input_pointers..., scalar_arguments..., output_pointers...). I have it working for a simple "add_one_kernel" (see the program listing below if interested).

Instead of writing the kernel with pointer arguments, I would like to write it with some StaticTensorPointer class that automatically turns the layout etc. into compile-time variables and only the pointer ends up as a PTX parameter. I guess it's possible with a custom `DynamicExpression`, but I find the documentation a bit vague on this. Any ideas how to achieve this?

Another question: Is it possible to get the shared memory needed for a compiled kernel? I need it for the kernel launch parameters of the kernel in the plugin.

```
import tensorrt as trt
import numpy as np
from quack.cute_dsl_utils import torch2cute_dtype_map
import tensorrt.plugin as trtp
import torch
import torch_tensorrt
import cutlass.cute as cute

from quack.cute_dsl_utils import torch2cute_dtype_map

trt_logger = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.VERBOSE)

STATIC_SHAPE = (16, 16)
STATIC_STRIDE = (1, 16)

@cute.kernel
def add_one_kernel(x: cute.Pointer, y: cute.Pointer):
    STATIC_LAYOUT = cute.make_layout(shape=STATIC_SHAPE, stride=STATIC_STRIDE)
    tensor_x = cute.make_tensor(x, STATIC_LAYOUT)
    tensor_y = cute.make_tensor(y, STATIC_LAYOUT)
    tidx, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
    bidx, _, _ = cute.arch.block_idx()
    idx = bidx * cute.arch.block_dim()[0] + tidx
    if idx < cute.size(tensor_x):
        tensor_y[idx] = tensor_x[idx] + 1

@cute.jit
def apply_add_one_kernel(x: cute.Pointer, y: cute.Pointer):
    BLOCK_SIZE = 256
    num_blocks = (np.prod(STATIC_SHAPE).item() + BLOCK_SIZE - 1) // BLOCK_SIZE

    add_one_kernel(x, y).launch(
        grid = [num_blocks, 1, 1],
        block = [BLOCK_SIZE, 1, 1],
    )


@torch.library.custom_op("my::add_one", mutates_args=())  # type: ignore[misc]
def add_one(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    assert x.is_cuda
    y = torch.empty_like(x)
    input_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[x.dtype]
    y_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, y.data_ptr(), cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)
    x_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, x.data_ptr(), cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)

    compiled = cute.compile(apply_add_one_kernel, x_ptr, y_ptr, options="--keep-ptx")
    compiled(x_ptr, y_ptr)

    return y


@torch.library.register_fake("my::add_one")
def _(X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    return X

@trtp.register("my::add_one")
def add_plugin_desc(X: trtp.TensorDesc) -> tuple[trtp.TensorDesc]:
    # Output has the same shape and dtype as the input.
    return X.like()


@trtp.aot_impl("my::add_one")
def add_plugin_aot_impl(
    X: trtp.TensorDesc, outputs: tuple[trtp.TensorDesc], tactic: int
) -> tuple[
    str | bytes, str | bytes, trtp.KernelLaunchParams, trtp.SymExprs
]:
    # Choose the pointer type based on the input dtype.
    if X.dtype == trt.float32:
        x_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[torch.float32]
    elif X.dtype == trt.float16:
        x_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[torch.float16]
    elif X.dtype == trt.bfloat16:
        x_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[torch.bfloat16]
    else:
        raise ValueError("Unexpected dtype")
    input_dtype = x_dtype
    y_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, 32, cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)
    x_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, 64, cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)

    compiled_kernel = cute.compile(apply_add_one_kernel, x_ptr, y_ptr, options="--keep-ptx")


    # Build symbolic launch parameters.
    BLOCK_SIZE = 256
    num_blocks = (np.prod(STATIC_SHAPE).item() + BLOCK_SIZE - 1) // BLOCK_SIZE
    launch_params = trtp.KernelLaunchParams()
    launch_params.grid_x = num_blocks  # number of thread blocks
    launch_params.block_x = BLOCK_SIZE  # threads per block
    launch_params.shared_mem = 0  # bytes of shared mem (I have no idea how to get this)

    # ``extra_args`` are scalar arguments appended to the kernel's argument list at
    # launch. Here ``n_elements`` is passed as a 32-bit symbolic integer so TRT
    # evaluates it from the actual tensor size at runtime.
    extra_args = trtp.SymIntExprs(0)

    kernel_name_ptx = list(compiled_kernel.kernel_info.keys())[0]
    return (
        kernel_name_ptx,  # kernel function name in PTX
        compiled_kernel.artifacts.PTX,  # PTX source — embedded in TRT engine
        launch_params,
        extra_args,
    )


torch_tensorrt.dynamo.conversion.plugins.generate_plugin_converter(
    "my::add_one",
    supports_dynamic_shapes=False,
    requires_output_allocator=False,
    use_aot_if_available=True,
)


class MyModel(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

    def forward(self, X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        res = torch.ops.my.add_one.default(X)
        return res


if __name__ == "__main__":


    my_model = MyModel().to("cuda").eval()
    m = torch.full(STATIC_SHAPE, 2, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)

    assert my_model(m)[0][0] == 3.0
    assert my_model(m)[1][1] == 3.0

    with torch_tensorrt.logging.debug():
        trt_inputs = [m]
        model_trt = torch_tensorrt.compile(
            my_model,
            inputs=trt_inputs,
            min_block_size=1,
        )
        print("Model compiled successfully!")
        print("Running inference with compiled model...")
        with torch.no_grad():
            for i in range(10):
                res = model_trt(m)
                assert torch.allclose(res, my_model(m)), "Results do not match!"

        program = torch_tensorrt.dynamo.trace(
            my_model,
            arg_inputs=trt_inputs,
        )
        engine_bytes: bytes = torch_tensorrt.dynamo.convert_exported_program_to_seri

items.title: copy_if with a Copy_Atom dispatches on the src slice only and can store out of bounds when dst extents differ
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe C++ - `include/cute/algorithm/copy.hpp`, the `copy_if` overloads

### Describe the bug

`copy_if(Copy_Atom<...>, pred, src, dst)` only static-asserts that src and dst have equal rank; it never compares extents. Per rest-slice it calls `Copy_Atom::call(pred_v, src_v, dst_v)`, and the atom's instruction dispatch tests the vector width against the **src** slice only (`copy_atom.hpp`, `is_constant<NumValSrc, size(src)>`). When dst has a smaller extent, one wide instruction is emitted into the smaller dst slice and stores out of bounds. There is no diagnostic of any kind before the corruption.

The sibling entry point `copy(src, dst)` handles the same mismatch safely: its vectorization machinery recomputes `max_common_vector`/alignment from both layouts and degrades to elementwise copies.

Minimal repro (host-only, ASan):

```cpp
#include <cute/tensor.hpp>
#include <cute/algorithm/copy.hpp>
#include <cstdio>
using namespace cute;

int main() {
  float sa[12], da[6];
  Tensor src = make_tensor(&sa[0], Shape<_4,_3>{});   // 12 elems
  Tensor dst = make_tensor(&da[0], Shape<_2,_3>{});   // 6 elems (typo)
  bool m[12]; for (int i=0;i<12;++i) m[i]=true;
  Tensor prd = make_tensor(&m[0], Shape<_4,_3>{});

  copy_if(Copy_Atom<UniversalCopy<uint128_t>, float>{}, prd, src, dst);
}
```

```
$ g++ -std=c++17 -g -fsanitize=address ... && ./a.out
==30==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow ...
WRITE of size 16 at 0x... thread T0
    #2 cute::copy_unpack<...> (include/cute/atom/copy_atom.hpp)
    #3 cute::Copy_Atom<...>::call(...)
    #4 cute::copy_if<...> (include/cute/algorithm/copy.hpp:69)
```

With plain `copy(src, dst)` on identical shapes the program runs ASan-clean and produces correct results, so the two entry points disagree on error behavior for the same misuse.

The generic elementwise `copy_if` at `copy.hpp:44-62` has a milder version of the same pattern: it bounds the loop by `size(dst)` and indexes `pred(i)`/`src(i)` without any cross-check.

### Expected behavior

Either a compile-time/static diagnostic when `size(src) != size(dst)` per rest-slice (mirroring what `copy()` effectively enforces), or dispatch keyed off both slices. Raw atom calls are normally fed by `TiledCopy` partitioning which guarantees matching widths, so this may be an accepted contract - but today the failure mode is silent memory corruption on a plausible typo, where the sibling API reports nothing yet also does the right thing.

### Environment details

- Current main, header-only, host-only repro (no GPU needed), g++ + AddressSanitizer

items.title: Example 64 (Ada FP8 grouped GEMM) refuses capable GPUs via exact CC 8.9 gate
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

examples/64_ada_fp8_gemm_grouped/ada_fp8_gemm_grouped.cu (~line 1107) gates execution on exactly compute capability 8.9:

```cpp
if (!(properties.major == 8 && properties.minor == 9)) {
    std::cerr << "... requires a device of compute capability 89." ...
```

The grouped FP8 kernels here compile cleanly for newer architectures, and the sibling example 58_ada_fp8_gemm uses the inclusive form:

```cpp
if (properties.major < 8 || (properties.major == 8 && properties.minor < 9))
```

On an RTX 5060 Ti (sm_120a, CUDA 12.8.1) the stock binary exits immediately with the capability message; with the gate relaxed to the sibling's form the example builds and runs to completion including device-reference verification (`Passed`). Example 64 is therefore refusing capable hardware for no functional reason.

### Suggested fix

Use the same `major*10+minor < 89` / `major < 8 || (major == 8 && minor < 9)` inclusive check as example 58.

items.title: linear_cross_entropy: chunked fast path is gated on is_cuda rather than the capabilities it requires
items.author: dwoai22
items.body_excerpt:
### Problem

`torch.nn.functional.linear_cross_entropy`'s chunked implementation has a fast path that avoids several scratch allocations by letting `mm` upcast internally via `out_dtype=`. Whether that path is taken is decided by `is_cuda` (`torch/nn/modules/linear_cross_entropy.py:486` on main), which is consulted by eleven downstream flags.

XPU implements every overload this path uses, but cannot reach it:

| Operator | native_functions.yaml | Dispatch |
|---|---|---|
| `mm.dtype_out` | 4164 | `CUDA: _mm_dtype_out_cuda`, `XPU: _mm_dtype_out_xpu` |
| `addmm.dtype_out` | 7092 | `CUDA`, `XPU` |
| `bmm.dtype_out` | 1387 | `CUDA`, `XPU` |
| `baddbmm.dtype_out` | 1066 | `CUDA`, `XPU` |

On XPU the module instead allocates `logits_acc_buf` and `input_chunk_acc_buf` and performs explicit casts it does not need. Since the purpose of this module is to avoid materializing the `(num_batches, num_classes)` logits tensor for large vocabularies, the unnecessary scratch is a direct cost to the case it exists to serve.

### Root cause

`is_cuda` is not wrong - CUDA is the only backend that satisfies both properties it stands for - but it bundles two independent capabilities under a name that mentions neither:

| Capability | Question | Uses |
|---|---|---|
| `mm(out_dtype=)` support | Can `mm` write a destination whose dtype differs from its operands? | 10 |
| fp32 GEMM accumulator | Does a same-dtype `addmm_` keep an fp32 accumulator internally? | 1 |

The second gates skipping a `(num_classes, in_features)` weight-grad scratch and is only observable at `grad_linear_weight.addmm_(logits_downcast.T, input_chunk)`, the single bf16 x bf16 -> bf16 GEMM in the file. Because the two travel together under one device name, a backend cannot satisfy or declare one without the other, and nothing in the file states what a new device would need.

The file's own comment acknowledges the situation as temporary:

```python
# CUDA gates the out_dtype= mm fast path; the non-CUDA path
# (CPU, MPS, XPU, ...) routes mixed-dtype mm through explicit
# casts until out_dtype= is validated on those backends.
```

### A second blocker on the same path

Enabling XPU needs one more change, in a different function. `LinearCrossEntropyOptions._resolve_auto_acc_dtype` (`torch/nn/modules/linear_cross_entropy_options.py:216`) returns fp32 only for CUDA and CPU. On XPU `acc_dtype` therefore never resolves to fp32 under `acc_policy="auto"`, `use_acc_dtype` stays `False`, and every gate above evaluates `False` regardless. Reaching the path today requires an explicit `acc_dtype=torch.float32`.

That check is a third, distinct capability - "does this device have hardware fp16/bf16 support" - and is dtype-dependent (CUDA gates bf16 at SM 8.0 and fp16 at SM 7.0). Both `torch.cuda` and `torch.xpu` expose `is_bf16_supported()`, though there is no fp16 counterpart and neither `torch.cpu` nor `torch.mps` provides either.

### Proposed fix

Split `is_cuda` into two named capability helpers, each with its own list of validated device types and a docstring stating what to verify before adding one. Behavior-preserving on its own; enabling XPU would then be a separate change with its own numerics validation, alongside the `_resolve_auto_acc_dtype` counterpart above. So, proposed solution does not add a new backend, but creates a structure that can be extended with multiple backends after they are validated.

Happy to send a PR if this is something the maintainers want.

### Versions

Source-structure issue, reproducible by reading the files. Observed against main at `3b4bcd4f227` (2026-08-20), `2.15.0a0+git3b4bcd4`.

items.title: [Inductor] `torch.add(inp, mm, alpha=...)` silently drops `alpha` (post-grad `addmm` fusion)
items.author: gau-nernst
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


```python
import torch

def f(inp, x, w):
    return torch.add(inp, x @ w, alpha=0.5)

inp, x, w = torch.randn(8, 8), torch.randn(8, 8), torch.randn(8, 8)
torch.testing.assert_close(torch.compile(f)(inp, x, w), f(inp, x, w))
```

```
AssertionError: Tensor-likes are not close!

Mismatched elements: 64 / 64 (100.0%)
Greatest absolute difference: 4.97156286239624 at index (3, 2) (up to 1e-05 allowed)
Greatest relative difference: 29.210800170898438 at index (1, 1) (up to 1.3e-06 allowed)
```

The compiled result equals `inp + x @ w`, i.e. `alpha` is ignored. Reproduces on CPU and CUDA, fp32 and bf16, with and without grad.
Correct with `pattern_matcher=False` or `backend="aot_eager_decomp_partition"`.

The following analysis was produced with an AI assistant (Claude);

> The `addmm` graph pattern in `torch/_inductor/fx_passes/post_grad.py` (`pass_patterns[2]`) matches
> `aten.add(inp, aten.mm(a, b))` in both operand orders and replaces it with `aten.addmm(inp, a, b)`.
> Neither the pattern nor `is_valid_addmm_fusion` checks `aten.add`'s `alpha` kwarg, and the pattern
> matcher drops kwargs a pattern doesn't declare, so `alpha` is lost. This is unchanged on current `main`.
> Same bug class in other passes: #196577 / #196588 (`decompose_addmm` drops `alpha`/`beta`), #195442
> (`batch_aten_sub` drops `alpha`). A fix could pin `alpha=1` in the pattern / check it in the
> extra_check, or forward it (`addmm(inp, a, b, alpha=alpha)` for `add(inp, mm)`, `beta=alpha` for
> `add(mm, inp)`).


### Error logs

_No response_

PyTorch version: 2.14.1+cu130 (git 5c4886908584029761b579af026dcfb627c84070)
CUDA used to build PyTorch: 13.0
OS: Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS (x86_64)

items.title: [Bug] Sync prefix indexer hashes every block of a BlockStored event against the first block's parent
items.author: ankit373
items.body_excerpt:
### What's wrong

`SyncPrefixHashTable.ProcessBlockStored` (`pkg/utils/syncprefixcacheindexer/sync_hash.go`) computes the AIBrix hash of every block in a `BlockStored` event from the same parent:

```go
for i, engineBlockHash := range event.BlockHashes {
    ...
    var parentAibrixHash = s.seed
    if event.ParentBlockHash != nil {
        if ph, exists := hashMapping.engineToAibrix[*event.ParentBlockHash]; exists {
            parentAibrixHash = ph
        }
    }
    aibrixHash := s.computeHash(parentAibrixHash, s.getBlockTokens(event, i))
```

`ParentBlockHash` is the parent of the first block only. Block `i > 0` should chain from block `i-1` of the same event. On the request path `GetPrefixHashes` builds a proper chain (`H(seed, b0)`, `H(h0, b1)`, ...), so every block after the first in a multi-block event gets a hash the gateway never produces.

vLLM emits one `BlockStored` per batch of newly full blocks, so a long prefill arrives as a single event with many blocks (the decoder splits the tokens per block in `convertTokenIDs`). In practice prefix matching from KV events stops after the first block of each event.

### Repro

Table with block size `bs`, three blocks `b0 b1 b2`:

```go
table.ProcessBlockStored(BlockStored{BlockHashes: []int64{1, 2, 3}, Tokens: [][]byte{b0, b1, b2}, ...})
table.MatchPrefix(model, -1, b0+b1+b2, {pod})
```

Expected 100, got 33. Same for an event whose first block was already known (33), and an event continuing from a parent block (66 instead of 100).

The existing `TestProcessBlockStored` only counts mappings, so it passes either way.

### Fix

Look up the parent once, then carry the previous block's AIBrix hash through the loop, including the already-mapped branch.

items.title: [RFC]: Autoscaler-driven elastic EP: observe-first staging, membership semantics, and failure rules
items.author: bolubo
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

AIBrix's PodAutoscaler scales replicas, and for MoE serving that unit is coarse: one replica can span dozens of GPUs, and traffic rarely varies in whole-replica quanta. vLLM can now resize DP/EP membership at runtime (`enable_elastic_ep`, `POST /scale_elastic_ep`, `POST /is_scaling_elastic_ep`, plus the DP-coordinator wave protocol), and #2288 asks AIBrix to drive it, starting observe-only. This RFC proposes how that drive should work, staged as observe, act, and graceful draining, and focuses on the platform-side semantics that are missing today: aligning three divergent states (Kubernetes resources, engine-committed membership, routable capacity), treating an engine resize as a transaction inside a reconcile loop, and writing down failure rules before production discovers them. The proposal is deliberately conservative: default off, hold rather than auto-recover, never act on unverified state. The observe stage is already in flight (#2812); we are asking for feedback on the act-side semantics before implementing them.

### Motivation

Whole-replica scaling is coarse and expensive for MoE: one replica may span dozens of GPUs, and traffic variation is rarely a whole-replica quantum. The engine now exposes the levers to resize DP/EP membership at runtime, but nothing in AIBrix drives them. Existing platform attempts in this space are either heavy (new CRDs, gated off) or still exploratory, and the upstream external-orchestration contract is not frozen yet (vllm/vllm#42515, vllm/vllm#43202).

**Benefit hypothesis (to be measured).** Two effects decide whether elastic EP is worth enabling. Sub-replica demand changes can be absorbed inside a footprint instead of moving whole replicas, which makes capacity quantization finer and avoids provisioning for step peaks; and ramps can be served as soon as the engine commits new ranks, without waiting for new pods. The cost side is the commit window (the engine answers 503 while resizing) and the added control complexity this RFC addresses. Enabling is least attractive when demand is stable at whole-replica quanta or when the window is not acceptable for the served workload. We plan to measure the deciding axes on one node first (time to add capacity for a width move versus a replica move, GPU-hours per unit of served traffic under bursty load, and error budget consumed during commit windows); multi-footprint economics need a larger setup and remain future work.

Three properties make this harder than an HPA-style target:

1. **Three states, not one.** Kubernetes knows which pods and processes exist; the engine knows which ranks are committed; the router knows which endpoints can take traffic. These states move at different speeds and in different orders: during a scale-up, capacity exists before the engine accepts it; during scale-down, the engine stops first and capacity is reclaimed after; after a rank failure, the desired state is unchanged while the engine serves degraded. "Replica count" cannot express any of this.

2. **A transaction inside a control loop.** An engine resize is a one-shot operation that takes tens of seconds, has intermediate states, and has no generic rollback. Today's known upstream bugs include a cancel path that corrupts engine state without rollback (vllm/vllm#57691) and a scale-up crash under EAGLE3 + CUDA graphs (vllm/vllm#58479). Kubernetes reconciliation, by contrast, assumes idempotent, replayable steps with eventual convergence; it has no word for "commit or hold". That gap has to be designed rather than coded ad hoc.

3. **No failure vocabulary.** Every step can fail quietly: partial joins, a controller restarting mid-commit, outcomes that cannot be verified after a timeout. Writing down the required behavior for these cases is the core of this RFC.

### Proposed Change

| Stage | What it adds | State |
|---|---|---|
| 0: observe | record engine scaling state in PodAutoscaler status; no decisions | in flight (#2812) |
| 1: act | opt-in width changes with transaction discipline and gates | this RFC |
| 2: draining | gateway policy for the engine's 503 window | this RFC (design) |

**Stage 0: observe (in flight: #2812).** PodAutoscaler records whether a scaling commit is in progress on the target's elastic-EP engines in `status.elasticEPScaling` (`inProgress`, `observedEngines`, `scalingEngines`, `lastTransitionTime`; no width read exists yet). No replica decisions change. This gives operators visibility and gives the controller a trustworthy read path for Stage 1.

**Stage 1: act with guardrails (opt-in, default off).** For deployments that enable elastic EP and opt in:

1. Read the **committed** width from the engine; never trust the last requested value.
2. Use target semantics: ask the engine to *be N* (the engine call takes `new_data_parallel_size` and a `drain_timeout`, default 120s), not to add one, so retries and re-ordering are harmless.
3. Treat each call as a transaction inside reconcile: one bounded operation per attempt (call, wait for commit up to a bound, verify, record the outcome, continue).
4. Gate every operation: never act while the engine reports scaling; never act on degraded or partially committed membership; enforce a settle window and hysteresis so a tens-of-seconds operation cannot oscillate.
5. Re-read state every reconcile; the controller never trusts its own last command (level-triggered).
6. Single writer for width: while act mode is on, the controller is the intended single writer for width; other writers are outside this contract and are surfaced as drift (F7).

**Stage 2: graceful draining.** While a commit is in flight, the engine answers 503 to all requests, including readiness probes. In our single-node test (4 x RTX 4090 48G, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, DP 2 to 4) the window lasted 37.2s on scale-up and 15.3s on scale-down; the raw evidence is recorded in #2812. The window affects the data plane of the deployment as a whole, not only the resized ranks. AIBrix holds the autoscal

items.title: [Feature][Gateway] Decode watchdog for SGLang PD requests whose decode pod stops responding
items.author: qidaye
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 Feature Description and Motivation

With SGLang PD disaggregation, the prefill request only returns once the decode pod has accepted the KV transfer. So when the gateway's prefill leg succeeds, the decode pod owes the client a response.

If the decode pod stops answering at that point, nothing in the gateway notices. This happens when its scheduler dies or wedges, either before the first token or in the middle of a stream.
- The client waits until Envoy's route timeout. For streaming LLM routes that timeout is usually very long or disabled.
- The routing context, and the load it holds on the chosen pods, stays live for the whole wait.
- The decode pod keeps the request's KV pages, because nobody tells it to drop the request.

The PD fail-fast path covers a prefill leg that fails. Nothing covers a decode leg that goes silent after a successful prefill.

### Use Case

SGLang PD deployments behind the aibrix gateway, where a decode pod can hang without its container exiting. Without a bound, such a pod turns every request routed to it into a client-side hang instead of a fast, retryable error.

### Proposed Solution

Add a decode watchdog to the ext_proc stream loop. It is armed only for requests that carry a gateway-owned `rid` (SGLang PD), and it has two phases.

1. **First response.** After the prefill leg succeeds, the decode pod has to send its first message within:
   - `AIBRIX_DECODE_FIRST_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT` for a streaming request (default 60s);
   - `AIBRIX_DECODE_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT` for a non-streaming request (default 0, off). Here the first message is the finished answer, so a safe value depends on `max_tokens`.

   On expiry the client gets a 504 with `x-error-pd-decode: true`, and the ext_proc stream is closed with `DeadlineExceeded`.

2. **Stream idle.** After the decode pod has started answering, `AIBRIX_DECODE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT` (default 120s) bounds the gap between two of its messages. Every message re-arms it.

   The response is already half-delivered, so no error response can be sent. Instead the ext_proc stream is closed with `DeadlineExceeded`, and Envoy resets the connection.

In both phases:
- the gateway sends one best-effort `/abort_request` for the `rid` to the decode pod;
- the request is counted as failed with `status="pd_decode_watchdog"`;
- a new counter `gateway_pd_decode_watchdog_total{phase}` records the kill;
- every timeout can be overridden per config profile under `routingConfig.pd`, and `0` disables it.

Planned as two PRs:
- first response (504 + abort);
- stream idle (stream reset + abort).

Each PR comes with unit tests, a mock-engine e2e test and docs.

### Area

Gateway

items.title: Runtime and metadata-service nightly images are unexpectedly large (~970 MB)
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

The current ARM64 nightly images for `aibrix/runtime` and `aibrix/metadata-service` are both approximately 970 MB unpacked:

```text
aibrix/runtime:nightly           970MB
aibrix/metadata-service:nightly  970MB
```

This appears unusually large for the runtime and metadata-service processes and is worth investigating.

Both images are built from `build/container/Dockerfile.python`, which installs the dependencies declared by the AIBrix Python wheel. The largest image layer is the `pip install` layer at approximately 814 MB.

## Measurements

| Component | Approximate size |
|---|---:|
| Debian + Python base layers | 156 MB |
| Final `pip install` layer | 814 MB |
| `site-packages` | 844 MiB |

The largest installed distributions are:

| Distribution | Size |
|---|---:|
| scipy | 142 MiB |
| pandas | 74 MiB |
| numpy | 59 MiB |
| plotly | 58 MiB |
| scikit-learn | 55 MiB |
| PuLP | 38 MiB |
| matplotlib | 37 MiB |
| dash | 32 MiB |
| kubernetes | 30 MiB |

Most of the scientific-computing and visualization imports appear under `aibrix.gpu_optimizer`, rather than the runtime or metadata-service entry points. Their installed dependency closure accounts for approximately 584 MiB.

There is also a mismatch between the Dockerfile comment and the package metadata: the Dockerfile says the profiling group is excluded to avoid packages such as pandas and matplotlib, but those packages are currently declared as main dependencies in `python/aibrix/pyproject.toml`. Therefore, `--without profiling` does not exclude them.

The two image names are also built independently from the same Dockerfile. In the inspected nightly builds, their large dependency layers have different digests, so those layers are not shared even though their installed contents and sizes are nearly identical.

## Impact

- Longer image pull and node startup times
- More registry and node storage usage
- Slower scale-out and cold starts for runtime workers
- Longer CI image builds and duplicate uploads
- Larger dependency and vulnerability-scanning surface

## Possible Changes

The exact implementation should be decided after confirming the dependency requirements of every published entry point. Possible changes include:

- Audit direct and transitive dependencies for `aibrix_runtime`, `aibrix_metadata`, `aibrix_batch_worker`, downloader, and GPU Optimizer.
- Adjust Python package metadata and container build targets so each published image installs only the dependencies required by the processes it runs.
- Preserve the storage backends and Kubernetes integrations currently supported by each entry point.
- If two published images remain identical, build the image once and apply both tags so their layers have the same digest.
- Correct the stale Dockerfile comment about excluded dependencies.
- Add image-size reporting or a regression threshold to CI, together with container smoke tests for the affected entry points.

The GPU Optimizer currently runs from `aibrix/metadata-service:nightly`, so any dependency changes must also update or preserve that deployment path.

## Environment

- Architecture: ARM64
- Tags: `nightly`
- Observed image sizes: approximately 970 MB each

items.title: [Bug] ModelAdapter ignores matchExpressions in podSelector
items.author: btxu-db
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

The ModelAdapter controller ignores `matchExpressions` in `spec.podSelector`. `getActivePodsForModelAdapter` lists pods with `client.MatchingLabels(instance.Spec.PodSelector.MatchLabels)`, so only `matchLabels` reaches the List call.

What this does in practice:

- A selector with only `matchExpressions` has empty `matchLabels`, so it matches every pod in the namespace. The adapter gets loaded on pods running a different base model.
- A selector that uses both picks up pods the expressions should have excluded.

`ModelClaim` already converts its selector with `metav1.LabelSelectorAsSelector`, so the two controllers behave differently for the same kind of selector.

### Steps to Reproduce

kind, AIBrix from `main`, `aibrix/vllm-mock:nightly` from `development/app` as the engine.

Three Deployments in one namespace, one pod each, labeled:

- `base-stable`: `model=base, tier=stable`
- `base-canary`: `model=base, tier=canary`
- `other-model`: `model=other`

Two adapters:

```yaml
apiVersion: model.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1
kind: ModelAdapter
metadata:
  name: lora-expr-only
spec:
  baseModel: base
  podSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - {key: model, operator: In, values: [base]}
  artifactURL: /models/lora-expr-only
---
apiVersion: model.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1
kind: ModelAdapter
metadata:
  name: lora-mixed
spec:
  baseModel: base
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: {model: base}
    matchExpressions:
    - {key: tier, operator: NotIn, values: [canary]}
  artifactURL: /models/lora-mixed
```

Result:

```
NAME             PHASE     CANDIDATES   INSTANCES
lora-expr-only   Running   3            [other-model-... base-stable-... base-canary-...]
lora-mixed       Running   2            [base-canary-... base-stable-...]
```

`/v1/models` on the pods confirms the adapters were actually loaded there: `other-model` has `lora-expr-only`, and `base-canary` has `lora-mixed`.

### Expected behavior

The full selector should be used, same as for any other `LabelSelector`. `lora-expr-only` should land on `base-stable` and `base-canary` only, and `lora-mixed` on `base-stable` only.

Fix is to build the selector with `metav1.LabelSelectorAsSelector` and pass it with `client.MatchingLabelsSelector`. I have a patch for this and will open a PR.

### Environment

- AIBrix: `main` @ `dcc8aa9a`
- Kubernetes: kind v1.30.0, 1 control-plane + 1 worker
- Engine: `aibrix/vllm-mock:nightly` from `development/app`

### Area

ModelAdapter / LoRA

items.title: [BUG | QST] CPU overhead regression with TVM-FFI
items.author: kainzhong
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**
In v4.6 update, the following is changed in `python/CuTeDSL/cutlass/cutlass_dsl/cutlass.py`:
```
-                if kwargs_wrapper_spec.kwonly_names or kwargs_wrapper_spec.arg_defaults:
+                # Route through the kwargs-capable compiled class whenever
+                # the signature has kwonly/defaults OR any positional arg
+                # carries a dataclass instance (detected by the spec
+                # converter, including Union[...] over dataclasses). The
+                # kwargs wrapper is the only place tvm-ffi's
+                # ``map_dataclass_to_tuple`` unpack hook fires.
+                if (
+                    kwargs_wrapper_spec.kwonly_names
+                    or kwargs_wrapper_spec.arg_defaults
+                    or kwargs_wrapper_spec.arg_names
+                    or map_dataclass_to_tuple
+                ):
```
So basically if a @cute.jit function satisfies one of the following:
- `kwonly_names`: have keyword only arguments (indicated by *)
- `arg_defaults`: have default arguments
- `arg_names`: have any argument that is not a keyword only argument
- `map_dataclass_to_tuple`: have dataclass arguments

With these restrictions (especially `kwonly_names` and `arg_names`), basically only a CuTeDSL function with no arguments can go to the else branch and become a `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunction` which is a subclass of `tvm_ffi.Function` so they get to be called in C++ and bypass python completely. For CuTeDSL functions with arguments, they now have to go through the `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunctionWithKwargs` path.

This will slightly slow down calling a CuTeDSL function from python due to extra python layers from in `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunctionWithKwargs`, which isn't a big deal since python is slow anyway. However, if you register the CuTeDSL function via tvm-ffi and call it from C++, the overhead becomes obvious because you will leave C++ and enter python (`TVMFFIJitCompiledFunctionWithKwargs.__call__`) and then enter the compiled CuTeDSL function. This makes the CPU overhead regress compared to pre-4.6 version since there wasn't going through python with GIL and argument wrapper stuff.

I also wonder what's the motivation behind this. My guess is this makes a @cute.jit function behave more like a python function where it can use kwargs instead of can only be called using positional args, but meanwhile when we do want to call it with positional args (in C++) this only makes it slower.

Currently there is a hack to fix this, which is instead of registering the compiled CuTeDSL function, we can register its `__tvm_ffi_object__` which would be a `tvm_ffi.Function` object, and we need to guarantee the args order is exactly the same in C++. I feel it's a bit hacky and fragile as cutlass evolves. 

Another proposition of mine is we can tell users (probably in docs) that if they define CuTeDSL functions in this format: `def func(a, b, c, /)` with nothing after / and no default values, then we can optimize this case into a `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunction` because we know nobody will use kwargs in this case. I think if this fix is OK I can open a PR on it.

Not sure what's the opinion of the CUTLASS people?

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**
I think my explanation should be clear enough so I don't think I need an example to reproduce.
You can just follow the example in https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/pull/3289 and measure the CPU time to notice the difference.

**Expected behavior**
Should be faster?

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
This regressed after v4.6 update

**Additional context**
Add any other context about the problem here.

comments.body:
Hi @kainzhong, thanks for reaching out! This is a known issue for us. Your understanding is correct - the condition you mention is generally `true`, except the trivial functions without any args. But per our benchmark, the overhead it introduces is < 1us, while the overall launch overhead is typically <10 us. We think it is fine to keep this overhead for compatibility of diversed inputs. And we agree to have more documents here. Any PR is appreciated.

items.title: Deadlock risk between snapshot restore and segment mount (segment_mutex_ / client_mutex_ ordering)
items.author: quantz8a
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

`MasterService::ApplySnapshotState()` reverses the lock order used by `MountSegment()` / `UnmountSegment()`, which can deadlock when snapshot restore races with a client mount or unmount.

## Affected path

- `ApplySnapshotState()` obtains an exclusive lock on `SegmentManager::segment_mutex_` via `segment_manager_.getSegmentAccess()` (`mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp:11232`).
- While still holding that lock it calls:
  - `UnmountSegment()` (`:11238`), and
  - `Ping(client_id)` (`:11248`).
- Both of those paths acquire `client_mutex_`:
  - `Ping()` does `std::shared_lock<std::shared_mutex> lock(client_mutex_)` (`:8405`).
  - `UnmountSegment()` does `std::shared_lock<std::shared_mutex> client_lock(client_mutex_)` (`:3127`) before re-acquiring `segment_mutex_` (`:3133`).

## Reverse order in the other callers

- `MountSegment()` first takes `client_mutex_` exclusively (`:900`) and then, inside its liveness callback, takes `snapshot_mutex_` and `segment_mutex_` via `segment_manager_.getSegmentAccess()` (`:909-:913`).
- `UnmountSegment()` takes `client_mutex_` before `segment_mutex_` as shown above.

So the code has both:

1. `segment_mutex_ (unique) -> client_mutex_ (shared)` in `ApplySnapshotState()`.
2. `client_mutex_ (unique) -> segment_mutex_ (unique)` in `MountSegment()`.

## Deadlock scenario

- Thread A is in `ApplySnapshotState()`: it holds `segment_mutex_` exclusively and blocks trying to take `client_mutex_` (via `Ping`).
- Thread B is in `MountSegment()`: it holds `client_mutex_` exclusively and blocks trying to take `segment_mutex_` (via `getSegmentAccess()`).

A and B wait on each other, forming a classic ABBA deadlock. The same inconsistent ordering exists for the snapshot-restore unmount path.

## Suggested fix

Do not call `UnmountSegment()` or `Ping()` while holding the snapshot-restore `segment_mutex_` hold. Collect the unready/all segment lists under `segment_mutex_`, release the lock, then unmount/ping/metric-update outside the lock. See the accompanying PR.

/cc @kvcache-ai/mooncake-core

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Verified both deadlock faces on current main (`ApplySnapshotState` at master_service.cpp:11142):

1. Self-deadlock on the unready path. The function holds `ScopedSegmentAccess` (unique on `segment_mutex_`) and calls `UnmountSegment` for each unready segment; `UnmountSegment` itself enters `ScopedSegmentAccess` at :3133. `std::shared_mutex` is non-recursive, so a second unique lock on the same thread is UB and blocks in practice. Any restore that actually has unready segments wedges the master right there.
2. ABBA on the ping path. Still holding `segment_mutex_`, it calls `Ping`, which takes `client_mutex_` shared (:8405). `MountSegment` takes `client_mutex_` exclusive first (:900) and then enters `getSegmentAccess()` in its liveness callback. Restore racing a client mount has each side waiting on the other.

So this is two distinct defects in one function, and the collect-then-act shape the issue suggests covers both.

One overlap worth settling before review effort gets duplicated: #4022 (Sep 11) already implements the same collect-under-lock, act-outside restructure for the unready path, with a test, and has been sitting without comments for three weeks. #4419 is the minimal version of the same idea. Same root cause, same fix shape; one of them should absorb the other. There is also prior art in #3152 (closed unmerged), which attacked the adjacent `snapshot_mutex_` ordering in this same function, in case the ordering argument there is still useful.

Context for prioritization: my open #3806 rewrites the repair side of this restore path. Whichever of #4022/#4419 lands, I will rebase and adapt #3806 to the new locking, so merging one of them does not strand the tolerance work.

items.title: torch.onnx.export produces invalid int32 QuantizeLinear
items.author: kyunggeunlee
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Problem Description
When exporting `torch.ops.quantized_decomposed.quantize_per_tensor` to ONNX, `torch.onnx.export` produces invalid ONNX QuantizeLinear nodes with output_dtype=int32.
According to ONNX spec, [QuantizeLinear](https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__QuantizeLinear.html) does not support int32; only [DequantizeLinear](https://onnx.ai/onnx/operators/onnx__DequantizeLinear.html) does.

### Suggestion
* `torch.onnx.export` should stop exporting int32 QuantizeLinear, **\*\*or\*\***
* ONNX spec should be extended to allow int32 as output dtype of QuantizeLinear

### How to Reproduce
```py
import onnx
import torch
import torch.ao.quantization.fx._decomposed
import onnx_ir


class Int32Quantize(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, input: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return torch.ops.quantized_decomposed.quantize_per_tensor(
            input,
            0.01,
            0,
            -2**31,
            2**31 - 1,
            torch.int32,
        )


def main():
    """
    Problem 1.
    ONNX QuantizeLinear doesn't support int32 quantization,
    but torch.onnx.export produces int32 QuantizeLinear
    """
    torch.onnx.export(
        Int32Quantize(),
        (torch.randn(10, 10),),
        "int32_quantize.onnx",
        input_names=["input"],
        output_names=["output"],
        dynamo=True,
        opset_version=21,
    )
    onnx_model = onnx_ir.load("int32_quantize.onnx")
    q, = onnx_model.graph.all_nodes()
    print(f"\nQuantizeLinear output_dtype: {q.inputs[-1].dtype}")

    """
    Problem 2. onnx model checker fails to detect int32 QuantizeLinear
    """
    onnx.checker.check_model(onnx_ir.to_proto(onnx_model))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```
```
[torch.onnx] Obtain model graph for `Int32Quantize()` with `torch.export.export(..., strict=False)`...
[torch.onnx] Obtain model graph for `Int32Quantize()` with `torch.export.export(..., strict=False)`... ✅

[torch.onnx] Optimize the ONNX graph...
[torch.onnx] Optimize the ONNX graph... ✅

QuantizeLinear (name: node_quantize_per_tensor) output_dtype: INT32
```

comments.author: anubhavagr
comments.body:
@justinchuby @titaiwangms — sharing my analysis of this issue and a proposed fix below:

### Root cause: 
With `dynamo=True`, `quantized_decomposed::quantize_per_tensor` is translated by onnxscript's torchlib (`onnxscript/function_libs/torch_lib/ops/quantized_decomposed.py`), which passes the quantized `dtype` straight into `QuantizeLinear`'s zero point. ONNX `QuantizeLinear`'s type constraint T3 (zero point and output) does not include int32, so exporting with `torch.int32` produces an invalid model. `DequantizeLinear` is unaffected — int32 is a valid input type there.

Of the dtypes the quantized_decomposed ops accept (`torch/ao/quantization/fx/_decomposed.py`:  uint8, int8, uint16, int16, int32, float8_e5m2, float8_e4m3fn), **int32** is the only one `QuantizeLinear` cannot emit — and it is a real use case (int32 bias quantization).

### Proposed fix (PyTorch side): 
Register repo-local implementations in `torch/onnx/_internal/exporter/_torchlib/ops/`, which take precedence over the onnxscript ones:

- dtypes `QuantizeLinear` supports: keep emitting `QuantizeLinear`;
- int32: lower to the PyTorch reference formula `clamp(round(input / scale) + zero_point, quant_min, quant_max).to(int32)` via
  Div/Round/Add/Clip/Cast — the same approach the legacy TorchScript exporter already uses for int32 bias requantization (`requantize_bias_helper` in `symbolic_helper.py`);
- same treatment for `quantize_per_channel` (broadcast scales/zero_points along `axis`).

I have a working implementation with e2e tests in `test/onnx/exporter/test_small_models_e2e.py` (numerics verified against onnxruntime for int8/uint8/int32, per-tensor and per-channel). Happy to send a PR if this approach sounds good.

Side note: the second problem in the report — `onnx.checker` not flagging the invalid int32 `QuantizeLinear` — looks like an onnx/onnx checker gap and probably deserves a separate issue in that repo.

items.title: `tt.scan`/`tl.cumsum` hits an internal `AddPartialReduce` assert when `num_ctas > 1`
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
Launching a kernel that runs `tl.cumsum` (any `tt.scan`) under a multi-CTA layout (`num_ctas >= 2`) triggers an internal consistency assertion in the scan lowering:

```
triton-opt: .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157:
void AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
```

**Expected**: either a clean diagnostic telling the user that scan is not supported under multi-CTA layouts, or correct codegen.
**Actual**: the internal assert fires. On a bare `triton-opt` run this is a `SIGABRT`; through the Python frontend the same assertion is surfaced as an opaque `RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed` after the assert text is printed, rather than a user-facing diagnostic.

The assert exists to catch a block-count mismatch, and it does — but the failure mode gives the user no hint that `num_ctas` is the problem.

This is **not** the same defect as the batched-dot `num_ctas` crash fixed by #11811 / reported in #11808. That bug lived in `TritonNvidiaGPUAssignCGALayoutsPass` (a rank mismatch while *assigning* the CGA layout). The IR reproducer below never runs that pass — the `CGALayout` is already written into the encoding and it crashes later, inside `ConvertTritonGPUToLLVM`'s scan lowering. On the Python frontend the same kernel does go through `AssignCGALayouts` successfully and only aborts at lowering. So this survives the #11811 fix; I have not rebuilt past that commit to confirm on current `main`, but the failing code path (`ScanOpToLLVM`, not `AssignCGALayouts`) is untouched by it.

## Reproducer 1 — `tl.cumsum` + `num_ctas=2`

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def scan_k(x_ptr, o_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, AX: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N)
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :])
    r = tl.cumsum(x, axis=AX)
    tl.store(o_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], r)

x = torch.randn(32, 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
o = torch.empty(32, 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
scan_k[(1,)](x, o, 32, 32, 0, num_ctas=2)   # <- num_ctas=2 triggers it
```

Output (the assert message is emitted, then the pipeline reports a generic failure):

```text
python: .../ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157: ... AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
...
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```

`num_ctas=1` compiles and runs correctly. The crash is independent of the scan axis and of which tensor dimension the CGA layout splits.

## Reproducer 2 — `triton-opt` (offline, no GPU)

`repro.mlir`:

```mlir
#b = #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread=[1,1],threadsPerWarp=[1,32],warpsPerCTA=[4,1],
                  order=[1,0], CGALayout=[[1,0]]}>
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas"=2:i32,"ttg.num-warps"=4:i32,
                   "ttg.threads-per-warp"=32:i32} {
  tt.func @p(%v:tensor<32x32xf32,#b>) {
    %r = "tt.scan"(%v) <{axis = 0 : i32, reverse = false}> ({
    ^bb0(%a:f32,%b:f32):
      %s = arith.addf %a, %b : f32
      "tt.scan.return"(%s) : (f32) -> ()
    }) : (tensor<32x32xf32,#b>) -> tensor<32x32xf32,#b>
    tt.return
  }
}
```

```text
$ triton-opt repro.mlir --allocate-shared-memory-nv \
    --convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm=compute-capability=90 -o /dev/null
triton-opt: .../ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157: ... AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
(SIGABRT, exit 134)
```

## Controls

- **`num_ctas=1`** (drop the `CGALayout`): compiles cleanly (rc 0).
- **`tt.reduce` with the same 2-CTA `CGALayout`**: compiles cleanly **and produces numerically correct output** (`tl.sum` + `num_ctas=2` matches the reference). Reduction lowering accounts for the CTA dimension; scan lowering does not.
- The assert fires for every scan configuration I tried: any scan axis, 2D or 3D tensors, `num_ctas=2` or `4`, and CGA splits on either dimension. The gap is systemic to `tt.scan` under multi-CTA, not tied to one config.
  - The **same assertion text is reached at two sites**, chosen by how many warps carry unique data along the scan axis (`axisNumWarps`). With the layouts Triton picks for the Python reproducer, `axis=0` goes through `AddPartialReduce` at `ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`, while `axis=1` on a 2D tensor (and the scan axis of a 3D tensor) takes the `axisNumWarps==1` fast path and fires the identical assert inside `AddPartialReduceOneWarp` at `ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:263`. A hand-written layout that puts several warps on the scan axis hits `:157` instead — so the site is decided by `axisNumWarps`, not by rank. Both come from the same `ScanLoweringHelper` block-count math, so the suggested fix below covers both.

<details>
<summary>Relevant native stack frames (triton-opt)</summary>

```text
#17 AddPartialReduce(...)
      .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:184:63
#21 (anonymous namespace)::ScanOpConversion::emitFastScan(
      mlir::triton::ScanOp, ..., mlir::triton::TargetInfoBase const&) const
      .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:522:3
#22 ConvertOpToLLVMPattern<mlir::triton::ScanOp>::matchAndRewrite(...)
#27 (anonymous namespace)::OperationLegalizer::legalize(mlir::Operation*)
```
</details>

Note on the two line numbers: the assert that fails is at **`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`** (the `numScanBlocks * ... == srcValues.size()` check). The `#17` frame prints `184:63` because `-O2` attributes the inlined cold `__assert_fail` block to the next source line — the `__assert_fail` call is preceded by `mov $0x9d, %edx` (`0x9d = 157`), confirming the assert's own line argument is 157. The `#18–#20` frames are inlined `SmallVector` destructors on the same PC, not real calls.

## Root cause

`AddPartialReduce` (`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`) asserts:

```cpp
assert(numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelE

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Verified against current main (`aad2a60d9`, local `triton-opt` built with `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`, pinned LLVM 24.0.0git): this is fixed by #11990.

Running the exact pipeline from the report (`--allocate-shared-memory-nv --convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm=compute-capability=90`):

| config | result |
|---|---|
| repro as posted (scan axis 0, `CGALayout=[[1,0]]`, split along the scan axis) | clean `error: TODO: unsupported scan layout`, exit 1, no assert |
| scan axis 1, split along axis 1 | same clean error |
| scan axis 0, `CGALayout=[[0,1]]` (split along the non-scan axis) | compiles, exit 0 |
| scan axis 1, split along axis 0 | compiles, exit 0 |
| `num_ctas=1` control | compiles, exit 0 |

No SIGABRT anywhere. The two assert sites (`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157` and `:263`) are still in the tree but no longer reachable from these inputs. The mechanism matches the #11990 description: scan-axis CTA splits now fail `ScanLoweringHelper::isSupported()` via `getCTASplitNum(...)[axis] != 1`, and non-scan-axis partitions use the per-CTA shape in `getNonAxisNumBlocks()` / `getAxisBlockStride()`, which is what the assert's block-count product needed.

One observation in case anyone touches this code: the rejection text is the pre-existing placeholder `TODO: unsupported scan layout`, which does not tell the user that `num_ctas` is the trigger. Not worth a PR on its own, but if the scan-axis case is meant to stay unsupported, naming the cause there would save the next person a source build.

Suggest closing this as fixed by #11990.

items.title: [Enhancement] Attention backend selection: name every fallback, reject invalid configs early
items.author: DhineshPonnarasan
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

TensorRT-LLM's PyTorch path selects an attention backend from `VANILLA` / `TRTLLM` / `FLASHINFER` via the `attn_backend` configuration. The current selection behavior has several gaps that make it hard to answer "which backend am I actually running, and why":

- An invalid or unknown `attn_backend` value is not rejected. `get_attention_backend()` logs a generic warning (`Falling back to TRTLLM attention backend`) and selects `TRTLLM`, so a typo can silently change the executed backend — along with its supported features and performance characteristics.
- A genuinely unavailable backend (e.g. `FLASHINFER` requested where the package is not installed) takes the same undifferentiated fallback path and is indistinguishable from an invalid name.
- Some backend-dependent constraints are detected late. The attention-sinks and relative-attention-bias `TRTLLM` requirements are asserted during forward execution, after the cost of a full build; this class of late failure has already surfaced in user reports (#13156).
- Some backend-dependent fallback/degradation messages do not clearly identify the backend or reason involved (e.g. rope-fusion handling), and at least one eligibility gate disables with no message.
- Backend selection is redundantly resolved on the per-layer construction path (`Attention.__init__` resolves the backend class, then `create_attention` resolves it again internally).

Requested behavior, stated as observable behavior rather than implementation:

- Validate backend names at configuration time against the supported set, with an actionable error listing valid values for invalid input.
- Make every backend fallback identify the requested backend, the reason it could not be selected, and the selected fallback.
- Move backend-dependent checks earlier (configuration/construction) where technically possible, while retaining genuinely runtime-dependent checks at runtime with improved diagnostics.
- Eliminate redundant backend dispatch during attention construction.
- Add no-GPU regression coverage for backend selection decisions.
- Preserve existing behavior for all valid configurations, and explicitly document the intentional change that invalid input raises instead of silently selecting `TRTLLM`.

### Alternatives

Several alternatives were considered.

Keeping the current generic warning-only behavior does not address invalid configuration input or late validation — the warning neither names the problem nor prevents a wasted build.

Introducing a large MoE-style or general attention resolution framework would be larger than necessary for the current backend-selection problem, which involves three backend classes and a small set of knowable conditions.

Extending only the existing `_resolve_*` feature-level checks would not address name validation, availability handling, or selection-time decisions because those checks operate inside an already-selected backend.

Redesigning FMHA/FmhaManager or FlashInfer internal kernel dispatch is also out of scope because inner-kernel selection is a separate layer with different inputs and constraints.

This request is therefore scoped to the existing attention backend selection/configuration boundary, leaving those layers untouched.

### Additional context

Verified against upstream `main` at commit `14729d4a3a` (synchronized with `origin/main`):

- The fallback warning in `tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/backends/utils.py` remains generic.
- `attn_backend` in `tensorrt_llm/llmapi/llm_args.py` remains a string field without supported-value validation.
- The attention-sinks / relative-attention-bias checks in `tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/attention.py` remain forward-time.
- Redundant backend resolution remains in the construction path.
- No dedicated selection/fallback test coverage was found; existing tests exercise backends rather than the selection decisions.

Related upstream PRs and issues — including #13156, #14635, #14942, #15417, #17800, #18025, #18520, and the FMHA selection work — were reviewed, and no exact or substantial duplicate of this proposal was found. They are cited here as precedent and context.

Testing plan:
- Parameterized no-GPU unit-test matrix covering backend × sparse configuration × FlashInfer availability × MLA/chunked and mocked capability conditions.
- Existing attention and `llmapi` test suites.
- Small-model integration runs confirming unchanged valid-configuration behavior.
- T4 validation of applicable FP16 selection and degradation paths.

I have access to a Tesla T4 (SM75, 16 GB) and will validate the applicable FP16 selection and degradation paths on real hardware. Newer-architecture-specific behavior will rely on mocked capability tests and existing CI hardware.

This proposal does not attempt to restore SM75/T4 kernel support.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the [documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/) and [examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples) for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL >= 4.6: FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward with block-sparse masks spills registers, up to 1.8x slower than 4.5.3 (same kernel source)
items.author: janhuenermann
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

With the same kernel source, CuTe DSL 4.6.0.dev0 and later generate PTX for the FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward kernel (`flash_attn.cute.flash_bwd_sm100.FlashAttentionBackwardSm100`) that spills registers. The spills appear when the kernel is specialized for block-sparse attention with a `mask_mod`. That is the path `torch.nn.attention.flex_attention(..., kernel_options={"BACKEND": "FLASH"})` takes. With CuTe DSL 4.5.3, the same source compiles to PTX with no spills, or almost none. The kernel is at the 128-register cap (512 threads per CTA), so the extra pressure becomes local-memory traffic. On B200 the backward kernel is 22% slower with a sliding-window mask and 82% slower with a document mask. The dense, causal, GQA and native `window_size` specializations of the same kernel are not affected.

This looks like the backward counterpart of #3701 (forward kernel, 4.7/4.8 vs 4.5.1), and it narrows down where the regression landed. 4.5.3 is fine. 4.6.0.dev0 already regresses, and it is the first release whose PTX header says `Based on NVVM 23.0.0` (4.5.3: `NVVM 20.0.0`).

**Backward kernel GPU time**, ms (B200, bf16, head dim 128, 16 heads; median of 50; main backward kernel only, from the torch profiler; a repeat run agrees within 1% for the block-sparse rows and within 5% for the others)

| attention | 4.5.3 | 4.6.0.dev0 | 4.8.0 ¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| full, batch 2 × 8192 | 2.039 | 2.010 (−1%) | 2.084 |
| causal, 2 × 8192 | 1.121 | 1.140 (+2%) | 1.177 |
| GQA causal (32 q / 4 kv heads), 2 × 8192 | 2.287 | 2.266 (−1%) | 2.366 |
| native sliding window 1024 (`window_size`), 2 × 16384 | 0.714 | 0.713 (0%) | 0.756 |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: sliding window 1024**, 2 × 16384 | 0.858 | **1.045 (+22%)** | **1.027 (+20%)** |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: document mask** (causal within random-length documents), 1 × 32768 | 1.279 | **2.329 (+82%)** | **2.209 (+73%)** |

The 4.5.3 and 4.6.0.dev0 columns run the same FA4 source (b20, see "Same source" below).
¹ The 4.8.0 column runs FA4 4.0.0b32, the latest release at the time of testing (b33 has a byte-identical backward kernel). FA4 changed between b20 and b32, so this column shows that the regression persists; it is not a clean A/B.

**The same PTX files assembled by one ptxas** (CUDA 13.0, V13.0.88, `ptxas -arch=sm_100a -O3 -v`)

| backward specialization | PTX from | spill stores / loads | SASS instr. | IMAD | STL / LDL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| causal | 4.5.3 (CUDA 12.9 / NVVM 20.0.0) | 0 / 0 B | 3496 | 242 | 0 / 0 |
| causal | 4.6.0.dev0 (CUDA 13.3 / NVVM 23.0.0) | 0 / 0 B | 3360 | 216 | 0 / 0 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.5.3 | 0 / 0 B | 3800 | 294 | 0 / 0 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.6.0.dev0 | 124 / 228 B | 4528 | 703 | 31 / 57 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.8.0 (CUDA 13.4 / NVVM 23.0.0) ¹ | 260 / 264 B | 4192 | 318 | 65 / 55 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.5.3 | 28 / 16 B | 4512 | 653 | 7 / 4 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.6.0.dev0 | 204 / 204 B | 5952 | 1049 | 51 / 42 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.8.0 ¹ | 184 / 184 B | 5456 | 968 | 46 / 37 |

All of these are at 128 registers (`.reqntid 512`), with warp-specialized budgets (`setmaxnreg.inc` 136/152, `setmaxnreg.dec` 88/24). The PTX files have no `.local` declarations, so ptxas introduces the spills from register pressure in the NVVM 23 PTX. The SASS that 4.8.0 ships through its own ptxas has 50 STL / 42 LDL for the document mask and 35 / 26 for the sliding window (causal: 2 / 2).

**Likely pressure region.** `CUTE_DSL_COMPILER_OPT="remarks{ptx}" CUTE_DSL_LINEINFO=1` on 4.8.0 marks `flash_attn/cute/block_sparse_utils.py:1564` in `get_block_sparse_iteration_info_bwd`. That line loads the block-sparse count and index tensors: `curr_q_cnt = q_cnt[batch_idx, head_idx, n_block]` and `q_idx[batch_idx, head_idx, n_block, None]`. #3701 found the same kind of small metadata-tensor load for the forward kernel (`cu_seqlens` in the varlen scheduler). Here the IMAD count rises together with the spills (document mask: 653 → 1049). We suspect the address arithmetic of these indexed loads, but have not verified it.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

The attached `nvvm23-sm100-bwd-repro.zip` has the scripts, the nine PTX files and our raw results. Its README has more detail.

*1. No GPU needed.* Assemble the attached PTX pair:

    152 bytes stack frame, 204 bytes spill stores, 204 bytes spill loads
```

```

pip install torch==2.14.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130

items.title: DGX Spark (SM121) Current Support Audit
items.author: kahyunnam
items.body_excerpt:
# FlashInfer — DGX Spark (SM121) Current Support Audit

**Date:** 2026-04-24
**Scope:** Audit of SM121 (compute capability 12.1, DGX Spark) support across FlashInfer ops, APIs, backends, and testing.
**Goal:** Improve Spark usability on FlashInfer by identifying existing gaps.

**Note: skip to "15. Consolidated Action Items" for TLDR.**

---

## Architecture Context

| Gencode | Target | CUDA Requirement |
|---------|--------|------------------|
| `compute_120a` / `sm_120a` | RTX 5090 (SM120) | CUDA 12.8 |
| `compute_120f` / `sm_120f` | SM12x family (120 + 121) | CUDA 12.9 |
| `compute_121a` / `sm_121a` | DGX Spark (SM121) | CUDA 12.9 |

### SM120 vs SM121: Implications for FlashInfer

Per the [CUDA 13.2 Programming Guide — Compute Capabilities](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.2.0/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html) (Tables 29–33), SM120 and SM121 share a single "12.x" spec column: identical shared memory (99 KB/block, 100 KB/SM), warps (48/SM), registers (64K/SM), tensor core data types (TF32, BF16, FP16, FP8, FP6, FP4, INT8), TMA, and cluster support. [Table 28](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.2.0/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html#compute-capabilities-family-specific-compatibility) confirms `compute_120f` is compatible with **both** CC 12.0 and 12.1. The chip-level differences (SM121 = aarch64 host, unified LPDDR5x, 84 SMs vs SM120's x86_64, discrete GDDR7, up to 170 SMs) do not affect kernel correctness — only SM-count-based heuristics and host toolchain.

### `f` vs `a` compilation targets: performance implications

Per the [PTX ISA 9.3](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/index.html) (§9.7.15.5.14 for dense `mma`, §9.7.15.6.3 for sparse `mma.sp`), `120f` (family) is a subset of `120a`/`121a` (arch-specific). Most SM12x features — including **dense** NVFP4/MXFP4 block-scaled MMA — are family-specific and available via `120f` from PTX ISA 8.8. The arch-specific restriction (requiring `sm_120a`/`sm_121a`) applies **only to sparse MMA** (`mma.sp`) with `.kind::mxf4nvf4`/`.kind::mxf4`:

| PTX Feature | `compute_120` (baseline) | `compute_120f` (family) | `compute_120a` / `compute_121a` (arch) |
|-------------|--------------------------|------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| FP4/FP6/FP8 conversions (`cvt`) | No | Yes | Yes |
| FP4/FP6 MMA, block-scaled MMA (`.kind::mxf8f6f4`) | No | Yes | Yes |
| **Dense** NVFP4 MMA (`.kind::mxf4nvf4`) | No | **Yes** (PTX ISA ≥ 8.8) | **Yes** |
| **Dense** MXFP4 MMA (`.kind::mxf4`) | No | **Yes** (PTX ISA ≥ 8.8) | **Yes** |
| **Sparse** NVFP4 MMA (`mma.sp` `.kind::mxf4nvf4`) | No | **No** | **Yes** |
| **Sparse** MXFP4 MMA (`mma.sp` `.kind::mxf4`) | No | **No** | **Yes** |

FlashInfer's b12x GEMM kernel (`dense_blockscaled_gemm_sm120_b12x.py`) uses `cute.nvgpu.warp.MmaMXF4NVF4Op` — a **dense** block-scaled MMA atom. This means `sm_120f` wheels already emit native NVFP4/MXFP4 dense MMA instructions. Only **sparse** NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA (not currently used in FlashInfer) requires `sm_120a`/`sm_121a`.

> **Correction (2026-06-12):** An earlier version of this table stated that ALL `.kind::mxf4nvf4`/`.kind::mxf4` MMA was arch-specific-only. Per [Harry-Chen's feedback](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/3170#issuecomment-4677810517) and PTX ISA §9.7.15.5.14 vs §9.7.15.6.3, the restriction is limited to the sparse (`mma.sp`) variant.

### Wheel build arch targets

The release wheel CI (`.github/workflows/release.yml`) builds the following SM12x targets:

| CUDA Version | SM12x target in `FLASHINFER_CUDA_ARCH_LIST` |
|---|---|
| < 12.9 | `12.0a` (SM120 arch-specific; no SM121 support) |
| >= 12.9, < 13.0 | `12.0f` (family; covers SM120 + SM121; includes dense NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA) |
| >= 13.0 | `12.0f` (same) |

**No `121a` target is included in any wheel build.** However, since FlashInfer's FP4 kernels use **dense** block-scaled MMA (`MmaMXF4NVF4Op`, not sparse), the `120f` wheels already emit native NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA instructions. The `121a` target would only be needed for future sparse MMA kernels. JIT compilation on SM121 still produces `121a` cubins for forward-compatibility.

### What this means for FlashInfer

- **Any kernel that runs on SM120 is architecturally compatible with SM121.** Hardcoded `sm_version == "sm_120"` or `minor == 0` checks in backend dispatch are over-restricting without justification.
- **Separate cubins matter for JIT but not for wheels.** `CompilationContext` correctly emits `sm_121a` for JIT on SM121. Since FlashInfer uses only dense block-scaled MMA (available on `120f`), the wheels do not lose FP4 GEMM performance. The `121a` JIT path provides forward-compatibility for future sparse MMA use.
- **SMEM capacity maps, tile configs, and MMA atoms are identical.** Code using `get_smem_capacity_in_bytes("sm_120")` returns the correct value for SM121 too — the only risk is `KeyError` if a map expects an `"sm_121"` key and doesn't have one.

### Key utility functions

| Function (`utils.py`) | Behavior for SM121 |
|------------------------|--------------------|
| `is_sm12x_supported` | True (CUDA ≥ 12.9) |
| `is_sm121a_supported` | True (CUDA ≥ 12.9) |
| `is_sm120a_supported` | **False** (12.0 only) |
| `device_support_pdl` | True (`major >= 9`) |
| `determine_attention_backend` | Returns `fa2` (fa3 is SM90-only) |
| `determine_gemm_backend` | Returns `sm80` (no SM12x branch) |

---

## 1. Attention

### 1.1 Decode (batch paged KV)

| Backend | CC Gate | SM121 Status | Notes |
|---------|---------|--------------|-------|
| **fa2** | Generic | **Supported** | Default via `determine_attention_backend` for non-FP8 tensor-core decode |
| **fa3** | SM90 only | **Not available** | `determine_attention_backend` returns fa3 only on SM90 |
| **xqa** | `major in {9, 10, 12}` | **Supported** | `trtllm_batch_decode` auto → xqa when `major != 10` |
| **trtllm-gen** | `major == 10` only | **Not available** | Auto selects this

items.title: torch.fx.Tracer.record_stack_traces is broken in torch 2.4.0
items.author: gilfree
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.fx.Tracer` has a `record_stack_traces` member. It does not give the correct stack trace, starting with torch  2.4 RC.

I am not sure it is part of the external API, but it was nice to have. The following is working in 2.3, but broken in 2.4RC


```python
import torch.fx
class M1(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = torch.nn.Linear(1, 1)
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.linear(x)
class M2(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.m1 = M1()
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.m1(x)
m = M2()
tracer = torch.fx.Tracer()
tracer.record_stack_traces=True
graph = tracer.trace(m)
sym=torch.fx.GraphModule(m,graph)
print(sym.print_readable())
assert 'code: return x + self.linear(x)' in sym.print_readable()
assert 'code: return x + self.m1(x)' in sym.print_readable()
```

It was broken in this PR: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/121449/ where you stopped using the find_user_frame (or an equivalent function) to filter non user stack traces.

Something along these lines can be probably used as a fix:

```python
    def create_proxy(self, kind, target,args, kwargs, name, type_expr = None, proxy_factory_fn = None):
....
     if self.record_stack_traces and not proxy.node.stack_trace:
            proxy.node.stack_trace = _find_user_frame2_4(''.join(CapturedTraceback.extract().format()))


    def _find_user_frame2_4(self, stack_trace):
        stack_trace=stack_trace.split('\n')
        if 'torch/fx/proxy.py' in stack_trace[-3]:
            stack_trace=stack_trace[:-1]
            while len(stack_trace)>2 and '/fx/' in stack_trace[-2]:
                stack_trace=stack_trace[:-2]
        return '\n'.join(stack_trace)
```

Notes:
- I am not sure why you don't see the effect in `torch.export.export`.
- `torch.export.unflatten` looses stack trace for collapsed modules.
