items.title: SM120: pip-installed FlashInfer missing CUTLASS/CCCL headers — all JIT compilation fails with `cutlass/arch/arch.h` not found
items.author: xzwgit
items.body_excerpt:
## Environment

- GPU: 8× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (SM120, cc 12.0)
- Driver / CUDA: 595.71.05 / CUDA 13.2.2
- FlashInfer: 0.7.1 (installed via `pip install .` from main) — also confirmed with the 0.7.0 wheel
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04.5
- vLLM: nightly dev511 (calls FlashInfer JIT for `mxfp8_gemm_cutlass_sm120`)

## Problem

The pip-installed FlashInfer package does not include the CUTLASS and CCCL headers needed for SM120 JIT compilation. The release wheels ship pre-built JIT cache only for `sm100a` (datacenter Blackwell); SM120 kernels are **JIT-only**, so the headers are required at runtime — but they are absent from `flashinfer/data/include/`.

Every JIT compilation on SM120 fails with:

```
flashinfer/data/include/flashinfer/gemm/mxfp8_gemm_cutlass_template...
    25 | #include "cutlass/arch/arch.h"
       |          ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
compilation terminated.
RuntimeError: Ninja build failed.
```

This makes any vLLM version that triggers FlashInfer's SM120 JIT path (recent nightlies call `gen_gemm_sm120_module_cutlass_mxfp8()` for MXFP8 GEMM) completely unable to start on consumer Blackwell.

## Root cause

The JIT env resolves these include paths:

```python
from flashinfer.jit import env
env.CUTLASS_INCLUDE_DIRS  # → flashinfer/data/cutlass/include, data/cutlass/tools/util/include
env.CCCL_INCLUDE_DIRS     # → flashinfer/data/cccl/cub, data/cccl/libcudacxx/include, data/cccl/thrust
```

But the installed package's `data/` directory contains only `include/` (flashinfer's own headers) and `csrc/` — no `cutlass/`, `cccl/`, or `spdlog/` directories. The 3rd-party submodules exist in the source tree (`3rdparty/cutlass`, `3rdparty/cccl`, `3rdparty/spdlog`) but are not copied into the installed package by `setup.py`.

## Workaround (verified)

Symlink the source-tree submodule headers into the installed package:

```bash
FI=$(python -c "import flashinfer, os; print(os.path.dirname(flashinfer.__file__))/data")
FLASHINFER_SRC=<path-to-flashinfer-source>

ln -sf $FLASHINFER_SRC/3rdparty/cutlass $FI/cutlass
ln -sf $FLASHINFER_SRC/3rdparty/cccl   $FI/cccl
ln -sf $FLASHINFER_SRC/3rdparty/spdlog $FI/spdlog
rm -rf ~/.cache/flashinfer/  # clear stale JIT cache
```

After this, all SM120 JIT kernels compile successfully (verified: full DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash serving on 8× RTX PRO 6000 starts and runs correctly).

## Suggested fix

One of:
1. **Bundle the headers**: copy `3rdparty/{cutlass,cccl,spdlog}` into the wheel's `data/` directory (the source is already a git submodule, just needs to be included in `setup.py`'s `package_data`)
2. **Ship SM120 pre-built kernels**: add `flashinfer_jit_cache_sm120` wheels (like the existing `sm100a` ones) so JIT is not needed
3. **Fallback gracefully**: when CUTLASS headers are missing and the target is SM120, emit a clear diagnostic pointing to the workaround instead of the opaque ninja error

Option 1 is the smallest change and benefits all SM120 users immediately.

## Additional context

- Release assets only include `flashinfer_jit_cache_sm100a-*` — no SM120 variant exists
- The `flashinfer_jit_cache-*` (non-arch-specific) wheels are 4.4 KB shims that depend on architecture-specific provider wheels — there is no SM120 provider
- This was verified independently on two machines: a fresh `pip install .` from a clean clone reproduces the issue; copying the headers fixes it

items.title: Auto GID selection picks a non-routable link-local GID on routed RoCEv2 fabrics using RFC1918 (10.0.0.0/8)
items.author: Lzy17
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary
On a routed RoCEv2 fabric where the RoCE IPv4 addresses live in RFC1918 space
(e.g. 10.0.0.0/8), automatic GID selection (when no explicit GID index is set)
picks a non-routable link-local GID instead of the routable IPv4 GID. Cross-node
QPs then never reach RTR and every cross-node transfer fails.

### Environment
- Transport: RDMA (RoCEv2), auto-GID (no `MC_GID_INDEX` / `gid_index < 0`)
- Fabric: routed RoCEv2, RoCE NIC IPv4 in 10.102.0.0/16 (i.e. inside 10.0.0.0/8)

### GID table (per rdma0, representative)
| index | type    | GID                       | address      |
|-------|---------|---------------------------|--------------|
| 0     | RoCE v2 | fe80::0690:81ff:fe37:a9e8 | link-local   |
| 1     | RoCE v2 | ::ffff:0a66:0965          | 10.102.9.101 |

### Root cause
`isOverlayIPv4` flags 10.0.0.0/8 (and 172.16/12, 100.64/10) as an "overlay"
address, so the routable IPv4 GID (index 1) is classified as
`kNetworkDegraded`. A network-backed link-local GID (index 0) is also classified
as `kNetworkDegraded`. With both candidates in the same class, the stable
tie-break on ascending `gid_index` selects index 0 — the link-local GID. A
`fe80::` GID cannot route across subnets, so the QP never reaches RTR:

    Failed to modify QP to RTR ... timed out [110]

### Impact
Any routed RoCEv2 deployment using RFC1918 10/8 (etc.) addressing must currently
work around this by pinning `MC_GID_INDEX` manually. A flat-L2 fabric that
exposes a normal (non-overlay) routable IPv4 GID is unaffected.

### Proposed fix
Rank a network-backed link-local GID strictly below every network-backed IPv4
GID (routable and degraded/overlay alike), so link-local is only chosen when no
network-backed IPv4 GID exists. PR to follow.

items.title: [Bug]: ~6 s fixed per-request latency on sm120 (4x RTX 5060 Ti TP4) with Qwen3.5 hybrid-GDN NVFP4 27B — 1.3.0rc29
items.author: sean640112
items.body_excerpt:
# ~6 s fixed per-request latency floor on sm120 (4× RTX 5060 Ti, TP4) with a Qwen3.5 hybrid-GDN 27B NVFP4 checkpoint

## Summary

On a 4× RTX 5060 Ti (sm120) box serving a **dense hybrid GDN + full-attention 27B** NVFP4 checkpoint with `trtllm-serve` (PyTorch backend, TP4), we measure a **~6 s per-request floor on time-to-first-token that is independent of prompt length**. A 212-token request takes **6.06 s** to first token (8.0 s total), and the floor persists at every length we tested (212 → 59,571 tokens). Requests are reproducible to ±5 ms across 12 measurements in 3 separate server starts.

The same hardware, same checkpoint, same prompt, same client, served by SGLang gives **0.26–0.30 s** for the identical request. `trtllm-serve` therefore looks ~20× slower on short requests, while its *marginal* prefill throughput is only ~2.6× lower (~2,143 tok/s vs ~5,600 tok/s).

We have ruled out MTP/spec-decode, scheduler policy, `max_seq_len`, chunked prefill, the CUDA caching allocator, and thinking-mode as causes (details below). We would like to know whether this per-request floor is **expected on sm120 for hybrid GDN models**, or a bug — and which knob/diagnostic we should look at next. We are happy to run any instrumentation you suggest.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | 4× NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, compute capability **12.0 (sm120)**, TP=4 |
| Driver | 610.57.04 |
| CUDA toolkit | 13.3 (`nvcc` 13.3, `CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-13.3`) |
| OS / Python | Linux, Python 3.12.11 (venv) |
| TensorRT-LLM | **1.3.0rc29.dev202609240000** (nightly from 2026-09-24; PyPI 1.2.1 does not contain `modeling_qwen3_5.py`, hence nightly) |
| torch | 2.14.0+cu132 |
| flashinfer-python | 0.6.18 |
| triton | 3.8.0 |
| nvidia-cutlass-dsl | 4.8.0.dev0 |
| tensorrt / tensorrt_cu13 | 10.14.1.48.post1 |
| MPI | OpenMPI 5.0.10 (`mpi4py` bootstrap path) |
| Model | `nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` — `architectures: ["Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration"]`, `model_type: qwen3_5`; 64 layers, hidden 5120, 24 Q heads, 4 KV heads |
| Quantization | ModelOpt `MIXED_PRECISION`: **FP8 per-tensor on 208 layers** (`block_size` absent) + **NVFP4 `group_size: 16` on 193 layers**, `kv_cache_quant_algo: null` |

Note on the attention backend: your hardware support matrix lists sm120 as supporting NVFP4 / MXFP4 / FP8 (per-tensor) / FP8 KV cache, which covers this checkpoint's formats — so the quantization scheme itself should be fully supported on sm120.

## How to reproduce

Server (the `mpirun -n 1` wrapper and `OMPI_MCA_*` are needed on this host because `import tensorrt_llm` otherwise blocks in the mpi4py `MPI.COMM_WORLD` initialization, and this host's own hostname resolves to loopback only):

```bash
export CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-13.3
export OMPI_MCA_btl_tcp_if_include=lo OMPI_MCA_oob_tcp_if_include=lo
mpirun -n 1 --oversubscribe trtllm-serve serve /path/to/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 1234 --tp_size 4 \
  --max_seq_len 140000 --max_batch_size 8 \
  --served_model_name qwen3.8-27b \
  --free_gpu_memory_fraction 0.80 \
  --extra_llm_api_options opts.yaml
```

`opts.yaml`:
```yaml
enable_chunked_prefill: true
max_num_tokens: 8192
speculative_config:
  decoding_type: MTP
  max_draft_len: 3
  speculative_model: /path/to/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4
```

Client — a minimal stdlib-only streaming client (this is the "probe" used for every number below; it measures the first chunk that carries `choices[0].text`/`delta.content`):

```python
import json, time, urllib.request
prompt = open("/path/to/corpus.txt").read()[:600]          # → 212 tokens
body = {"model": "qwen3.8-27b", "prompt": prompt, "max_tokens": 1, "temperature": 0, "stream": True}
req = urllib.request.Request("http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1/completions",
        data=json.dumps(body).encode(), headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
t0 = time.time(); ttft = None
with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=900) as r:
    for raw in r:
        s = raw.decode().strip()
        if not s.startswith("data: "): continue
        if s[6:] == "[DONE]": break
        d = json.loads(s[6:])
        ch = d.get("choices") or []
        if ch and ch[0].get("text"):
            ttft = time.time() - t0; break
print("TTFT", ttft)
```

## Measured results (same probe, same prompts, same box)

| prompt tokens | path | TRT-LLM stream TTFT | TRT-LLM non-stream total | SGLang stream TTFT | SGLang non-stream total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **212** | completions | **6.053–6.062 s** (n=5) | 7.995–8.035 s | **0.262 s** | 0.304 s |
| 222 | chat (medium template) | 12.11 – **22.21 s** (unstable across restarts) | 14.06 – 26.19 s | 0.268 s | — |
| 7,172 | completions | 10.10 s | 12.02 s | 0.243 s *cached* | 1.84 s *cached* |
| 12,131 | completions | 12.12 s | 14.06 s | — | — |
| 28,008 | completions | — | 20.13 s | — | 6.15 s *cached* |
| 59,571 | completions | — | 36.26 s | — | — |
| 65,032 | chat | 56.52 s | 56.45 s | — | — |

*("cached" = the SGLang side hit its radix prefix cache on the shared corpus prefix, so those cells are not a like-for-like prefill comparison.)*

Least-squares fit of the completions path (`total = C + N/R`, 5 points spanning 212 → 59,571 tokens):
**C = 8.10 s, R = 2,143 tok/s, R² = 0.9966** — i.e. a very large constant plus a modest rate term. (The streaming TTFT is ≈ 1.9 s lower at every point, i.e. TTFT ≈ 6.1 s + N/2143.)

For reference, an independent client (vLLM's `bench serve` against the same server) measured prefill throughput of **453 / 1,014 / 1,302 tok/s** at 8K / 32K / 64K with meanTTFT 16.15 / 29.28 / 46.44 s, i.e. the same shape: mostly a constant, with the rate part improving with length.

The SGLang side on this box (same checkpoint, TP4, DFlash2, fp8 KV, same client) measures ~5,600 tok/s marginal prefill and a per-request overhead of ≲0.3 s. So the fixed component, not the rate, is what dominates short requests for us.

## What we ruled out (each was an actual A/B on a server restart)

| Variant | tiny-request TTFT | 8K-prefill |
|---|---|-

CuTe DSL

@cute.jit

    print("coalesced:", cute.coalesce(layout))
    print("expected: ", expected)


tensor = from_dlpack(torch.empty((4096, 8192), device="cuda"))
tensor = tensor.mark_compact_shape_dynamic(mode=1)
repro(tensor)
```

input:     (16,?):(8,128)

items.title: numeric_limits< float_e2m3_t / float_e3m2_t >::lowest() returns a small negative value instead of the format minimum
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`numeric_limits<cutlass::float_e2m3_t>::lowest()` and `numeric_limits<cutlass::float_e3m2_t>::lowest()` return values near -1.8 / -1.75 instead of the most negative finite value of each format. The same wrong constant is used in the `std::` specializations, the `cutlass::platform::` specializations, and the `float_e2m3_unpack8bits_t` / `float_e3m2_unpack8bits_t` variants, six call sites in total.

The type's own metadata disagrees with the hardcoded constant: `BitRepresentation::MIN_VALUE` for both formats is `0x3F`, and `max()` (which uses `MAX_VALUE = 0x1F`) is correct.

### Evidence

For E2M3 (bias 1) the most negative finite pattern is `0x3F` (`s=1, exp=11, man=111`, value -(1+7/8)*2^2 = -7.5). The code returns `bitcast(0x2f)`, which decodes to `s=1, exp=01, man=111` = -1.875.

For E3M2 (bias 3) the most negative finite pattern is `0x3F` (`s=1, exp=111, man=11`, value -(1+3/4)*2^4 = -28). The returned `0x2f` decodes to `s=1, exp=011, man=11` = -1.75.

Repro (g++ -std=c++17 -O2 against include/ only):

```cpp
#include "cutlass/float_subbyte.h"
#include <cstdio>
#include <limits>

int main() {
    printf("e2m3: max=%g lowest=%g\n",
        float(std::numeric_limits<cutlass::float_e2m3_t>::max()),
        float(std::numeric_limits<cutlass::float_e2m3_t>::lowest()));
    printf("e3m2: max=%g lowest=%g\n",
        float(std::numeric_limits<cutlass::float_e3m2_t>::max()),
        float(std::numeric_limits<cutlass::float_e3m2_t>::lowest()));
}
```

Actual output:

```
e2m3: max=7.5 lowest=-1.875
e3m2: max=28 lowest=-1.75
```

Expected: `-7.5` and `-28`. Note `lowest()` for `float_e2m1_t` (`0xf`) is correct, which shows the intent was sign bit | MAX_VALUE.

### Suggested fix

Replace `bitcast(0x2f)` with `bitcast(0x3f)` in all six places (include/cutlass/float_subbyte.h lines 628, 640, 715, 727, 738, and the e3m2_unpack8bits equivalent), or better, derive it as `type::bitcast(type::Base::BitRepresentation::MIN_VALUE)` so it cannot drift from the encoding again. `epsilon()` on these types checks out and needs no change.

No in-tree caller currently reads `lowest()` on these types, so the defect is latent but silently wrong for any external user relying on numeric_limits.

items.title: EpilogueDirectStore warp decomposition uses WarpShape::kN where WarpCount is meant
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`EpilogueDirectStore`'s constructor computes the warp decomposition as:

```cpp
int warp_id_mn = warp_idx % (WarpCount::kM * WarpShape::kN);
```

(include/cutlass/epilogue/threadblock/epilogue_direct_store.h line 171)

The second factor is a typo: it mixes the warp shape's `WarpShape::kN` into what should be the warp count. `EpilogueBase` does this correctly (include/cutlass/epilogue/threadblock/epilogue_base.h lines 219-220):

```cpp
int warp_mn = warp_idx % (WarpCount::kM * WarpCount::kN);
```

When `WarpCount::kN > WarpShape::kN` the modulo truncates `warp_idx` early and two different warps receive the same `(warp_m, warp_n)` coordinates. For all currently instantiated direct-store configs `WarpCount::kN <= WarpShape::kN`, so nothing is observably wrong today; the defect surfaces only for shapes where `Shape::kN > WarpShape::kN^2`.

### Suggested fix

Use `warp_idx % WarpCount::kCount` (or `% (WarpCount::kM * WarpCount::kN)` to mirror `EpilogueBase`).

items.title: CuTeDSL: nested comprehension breaks staged control flow later in the outer comprehension (NameError on the generator variable)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`_visit_Comprehension` in `cutlass/base_dsl/ast_preprocessor.py` (~lines 2424-2428) sets `session_data.generator_targets` for the comprehension being visited, then unconditionally resets it to `[]` afterwards:

```python
self.session_data.generator_targets = targets
ele_visitor(node)
self.session_data.generator_targets = []
```

When the element expression contains a *nested* comprehension, the inner `_visit_Comprehension` overwrites `generator_targets` with the inner targets and resets it to empty on exit. The outer comprehension's remaining element processing then runs with no generator targets, so any later construct that synthesizes staged control flow (e.g. an `IfExp`) treats the outer generator variable as a free/global name and fails.

Minimal repro (verified against `nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.7.0`; the control version without the inner comprehension compiles and runs):

```python
import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute

@cute.jit
def f(flag: cutlass.Boolean) -> cutlass.Int32:
    vals = [(len([0 for _ in range(2)]), (y if flag else -y)) for y in range(4)]
    return cutlass.Int32(sum(v[0] * v[1] for v in vals))

print(f(cutlass.Boolean(True)))
```

Actual error:

```
Caused exception: name 'y' is not defined
suggestion: Variables used inside staged control flow (for/if/while) must be defined before the
control flow region. Give the variable an initial value before the loop or branch.
```

The suggestion is misleading: `y` is the comprehension variable, not a user mistake.

### Suggested fix

Save the previous value of `session_data.generator_targets` before visiting and restore it after `ele_visitor(node)` returns (a `try/finally`, which also protects the session state on exception paths), instead of resetting to `[]`.

items.title: Conv2d/Conv3d output-size constructors use R*dilation instead of the effective filter size ((R-1)*dilation+1)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

The output-size computing constructors in `include/cutlass/conv/conv2d_problem_size.h` (lines ~175-176) and `include/cutlass/conv/conv3d_problem_size.h` (~196 and ~224) subtract `R * dilation` instead of the effective filter extent `((R - 1) * dilation + 1)`:

```cpp
P = ((H + pad_h + padding[1] - R * dilation_h) / stride_h) + 1;
Q = ((W + pad_w + padding[3] - S * dilation_w) / stride_w) + 1;
Z = ((D + pad_d + ... - T * dilation_d) / stride_d) + 1;
```

The library's own profiler computes cuDNN-compliant sizes with the standard formula (tools/profiler/src/conv2d_operation_profiler.cu lines ~275-303):

```
output = div_up(input + 2*pad - ((filter - 1) * dilation + 1) + 1, stride)
```

For dilation == 1 the two agree (`R*1 == (R-1)*1+1`), which is why existing tests pass. For dilation > 1 the constructors undersize P/Q/Z: e.g. H=8, R=3, dilation_h=2, pad=0, stride=1 gives P = 8-6+1 = 3 instead of the correct 8-5+1 = 4. Degenerate combinations can even produce non-positive extents (H=1, R=1, dil=3, pad=0 gives P=-1).

Any caller constructing a problem via these Tensor4DCoord/Tensor5DCoord constructors with dilation > 1 gets wrong output extents; downstream kernels then truncate or mis-map the output.

### Suggested fix

Use `(R - 1) * dilation_h + 1` (and the S/T analogues) in all three places.

items.title: uint1b_t ReduceArray specializations are broken (logical_or never compiles / always true; logical_and tests bytes not bits)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

The `uint1b_t` specializations of `ReduceArrayOperation` in include/cutlass/reduction/thread/reduction_operators.h (lines ~157-204) are broken in three independent ways.

#### logical_or: wrong parameter type AND constant-true result

```cpp
template <int N>
struct ReduceArrayOperation<logical_or<uint1b_t>, uint1b_t, N> {
  ...
  uint1b_t operator()(
    logical_and<uint1b_t> const &reduction_op,   // <-- copy-paste: accepts only logical_and
    ArrayType const &array) const {
    ...
    bool item = true;                            // <-- identity of OR is false
    for (...) { bits = ptr[byte]; item = (item || bits); }
    return uint1b_t{item};                       // <-- always true
```

Consequences, both verified against the current tree:

1. The public helper does not compile:
   `cutlass::reduction::thread::detail::ReduceArray(logical_or<uint1b_t>{}, array)` fails with *"operator() cannot be called with the given argument list"* because the parameter type names `logical_and`.
2. Even calling it directly with a `logical_and` argument compiles but ignores its input entirely: `item` starts `true` and is only ever OR-ed into, so the result is constant `true`.

#### logical_and: tests whole bytes, not bits

```cpp
bool item = false;
for (int byte = 0; byte < (N + 7) / 8; ++byte) {
  uint8_t bits = ptr[byte];
  item = (item || !bits);      // "some byte is entirely zero"
}
return uint1b_t{!item};
```

This returns "no byte is entirely zero", not "all elements are set". With `N = 8` and element 7 cleared, byte 0 is `0x7F`, no byte is zero, and the reduction reports true:

```
AND [1]*7+[0]: got=1 expected=0
```

There is also no masking of padding bits when N is not a multiple of 8.

Neither specialization has in-tree callers today, so both are latent public-API defects.

### Suggested fix

For logical_or: change the parameter type to `logical_or<uint1b_t>` and initialize `bool item = false;`.
For logical_and: loop over the ceil(N/8) bytes, mask the final byte's padding bits, and test per-byte zero as intended - or simply iterate elements via the array API.

items.title: TensorView::operator- does not compile; TensorViewPlanarComplex::reset ignores its size parameter
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

Two small public-API breakages in the tensor view headers, both verified by compiling against include/ only.

#### 1. `TensorView::operator-(TensorCoord)` cannot compile

include/cutlass/tensor_view.h ~lines 258-267 constructs a base-class object but returns it as the derived type:

```cpp
TensorView operator-(TensorCoord const& b) const {
    TensorRef result(*this);                       // base-class alias
    result.add_pointer_offset(-this->offset(b));
    return result;                                 // no base->derived conversion
}
```

```
tensor_view.h:266:12: error: could not convert 'result' from
'cutlass::TensorRef<float, cutlass::layout::RowMajor>' to 'cutlass::TensorView<float, cutlass::layout::RowMajor>'
```

`operator+`, `+=`, `-=` are all fine; this one looks like a copy-paste from `TensorRef`. The identical pattern exists in include/cutlass/tensor_view_planar_complex.h ~lines 250-259.

#### 2. `TensorViewPlanarComplex::reset` ignores its size parameter

include/cutlass/tensor_view_planar_complex.h ~lines 162-165:

```cpp
void reset(Element* ptr, Layout const &layout, LongIndex imaginary_stride, TensorCoord size) {
    Base::reset(ptr, layout, imaginary_stride);
    this->resize(extent_);        // self-assignment; parameter 'size' never used
}
```

After `pv.reset(pbuf, RowMajor(8), 32, {8,8})` on a view that was 4x4, the pointer and stride update but `extent()` still reports 4x4. Plain `TensorView::reset` correctly resizes to its argument.

### Suggested fix

Mirror `operator+`: construct `TensorView result(*this); result.add_pointer_offset(...); return result;` (and the planar-complex analogue). In `reset`, call `this->resize(size);`.

items.title: SubbyteReference breaks its offset invariant for negative offsets (constructor and operator+=)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`SubbyteReference` (both the primary template and the `StorageVec` partial specialization in include/cutlass/subbyte_reference.h) mishandles **negative** offsets: the constructor and `operator+=` with a negative argument use truncating division without normalizing, leaving the object in a state that violates its own invariant.

Verified by execution on a minimal host build (Storage = uint8_t, Element = int4b_t):

```
control  -= (+3)  : storage_delta=-2 off=1   get=-3   correct
case B   += (-3)  : storage_delta=-1 off=-1            (invariant requires off in [0, 1])
FAIL: += negative breaks offset_ invariant
case C   ctor(ptr, -3): storage_delta=-1 off=-1        same broken state
```

Correct state for element -3 is one storage unit further back (`storage_delta == -2`, `offset_ == 1`). Instead `offset_ < 0`, and any subsequent `get()`/`set()` shifts by a negative bit count (undefined behavior) or reads the wrong nibble. The mirrored `operator-=` with a positive argument is correct - its borrow logic compensates - which is why only the negative-input paths were affected.

Reachability: `TensorRef::operator-(coord)` and negative `add_pointer_offset` feed this constructor through `ReferenceFactory` for sub-byte tensors. Nothing in-tree navigates sub-byte tensors backward across vector boundaries today, so this is latent public-API breakage.

### Suggested fix

Normalize negative deltas exactly like the positive path does: fold the current `offset_` in first, then use floor-style division/borrow so that the postcondition `0 <= offset_ < kElementsPerVector` always holds.

items.title: TensorNHWC::inverse device path diverges from host path when strides are not w-multiples
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`TensorNHWC::inverse(LongIndex)` (include/cutlass/layout/tensor.h ~lines 158-188) computes different results on device and host whenever `stride_h` or `stride_n` is not a multiple of `stride_w`.

The device branch computes

```cpp
c = int(index % static_cast<int>(stride_[0]));   // provisional, before any division
...
fast_divmod(n, tmp, index, stride_[2], hw_mul, hw_shr);
fast_divmod(h, w, tmp,  stride_[1], w_mul, w_shr);
fast_divmod(w, tmp, w,  stride_[0], c_mul, c_shr);   // final remainder -> tmp, discarded
```

The channel coordinate is taken from the pre-division remainder expression and never updated; the actual post-divide residual lands in `tmp` and is thrown away. The host branch derives `c = residual % stride_[0]` from the final residual, which is the correct inverse of the packed/strided forward mapping.

Simulating the verbatim device branch with cutlass's own `find_divisor`/`fast_divmod` for strides (6, 15, 45) and index = 15 gives (n=0, h=1, w=0, **c=3**) where the host path returns (n=0, h=1, w=0, **c=0**). The only in-tree caller (`test/unit/layout/tensor_nhwc.cu`) uses packed strides where both paths agree, so the divergence has gone unnoticed. Minor adjacent note: `find_divisor` also assumes positive strides.

### Suggested fix

Set `c` from the final `fast_divmod` remainder (the value currently discarded into `tmp`), matching the host branch.

items.title: torch.compile silently accepts invalid Bernoulli probabilities that eager mode rejects
items.author: jasminetrail
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When calling `torch.bernoulli()` with out-of-range probabilities (e.g., `p = 2.0`), eager mode correctly raises a `RuntimeError`. However, `torch.compile` with the `inductor` backend silently bypasses this validation and returns a result, producing a silent correctness divergence.

### Reproducer

```python
import traceback
import torch

def model():
    # Invalid Bernoulli probabilities — eager checks p in [0, 1]
    p = torch.full((4,), 2.0, dtype=torch.float32)
    return torch.bernoulli(p)

def run(label, fn):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    try:
        out = fn()
    except Exception:
        print(f"{label}: raised")
        print(traceback.format_exc())
        return None
    print(f"{label}: returned {out}")
    return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("torch", torch.__version__)
    eager = run("eager", model)
    compiled = run("compiled", lambda: torch.compile(model, backend="inductor")())
    if eager is None and compiled is not None:
        print("BUG: compiled execution accepted invalid Bernoulli probabilities.")

items.title: torch.distributions.Laplace.icdf returns -inf (and loses accuracy) for small tail probabilities
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
Description

`Laplace.icdf(p)` computes `term = p - 0.5` and then `loc - scale * sign(term) * log1p(-2 * |term|)`. For
`p` below about 5.5e-17 (float64) `p - 0.5` rounds to exactly `-0.5`, `log1p(-1) = -inf`, and the result
is `-inf` although the true quantile `loc + scale * log(2p)` is finite. Accuracy is already lost before
that: `icdf(1e-16)` is wrong in the third significant digit. The upper tail behaves the same way.

### Steps to reproduce

```python
import torch
from torch.distributions import Laplace
d = Laplace(torch.tensor(0.0, dtype=torch.float64), torch.tensor(1.0, dtype=torch.float64))
print(d.icdf(torch.tensor(1e-17, dtype=torch.float64)))  # -inf      (exact: log(2e-17) = -38.45)
print(d.icdf(torch.tensor(1e-16, dtype=torch.float64)))  # -36.0437  (exact: -36.1482)
```

### Expected

`icdf(p) = loc + scale * log(2p)` for `p < 0.5` (and `loc - scale * log(2(1-p))` above), accurate in the tails.

### Versions

Environment

PyTorch 2.14.0 (the latest release, CPU wheel) and 2.12.0, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64

cc @fritzo @neerajprad @alicanb @nikitaved

items.title: [Tune] Synch PBT - Trials should be paused on Restore:  ALL Trials continue and no perturbation is done
items.author: Daraan
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

When we use PBT in synch mode and restore the tuning process from a checkpoint then all restored trials are put into a PENDING and soon RUNNING state, however this includes trials that should stay paused.

For example in belows example the perturbation interval is at `884736`. The first trial was lacking behind and the process was interrupted.
On restore all trials are put into PENDING -> RUNNING again, ignoring that the trials at the perturbation interval should wait for the last trial.
This then also prevents the perturbation at 884736.

```python
╭────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ name      status       iter     total time (s)     current_step   
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PBT       RUNNING       108            4800.78           737280   # <-- All should wait until this reaches 884736 
│ PBT       RUNNING       684           11964.2            884736    # should be PAUSED / PENDING after restore and wait for first trial
│ PBT       RUNNING       396            8746.1            884736 
│ PBT       RUNNING       126            5353.79           884736 
│ PBT	    PENDING       117            5258.1            884736
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

---

Another problem is that after a restore `self._next_perturbation_sync` is not correct (the PBT has no state loaded as far as I see).
In sync mode this causes that `choose_trial_to_run` will never unpause a paused trial as both conditions are False:


```python
                if not self._synch:  # False
                    candidates.append(trial)
                elif (
                    self._trial_state[trial].last_train_time
                    < self._next_perturbation_sync  # not restored
                ):
                    candidates.append(trial)
```

So on the next perturbation interval all trials will be paused and stay paused forever.

### Versions / Dependencies

2.49.2

### Reproduction script

Run a PBT script with synch. Interrupt it restore.

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

Currently operations on (reads) a Databricks Unity Catalog on GCP doesn't work with the `Catalog` abstraction for Delta tables.

The reason for this is because internally we use the `delta-rs` library to write to delta tables, and `delta-rs` relies on an older version of `object_store` which doesm't support google oauth bearer tokens (the latest version does). We should upgrade our `delta-rs` dependency when they release a new version and update code as necessary.

Issue on `delta-rs`: https://github.com/delta-io/delta-rs/issues/4566

items.title: [Serve] Allow app-defined health routes to bypass `max_ongoing_requests`
items.author: codechrl
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

Every request to a route on a `@serve.ingress` FastAPI app counts toward the deployment's `max_ongoing_requests`. A health route such as `GET /healthz` therefore waits for a free slot while the replicas are saturated. External health checkers (load balancers, Kubernetes probes) time out on it and mark a working application as down.

Repro on Ray 2.54.1 and FastAPI 0.116.0:

```python
import asyncio
import threading
import time

import requests
from fastapi import FastAPI
from ray import serve

app = FastAPI()


@serve.deployment(max_ongoing_requests=2)
@serve.ingress(app)
class Api:
    @app.get("/work")
    async def work(self):
        await asyncio.sleep(6)

    @app.get("/healthz")
    async def healthz(self):
        return "ok"


def timed_get(path):
    start = time.time()
    status = requests.get(f"http://127.0.0.1:8000{path}").status_code
    print(path, status, f"{time.time() - start:.2f}s")


serve.run(Api.bind())
timed_get("/healthz")

for _ in range(2):
    threading.Thread(target=timed_get, args=("/work",)).start()
time.sleep(1)
timed_get("/-/healthz")
timed_get("/healthz")
```

```text
/healthz 200 0.65s
/-/healthz 200 0.03s
/work 200 6.04s
/work 200 6.04s
/healthz 200 5.40s
```

The replica logs `GET /healthz 200 2.7ms` for the last call. The rest of the 5.40s is spent waiting for a free slot.

The built-in routes do not cover this case. The proxy's `/-/healthz` reports whether the proxy is draining, has a route table and, on worker nodes, knows a running replica. The replica's `/-/healthz` exists only with direct ingress, which `RAY_SERVE_ENABLE_DIRECT_INGRESS` leaves off by default. It returns the result of the controller's last `check_health` call. Neither runs a request through the application. #33979 asked for a per-application route that calls `check_health`. It was closed in a backlog sweep for inactivity.

Two possible shapes:

- An option on `@serve.ingress` or `@serve.deployment` that lists routes exempt from `max_ongoing_requests`, e.g. `exempt_routes=["/healthz"]`.
- A per-application `/{route_prefix}/-/healthz` that calls `check_health` outside the request semaphore.

Documented guidance on the recommended pattern would also work.

### Use case

A FastAPI ingress deployment forwards each request to model deployments through handles. Each forwarded call takes several seconds. A container health check calls the app's `/healthz`, which reports `serve.status()`. With the default `max_ongoing_requests=5`, five concurrent calls left `/healthz` unroutable. The health check failed. The container supervisor then restarted the service, which failed every in-flight request. Raising `max_ongoing_requests` to 200 only moves the threshold. A separate health deployment does not exercise the ingress deployment that serves the traffic.

items.title: Autoscaler-driven elastic expert/data parallelism for MoE
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### Feature Description and Motivation

For large MoE models we only scale whole replicas, which is coarse and expensive. vLLM has elastic EP (`enable_elastic_ep`, `/is_scaling_elastic_ep`, the DP coordinator request-wave protocol in `vllm/v1/engine/coordinator.py`) to add/remove DP/EP ranks at runtime. The autoscaler doesn't drive it. Scaling EP width by load would right-size MoE serving without full-replica steps.

### Use Case

DeepSeek / Qwen-MoE style deployments where per-replica cost is high and traffic varies; scale expert parallelism up and down instead of adding or removing entire replicas.

### Proposed Solution

Let PodAutoscaler target EP/DP width for elastic-EP-enabled deployments and drive scaling via the engine's elastic-EP endpoints + the DP coordinator wave protocol. Start observe-only (read `/is_scaling_elastic_ep` and wave state) before acting on it.

items.author: Jeffwan

## Summary

When an engine exhausts its local restart budget, reschedule the affected ModelClaim to another eligible warm pool Pod and restore routing after activation.

## Scope

- Trigger only after the runtime reports a terminal engine failure.
- Keep co-resident engines on the original Pod unaffected.
- Reuse normal placement and activation; no live migration or in-flight request preservation.
- Allow gateway retries to succeed after the new route becomes ready.

items.title: feat: Add AIBrix Chat - a frontend demo portal for LLM inference
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 Feature Description and Motivation

AIBrix provides powerful infrastructure for LLM inference, but we lack a user-facing demo to showcase its capabilities. Currently, users need to interact with AIBrix through API calls, or third-party clients, which creates friction when:

- Live demos — Presenting AIBrix at conferences, meetups, or internal reviews requires a polished UI
- End-to-end validation — Testing the full stack (gateway routing, model serving, load balancing) benefits from a real frontend client
- Onboarding — A working chat UI makes it easier for new contributors to understand the user-facing value of the infrastructure

### Use Case

Add a lightweight chat portal under apps/chat/web/ that serves as both a demo and a functional frontend for AIBrix-managed LLM endpoints.

What it includes:
- Chat interface with conversation management (create, search, delete, move)
- Project organization for grouping related conversations
- Model selector supporting multiple backends
- Sidebar navigation with chat history
- Dark-themed, responsive UI built with React + Vite + Tailwind CSS


Architecture:
```
  apps/
  ├── chat/
   │   ├── web/          # React frontend
   │   └── api/          # Backend proxy for LLM endpoints (planned)
```

### Proposed Solution

Why in-repo (not a separate project)?

1. Dogfooding — The chat portal consumes AIBrix gateway APIs directly, validating routing algorithms, model selection, and streaming behavior from a real client
2. Faster iteration — Co-locating with infrastructure code means API and frontend changes can land together
3. Visibility — Contributors are more likely to maintain something that lives alongside the core project
4. Demo-ready — A single repo clone gives users everything needed for a complete demo

### Task break down

#### Models and vLLM adaptatio

> Note: we do not necessarily need to host every model, each model endpoint should be fully replaced by cloud api. that means if we find some model are not supported in vllm-omni, we just use openai endpoint as replacement.

items.title: [Feature]: Experimental NVFP4 sparse MLA decode for SM100/SM103 (vLLM nvfp4_ds_mla, DeepSeek-V3.2 / GLM-5)
items.author: stu-cao
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this request has not been filed yet.

### Problem

vLLM can store the KV cache of DSA-style sparse MLA models (DeepSeek-V3.2, GLM-5) in `nvfp4_ds_mla`, a 352-byte-per-token layout: 256 B of e2m1 NoPE values, 64 B of e4m3 RoPE values and 32 B of e4m3 block-16 scales. It holds 1.6x the tokens of an FP8 cache (576 B per token).

FlashInfer has no SM100/SM103 sparse MLA decode that reads it. The SM100 sparse path (`trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla` with `sparse_mla_top_k`) reads FP8/BF16 rows only, and the existing NVFP4 sparse MLA (#4955) is SM120-only DeepSeek-V4 with 384 B rows. An engine that stores `nvfp4_ds_mla` therefore either restages the selected top-k rows as FP8 in every layer (on GB200 at 15 tokens per step that gather costs 5.3 us on top of TRTLLM-gen's 12.4 us, and re-rounding every dequantized value to e4m3 costs 3.0-4.7 % relative error) or uses FlashMLA's NVFP4 kernel, which pads the 16 heads per rank to 64.

### Requested outcome

An experimental `flashinfer.mla.nvfp4_sparse_mla_decode` that reads `nvfp4_ds_mla` rows as stored (dequantized in shared memory, nothing staged in global memory) for 16 query heads per rank, top-k 512/1024/2048, e4m3 queries and bf16 output, on SM100 and SM103. The implementation is in PR #5717.

### Target hardware

SM100 (B200, GB200), SM103 (B300, GB300)

### Inference engine

vLLM

### Affected model or model family

DeepSeek-V3.2 at TP8 and GLM-5 at TP4 (16 attention heads per rank), served with `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4_ds_mla`.

### Workload and configuration

- Data type and quantization: NVFP4 KV cache (e2m1 values, e4m3 block-16 scales, e4m3 RoPE), e4m3 query, bf16 output
- Batch size or request concurrency: speculative-decode steps, 5 to 45 query tokens per launch
- Sequence lengths or token counts: top-k 2048 rows selected per token by the sparse indexer
- Parallelism: TP4/TP8 attention, also decode workers of a prefill/decode split
- Relevant shapes: 16 heads, 576-dim latent (512 NoPE + 64 RoPE), 512-dim values, top-k 512/1024/2048, flat row ids `block_id * block_size + offset`, `-1` marks an empty slot
- Environment: B300 SXM6 (SM103, 148 SMs), driver 580.173.02, CUDA 13.0 (nvcc 13.0.88), torch 2.14.0+cu130, Python 3.12.3, Ubuntu 24.04

### Current workaround

FP8 staging gather + TRTLLM-gen sparse MLA (extra HBM traffic, 3.0-4.7 % relative error), or FlashMLA's NVFP4 sparse decode (pads to 64 heads).

### Impact

Memory capacity or bandwidth; Correctness or numerical-quality risk.

### Acceptance criteria

- Passes the correctness tests in `tests/experimental/test_nvfp4_sparse_mla_decode.py` against an exact FP32 reference on SM100 and SM103: every cluster size, three top-k widths, padded indices, a block-shaped cache, CUDA-graph replay.
- Relative error below 1 % (measured 0.29 % on B300).
- A benchmark against FP8 TRTLLM-gen sparse MLA at the same request-shaped indices (`benchmarks/bench_nvfp4_sparse_mla_decode.py`).

### Related work, dependencies, or suggested scope

- #5443 (merged): dense NVFP4 DeepSeek-V4 decode. Different operator: paged MQA, 64 heads, NVFP4 Q/K/V, tcgen05. This one is top-k sparse, 16 heads, e4m3 Q, 352 B rows, `mma.sync`.
- #4955 (merged): SM120 NVFP4 sparse MLA for DeepSeek-V4 (384 B rows). This one is SM100/SM103 and vLLM's `nvfp4_ds_mla` rows.
- vLLM integration: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59342 (draft), in which FlashInfer's sparse MLA backend accepts `nvfp4_ds_mla` and decodes through this API.
- Not a parameter-space extension of `trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla`: the KV operand is a different type (uint8 rows of 352 B with mixed e2m1/e4m3 fields addressed by flat row ids, no page table), which is the "materially different API contract" case in `flashinfer/experimental/README.md`.

### Timing or release need

None.

### Experimental track

- **Owner:** @stu-cao
- **Reason for the experimental path:**
  - new operator for a KV format defined by an engine (vLLM's `nvfp4_ds_mla`), with an API contract that is not final: fixed 16 heads, e4m3 query only, no LSE output, no attention sinks;
  - architecture-specific implementation (SM100a/SM103a e2m1 conversions, thread-block clusters with distributed shared memory);
  - the packaged tests have run on SM103 (B300) only; SM100 (B200/GB200) runs the same kernel body inside vLLM but the FlashInfer packaging has not been run there;
  - the `mma.sync` pipeline is expected to be superseded by a tcgen05 kernel.
- **Graduation plan, target: the first release cut after 2026-10-27 (four weeks):**
  1. run `tests/experimental/test_nvfp4_sparse_mla_decode.py` and the benchmark on B200/GB200 (compute capability 10.0), the remaining validation gap;
  2. the vLLM integration lands, which shows the API holds up against a real engine;
  3. finalize the API: keyword-only tuning parameters (`num_ctas_per_token`), and decide whether LSE output, attention sinks or other head counts are needed;
  4. complete the stable-API checklist: trace template, docs page, top-level export, and an AOT decision;
  5. compare with a tcgen05 kernel at the same shapes; keep it as a second backend behind this API if it is faster, otherwise drop it.
- **Removal:** if step 1 fails or no engine adopts the API within the window, delete `flashinfer/experimental/nvfp4_sparse_mla_decode/`, the tagged API in `flashinfer/mla/_core.py` and the tests.

items.title: [Feature request] `torch.export` .save/.load could support `safetensors` and/or `weights_only=True`
items.author: stu-twelvelabs
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Today, torch.export will load tensors via
```
def deserialize_torch_artifact(serialized: Union[Dict[str, Any], Tuple[Any, ...], bytes]):
    if isinstance(serialized, (dict, tuple)):
        return serialized
    if len(serialized) == 0:
        return {}
    buffer = io.BytesIO(serialized)
    buffer.seek(0)
    # weights_only=False as we want to load custom objects here (e.g. ScriptObject)
    artifact = torch.load(buffer, weights_only=False)
    assert isinstance(artifact, (tuple, dict))
    return artifact
```
Security teams really don't like this I have learned 🙂. In the interest of leveraging the awesome benefits of export more safely, it would be amazing to add optional support for any or all of `safetensors` and/or `weights_only=True`!

Thank you for all the work on `torch.export`, it has a very promising future!

### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

cc @chauhang @penguinwu @avikchaudhuri @gmagogsfm @zhxchen17 @tugsbayasgalan @angelayi @suo @ydwu4

items.title: torch.baddbmm with valid batched CSR input triggers INTERNAL ASSERT instead of a user-facing error
items.author: tangyuan499-commits
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.baddbmm` with a valid batched CSR tensor on CUDA triggers an internal assertion:

```text
RuntimeError: false INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at
"../aten/src/ATen/cuda/CUDASparseDescriptors.cpp":185,
please report a bug to PyTorch.
Support for batched CSR indices and values is not implemented.
```

I understand that CUDA support for batched CSR indices/values may currently be unsupported. The issue here is that a valid user input reaches `TORCH_INTERNAL_ASSERT` and produces a "please report a bug to PyTorch" message, rather than a normal user-facing `RuntimeError` or `NotImplementedError` explaining that this operation is unsupported.

Minimal reproducer:

```python
import torch

torch.manual_seed(5)

input = torch.randn(2, 3, 4, device="cuda")

batch1 = torch.randn(
    2, 3, 5, device="cuda"
).to_sparse_csr()

batch2 = torch.randn(
    2, 5, 4, device="cuda"
)

torch.baddbmm(
    input,
    batch1,
    batch2,
    beta=1.0,
    alpha=1.0,
)
```

Observed result:

```text
RuntimeError: false INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at
"../aten/src/ATen/cuda/CUDASparseDescriptors.cpp":185,
please report a bug to PyTorch.
Support for batched CSR indices and values is not implemented.
```

The batched CSR tensor itself is valid and is produced directly using:

```python
batch1 = dense_tensor.to_sparse_csr()
```

If batched CSR input is not supported by the CUDA `baddbmm` implementation, I would expect this case to fail with a regular user-facing error such as `RuntimeError` or `NotImplementedError`, rather than an internal assertion.

This seems related to the existing limitation around batched CSR CUDA support discussed in #60854, but this report is specifically about the error handling path reaching `TORCH_INTERNAL_ASSERT`.

comments.author: Mohit-25-tech
comments.body:
Hi, I've opened a PR for this: #199650 

It replaces the `TORCH_INTERNAL_ASSERT` in `CuSparseSpMatCsrDescriptor` with a `TORCH_CHECK`, so batched CSR indices/values on CUDA raise a normal `RuntimeError` instead of "please report a bug". This covers both `torch.baddbmm` and `torch.bmm`, which go through the same guard. The check now runs before `cusparseCreateCsr`, so the raw descriptor isn't leaked when it fails. I also added a regression test for both ops. No batched CSR support is added.

I reproduced the original failure on a Tesla T4 (PyTorch 2.11.0+cu128) and confirmed the modified file compiles. I couldn't run the new test locally, so I'm relying on CI for that. Happy to adjust anything, for example switching to `NotImplementedError` if you'd prefer that.

Could someone mark this actionable when you get a chance? I used an AI coding assistant (Codex) while preparing the change and reviewed the diff myself.

comments.author: pearu
comments.body:
I looked into whether this is genuinely a backend limitation, and it is not. cuSPARSE has supported batched CSR SpMM since CUDA 11.6 Update 1 and rocSPARSE since ROCm 5.2.0 — both well below the versions PyTorch requires. Our batched CSR storage layout is already exactly what cuSPARSE expects, and the `cusparseCsrSetStridedBatch` call that makes it work is already in the descriptor, sitting dead behind the assert this issue reports. So my preference is that we implement the missing feature rather than re-word the exception: a fix that only renames the error leaves the actual work undone and makes it harder to pick up later. To check that the proper fix is not large, I had Claude Code prepare and verify a minimal patch against the reproducer above; the details, the diff and the verification results are below.

> **cuSPARSE** supports batched CSR `Cᵢ = Aᵢ·Bᵢ` from **CUDA 11.6 Update 1**
> ("cusparseSpMM now supports batches of sparse matrices"), for all algorithms
> except `CUSPARSE_SPMM_CSR_ALG3`. `spmm()` uses `CUSPARSE_SPMM_CSR_ALG2`
> (`SparseBlasImpl.cpp:563`). PyTorch requires CUDA >= 12.6
> (`cmake/public/cuda.cmake`).
>
> **rocSPARSE** added "Batched SpMM for CSR, CSC, and COO formats" in rocSPARSE
> 2.2.0 / ROCm 5.2.0; CI runs ROCm 7.x and above.
>
> So no version gate is needed on either backend.
>
> **The storage layout already matches.** cuSPARSE wants one row-offsets stride
> and one shared stride for column indices and values, with the same nnz in
> every batch. A PyTorch batched CSR stores `crow_indices` as
> `(*batch, nrows+1)` and `col_indices`/`values` as `(*batch, nnz)`, so nnz is
> equal across batches by construction (`TensorConversions.cpp:100`) and the
> col/value batch strides coincide.
>
> **The call is already written**, dead behind the assert. Making it live is
> the whole change:
>
> ```diff
> --- a/aten/src/ATen/cuda/CUDASparseDescriptors.cpp
> +++ b/aten/src/ATen/cuda/CUDASparseDescriptors.cpp
> @@ -180,16 +180,27 @@ CuSparseSpMatCsrDescriptor::CuSparseSpMatCsrDescriptor(const Tensor& input, int6
>        CUSPARSE_INDEX_BASE_ZERO, // base index of row offset and col index
>        value_type // data type of values
>        ));
> +  // Take ownership before the checks below so that a failure cannot leak the
> +  // raw descriptor.
> +  descriptor_.reset(raw_descriptor);
>  
>    if (ndim == 3 && batch_offset == -1) {
>      int batch_count =
>          at::native::cuda_int_cast(at::native::batchCount(input), "batch_count");
>      if (crow_indices.dim() >= 2 || values.dim() >= 2 ||
>          col_indices.dim() >= 2) {
> -      // cuSPARSE ignores the strides and uses only the first batch
> -      TORCH_INTERNAL_ASSERT(
> -          false,
> -          "Support for batched CSR indices and values is not implemented.");
> +      TORCH_CHECK(
> +          crow_indices.dim() >= 2 && col_indices.dim() >= 2 &&
> +              values.dim() >= 2,
> +          "Expected crow_indices, col_indices and values of a batched CSR "
> +          "tensor to be batched, got dimensionalities ",
> +          crow_indices.dim(), ", ", col_indices.dim(), " and ", values.dim());
> +      // cuSPARSE uses a single batch stride for column indices and values.
> +      TORCH_CHECK(
> +          col_indices.stride(-2) == values_->stride(-2),
> +          "Expected col_indices and values of a batched CSR tensor to have "
> +          "equal batch strides, got ",
> +          col_indices.stride(-2), " and ", values_->stride(-2));
>        TORCH_CUDASPARSE_CHECK(cusparseCsrSetStridedBatch(
>            raw_descriptor,
>            batch_count,
> @@ -202,8 +213,6 @@ CuSparseSpMatCsrDescriptor::CuSparseSpMatCsrDescriptor(const Tensor& input, int6
>            cusparseCsrSetStridedBatch(raw_descriptor, batch_count, 0, 0));
>      }
>    }
> -
> -  descriptor_.reset(raw_descriptor);
>  }
> ```
>

items.title: [Bug]: Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 cannot load with the PyTorch backend
items.author: mihai-chiorean
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM: current `main`
- Backend: PyTorch
- Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4`
- Reproduced on: DGX Spark / SM121

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [x] The official example scripts
- [x] The `transformers` checkpoint loader
- [x] The PyTorch backend

### Reproduction

Attempt to load the checkpoint through `LLM(...)` or `trtllm-serve` with the PyTorch backend and text-only multimodal execution (`disable_mm_encoder=True`).

The checkpoint is a dense Qwen3.8/Qwen3.5-family VLM with mixed compressed-tensors quantization: packed NVFP4 dense MLP weights, FP8 attention/GDN/lm_head weights, FP8 KV cache, and one MTP layer.

### Expected behavior

The checkpoint should select `Qwen3_5VLModel`, preserve each config group's quantization, map packed compressed-tensors names to TRT-LLM parameters, construct a rowwise-FP8 `lm_head`, and generate coherent text with and without MTP.

### Actual behavior

Current `main` has several independent blockers:

1. Generic dense Qwen3.6/3.8 VLM configs are classified as Qwen-Image-Bench configs.
2. The compressed-tensors parser rejects or loses multiple `config_groups`.
3. Packed NVFP4 names/scales are not normalized for the Qwen mapper.
4. Dense MLP quant-config keys do not match the `_DenseMlpAdapter` runtime module path.
5. The explicit FP8 `lm_head` entry is dropped, which would cast the FP8 weight to bf16 and discard its scale.

### Validation

With focused fixes for those concerns, an SM121 full-model smoke loaded 23.91 GiB of model weights, selected native `trtllm::nvfp4_gemm`, constructed `lm_head` as `FP8_PER_CHANNEL_PER_TOKEN`, and generated coherent 64-token responses for two prompts. The same stack also generated coherently with the checkpoint MTP layer enabled.

The changes will be proposed as small dependent PRs so each concern can be reviewed independently.

items.title: EngineDeadError message compounds a prefix each time it is unpickled
items.author: StephenLReed
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM: 1.3.0rc23 (built from `f20ea652`); behaviour re-checked against `main` @ `fbda11f5`
- GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 (sm_120), driver 595.71.05
- PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, Python 3.12.13
- Ubuntu 25.10, kernel 6.17.0-41-generic
- Backend: PyTorch; single GPU, no TP/PP
- Model where observed: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 with FP8 KV cache (where model-specific)

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Reproduction

`EngineDeadError.__init__` renders `root_cause` into the message, and default exception pickling
round-trips through `args` — which holds that rendered message. Unpickling re-invokes `__init__` with
the message string as the cause, so the prefix is prepended again on every hop:

```
original : Engine has died: RuntimeError: PyExecutor has already been shutdown
1 hop    : Engine has died: str: Engine has died: RuntimeError: PyExecutor has already been shutdown
2 hops   : Engine has died: str: Engine has died: str: Engine has died: RuntimeError: ...
```

The class is raised when a worker process dies, i.e. exactly where it crosses a process boundary, so
the mangled text is the form users are most likely to encounter.

### Expected behavior

An EngineDeadError reconstructed in another process renders the same message as the original.

### actual behavior

Each unpickle prepends the prefix again, so the message grows one 'Engine has died: str: ' per hop. .root_cause is unaffected.

### additional notes

Message only. `__dict__` is restored after `__init__`, so `.root_cause` survives as the original
exception and the attribute contract holds. This is log legibility and unbounded message growth, not
a broken consumer contract.

Add `__reduce__` returning `(self.__class__, (self.root_cause,))` so reconstruction uses the cause
rather than the rendered text. `root_cause` is already pickled as part of `__dict__`, so no new
picklability requirement is introduced.

We have the patch with four CPU-only tests (2 fail before, 4 pass after) and are raising this Issue
Request first per CONTRIBUTING.md.

**Questions for maintainers**

1. Would you prefer `__reduce__`, or moving the rendering out of `__init__` into `__str__` so `args`
   never holds the formatted text?
2. Are there other exception types in `tensorrt_llm/executor` that render constructor arguments into
   the message and would have the same issue?

items.title: [RFC] Training/Inference Numerical Consistency for RL Post-Training
items.author: shikicloud
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

In RL post-training, the rollout engine samples tokens and the trainer recomputes logprobs on those same tokens with the same weights. When the two disagree, PPO's importance ratio is computed against the wrong denominator; low-probability tokens can spike the ratio and blow up gradients; training can collapse.

Four causes, each with published evidence:

1. **Kernels are not batch-invariant.** The same request can produce different logits depending on what else is in the batch, because RMSNorm/matmul/attention pick their reduction strategy from batch shape ([Thinking Machines, "Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference"](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/defeating-nondeterminism-in-llm-inference/), 2025-09-10).
2. **MoE routing disagrees between engines even with identical weights** — ~10% of per-layer routing decisions differ, 94% of tokens affected in ≥1 layer, on Qwen3-30B-A3B ([R3 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11370), arXiv 2510.11370). R3 (#18397) is an initial solution to fix this cause.
3. **LM-head / router precision.** BF16 alone dropped train/inference token-probability correlation to ~0.9; FP32 restored ~0.99 ([MiniMax-M1 tech report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13585), arXiv 2506.13585).
4. **Severity is hardware- and kernel-dependent and compounds with length.** Same code: KL ≈ 5e-4–1e-3 on one GPU, 1e-2–1e-1 on another, traced to a specific attention-kernel bug ([ByteDance Seed, "When Speed Kills Stability"](https://yingru.notion.site/When-Speed-Kills-Stability-Demystifying-RL-Collapse-from-the-Training-Inference-Mismatch-271211a558b7808d8b12d403fd15edda)).

R3 addresses cause 2. This RFC covers what's left of R3 (cause 2's remaining edges) plus causes 1, 3, and a sampling-semantics issue that compounds all of them. Other useful features like TIS/MIS/KPop remain in RL frameworks but not inference engines. Futhermore, this RFC targets on important features for TRTLLM, we will explore new features to solve this problem on an new issue.

This RFC is generated by codex with human's instructions and supervision. Also thanks @NolenLiang and @JeffPengCoder's help. CC's @joyang-nv @xuantengh @yuki-97 

## What exists today

- **Router Replay**: `LlmArgs.enable_return_routed_experts` + `SamplingParams.return_routed_experts` → `CompletionOutput.routed_experts`, `int16`, `[seq_len-1, num_moe_layers, top_k]`, pre-EPLB logical ids. Separated-routing MoE backends only; fails closed on PP>1, spec decode, fused routing(TBD).
- **`logprobs_mode`**: `RAW` (pre-sampling-params) / `PROCESSED` (post). No `raw_logits`/`processed_logits` variants.
- **`FORCE_DETERMINISTIC`**: a C++ env var, not exposed via `LlmArgs`. Covers attention multi-block, KV-cache reuse, and all-reduce workspace size. Does not cover autotuner tactic selection, FMHA library selection, all-reduce *strategy* selection, or CUDA-graph padding(TBD).
- **`MoeConfig.disable_finalize_fusion`**: CUTLASS only; the LlmArgs docstring states the fused path is non-deterministic for top-k > 2.

Two items already landed for Router Replay: per-request gating (`SamplingParams.return_routed_experts=False` now correctly attaches nothing), and the output dtype is `int16`.

Reading the PyTorch backend (`tensorrt_llm/_torch/`) turns up nine places where a numeric result depends on batch shape or token count, not just the sequence — this is what drives the Deterministic inference work below:

| # | Source | Class | Covered by `FORCE_DETERMINISTIC`? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Attention multi-block/split-KV (MMHA/XQA/TRTLLM-Gen); split count = `f(SM_count, batch*heads)` | batch-dependent | Yes — but a shared-memory guard can silently re-enable multi-block regardless of the flag |
| 2 | FMHA library selection by batch bucket (`fmha/manager.py`) | batch-dependent | No — `TLLM_FMHA_LIBS` can pin one manually |
| 3 | Dense GEMM tactic selection by M (autotuner) | batch-dependent, plus profiling-noise without a persisted cache | No — `enable_autotuner=False` falls back to `tactic=-1`, but the fallback cuBLASLt path's own algorithm choice is unexamined |
| 4 | MoE grouped-GEMM tactic selection by token count | batch-dependent | No |
| 5 | MoE finalize/unpermute reduction, CUTLASS top-k>2 | non-deterministic per LlmArgs docstring | Partially — `disable_finalize_fusion=True`; TRTLLM-Gen has no unfused path |
| 6 | All-reduce *strategy* selection by message size | batch-dependent | No — only workspace *size* is fixed, strategy selection isn't |
| 7 | CUDA-graph batch-size padding ladder | batch-dependent | No |
| 8 | Chunked-prefill / KV-reuse boundary placement | depends on scheduler budget, not just the sequence | Yes — both disabled |

Two bugs found while reading the same code, independent of scope: `getBoolEnv` matches only the exact string `"1"` (`FORCE_DETERMINISTIC=true` is silently ignored), and MMHA's multi-block override under shared-memory pressure bypasses the flag entirely.

## Proposed Change.

Organized by delivery phase. Each phase lists what happens to every workstream in that phase, rather than each workstream carrying its own separate phase numbering.

### Phase 1 — config only, no new kernels, land first

- **Router Replay:**
  - Validate TRTLLM-Gen, DeepGEMM, and WideEP end to end. Today only CUTLASS has a GPU test, on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B-Chat; the other backends' support is inferred from `_supports_load_balancer()`, not tested.
  - Optional `uint8` output for `num_experts <= 256` models. `int16` already halves the naive `int32` footprint, but large payloads are a real failure mode at scale — a comparable rollout system hit ~35GB/actor, ~280GB across 8 actors, on a 96-layer MoE model with long context. Worth having the compact path ready before someone hits this on TRT-LLM.
- **Deterministic inference:**
  - Config-only surface over the gaps in the table above:

    ```python
    class TorchLlmArgs:
        enable_deterministic_inference: bool = False
        # Superset of FORCE_DETERMINISTIC=1:
        #   - autotuner f

items.title: [Bug] sm12x MoE CuTe-DSL kernels are never disk-cached — cute.compile hardcodes no_cache=True, so every fresh engine re-pays 15–40 s MLIR compiles per kernel shape
items.author: jhsmith409
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The Blackwell sm12x fused-MoE path compiles all of its CuTe-DSL kernels through explicit
`cute.compile(...)`, which unconditionally disables the DSL's file cache. The only caching
layer is three in-process Python dicts, so **every engine start re-pays the full MLIR JIT
cost for every kernel specialization it touches** — measured at **~40 s** for the dynamic
kernel's first hit and **~15–18 s per small-`m` micro-kernel specialization**. In a serving
context (vLLM `--moe-backend=flashinfer_b12x`) these compiles land mid-request and freeze
the whole engine (vllm#47458: ~17.5 s stop-the-world stalls, all in-flight requests frozen
including mid-decode).

`CUTE_DSL_CACHE_DIR` / `CUTE_DSL_DISABLE_FILE_CACHING` have no effect on this path — the
gate that would consult them is short-circuited before they are read.

## Environment

- flashinfer 0.6.12, 0.6.13, and **0.6.15.post1** (all verified; `moe_dispatch.py` cache
  structure unchanged across them)
- nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.5.0 and **4.6.0** (both verified)
- SM120: RTX 5070 Ti (×2, TP/PP), RTX 5090 (unsharded), RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell — reproduced
  on all three in the vllm#47458 thread
- Model: `nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4` via vLLM `--moe-backend=flashinfer_b12x`

## Mechanism (exact code paths)

1. **The DSL hardcodes `no_cache=True` for explicit compiles.**
   `CompileCallable._compile` sets `kwargs["no_cache"] = True` unconditionally:
   - nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.5.0: `base_dsl/compiler.py:604-605`
   - nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.6.0: `base_dsl/compiler.py:1319`

2. **The file cache is gated behind `if not no_cache`** — both the load and the dump —
   so the env vars are never even consulted for explicit compiles:
   - 4.5.0: `base_dsl/dsl.py:1645` (load), `:1736` (dump)
   - 4.6.0: `base_dsl/dsl.py:2004` (load), `:2105` (dump); in-memory `jit_cache` lookups
     likewise skipped under `no_cache` at `:2012`, `:2293`

3. **The sm12x MoE dispatch only ever compiles through `cute.compile`,** with plain
   in-process dicts on top — nothing reaches disk:
   - 0.6.12/0.6.13: `blackwell_sm12x/moe_dispatch.py:676/912/1675` (compile sites);
     `_STATIC/_MICRO/_DYNAMIC_KERNEL_CACHE`
   - 0.6.15.post1: compile sites at `:697/:942/:1723`; caches at `:486/:733/:1524`

4. Compounding factor (tracked separately as #3836): the micro-kernel `cache_key`
   includes both `m` and `workspace.max_rows` (0.6.15.post1 `moe_dispatch.py:770-791`,
   fields at `:774`/`:778`), so workspace growth invalidates already-compiled small-batch
   entries even *within* a process lifetime. With no disk layer underneath, each
   invalidation is a full 15 s+ recompile, not a reload.

## Verification

Behavioral check from the vllm#47458 thread (credit @waynehacking8, on 0.6.12 / DSL 4.5.0):

- `cute.compile` of a trivial `@cute.jit` function leaves `CUTE_DSL_CACHE_DIR` **empty**.
- Calling the same jit function **directly** (implicit compile path) writes
  `cute_dsl_<hash>.mlir`, and a fresh process then logs `JIT cache hit IN-FILE`.
- Only the implicit direct-call path caches; flashinfer's MoE dispatch never uses it.

Source-level re-verification on 0.6.15.post1 / DSL 4.6.0 (2026-08-02, inside the
`vllm/vllm-openai` nightly image): every line cite in the Mechanism section above was
confirmed against the installed packages — the hardcoded `no_cache=True`, the
`if not no_cache` gates around both file-cache load and dump, the three `cute.compile`
sites, the three in-process dicts, and `m`/`max_rows` still present in the micro-kernel
cache key.

Measured first-hit compile costs (RTX PRO 6000, synthetic MoE E=32/topk=4 driving
`B12xMoEWrapper.run` exactly as vLLM's `FlashInferB12xExperts` does):

| kernel path | first hit | subsequent (same key) |
|---|---|---|
| dynamic (m-independent key) | ~40 s | 1–3 ms |
| micro m=1 | 14.9 s | ms |
| micro m=2 | 15.2 s | ms |
| micro m=64 | 18.3 s | ms |

Production symptom: vllm#47458 — py-spy captured 16 consecutive samples over 8.35 s pinned
in `b12x_fused_moe (flashinfer/fused_moe/cute_dsl/b12x_moe.py:166)` during a live
~17.5 s engine-wide stall; `perf` showed `_cutlass_ir.cpython-312.so` frames present only
during stalls.

## Why this deserves a disk layer even after #3836

#3836 stops *rekeying* (recompiles within one process). But serving engines restart —
deploys, config changes, crash recovery, autoscaling — and each fresh process re-pays the
entire compile set: ~40 s dynamic + 15–18 s per small-shape class. For a model like
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B this is 1–2 minutes of mid-serving stalls per engine lifetime that a
disk cache would reduce to milliseconds. The artifacts are deterministic products of
(kernel source, shape/config tuple, DSL version, arch) — exactly what file caches are for.

## Suggested fix directions

Either would resolve it; the first is contained entirely in flashinfer:

1. **flashinfer grows its own disk layer for sm12x MoE kernels**: serialize the compiled
   artifact keyed by the existing `cache_key` tuples + flashinfer version +
   nvidia-cutlass-dsl version + SM arch, under `FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_DIR` (or a new env),
   loading into `_STATIC/_MICRO/_DYNAMIC_KERNEL_CACHE` on miss. The DSL's own
   `compile_and_cache` machinery demonstrates the artifact is serializable (the implicit
   path already writes/reads `.mlir` + compiled objects).
2. **Upstream: nvidia-cutlass-dsl honors its file cache under explicit `cute.compile`**
   (stop hardcoding `no_cache=True`, or add an opt-in kwarg flashinfer can pass).

A third, cheaper-but-partial option is an official warm-up API (the attempt in
vllm#47599 was closed unmerged): it moves the cost to boot but still re-pays it every
process start, and needs the largest-workspace-first ordering to avoid #3836 rekeying —
a disk cache composes with, rather than replaces, that.

## Cross-references

- vllm#47458 — serving-stall report this splits from (mechanism established in-thread by
  @waynehacking8; py-spy confirmation by me)
- flashinfer#3836 — the workspace-rekeying half (open)

items.title: [Bug] CuTe-DSL MXFP8 quantization zeros nonzero BF16 blocks when E8M0 scale byte is 0
items.author: youngeunkwon0405
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting

- [x] I searched existing issues and pull requests and did not find an open report or fix for this exact CuTe-DSL scale-byte-0 case. Related reports are listed below.

### Bug description

`flashinfer.mxfp8_quantize(..., backend="cute-dsl")` turns nonzero, exactly representable BF16 values into zero when it selects E8M0 scale byte `0`.

E8M0 byte `0` represents **2^-127**, not zero. Quantization should therefore use the finite FP32 inverse scale **2^127**. The CuTe-DSL inverse-scale helper instead explicitly returns zero for this code, so the FP8 payloads become zero.

This reproduces on FlashInfer **0.6.18**, NVIDIA **GB200**, CUDA **13.4**, PyTorch **2.14.0a0+b2c75dd062.nv26.09**, and **nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.6.2** as reported by `importlib.metadata.version()` in the reproducer. The same zero override is present in the inspected main revision `46340689a5ab5665ab39f6281dac4d021d7ae94b`; I have not run that main revision.

The synthetic inputs below are all **normal BF16 values**, so this loss does not come from BF16 underflow. They are also exactly representable in MXFP8 E4M3. No model weights, TE dequantization, or external scale-byte postprocessing is involved in this reproduction.

### Minimal reproduction

```python
import torch
import flashinfer

# Four constant 32-value blocks per row; the last is a control.
s = 2.0 ** -127
values = torch.tensor([20*s, -20*s, 448*s, 448*2*s], dtype=torch.float64)
x = values.to(device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16).repeat_interleave(32).repeat(32, 1)
assert torch.equal(x[0, ::32].double().cpu(), values)

q, sf = flashinfer.mxfp8_quantize(
    x, backend="cute-dsl", is_sf_swizzled_layout=False, alignment=32
)
sf = sf.reshape(32, 4)
# Independent FP64 decode: E8M0 byte 0 is a valid nonzero scale.
scale = torch.exp2(sf.double() - 127).repeat_interleave(32, dim=1)
decoded = q.double() * scale

print("input:", x[0, ::32].double().tolist())
print("scale bytes:", sf[0].tolist())
print("FP8 payload:", q[0, ::32].float().tolist())
print("decoded:", decoded[0, ::32].tolist())
print("changed elements:", (decoded != x.double()).sum().item(), "/", x.numel())
print("control exact:", torch.equal(decoded[:, 96:], x[:, 96:].double()))
```

### Actual and expected results

The verified run produced:

```text
input: [1.1754943508222875e-37, -1.1754943508222875e-37, 2.633107345841924e-36, 5.266214691683848e-36]
scale bytes: [0, 0, 0, 1]
FP8 payload: [0.0, -0.0, 0.0, 448.0]
decoded: [0.0, -0.0, 0.0, 5.266214691683848e-36]
changed elements: 3072 / 4096
control exact: True
```

For the selected scale bytes `[0, 0, 0, 1]`, the expected payloads are `[20.0, -20.0, 448.0, 448.0]`, giving **zero changed elements**. The scale-byte-1 control already passes.

### Suspected cause and requested fix

The [inverse-scale helper](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/46340689a5ab5665ab39f6281dac4d021d7ae94b/flashinfer/quantization/quantization_cute_dsl_utils.py#L209-L242) constructs the exponent for `2^(127 - code)`, then overrides the result with `0` when `code == 0`. For code 0, the initially constructed value `2^127` is finite and is the required multiplier.

Could you fix the code-0 inverse-scale handling and add regression coverage that checks preservation of nonzero values, including positive/negative constant blocks and an all-zero block? Checking only for the absence of NaNs does not catch this loss. The helper is shared with MXFP4, so its callers would also benefit from boundary coverage; this report's GPU reproduction covers MXFP8 E4M3 only.

### Related TE fix and FlashInfer reports

- **[NVIDIA/TransformerEngine#3262](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TransformerEngine/pull/3262)**, merged August 5, fixes the related E8M0 code-0 decoding bug: the forward scale expansion must produce `2^-127` rather than zero. This is the same format-boundary problem in a different operation: TE fixes forward scale expansion during dequantization; FlashInfer needs the inverse scale `2^127` during quantization.
- **#4023** fixes inverse-scale handling for **code 254** and explicitly retains the code-0 zero override, so it does not address this reproduction.
- **#2440 / #2441** address tiny-input NaNs in the CUDA path by producing zeros. The issue here is preserving valid nonzero values in the CuTe-DSL path.

### Environment

Collected with `python -m flashinfer.collect_env` in the same venv/container used for the reproduction. Private checkout, venv, and cache paths are replaced with placeholders; package and library information is retained.

The venv inherits system-site packages. The reproducer directly reported `importlib.metadata.version("nvidia-cutlass-dsl") == "4.6.2"` and `importlib.metadata.version("apache-tvm-ffi") == "0.1.11"`. The collector's package inventory below enumerates all visible distributions into a dictionary, so the inherited system versions `4.8.0.dev0` and `0.1.14` overwrite those entries in its display. Both observations are included here to make the environment explicit.

<details>
<summary>Full environment report (private paths redacted)</summary>

```text

<!-- generated by `python -m flashinfer.collect_env`; paste into your issue -->

==== FlashInfer ====
flashinfer                   : 0.6.18
flashinfer commit            : 69ff11fc4954396d98326656dc85debd2223f637
flashinfer file              : <venv>/lib/python3.12/site-packages/flashinfer/__init__.py

items.title: [Bug]: MiniMax-M2 streaming tool parser re-sends full arguments and duplicates the tool call
items.author: MohammadHijjawi97
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

CPU only (parser logic, no GPU needed); TensorRT-LLM main @ 534e1f8a.

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

With `--tool_parser minimax_m2` and `stream=true`, a tool call that streams over several chunks produces broken output. Minimal repro without a model: feed this text to `MiniMaxM2ToolParser.parse_streaming_increment` in 4-character chunks:

```
<minimax:tool_call><invoke name="get_weather"><parameter name="city">Paris</parameter><parameter name="unit">celsius</parameter></invoke></minimax:tool_call>
```

### Expected behavior

The concatenated `function.arguments` deltas form `{"city": "Paris", "unit": "celsius"}`, and there is a single tool call (index 0) — the same result as the non-streaming `detect_and_parse`.

### actual behavior

- The full arguments JSON is re-sent each time a parameter completes, so the concatenated deltas are `{"city": "Paris"}{"city": "Paris", "unit": "celsius"}` (invalid JSON).
- When `</invoke>` arrives, the function name is emitted again under tool index 1, creating a phantom second call.

### additional notes

The partial-invoke regex can also match across an already-closed `<invoke>` and emit a garbage tool name. I have a fix with a regression test and will open a PR.
