items.title: Matrix<R,C>::at() strides by row count: wrong values and out-of-bounds access for all non-square shapes (diagonal/hcat/vcat affected)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

The value-semantics `Matrix<R, C>` specializations in include/cutlass/matrix.h implement `at(i, j)` with a **row-count** stride instead of a column-count stride:

```cpp
Element at(int i, int j) const {
    return data[i * kRows + j];   // should be i * kColumns
}
```

Every non-square specialization is affected (square ones coincide). Consequences for non-square shapes:

- wrong element returned/stored whenever row >= 1 and R != C;
- out-of-bounds reads **and writes** when R > C (e.g. `Matrix<float,4,1>::at(3,0)` touches `data[12]` of a 4-element array);
- GCC at -O2 even warns "iteration invokes undefined behavior" on loops over `at()` for 3x2/4x2/4x3.

Downstream members built on `at()` inherit the defect:

- `diagonal()` returns wrong values for every non-square shape and performs OOB accesses for R > C shapes (e.g. `Matrix<float,3,2>::diagonal()` writes 3 entries into its 2-element result while reading `data[8]` of 6); AddressSanitizer flags it: `heap-buffer-overflow READ ... Matrix<float,3,2>::diagonal() const matrix.h`.
- the element-wise forms of `hcat`/`vcat` read their operands through `at()`, so concatenations are wrong for any operand with more than one row and non-square shape. A full differential over all 15 shapes shows 28 hcat-lhs + 18 hcat-rhs + 19 vcat-lhs mismatches plus transpose round-trip failures (`t.transpose()` != original), all confined to non-square operands.

Everything else in the header (products, transpose storage maps, slice_/set_slice_, dot/sum/norm/trace, uniform constructors) sweeps clean against reference implementations; the defects are exactly the `at()`-derived paths. No in-tree caller exercises these members on non-square matrices today (`test/unit/core/matrix.cu` is 4x4 only), so this has stayed latent, but the class is public API.

### Suggested fix

Regenerate the specializations with `at()` striding by `kColumns`; make `diagonal()` emit `min(kRows, kColumns)` entries from `data[i * kColumns + i]` into a matching-size result; regenerate the element-wise `hcat`/`vcat` statics (or index operands directly). A unit test covering at/diagonal/hcat/vcat on non-square shapes would pin it.

items.title: [Serve] [RFC] Computed Retry-After for backpressure rejections
items.author: vinay7373
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

PR #65193 added `BackpressureConfig`. Deployments can now reject backpressured requests with a 429 and a static `Retry-After` header. Each caller (proxy or `DeploymentHandle`) has its own request queue, and at the time of a backpressure rejection a static `Retry-After` value can be incorrect in both directions. If the queue is deep and the static value is too short, clients retry into another rejection, adding load exactly when the system is trying to shed it. If the queue drains fast and the value is too long, capacity sits idle while clients wait.

This proposal computes the `Retry-After` value from observed load. This makes the header a reliable estimate of when capacity will be available, instead of a number the operator guessed. This was the original shape of the production request behind #65193 and it fits the discussion there about making 429 the default at some point.

No OSS inference server does this today (TGI, Triton, NVIDIA Dynamo and TorchServe all reject without a retry hint). The closest prior art is cloud-side (Azure OpenAI's `retry-after-ms`, AWS's `x-amz-retry-after`) and per-client rate limiters, where the value can be exact because a rate window is a clock. Capacity recovery is not a clock, so here the value is an estimate at any layer.

## Goals

- An opt-in `BackpressureConfig` policy that computes `Retry-After` from load signals the rejecting component already has.
- Keep the rejection path as cheap as it is today. No RPCs, locks or extra work on reject-and-respond.
- Degrade gracefully: computed, else static, else no header. Never fail or delay a rejection.

## Non-goals

- Changing when requests are rejected. Admission control is a separate discussion.
- Guaranteeing admission at the suggested time. The header is a hint, not a reservation.
- Changing the default rejection status code. Tracked separately.
- Implementing any further policy, such as the cluster-informed one (see "Future policies").

## Proposed API

```python
from ray.serve.config import BackpressureConfig

@serve.deployment(
    max_queued_requests=64,
    backpressure_config=BackpressureConfig(
        status_code=429,
        retry_after_policy="queue_drain_rate",   # NEW: "static" (default) | "queue_drain_rate"
        retry_after_s=5,                         # static value; also the fallback for computed policies
    ),
)
```

`retry_after_policy` is a named policy instead of a bare `"auto"` so future strategies can be added without changing what existing configs mean.

## Proposed design

This design adds a new field to `BackpressureConfig` called `retry_after_policy`, and one new policy named `queue_drain_rate` that computes `Retry-After` from the rejecting component's observed queue depth and drain rate.

The overall mechanism has 3 basic aspects: (i) how to compute the `Retry-After` value (what the `queue_drain_rate` policy implements), (ii) where to compute it, and (iii) who stamps the header and emits it to the client.

These boil down to emission and estimation. Emission answers (iii) and is fixed: the rejecting component stamps the header. Estimation covers (i) and (ii): one shared implementation, invoked at the two places Serve rejects today, each feeding its own local signals.

### The `queue_drain_rate` policy (this proposal)

```
retry_after = ceil(observed_queue_depth / drain_rate)
```

- **The numerator is the depth observed at rejection.** It is at least `max_queued_requests`, since a rejection only fires once the queue has reached the cap, and occasionally a little above it: the router's check is not atomic, and replica-rejected requests re-enter the queue behind new arrivals. The raise site already holds this number (it is in the `BackPressureError` message today), so using the observed value costs nothing and is exact.
- **`drain_rate` is the live signal**: how fast the queue empties, updated at the end of every interval as `drain_rate = 0.3 * rate_over_last_interval + 0.7 * previous_drain_rate`. `rate_over_last_interval` is the fresh measurement: requests drained during the interval that just ended. `previous_drain_rate` is this same formula's output from the previous update, so it carries the whole history with older intervals fading out. The 70% weight on the trend keeps lumpy traffic from whipping the value around (completions land in bursts, so a single interval can read 0 or 3x the true rate), and the 30% on the fresh measurement keeps the estimate chasing real load changes within a few intervals. The split, the interval length and the warmup threshold are implementation constants with environment-variable overrides, like Serve's other internal tunables, not new `BackpressureConfig` fields. The update runs on a lightweight background timer in the component's existing metrics machinery (default 1s). An interval with zero completions counts as a real observation when work is in flight, since that is what slow drain looks like, but idle intervals (nothing running or queued) skip the update instead of decaying the rate. The rate counts as warm after a configurable minimum number of counted intervals; until then the fallback applies.
- **Two call sites, one implementation.** On the proxy path the router rejects; its drain rate is its own assignment throughput, from a monotonic counter added at the existing send event (the current per-replica counter is an in-flight gauge, so it can't provide a rate). The rate is fleet-blended: faster replicas take more assignments, so mixed hardware is priced in. On direct ingress the replica rejects; its drain rate is its own completion rate, and its queue is drained only by itself. Same formula, different local inputs, different values, each describing its own queue. A replica's value is a conservative upper bound, since a retry may be re-balanced to a replica that frees up sooner.
- **Clamp to [1, 60] seconds.** Common client SDKs ignore `Retry-After` above 60s.
- **Jitter (for example +/-20%) is applied in the shared heade

comments.author: johntaylor-cell
comments.body:
My main concern is how this RFC and direct-ingress work together.  Serve is moving toward direct-ingress with HAProxy as the default, and on that path the router is no longer the module that rejects the request.  HAProxy will sit between the client and Serve, and it already has retry-after functionality (as does Envoy).  Both implement it very differently from what the RFC proposes.  Their calculation is time-based so it is more exact than the proposed prediction.  It is also per-client, and HAProxy exposes queue-based metrics so the limit can fire only under real back pressure.  I suggest we provide a way to enable that functionality in HAProxy, which Serve already generates config for but does not use today.

If we also want retry-after on the router path (when direct-ingress is disabled), I would try to duplicate HAProxy's time-based functionality, rather than use a forecast. That is a larger change than this RFC scopes, since admission control is listed as a non-goal, but I think it is worth deciding explicitly rather than estimating.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
Thanks for the review. Breaking it down into where we agree and where we don't.

**Where we agree:**

1. The RFC did not cover the direct-ingress path. That was a real gap and I updated the RFC. Short version: on direct ingress the same policy runs at the replica, using its own queue depth divided by an EWMA of its own completion rate. Same formula, one shared estimator implementation, two call sites. A replica's queue is drained only by itself, so that vantage is even simpler than the router's.

2. Per-client rate limiting at the HAProxy layer is valuable. It answers "this client exceeded its quota", and its Retry-After can be exact because a rate window is a clock. That is complementary to this RFC, which answers "the deployment is out of capacity, here is when to come back". I would support that as a separate proposal and am happy to file it.

**Where we don't agree, and why:**

1. "HAProxy will sit between the client and Serve" as the rejector. Not for backpressure today. On the direct-ingress path the replica rejects the request (see the "Request dropped due to backpressure" emission sites in [replica.py on the ray-2.58.0 tag](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/python/ray/serve/_private/replica.py)). HAProxy passes the replica's response through, and its errorfiles only rewrite HAProxy-generated errors. #65193 shipped 429 + Retry-After on this path, tested with `RAY_SERVE_ENABLE_DIRECT_INGRESS=1`.

2. "Functionality Serve already generates config for but does not use". I checked `haproxy_templates.py`: no stick-tables, no track-sc, no deny rules, no Retry-After anywhere in the generated config. Enabling this would be new work, not switching on something dormant.

3. "Their calculation is time-based so it is more exact than the proposed prediction". I checked the [HAProxy docs](https://www.haproxy.com/documentation/haproxy-configuration-tutorials/security/traffic-policing/) on this. HAProxy's computed Retry-After is `http-after-response set-header Retry-After %[src,table_expire(...)]`: the time until the client's stick-table rate-limit record expires. That is per-client policing, and it is exact because a rate window is deterministic. For capacity overload (server maxconn queue full, `timeout queue` expiring) the docs show no Retry-After computation: that 503 ships without a hint. The queue timer measures elapsed wait, not time until capacity returns. When capacity frees depends on service completions and arrivals, and no layer can know that exactly, including HAProxy, which cannot see how long the inference ahead of a request will take. Any capacity Retry-After is an estimate at every layer. That is why the RFC ships an acceptance criterion and telemetry to measure the estimate, instead of claiming exactness.

Rate limiting and capacity backpressure are different problems. An exact time-based Retry-After exists for the first and cannot exist for the second. This RFC is scoped to the second, now explicitly works on both ingress paths, and leaves room for a HAProxy rate-limiting proposal alongside it.

comments.author: suppagoddo
comments.body:
@vinay7373 - Couple of questions or feedback on this:

1. In case of direct-ingress path, the `router_queue_drain_rate` would become a bit misleading as the requests are rejected by the replicas here. 
2. For the direct-ingress path, I am thinking can we also add another saturation_factor. Fleet level info does not exists here, so it can be local value here.
3. For the EWMA warmup, I am thinking can this be a configurable variable.

Also I agree on the Rate limit and capacity back-pressure differentiation made above. 

Overall, I like the idea of calculating the `retry_after_s` on router/replica level before the `cluster_informed` policy.

comments.author: suppagoddo
comments.body:
@vinay7373 - For 
> retry at the suggested delay is admitted X% of the time” 

metric, in case of arbitrary production traffic, how can the serve proxy/router reliably correlate a 429 with a subsequent retry, because the client may generate a new request ID, retry through a different proxy/router, or not retry at all.

In order to measure efficiency without client correlation, shall we also compare the suggested/computed delay against an observable local recovery/drain-time metric [The calculation for this might get tricky under continuous load]?

> Rate limiting and capacity backpressure are different problems. An exact time-based Retry-After exists for the first and cannot exist for the second. This RFC is scoped to the second, now explicitly works on both ingress paths, and leaves room for a HAProxy rate-limiting proposal alongside it.

Unfortunately, there is no data plane component with the entire fleet view, and it can take seconds for the controller to respond to any situation. So I beleive the best decision point is the one closest to the client, where a refusal costs no downstream resources. That is why I have been focusing on HAProxy and with a goal to keep any solm isolated and simple.

You are right on the three points above. I also tried to construct a computed version at HAProxy and it fails for your reasons plus one more: queue state resets on every reload, which fires whenever the replica set changes.

I think the RFC runs two problems together. Admission control keeps the fleet from being overloaded, `Retry-After` only shapes when refused load comes back. Shed at HAProxy by

Most of the dynamic information in the proposed estimator comes from the `drain-rate EWMA` and `saturation signals`. I would suggest it make more sense for the acceptance criteria to explicitly compare the `computed policy` against a `jittered-static baseline` under the same workloads?

Retry-After estimator should be independent of admission control here, which I guess you also agree upon.

</strike>
@johntaylor-cell - Your proposal seems to change both the admission-control point and the retry-shaping strategy.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@johntaylor-cell 

My thoughts on your a HA Proxy based admission control and what I see as limitations:

- As you mentioned the HAProxy queue resets on every reload and Serve reloads HAProxy on every replica-set change. So the primary queue evaporates exactly during autoscaling churn (your own finding).
- Composition traffic never passes HAProxy, so the Serve backstop must stay. That means 3 admission systems with 3 threshold vocabularies to keep coherent.
    - Users configuring three queueing layers instead of one: per-server `maxconn` plus timeout queue in HAProxy, `max_queued_requests` at handles, `max_ongoing_requests` at replicas. Three knobs at three levels in different units (connections vs requests, per instance vs per caller vs per replica) that all have to be sized against each other and re-sized as the cluster scales. Mis-size any pair and you get double queueing or shedding while replicas sit idle. That is more error prone, not simpler.
- The default proxy path gets nothing from it.
- Per-deployment BackpressureConfig granularity would have to be re-expressed in generated HAProxy config.
- Moving where queueing happens is an admission-control redesign, which this RFC explicitly scopes out as a non-goal.
- On jittered-static vs computed: 
    - jitter only spreads retries around a center, it cannot make the center reliable. With `retry_after_s` we already ship the option to set a fixed, guessed value at config time, so a jittered constant is not a new proposal, it is [#65193](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65193) plus jitter. Drain rate moves 10-100x across load regimes, so the constant is wrong exactly when it matters. A 5s center against a 60s real drain means every jittered retry comes back early and gets refused again. Guessing that constant is the problem this RFC exists to remove. So a computed value using drain rate is more reliable. And @suppagoddo 's suggestion for A/B against a jittered-static baseline will show it under real workloads and make this measurable.

comments.author: johntaylor-cell
comments.body:
> [@johntaylor-cell](https://github.com/johntaylor-cell)
> 
> My thoughts on your a HA Proxy based admission control and what I see as limitations:
> 
> * As you mentioned the HAProxy queue resets on every reload and Serve reloads HAProxy on every replica-set change. So the primary queue evaporates exactly during autoscaling churn (your own finding).

Three knobs at three levels in different units (connections vs requests, per instance vs per caller vs per replica) that all have to be sized against each other and re-sized as the cluster scales. Mis-size any pair and you get double queueing or shedding while replicas sit idle. That is more error prone, not simpler.
> * The default proxy path gets nothing from it.
> * Per-deployment BackpressureConfig granularity would have to be re-expressed in generated HAProxy config.

With `retry_after_s` we already ship the option to set a fixed, guessed value at config time, so a jittered constant is not a new proposal, it is [#65193](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65193) plus jitter. Drain rate moves 10-100x across load regimes, so the constant is wrong exactly when it matters. A 5s center against a 60s real drain means every jittered retry comes back early and gets refused again. Guessing that constant is the problem this RFC exists to remove. So a computed value using drain rate is more reliable. And [@suppagoddo](https://github.com/suppagoddo) 's suggestion for A/B against a jittered-static baseline will show it under real workloads and make this measurable.

I have one last set of comments, but I think I have explored an HAProxy centric solution enough at this point.    A less invasive change as proposed in your RFC is likely the safest approach.  I do have two comments about the estimation calculation as presented below in #6 and #7.
1. The reload is really a gap.  There is no reason to wipe out the HAProxy state unless there is a configuration change that requires such a drastic step.  HAproxy can add/remove servers dynamically of course
2. If HAProxy did perform admission control (set per-server maxconn), composition traffic would become indirectly visible, since it slows the replica and HAProxy's queue fills behind it, at least while the replica holds the overflow rather than fast-rejecting it.
3. Yes, an HAProxy approach doesnt work if there is no HAProxy :slightly_smiling_face: Hopefully that path is rare as direct-ingress will become the default very soon
4. Yes, but entirely doable and not difficult
5. No reason to not explore admission control even though the RFC mentions it as a non-goal.  Seems limiting if we are trying to find best long-term soln
6. The estimator has three inputs and I do not think any of them hold up.  Queue depth is not an observation, a rejection only fires once depth has reached `max_queued_requests`, so it is always the configured cap.  Occupancy is zero for LLM deployments, where `max_ongoing_requests` defaults to a billion.  And I could not find any signal behind the backoff term.  That leaves the drain rate, which the RFC agrees carries the estimate, but the router has no counter for it today and the code that raises the rejection cannot reach the router state it would need.
7. Regarding adding jitter, today's static path has none, `retry_after_s` is emitted verbatim by every path through one helper.  That makes the A/B @suppagoddo suggested a comparison bet

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@johntaylor-cell took your 6 and 7 into the RFC:

On 6: you are right that queue depth is the configured cap at rejection, and right about occupancy. I checked: `serve.llm` sets `DEFAULT_MAX_ONGOING_REQUESTS = int(1e9)` (python/ray/llm/_internal/serve/constants.py), so occupancy against configured capacity reads zero. The saturation factor is dropped entirely and the formula is now `ceil(max_queued_requests / drain_rate)`. 

One clarification on the drain rate, since implementability was questioned: the router already counts assignments per replica (num_requests_sent_to_replicas, router.py:152) and the rejection is raised from a method on the same `RouterMetricsManager` that owns those counters, so the EWMA is a derivation over state the raise site already holds, not new plumbing.

On 7: agreed and adopted. Jitter moves into the shared header helper, so the static retry_after_s path gets it too, which both fixes today's verbatim emission and keeps the A/B fair. Good catch, credited in the RFC.

Separately, your reload observation (HAProxy state wiped on replica-set changes when dynamic server updates would do) is a real standalone improvement to the HAProxy ingress, worth its own issue regardless of this RFC.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@suppagoddo thanks for your review, all of your points are in the updated RFC:

1. Renamed to queue_drain_rate, since the same policy runs at the router or the replica, whichever rejects.
2. On a local saturation factor for direct ingress: we ended up dropping the saturation factor everywhere instead. From @johntaylor-cell 's finding `serve.llm` defaults `max_ongoing_requests` to `1e9`, so occupancy measured against configured capacity reads zero for the main workload class, and the backoff term had no existing signal behind it. It isn't gone forever though: if the A/B data shows the simple formula consistently errs in a way a saturation signal would fix, that data is the justification to bring one back. Evidence first, term later.
3. EWMA warmup is configurable as an implementation constant with an environment-variable override, alongside the smoothing split and the interval length, same as Serve's other internal tunables. Deliberately not a new BackpressureConfig field, to keep the public API at two fields plus the policy name.
4. Adopted your measurement point: since retries can't be reliably correlated (new request IDs, different proxy, or no retry at all), the primary measure is suggested delay vs the locally observed queue drain time, with admitted-retry rate secondary where correlation does exist.
5. Your A/B against a jittered-static baseline is now the acceptance test itself.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@abrarsheikh to summarize the whole review thread and the current state of RFC:

Updated the RFC based on the review so far and it came out simpler. 
One policy, `queue_drain_rate` which computes `retry_after` on rejection using below formula:
```
retry_after = ceil(max_queued_requests / drain_rate)
```
Where:
- `max_queued_requests`: the numerator is the configured cap (depth at rejection is always the cap) and 
- `drain_rate` is a smoothed measure of how fast the rejecting component's queue empties which is assignment throughput at the router, completion rate at the replica. 

The value is clamped to [1, 60]s and jittered in the shared header helper so the static path gets jitter too, falls back to the static retry_after_s when the rate isn't warm, and the acceptance test is an A/B against a jittered-static baseline measured on suggested delay vs observed local drain time.

comments.author: suppagoddo
comments.body: @abrarsheikh @vinay7373 - Can I take this feature implementation?

comments.author: JerryChaox
comments.body:
hello guys, some information and test for this RFC.

I tested the proposal on Ray 2.58.0 and found two implementation details worth checking before coding it.

First, num_requests_sent_to_replicas is an in-flight gauge: it increments on send and decrements on completion. It cannot directly provide assignment throughput, so the router likely needs a monotonic counter at the accepted-assignment event.

Second, router queue depth is not always equal to max_queued_requests at rejection. Internal replica rejection can cause requests to re-enter after new requests occupy temporarily freed slots. With a cap of 8, 1,418 of 17,270 router rejection events had an observed depth of 9–11. I did not observe this on the direct-replica path.

I also compared the computed policy with a tuned jittered-static baseline over 90 held-out distributed runs. Conditional local-drain header MAE was 1.865s for the computed policy and 1.141s for static 2s. The computed policy generated fewer attempts, so this looks like a precision versus retry-cost tradeoff rather than a clear winner.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@JerryChaox Thanks for testing the approach and for those valuable findings. Here are my thoughts on each of them:

1. Agree (and my earlier comment was wrong on this) that `num_requests_sent_to_replicas` is an in-flight gauge, increments on send (`router.py:404`) and decrements on completion (`router.py:412`). I will fix this by adding a new monotonic assignment counter at the same send event. So the raise site and the counters live on the same object and the drain rate is still a derivation over local state.

2. This is a great find. Agreed. This finding makes the formula better: use the observed depth at rejection as the numerator instead of the configured cap. The raise site already holds that number, it is in the BackPressureError message today.

3. On your third observation, the A/B test: I see how a static value wins on a homogeneous workload, where a good constant like your 2s can be guessed or tuned in advance. But the whole purpose of this RFC is the case where the constant cannot be guessed in advance, because load regimes vary and move the drain rate. I'd like to know: a) Did drain time vary across your 90 runs? b) Was the 2s tuned per workload or once overall?

Your fewer attempts observation is the most interesting part. MAE weighs a 1s early and a 1s late suggestion equally, but the costs are not equal: early means a wasted attempt plus more load on a system that is already shedding, late means idle wait. So I think we should use a asymmetric or composite metric that penalizes wasted attempts (penalize early more than late).

comments.author: vinay7373
suppagoddo
comments.body: @vinay7373 - Sounds good, will start the implementation work!

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
Acceptance criteria spec:

1. Ground truth: Each rejection records the observed depth D and the drain counter value at that moment. Ground truth T is the wall time until the counter advances by D: assignments at the router, completions at the replica on direct ingress. This measures what the header claims, that the observed backlog clears. It does not measure whether a specific retry gets admitted, since that depends on other clients' arrivals. T stays measurable under continuous overload because the counter keeps advancing even when the queue never dips below the cap.
2. Metric: An asymmetric loss between the suggested delay `s` and `T`: `0.75 * max(T - s, 0) + 0.25 * max(s - T, 0)`. One second too early costs 3x one second too late, because an early retry wastes an attempt and adds load while the system is shedding and a late one only waits, bounded by the clamp. The minimizer of this loss is the 75th percentile of the drain time distribution, so the estimator gets a concrete target. MAE is reported as secondary for comparability. Scoring is offline over logged pairs, on the pre-jitter post-clamp value.
3. Baseline: The comparison arm is jittered static, with the constant tuned only on calibration runs disjoint from the evaluation set (rule: 75th percentile of calibration drain times, one global constant). A per-scenario tuned static is also reported. Runs are open loop (clients ignore the header) with autoscaling off and a pinned replica set.

@suppagoddo For me to run the above acceptance test I'll need one structured record per rejection with `policy id, fallback rung used, observed depth, drain rate estimate and warm flag, pre-jitter and post-jitter values, and the counter value at rejection`. Plus the counter itself readable by a test harness at sub-second granularity. Everything already exists at the raise site or in estimator state; the cost is one log line on a path that already logs a warning today. Please make sure this record emission is part of your implementation.

Pass bar (proposal): 
- Computed beats the static baseline on the primary loss by at least 20% in aggregate across the scenarios
- is never more than 10% worse in any single scenario
- the undershoot rate lands at 25 +/- 10 points
- and cold start falls back to the static value cleanly.

cc. @JerryChaox @abrarsheikh @johntaylor-cell

items.title: Illegal memory access in triton kernel and non-determinism codegen
items.author: xw285cornell
items.body_excerpt:
Hi team, we seem to identified an issue that triton is generating non-deterministic codegen results, and in certain cases (small chances) it seems to have illegal memory access due to out of bound access in shared memory. 
The triton code is fairly simple (shown below). We run the code many times (disabled pytorch's codegen cache) and it seems it produced different shared memory: 
Most of times: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 2560, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}
Sometimes: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 544, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}

So sometimes it only asks for 544 bytes for shared memory space which might lead to out of bound access to shared mem. We checked and ttir is the same across the two runs, but llir is different. Wondering if you can shed some lights on this (and whether the codegen is deterministic. Also this is still on llvm IR - not sure if it repros in MLIR. 

```
from torch._inductor.triton_ops.autotune import pointwise

@pointwise(
    size_hints=[262144, 64],
    tile_hint=TileHint.DEFAULT,
    filename="notebook",
    meta={
        "signature": {0: "*bf16", 1: "*fp32", 2: "*bf16", 3: "i32", 4: "i32"},
        "device": 0,
        "constants": {},
        "mutated_arg_names": [],
        "configs": [instance_descriptor(divisible_by_16=(0, 1, 2, 3), equal_to_1=())],
    },
)
@triton.jit
def triton_(
    in_ptr0,
    in_ptr1,
    out_ptr0,
    xnumel,
    ynumel,
    XBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
    YBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
):
    xnumel = 262144
    ynumel = 62
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:, None]
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    yoffset = tl.program_id(1) * YBLOCK
    yindex = yoffset + tl.arange(0, YBLOCK)[None, :]
    ymask = yindex < ynumel
    x0 = xindex % 512
    x1 = xindex // 512
    y2 = yindex
    x3 = xindex
    tmp0 = tl.load(
        in_ptr0
        + (
            512
            + x0
            + (1536 * x1)
            + (786432 * y2)
            + (786432 * (((x0 + (512 * x1)) // 262144)))
        ),
        xmask & ymask,
    ).to(tl.float32)
    tmp1 = tl.load(in_ptr1 + (512 + x0), xmask)
    tmp2 = tmp1.to(tl.float32)
    tmp3 = tmp0 + tmp2
    tmp4 = 2.8284271247461903
    tmp5 = tmp3 / tmp4
    tl.store(
        out_ptr0 + (y2 + (62 * x3) + tl.zeros([XBLOCK, YBLOCK], tl.int32)),
        tmp5,
        xmask & ymask,
    )
```

items.title: Discussion: First-class image warmup workflow for AIBrix model workloads
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
## Proposal

Add a first-class `ModelWarmup` workflow for AIBrix model workloads.

The initial scope is intentionally small: preload large inference/runtime images onto nodes before rollout or scale-out. This addresses cases where traffic arrives while a newly-created Pod is still waiting for the container runtime to pull and unpack images.

This issue is for design discussion. The API and controller behavior are not finalized.

## Business value

Image pulling is a major source of cold-start latency for model-serving workloads. It is especially visible during:

- autoscaler scale-out, when a new replica lands on a node without the required image cache;
- StormService or RoleSet rolling updates, when the new revision is not yet ready but traffic is already increasing;
- manual capacity preparation, where operators want to warm nodes before exposing them to serving traffic.

A first-class workflow should make image warmup observable through Kubernetes status and provide a verify-before-rollout/scale workflow.

## Proposed MVP

Introduce a standalone `ModelWarmup` CRD under `model.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1`.

```yaml
apiVersion: model.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1
kind: ModelWarmup
metadata:
  name: qwen-image-warmup
spec:
  targets:
  - nodes:
      names:
      - gpu-node-a
      - gpu-node-b
  - nodeSelector:
      matchLabels:
        resource-pool.aibrix.ai/name: latency-pool
  - workload:
      ref:
        apiVersion: orchestration.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1
        kind: StormService
        name: qwen
      subTarget:
        roleName: prefill

  imagePreload:
    images:
    - registry.example.com/vllm@sha256:...
    - registry.example.com/aibrix-runtime@sha256:...
    pullSecrets:
    - name: registry-secret

  policies:
    parallelism: 8
    globalTimeoutSeconds: 1800
    retryLimit: 2
    ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600
```

## Target selection

All of the following target sources should be supported:

1. **Explicit nodes**: a list of node names.
2. **Node labels, capabilities, or resource pools**: a Kubernetes `LabelSelector`, for example an AIBrix resource-pool label. This mode should discover matching nodes added later for autoscaler scale-out.
3. **AIBrix workloads**: resolve nodes from `StormService`, `RoleSet`, `Deployment`, `ModelClaim`, or `ModelAdapter` Pods, with role-level filtering such as `prefill` or `decode` where applicable.

Multiple target entries are allowed. The controller should take the union of all resolved targets and deduplicate by node name. This allows operators to combine a resource pool, a workload's current nodes, and explicitly reserved nodes.

A workload reference describes the current workload placement. It does not by itself guarantee coverage of future scale-out nodes; use a node selector/resource-pool target for that purpose.

## Execution model

The controller should:

1. Resolve all target sources.
2. Union and deduplicate target nodes.
3. Calculate a deterministic revision from the target and image configuration.
4. Create one node-pinned warmup Job per target node and revision.
5. Run one short-lived regular container per unique image so image pulls can proceed independently.
6. Update per-node and aggregate status from Job completion.
7. Reconcile newly matching nodes, failed Jobs, stale targets, retries, and TTL cleanup.

Warmup Jobs should use `nodeName` or required node affinity, support the target node's taints and architecture, use configured pull secrets, and avoid requesting GPU resources for image-only warmup. Image entrypoints should be overridden so an inference server does not start accidentally.

A Job is preferred over a bare Pod because it provides retry and completion semantics and can recreate a deleted warmup Pod.

## Suggested status

```yaml
status:
  phase: Pending|Running|Succeeded|Failed|Degraded
  observedRevision: ...
  desiredNodes: 2
  activeNodes: 1
  succeededNodes: 1
  failedNodes: 0
  startTime: ...
  completionTime: ...
  targets:
  - nodeName: gpu-node-a
    source: NodeSelector
    phase: Succeeded
    jobName: qwen-image-warmup-gpu-node-a
    reason: ImagePreloadSucceeded
    message: ...
  conditions: []
```

Image references should preferably be immutable digests, or the controller should record the resolved digest. A changed image list or target configuration must create a new revision and invalidate the previous result.

## MVP boundaries

The first implementation focuses on image preloading only. It should not yet include:

- model artifact/file download;
- engine startup or inference warmup;
- generic arbitrary commands or custom actions;
- automatic rollout blocking or autoscaler mutation;
- direct runtime sidecar RPC integration.

The status and API should remain extensible for later artifact, engine, and precheck stages. Existing StormService, RoleSet, ModelClaim, and PodAutoscaler behavior must remain unchanged unless warmup integration is explicitly enabled.

## Why keep warmup independent?

Warmup is useful before rollout, scale-out, and manual capacity preparation. A standalone resource provides reusable target selection, independent lifecycle and status, and a foundation for future integration with workload controllers without coupling the first implementation to a single workload type.

## Open questions

- Should the kind remain `ModelWarmup`, or should the image-only MVP use `ModelImageWarmup`?
- Should `StormService`, `RoleSet`, and `NodeSelector` be the initial supported target sources, with other workload kinds added later?
- Should failed Jobs be retained by default until TTL cleanup?
- Should the default failure behavior be fail-closed, degraded success, or require an explicit policy?

items.title: [Docs] Add Chinese localization and language switching for the documentation site
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
## Feature Description and Motivation

 provide a Chinese version for the entire [AIBrix documentation site](https://aibrix.readthedocs.io/latest/)

A site-wide Chinese localization would make AIBrix more accessible to Chinese-speaking users and contributors, improve onboarding, and reduce the effort required to understand concepts, deployment guides, API references, and troubleshooting documentation.

## Use Case

Chinese-speaking users who are evaluating, deploying, or contributing to AIBrix currently need to translate the documentation page by page. A consistent official Chinese version would provide a more coherent reading experience across the whole documentation site.

## Proposed Solution

Consider adding Chinese localization for the documentation site with a visible language switcher, for example:

- Add a `中文` / `English` switcher in the documentation header or navigation.
- Use a stable localized URL structure such as `https://aibrix.readthedocs.io/zh-CN/latest/`.
- Translate the existing documentation progressively, starting with Getting Started, Installation, Architecture, and core user guides.
- Preserve matching navigation and page structure between English and Chinese where possible.
- Define a lightweight synchronization process so translated pages stay aligned with the English source, including a way to identify pages that need updates.
- Reuse any localization support already available in the current documentation toolchain.

items.title: [Bug] ModelRouter never recreates a missing HTTPRoute (deleted route, or model label added later)
items.author: btxu-db
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

ModelRouter only creates the HTTPRoute from a workload's Add event. There's no `UpdateFunc` and no periodic resync, so once the route is missing it stays missing until the controller restarts.

Two ways I ran into it:

- I deleted `deepseek-coder-7b-router` by hand. It never came back, and requests for the model kept failing with 503 while the pod was fine.
- I created a Deployment and added `model.aibrix.ai/name` with `kubectl label` afterwards. No route was created.

Without a routing strategy the gateway needs this route and returns 503 when it's missing. `config/default` doesn't set `ROUTING_ALGORITHM`, so plain OpenAI clients on a default install hit this.

#2831 fixed the delete-workload case from #2824. These two don't go through that path.

### Steps to Reproduce

kind (`hack/ci/kind-config.yaml`), AIBrix installed from `main` the way `test/run-e2e-tests.sh` does it, `aibrix/vllm-mock:nightly` from `development/app` as the engine.

**Deleting the route**

`deepseek-coder-7b` is served by the Deployment `deepseek-coder-7b-l20`, and requests return 200.

```bash
kubectl -n envoy-gateway-system port-forward svc/envoy-aibrix-system-aibrix-eg-903790dc 8888:80 &

req() {
  curl -s -o /tmp/resp.json -w '%{http_code}' localhost:8888/v1/chat/completions \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"model":"deepseek-coder-7b","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}],"max_tokens":8}'
}

kubectl -n aibrix-system delete httproute deepseek-coder-7b-router
start=$(date +%s)
for i in $(seq 1 30); do
  code=$(req)
  route=$(kubectl -n aibrix-system get httproute deepseek-coder-7b-router -o name 2>/dev/null || echo none)
  echo "t=$(( $(date +%s) - start ))s HTTP $code route=$route $(head -c 90 /tmp/resp.json)"
  sleep 3
done
```

Output (bodies truncated):

```
t=0s  HTTP 502 route=none upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers. reset reason: protocol error
t=3s  HTTP 502 route=none upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers. reset reason: protocol error
t=6s  HTTP 503 route=none {"error":{"type":"overloaded_error","code":"service_unavailable",...
...
t=89s HTTP 503 route=none {"error":{"code":"service_unavailable",...,"message":"httproutes.gateway.networki...
```

4 × 502 and 26 × 503 out of 30. The route never came back and the controller didn't log anything about it. The L20 pod stayed 1/1 Running.

**Adding the model label later**

A Deployment without `model.aibrix.ai/name`:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: late-label-2
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: late-label-2}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: late-label-2}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: vllm-openai
        image: aibrix/vllm-mock:nightly
        command: ["python3", "app.py"]
        env:
        - {name: MODEL_NAME, value: late-model-2}
        ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
```

```bash
kubectl apply -f late-label.yaml
kubectl rollout status deploy/late-label-2
kubectl label deploy late-label-2 model.aibrix.ai/name=late-model-2 model.aibrix.ai/port=8000
kubectl -n aibrix-system get httproute late-model-2-router
```

I checked for `late-model-2-router` every 10 seconds for 3 minutes. It wasn't there in any of the 18 checks, and the controller logged nothing about it.

**After restarting the controller**

```bash
kubectl -n aibrix-system rollout restart deploy/aibrix-controller-manager
```

After a restart, both routes come back right away. In the delete case, `deepseek-coder-7b-router` was back within about 8 seconds and requests returned 200 again. In the label case, `late-model-2-router` (backend `default/late-model-2:8000`) already existed when the rollout finished.


### Expected behavior

The route should exist whenever a workload serves the model, and come back on its own if it goes missing.

What I have in mind, keeping the current create-only behavior:

- An `UpdateFunc` that only reacts when the model labels or annotations change, and ignores objects that are being deleted.
- A ticker, like the periodic enqueue in ModelAdapter and PodAutoscaler, that lists workloads from the cache and creates any route that's missing. It checks the cache first, so nothing is written when all routes exist.

This doesn't try to update existing routes or handle the same model name in several namespaces. Happy to send a PR if this sounds OK.


### Environment

- AIBrix: tested on `main` @ `dcc8aa9a`. Latest `main` (`be4dcd30`, includes #2831) still only registers Add and Delete handlers in ModelRouter.
- Kubernetes: kind v1.30.0, 1 control-plane + 1 worker
- Envoy Gateway v1.2.8 from `config/dependency`
- Engine: `aibrix/vllm-mock:nightly` from `development/app`

### Area

Gateway

items.title: [Bug] KV event replay never applies the replayed batches
items.author: sohom-cs
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`ZMQClient` asks the vLLM KV event publisher for a replay when it starts, from seq 0 ([zmq_client.go#L149](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a26d827c0bbb0dd43079c7d7853a7bd32d89eb1e/pkg/cache/kvcache/zmq_client.go#L149)), and after every reconnect, from `lastSeq+1` ([#L251](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a26d827c0bbb0dd43079c7d7853a7bd32d89eb1e/pkg/cache/kvcache/zmq_client.go#L251)). The replayed batches never reach the prefix index.

vLLM answers a replay request with one message per buffered batch and then an end marker with seq -1 ([`_service_replay`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/111f71a6dbf1fe517f6164e1059a2837bb0a8b4e/vllm/distributed/kv_events.py#L509-L527)). `requestReplay` reads a single frame ([#L394](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a26d827c0bbb0dd43079c7d7853a7bd32d89eb1e/pkg/cache/kvcache/zmq_client.go#L394)), which is the empty delimiter of the first replayed message. It logs `Successfully requested replay from seq 0 for <pod> (response: 0 bytes)` and returns. The batches and the end marker stay unread in the DEALER socket.

What this breaks:

- A gateway that subscribes after the engine has cached blocks never indexes those blocks. Later `BlockStored` events whose parent is one of them are skipped as "unknown parent" ([sync_hash.go#L280-L287](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a26d827c0bbb0dd43079c7d7853a7bd32d89eb1e/pkg/utils/syncprefixcacheindexer/sync_hash.go#L280-L287)), so prefixes that extend an earlier cached prefix are not indexed either.
- Events published while the client was disconnected are not recovered.
- The frames left in the socket are read by the next replay request as its response.

The unit tests did not catch it because the mock publisher answers a replay request with a single `"OK"` frame ([zmq_client_test.go#L635](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a26d827c0bbb0dd43079c7d7853a7bd32d89eb1e/pkg/cache/kvcache/zmq_client_test.go#L635)).

A separate thing I noticed while reading this code, not part of this bug: the replay port is fixed at `DefaultRouterPort = 5558`, while `samples/semantic-router/models/qwen3-8b.yaml` publishes replay on 5559 and the vLLM P/D samples in `samples/disaggregation/vllm/` use 5558 for the NIXL side channel.

### Steps to Reproduce

A ROUTER that follows vLLM's replay protocol, plus the send and receive steps of `requestReplay` (pebbe/zmq4 v1.4.0, libzmq 4.3.5, Go 1.24):

```go
package main

import (
	"encoding/binary"
	"fmt"
	"time"

	zmq "github.com/pebbe/zmq4"
)

func seqBytes(s int64) []byte { b := make([]byte, 8); binary.BigEndian.PutUint64(b, uint64(s)); return b }

func main() {
	router, _ := zmq.NewSocket(zmq.ROUTER)
	router.Bind("tcp://127.0.0.1:15558")
	// vLLM side: replay buffer holds batches seq 7..9
	go func() {
		frame, _ := router.RecvMessageBytes(0) // [client_id, "", start_seq]
		client := frame[0]
		start := int64(binary.BigEndian.Uint64(frame[2]))
		for s := int64(7); s <= 9; s++ {
			if s >= start {
				router.SendMessage(client, []byte{}, []byte("kv-events"), seqBytes(s), []byte(fmt.Sprintf("payload-%d", s)))
			}
		}
		router.SendMessage(client, []byte{}, []byte{}, seqBytes(-1), []byte{}) // END_SEQ
	}()
	dealer, _ := zmq.NewSocket(zmq.DEALER)
	dealer.Connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:15558")
	time.Sleep(100 * time.Millisecond)
	// same send/receive steps as aibrix requestReplay
	dealer.SendMessage([]byte{}, seqBytes(0))
	dealer.SetRcvtimeo(5 * time.Second)
	resp, err := dealer.RecvBytes(0)
	fmt.Printf("requestReplay returns: err=%v, response %d bytes (logged as success)\n", err, len(resp))
	// what is left unread in the DEALER queue
	time.Sleep(200 * time.Millisecond)
	n := 0
	for {
		parts, err := dealer.RecvMessageBytes(zmq.DONTWAIT)
		if err != nil {
			break
		}
		n++
		fmt.Printf("  unread message %d: %d frames, seq frame=%v\n", n, len(parts), parts[len(parts)-2])
	}
	fmt.Printf("replayed batches never decoded/applied: %d messages left in socket\n", n)
}
```

Output:

```
requestReplay returns: err=<nil>, response 0 bytes (logged as success)
  unread message 1: 3 frames, seq frame=[0 0 0 0 0 0 0 7]
  unread message 2: 4 frames, seq frame=[0 0 0 0 0 0 0 8]
  unread message 3: 4 frames, seq frame=[0 0 0 0 0 0 0 9]
  unread message 4: 4 frames, seq frame=[255 255 255 255 255 255 255 255]
replayed batches never decoded/applied: 4 messages left in socket
```

This uses the framing of vLLM v0.26 and later, `[empty, topic, seq, payload]`. vLLM v0.25 and earlier send `[empty, seq, payload]` (the topic frame was added in vllm-project/vllm#45177). The first frame is the empty delimiter in both, so the result is the same.

### Expected behavior

`requestReplay` reads replies until the end marker, applies each replayed batch newer than `lastSeq` the same way as live batches, and bounds the whole replay by `ReplayTimeout`. A reply that times out is not read as the answer to the next request.

I'm opening a PR with a fix and tests.

### Environment

- AIBrix: main at a26d827
- vLLM: any version started with a `replay_endpoint` in `--kv-events-config`. I checked the replay code in `vllm/distributed/kv_events.py` for v0.11.0 through v0.30.0; only the topic frame changed.
- Found by reading the code and reproduced with the program above, not in a cluster.

### Area

Gateway

items.title: [ModelClaim] Add operational metrics for pooled runtimes and policy actions
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### Feature Description and Motivation

ModelClaim exposes basic desired/ready/activation metrics and runtime KV/HBM gauges, but operators cannot currently tell whether an engine is repeatedly restarting, was re-adopted after an agent restart, exhausted its restart budget, or whether the pool KV policy applied or skipped a decision.

ModelClaim is still experimental, so this issue is limited to additive observability. 

### Use Case

When several model engines share one GPU, an operator needs to distinguish a healthy dense pool from a pool that is silently converging through engine restarts or repeatedly failing policy actions. The signals must support alerts and post-incident diagnosis without requiring runtime snapshot or controller log inspection.

### Proposed Solution

Add low-cardinality Prometheus metrics covering:

- engine restart attempts and restart-budget exhaustion;
- runtime agent re-adoption outcomes;
- engine state counts by phase (`active`, `sleeping`, `restarting`, `failed`);
- pool-policy evaluation and action outcomes (`applied`, `skipped`, `failed`) with a bounded reason label;
- requested and successfully applied KV limits per model;
- sleep and wake operation count and duration;
- duration for which a ModelClaim has no ready engine.

Keep labels bounded to namespace, model, pod/pool where necessary, action/result, and an enumerated reason. Do not expose free-form errors, operation IDs, PIDs, or claim UIDs as metric labels. Detailed errors should remain in logs and Kubernetes Events.

Add focused unit tests for registration, values, cleanup of deleted gauge series, and bounded label values. Document metric names and semantics alongside the ModelClaim runbook.

### Acceptance Criteria

- Metrics are exported from the existing controller-manager or runtime `/metrics` endpoints.
- A terminal engine failure, successful re-adoption, successful/failed KV update, and sleep/wake operation are observable without reading logs.
- Policy skip reasons are from a fixed enum and cannot introduce unbounded cardinality.
- Existing ModelClaim APIs and reconciliation behavior remain unchanged.

items.title: [Store] Does Mooncake store plan to support awareness of layers, chunk ordering, and TP?
items.author: Hadigan
items.body_excerpt:
It looks like the current Mooncake store does not have awareness of layer granularity, chunk order (earlier vs. later chunks), or TP ranks. This can cause problems during cache eviction:

1. The store might evict KVs for only some layers, forcing prefill to recompute all layer KVs for those tokens.
2. The store might evict the KVs corresponding to the earliest chunk(s) of a token sequence, forcing prefill to recompute KVs for all chunks/tokens.
3. The store might evict KVs produced by some TP ranks, forcing all TP ranks to recompute KVs.

I think the Mooncake store should be aware of layers, chunk ordering, and TP. On eviction, it should evict a token’s KV caches for all layers and for all TP ranks together (i.e., keep KV state complete per token). 
From the chunk-order perspective, eviction policies should prefer removing KVs for later chunks first rather than evicting early-chunk KVs that make prefill expensive.

items.title: MapAllocator hardcodes PROT_WRITE, causing OOM on unified-memory systems: no way to request a read-only file mapping
items.author: nvbfalk
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Bug Description
`MapAllocator` maps checkpoint files `PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE` on both branches, even though the
non-shared path opens the fd `O_RDONLY`:
 
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/aten/src/ATen/MapAllocator.cpp
 
```cpp
if (flags_ & (ALLOCATOR_MAPPED_SHARED | ALLOCATOR_MAPPED_SHAREDMEM)) {
  base_ptr_ = mmap(nullptr, size_, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_SHARED, fd, 0);
} else {
  base_ptr_ = mmap(nullptr, size_, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE, fd, 0);
}
```
 
A private writable mapping over a read-only fd is legal, so this works, and on discrete-GPU systems
the write permission is harmless - nothing writes, pages stay clean and file-backed.
 
On systems with coherent CPU/GPU memory (`is_integrated=1`: Jetson Thor/Orin, GB10, GH200/GB200) it
is not harmless. A pageable H2D copy whose **source** is such a mapping causes the entire source
range to be faulted as a write, COW'ing every touched page into anonymous memory. Because host and
device draw on one physical pool, the process is OOM-killed partway through loading a checkpoint that
otherwise fits comfortably.
 
There is currently no way for a caller to ask for a read-only mapping:
 
- `UntypedStorage.from_file` exposes only `shared`, which selects `MAP_SHARED` vs `MAP_PRIVATE`.
- The `ALLOCATOR_MAPPED_*` flag enum has no protection member, so nothing can be threaded through.
- `torch.serialization.set_default_mmap_options` accepts only `MAP_PRIVATE`/`MAP_SHARED` and does not
  affect `prot`.
This affects both `torch.load(mmap=True)` and `UntypedStorage.from_file` directly.

## Reproduction

Minimal, run on any `is_integrated=1` device:
 
```python
import os, subprocess, torch
 
PATH, N = "/tmp/big.pt", 4 * 1024**3  # 4 GiB
 
def rss():
    d = {}
    for line in open("/proc/self/status"):
        if line.startswith(("RssAnon:", "RssFile:")):
            k, v = line.split()[:2]
            d[k.rstrip(":")] = int(v) / 1024**2
    return d
 
if not os.path.exists(PATH):
    torch.save(torch.empty(N, dtype=torch.uint8), PATH)
 
t = torch.load(PATH, map_location="cpu", mmap=True, weights_only=True)
before = rss()
print(subprocess.run(
    ["grep", "-E", r"rw-p|r--p", "/proc/self/maps"], capture_output=True, text=True
).stdout.splitlines()[-1])   # the checkpoint VMA: rw-p
 
d = t.to("cuda")             # pageable H2D, source is the mapping
torch.cuda.synchronize()
after = rss()
 
print(f"RssAnon  {before['RssAnon']:8.2f} -> {after['RssAnon']:8.2f} GiB")
print(f"RssFile  {before['RssFile']:8.2f} -> {after['RssFile']:8.2f} GiB")
```
 
**Expected:** the copy reads the source, so pages stay clean and file-backed. `RssFile` grows by the
tensor size, `RssAnon` is flat.
 
**Actual, on integrated:** `RssAnon` grows 1:1 with bytes copied and `RssFile` stays flat. Every page
of the mapping becomes unreclaimable anonymous memory. With a checkpoint approaching the size of the
pool, the process is killed before the copy finishes.
 
This does not reproduce on discrete GPUs.

Happy to help put up the PR.

### Versions

PyTorch version: 2.11.0+cu130
CUDA used to build PyTorch: 13.0
OS: Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS (aarch64)
Python: 3.12.13
Python platform: Linux-6.8.12-1021-tegra-aarch64-with-glibc2.35
Is CUDA available: True
CUDA runtime version: 13.0.88
GPU models and configuration: GPU 0: NVIDIA Thor
Nvidia driver version: 595.73
Libc version: glibc-2.35
CPU: aarch64, 14 cores (ARM, sve2)


cc @andrewkho @divyanshk @SsnL @VitalyFedyunin @dzhulgakov @scotts @mruberry @mikaylagawarecki

When execing into a ray pod and running a curl against localhost:8080/metrics, I see duplicate headers for the same metric:

# HELP ray_component_cpu_percentage Total CPU usage of the components on a node.

ray_component_cpu_percentage{Component="raylet",SessionName="session_2026-07-08_15-50-24_749109_290",Version="2.54.0",ip="10.72.69.156",pid="359"} 1.0
ray_component_cpu_percentage{Component="agent",SessionName="session_2026-07-08_15-50-24_749109_290",Version="2.54.0",ip="10.72.69.156",pid="412"} 1.2

items.title: [Core] image_uri / container runtime env workers can't get the token under Kubernetes token auth
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

With Kubernetes token auth (`RAY_ENABLE_K8S_TOKEN_AUTH=true`, which KubeRay sets for K8s auth mode), workers started through the `image_uri` or `container` runtime env probably can't authenticate.

KubeRay mounts a projected service account token at `/var/run/secrets/ray.io/serviceaccount/token` in the Ray container, and the token loader reads it from there. The runtime env plugin in `python/ray/_private/runtime_env/image_uri.py` forwards `RAY_AUTH_MODE` and `RAY_ENABLE_K8S_TOKEN_AUTH` into the podman worker container, but only mounts the Ray temp dir, so the worker has no token.

There may be other files need to be mounted, so contributor should mount those files too.

This comes from reading the code and hasn't been reproduced. Contributors should verify it on a KubeRay cluster with K8s token auth enabled first, then decide on a fix, for example mounting the token directory into the container. The kubelet rotates projected tokens, so a fix should keep working after rotation.

Related: #66467 mounts the regular token file (`~/.ray/auth_token` or `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH`) into these containers but doesn't cover the K8s token.

items.title: External routing does not support prefill/decode disaggregated Pods
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
## Feature Description and Motivation

The current external routing implementation supports single-target replica selection. It can receive candidate Pods with prefill/decode role attributes, but one external decision returns only one target Pod.

As a result, prefill/decode disaggregated Pods are not currently supported by the external routing path: selecting one role-labelled Pod does not select a P/D pair or invoke AIBrix's existing P/D orchestration and handoff flow.

This issue tracks that missing capability as a future external-routing enhancement. The existing single-target behavior remains valid and should stay backward compatible.

## Use Case

Operators may want to use an external decision service for workloads deployed as separate prefill and decode Pods, while retaining AIBrix's P/D execution flow.

Today they must use the built-in `pd` strategy; the `external` strategy cannot represent or apply the coordinated P/D decision.

## Proposed Solution

Investigate how external routing can support prefill/decode disaggregated Pods and integrate with the existing P/D router.

The implementation approach is intentionally left open. Follow-up design work should determine the protocol shape, compatibility with the current single-target API, target validation, fallback behavior, and reuse of the existing P/D orchestration path.

Related P/D work: #1134 and #1223.

## Area

Gateway

items.title: [cake deslop] cake_kimi_k3_situ: remove never-compiled bindings/sequences, merge SM100/SM103, parametrize FC1/FC2 tile-N clones
items.author: yzh119
items.body_excerpt:
The Cake SiTU backend of `cutlass_fused_moe` (`csrc/fused_moe/cake_kimi_k3_situ`, #5183) adds ~162K lines.

**Findings**
- 64 per-stage `*_binding.cu` files (26K lines) and their registry records are never compiled: only the prepared-sequence bindings are loaded.
- 4 of 22 sequences (2 per arch) are not reachable from `ROUTES`; with the kernels only they use, that is another 16K lines. The `m256_c12` selector maps to the same sequence as `m64_claim8` and is otherwise unused.
- Of the 39 routed SM100/SM103 file pairs, 22 are identical except hashes and 17 differ only in the shared-memory base line.
- Per arch, 9 FC1 and 10 FC2 kernels are tile-N (8/16/32/128) and feature-flag clones.
- Each submit re-validates ~15 tensors, rebuilds stage dicts, walks a 66–100-entry argument plan with string splitting, and re-encodes TMA descriptors in C++.
- GPU tests launch only 64/256/512/2048 tokens; 6 of 9 routed sequences per arch are never launched.

**Proposed steps**
- [ ] Delete never-compiled bindings, unreachable sequences and the `m256_c12` selector.
- [ ] Merge SM100a/SM103a sources (one guarded line); compile each source for both arches.
- [ ] Add GPU tests covering every routed sequence (1, 8, 16, generic tile 8/16/32/128 counts).
- [ ] Pre-flatten the argument vector and cache TMA descriptors at prepare time.
- [ ] Regenerate FC1/FC2 as templates over tile-N and feature flags.

Expected size: ~162K → ~60K (mechanical) → ~12K (regenerated).

items.title: SM120 (RTX PRO 6000) MoE backend gaps: MoeConfig.backend schema missing MegaMoE entries, and no EP-capable path for this hardware
items.author: ItamarTerem
items.body_excerpt:
Hi TensorRT-LLM team,
Deploying a large MoE model (Kimi-K2.7-Code-NVFP4, 384 experts) on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (SM120) via the pytorch backend, trtllm-serve, version 1.3.0rc20. Two related findings we wanted to raise:

1. MoeConfig.backend's pydantic Literal doesn't include MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL/MEGAMOE_DEEPGEMM, even though create_moe.py's dispatch logic already handles both as real branches. Setting moe_config.backend: MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL in extra_llm_api_options.yaml fails pydantic validation before create_moe.py is ever reached, even though the underlying backend selection logic supports it. This looks like the config schema hasn't caught up to the dispatch logic yet.
2. More fundamentally: none of the EP-capable MoE backends currently work on SM120 in this build.
 - MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL / MEGAMOE_DEEPGEMM: both explicitly require SM100/SM103 ("MegaMoECuteDsl requires SM100 family (SM100 or SM103); got SM120"), and fall back to CutlassFusedMoE.
 - WIDEEP: not SM-gated, but its GEMM compute still routes through the same CUTLASS kernel that produces silently incorrect output on SM120 in our testing, and additionally hit a binding mismatch in this build (run_moe() is missing value for argument '_37') before we could evaluate EP itself.
 - CUTEDSL (b12x): the only backend we've confirmed produces correct output on SM120, but has no EP support at the flashinfer level (num_local_experts != num_experts raises NotImplementedError in b12x_fused_moe).

Net result: there is currently no correct + EP-capable MoE path for SM120 in this stack, which limits per-GPU memory headroom for large-expert-count models on this hardware class.
Questions:

1. Is SM120 support planned for any of the MegaMoE/WideEP paths, or is SM100/SM103-first prioritization intentional for the near term?
2. Should we file the MoeConfig.backend schema gap as a separate, smaller issue, since that looks like a straightforward fix independent of the larger EP question?
3. Is there a recommended path for SM120 users running large MoE models today, or is CUTEDSL/no-EP the expected configuration for this hardware class in the current release?

Happy to share full repro steps/configs if helpful. Thanks for your work on this — appreciate the pointers.

items.title: [Data] read_iceberg migration to Datasource V2 (tracking issue)
items.author: AarryaSaraf
items.body_excerpt: ### Description `read_iceberg` is still on the V1 `Datasource` abstraction. We are porting it to Datasource V2 (`ListFiles` / `ReadFiles`), initially behind an opt-in flag. This issue tracks the work and collects design feedback before the flag flips. Three problems come out of the left column: 1. **The pushed-down filter never reaches planning.** Memoization happens at construction, before `.filter()` exists, and pushdown `copy.copy()`s the datasource, carrying the stale plan across. On a 3-file table where 2 match, `.filter(region == "US")` plans 3 files; the identical predicate as `read_iceberg(row_filter=...)` plans 2. Results stay correct, but the whole table is listed and planning is a single-node step that grows with table size. 2. **Sizing uses compressed bytes.** Measured expansion: 440x on one file, 1839x on another. A chunk nominally "128 MB" can be tens of GB decoded. 3. **Peak memory equals chunk size** — the chunk is materialized as one Arrow table before anything is yielded. On the right, `plan_files()` runs once inside the listing task with the filter already attached; its scan tasks become typed manifest columns rather than a driver-side object graph; bin packing counts estimated decoded bytes; and the reader yields one block per record batch. ### Status In progress. Stage 1 — the shared V2 seams Iceberg needs (schema without a file sample, an exact-metadata-count hook, a whole-file-indexer hook) — merged as #65908. Stage 2 is the Iceberg source itself: manifest codec, listing indexer, bin-packing partitioner, scanner, reader, and the flag and dispatch; it is built and green locally and lands as three PRs to stay reviewable. Stage 3 then makes `count()` metadata-only, answered from the manifest's per-file `record_count` wherever Iceberg's per-file residual is `AlwaysTrue` — so `WHERE partition_col = x` counts without reading data. Work planned after that is described in the draft PR linked below. All of it sits behind `DataContext.use_iceberg_datasource_v2` (default `False`, env `RAY_DATA_USE_ICEBERG_DATASOURCE_V2`), and the public `read_iceberg` signature does not change. One behaviour change for the release notes: `parallelism` / `override_num_blocks` become warning no-ops on this path, since task count now comes from bin packing. ### Use case Anyone reading a large Iceberg table with Ray Data: today a filtered read still lists and reads the whole table, and worker peak memory is sized from compressed bytes — a number that can be three orders of magnitude off. ### Related issues Related to #66147, #64464, #65581. Not a duplicate of any: no open issue or PR covers moving `read_iceberg` to Datasource V2 (#66133 / #66145 / #51951 are the write path). Feedback especially welcome on the opt-in-then-flip rollout and the `parallelism` no-op.

items.title: Ray's site serves no /.well-known/security.txt (RFC 9116)
items.author: kobihikri
items.body_excerpt:
`https://docs.ray.io/.well-known/security.txt` returns 404 (and `ray.io` redirects without serving one). [RFC 9116](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116) defines `/.well-known/security.txt` as the standard, machine-discoverable place a security researcher (or automated tooling) looks first to find how to report an issue. Ray has a [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/master/SECURITY.md), but there's no security.txt advertising it at the well-known path.

A small security.txt (Contact → your reporting channel, a future `Expires` per §2.5.5, Policy → SECURITY.md) served from the site's static directory would resolve it. Happy to help however is easiest.

I used AI assistance to investigate and draft this; I reproduced the 404 myself.

> AI-assisted status update — 4 October 2026.
>
> [Malfet acknowledged this proposal on June 22](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/187827#issuecomment-4768918941) and is assigned. This remains a separate documentation proposal alongside the migration tracker #187455; the original request is preserved below.
>
> At main `9a3eac3b8ffb`, the [general review checklist](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/9a3eac3b8ffba6e54e61df7ebecfb0afcc5e5a74/.claude/skills/pr-review/review-checklist.md) still has one generic MPS-compatibility item. A separate [Metal kernel guide](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/9a3eac3b8ffba6e54e61df7ebecfb0afcc5e5a74/.claude/skills/metal-kernel/SKILL.md) already covers implementation conventions and testing. The proposal here concerns focused review checks. The checked issue timeline links no implementation PR.

---

The `pr-review` skill is explicitly for "areas CI cannot check," and it's thorough for CPU/CUDA/Python — but ~one line on MPS. As more ops move from MPSGraph to hand-written Metal kernels, a few things tend to get missed in review that the correctness-only MPS CI shard doesn't gate.

Would there be interest in a small `### MPS / Metal Kernels` subsection in `review-checklist.md`, grown one check per PR (like the existing `[BE]` updates)? A few common ones:

- perf vs the MPSGraph path being replaced (the shard is correctness-only, so a correct-but-slower kernel still passes)
- whether the change actually removes the old shape-cached graph path, rather than adding a fast kernel beside it
- test coverage that exercises the shapes/dtypes Metal kernels tend to break on (CI only catches what's tested)
- `metal::fast::*` math (within tolerance, but precision compounds in training)
- reaching for a bespoke kernel where the existing `c10/metal` lineage would do

Happy to send these as separate small PRs if useful — flagging here first to check it's wanted. Scope: skill docs only.

shortlist.title: [Performance]: spec-decode boot-to-boot throughput dispersion on L4 (CV up to 13.92%), resolved in 0.30.0
shortlist.author: akshathtiwari
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

Not a proposal so much as a measurement suggestion. Speculative-decoding throughput on this stack is boot-dependent to a degree a single-boot benchmark cannot see: on 0.29.0 / L4, twelve boots of a byte-identical configuration gave CV 13.92% in one container and 3.73% in another. Anything comparing speculative configurations from one boot each is partly measuring which boot it got.

0.30.0 looks much better on this axis (0.99% and 1.61% across two containers on different physical cards), so this may already be resolved. I am reporting it mainly because the mechanism is not what I assumed, and the protocol seems worth having on record either way.

### Report of performance regression

Reporting this because 0.30.0 appears to resolve it, and the obvious explanation turns out to be wrong, so something else changed and I would like to know what.

**Setup.** Qwen3-4B target, `z-lab/Qwen3-4B-DFlash-b16` drafter, 5 speculative tokens, bf16 weights, `--kv-cache-dtype auto`, FlashInfer pinned. GSM8K, concurrency 1, one fixed prompt set replayed on every boot. 12 boots per arm inside a single container, one physical GPU per session (UUID recorded). The harness speaks HTTP only and never imports vLLM.

Throughput at concurrency 1, output tokens/s:

| card | engine | session | default | --enforce-eager | ratio | default CV |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| L4 (SM89) | 0.29.0 | A | 39.2 | 80.5 | **0.487** | **13.92%** |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.29.0 | B | 61.2 | 79.7 | **0.768** | **3.73%** |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.30.0 | C | 82.8 | 81.6 | **1.014** | 0.99% |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.30.0 | D | 78.2 | 77.0 | **1.017** | 1.61% |
| A10 (SM86) | 0.29.0 | E | 132.6 | 138.3 | 0.959 | 2.08% |

Each ratio is the default arm divided by the eager arm measured in the same container, so session and card effects cancel. On 0.29.0/L4 the CUDA-graph path runs at 49% and 77% of the eager path; on 0.30.0 it reaches parity. Acceptance length is flat throughout (tau 4.11-4.15), so this is throughput rather than a change in what the drafter gets accepted.

### Misc discussion on performance

Two observations, one related issue, and a question.

**1. The CUDA-graph fallback still fires on 0.30.0.** I had assumed the improvement was the speculative path gaining full graphs. It is not. The warning is byte-identical on both versions and capture proceeds under PIECEWISE in each:

> CUDAGraphMode.FULL_AND_PIECEWISE is not supported with spec-decode for attention backend FlashInferBackend (support: AttentionCGSupport.UNIFORM_SINGLE_TOKEN_DECODE); setting cudagraph_mode=PIECEWISE

Backend selection is unchanged too: both versions log FLASHINFER for the target and FLASH_ATTN for the second selection. So neither graph mode nor backend choice explains the difference.

**2. On 0.29.0 the dispersion magnitude is itself not reproducible.** Two twelve-boot measurements of the identical configuration gave CV 13.92% and 3.73%, with means 39.2 and 61.2 tok/s. The effect is present in both; its size is not a property of the configuration. The eager arm is stable across every session measured (80.5, 79.7, 81.6, 77.0 on L4; 138.3 on A10), which is what makes it usable as a control.

**Related, but I do not think it is the same thing: #58677.** That reports the draft model's torch.compile cache identity flipping between exactly two values across restarts with byte-identical argv, attributed to the shared VllmConfig being mutated in-place during the main model's warmup and CUDA-graph-capture phase, before the draft head compiles. Two differences: the symptom there is startup recompile cost rather than steady-state throughput, and it reports 0.27.1 affected with 0.29 appearing immune, whereas what I measure is on 0.29.0.

Still, the shape is close enough that I would rather ask than assume: **if VllmConfig is mutated in place during graph capture and that mutation reaches what the draft compiles to, could the same mechanism produce a steady-state throughput difference and not only a cache-key difference?** My measurements begin after the server reports healthy, so any recompilation has finished by then.


**The question.** What changed between 0.29.0 and 0.30.0 on this path, given the fallback and the backend selection are identical in both? If a specific PR is responsible I would rather cite it than guess. I looked at #53867, #51700, #54646 and #52228 and could not attribute it from the release notes alone.

**Possibly relevant.** The effect is much weaker on an A10 (ratio 0.959) than on an L4 (0.487 and 0.768) at the same engine version. The A10 has 24 GiB against the L4's 22.03 GiB usable, and this configuration sits close enough to the memory ceiling that --enforce-eager alone decides whether an fp8_e4m3-KV variant boots at all. So capacity pressure may matter more here than architecture. I have not separated the two.

**Reproduction.** Harness, raw append-only records, analysis scripts and the engine logs are at https://github.com/akshathtiwari/spec-fp8-study (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23033168). The boot-variance runs are one command each and the per-session numbers regenerate from the stored records. Happy to run further configurations if a specific one would help; the full sweep is a couple of GPU-hours.

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

Not `collect_env.py` output: the engine runs in an ephemeral container on a rented GPU, so this machine's environment is not the one under test. These are the fields the harness records per measurement, read from nvidia-smi and from the running server.

```text
GPU         NVIDIA L4 (SM89, 22.03 GiB usable) and NVIDIA A10 (SM86)
            one physical card per session, gpu_uuid recorded per record
driver      580.95.05
CUDA        13.0
torch       2.13.0+cu130
vLLM        0.29.0 and 0.30.0, pinned by image digest. Version is read from
            the server's /version endpoint and checked against the declared
            value before any measu

comments.author: akshathtiwari
comments.body:
Correction to the "possibly relevant" paragraph in my original post.

I wrote that the A10 has 24 GiB against the L4's 22.03 GiB usable, and offered memory capacity as the likelier of two readings for why the deficit is weak on the A10. **That is wrong.** Both cards report **22.5 GiB** in my own records, and I had never checked the field before writing it. Capacity is not the difference between them.

What does differ, from the same records:

| | VRAM | arch | max SM clock | power limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L4 | 22.5 GiB | SM8.9 | 2040 MHz | **72 W** |
| A10 | 22.5 GiB | SM8.6 | 1695 MHz | **150 W** |

So the card showing the deficit has less than half the power budget. That is a better fit for the symptom than capacity ever was: CUDA graphs run the work faster, faster work draws more power, and a 72 W part can hit its cap and clamp — variably, depending on thermal history, which would also explain why the dispersion magnitude itself does not reproduce between sessions. The eager arm runs slower, stays under the cap, and is stable in every session measured.

I want to be clear that this is a hypothesis and **my data cannot test it.** I was recording `clocks.max.sm` and `power.limit`, which are what the card is permitted to do, not what it did. A throttling explanation is precisely what configured limits cannot see.

I have since added sampling of achieved SM clock, power draw and `clocks_throttle_reasons.*` across the measurement window, and a run is in flight. If `sw_power_cap` is active during the default arm and not during the eager arm, that is the driver answering the question directly rather than me inferring it from a clock curve. I will post the result either way, including if it kills the hypothesis.

The throughput numbers and the ratio table in the original post are unaffected by this — they are measured, and the correction is to an explanation I attached to them.
